0.title: Job: Does He Fear God for No Reason?
0.overview:
The message. The book of Job asks whether God is worth loving for himself, or only for what he gives. Satan puts the question about a real man, behind his back: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9). Then Job loses his wealth, his ten children and his health, and is never told why. His friends insist that suffering on this scale must be punishment for sin; Job knows it is not, and pours out his anguish to God himself. At last God comes, not with an explanation but with himself, and that proves to be enough: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (42:5). God is good when his ways are hidden, suffering is not always a verdict on the sufferer, and one who has lost everything but God has not lost what matters most.

Background: the man. Job lived in “the land of Uz” (1:1), outside Israel, probably in Edom or northern Arabia. He was “the greatest of all the people of the east” (1:3), honoured at the gate of the city (29:7). The story belongs to the age of the patriarchs: wealth counted in livestock, a father offering sacrifices for his family with no priest or temple, a further 140 years of life after his trials (42:16), and a word for money (42:11) found elsewhere only in the story of Jacob (Genesis 33:19). The book never mentions Israel, Sinai or the law of Moses. Job was a real man: the LORD names him through Ezekiel beside Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14), and James holds him up to Christians as a pattern of steadfastness (James 5:11).

The writer and the date. Scripture does not say who wrote Job or when. An old Jewish tradition credited Moses; others suggest the age of Solomon, when Israel’s wisdom writing flourished, or the exile. The book may well have been written down long after the events, by an Israelite: the narrator calls God “the LORD”, his covenant name, while Job and his friends nearly always say “God” or “the Almighty”. This commentary leaves author and date open, as the book does. Nothing in its message depends on them.

The kind of writing. Job stands with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes among Scripture’s wisdom books, but it is wisdom in the form of a drama of argument. A short prose story opens it (chapters 1–2) and closes it (42:7–17); between them stands a long poem, some of the finest and hardest Hebrew in the Old Testament. Read it as poetry, which says a thing and then says it again another way, and meant to be felt as well as understood. Above all, notice who is speaking. The book records truly what each speaker said, but not every speaker spoke truly: God tells Eliphaz, “you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (42:7). So the friends’ speeches, though they often sound like sound doctrine, must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer. Paul can quote a single true line of theirs (5:13, in 1 Corinthians 3:19), but their argument as a whole God rejects.

Is Job history? Some Christians read the book as a parable or an inspired drama, pointing to its poetry and round numbers. This commentary’s view is that Job was a real man and the book records real events, with the speeches shaped into great poetry, as the Psalms shape real prayers. Ezekiel and James speak of Job as they speak of Noah and the prophets (Ezekiel 14:14; James 5:10–11). The shaping does not make the book less true; with the historic confessions, this commentary receives it as God’s inspired and wholly true word.

How the book makes its case. The prologue (chapters 1–2) lets the reader into the heavenly court and tells us twice, from God’s own mouth, that Job is “a blameless and upright man” (1:8; 2:3). Job first worships: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (1:21). After seven silent days with his friends, he curses the day he was born (chapter 3). Three rounds of debate follow (chapters 4–14, 15–21 and 22–27). Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar repeat one tidy idea: God repays, so great suffering means great sin. They grow harsher, until Eliphaz invents crimes for Job (22:5–9), and then the debate runs down. Job protests his innocence and accuses God of treating him as an enemy, yet keeps reaching past God’s hand to God himself: for an arbiter (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), and at last a living Redeemer (19:25). A quiet poem asks where wisdom is found (chapter 28). Job makes his last defence (chapters 29–31). A younger man, Elihu, speaks (chapters 32–37), partly truly and partly not, and the book gives no verdict on him. Then “the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (38:1). He answers none of Job’s questions, but questions Job about the earth, the sea and the wild creatures, Behemoth and Leviathan (chapters 38–41), until Job lays his hand on his mouth (40:4) and repents in dust and ashes (42:6). The epilogue (42:7–17) vindicates Job, rebukes the friends, has Job pray for them, and restores his fortunes twice over.

What the book does not say. The book never answers in general terms why the innocent suffer, and Job himself is never told about the heavenly court. What it shows is that hard providences are never in themselves a verdict on the sufferer, that God may have good reasons we cannot see, and that every power, Satan included, can go no further than God allows (1:12; 2:6).

Where it leads: to Christ. Job points to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes and the pattern it sets. Its deepest cry is for someone to stand between God and man: “There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both” (9:33). The New Testament answers that “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Job’s Redeemer (Hebrew go’el, the nearest kinsman who rescues family in trouble) is most likely God himself; but a kinsman must share our flesh, and the Son of God did (Hebrews 2:14). Job’s story is also a pattern of Christ’s. Job was blameless and suffered without knowing why; Jesus, wholly without sin, was stripped, deserted by his friends, condemned by the religious leaders of his day, and cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Satan asked whether anyone would serve God for nothing; Jesus did, and was hated “without a cause” (John 15:25). And his resurrection makes good Job’s hope: “yet in my flesh I shall see God” (19:26). Paul even takes up God’s question from the whirlwind (41:11) to praise a grace no one can earn: “Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35).

For us. Job gives suffering believers permission to be honest: to say the true thing to God rather than the pious thing, to bring their complaints to him rather than away from him, and to refuse the confident explanations of people who are sure they know why this has happened. It warns comforters to sit longer in silence. It answers Satan’s question in every generation: a believer who has lost everything can still want God for himself, because grace has made him so. And it shows us a God who does not owe us an explanation, but has done more than explain: in Christ he came and suffered with us and for us. “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (James 5:11).

1.title: Does Job Fear God for No Reason?
1.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.<sup>2</sup>There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.<sup>3</sup>He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.<sup>4</sup>His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.<sup>5</sup>And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.<sup>6</sup>Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"<sup>9</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason?<sup>10</sup>Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.<sup>11</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>14</sup>and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them,<sup>15</sup>and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>16</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>17</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>18</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>19</sup>and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>20</sup>Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.<sup>21</sup>And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."<sup>22</sup>In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens with a prose prologue (chapters 1–2) that lets the reader see what Job himself never sees. Before a word of the long debate is spoken, we meet the man, hear God’s verdict on him, overhear a conversation in heaven, and watch him lose everything in a single day.

The message. God is worth loving for himself, not only for what he gives, and his grace can make a human heart love him so. Satan says Job’s faith is a wage; God lets it be tested within limits he sets; and Job, stripped of his wealth and his ten children, falls to the ground and worships. His suffering is neither deserved nor meaningless: it begins in heaven, with God’s delight in his servant.

Why it was said. Readers who knew that God blesses the obedient were always tempted to read every disaster as a verdict on the sufferer (see the introduction). The first line of the book shuts that door: the man who suffers most is the man God calls blameless.

How the chapter makes its case. Job is introduced as blameless and upright, rich in children and goods, and praying even for his children’s hidden hearts (vv. 1–5). In the council of heaven the LORD points Job out, Satan asks, “Does Job fear God for no reason?”, and the LORD allows everything Job has to be touched, but not Job himself (vv. 6–12). On one ordinary day four messengers bring news of raiders, fire, more raiders and a great wind that kills all ten children (vv. 13–19). Job tears his robe and worships: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.” In all this he does not sin or charge God with wrong (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. Satan’s word “for no reason” comes into the New Testament as the word for Christ, hated “without a cause” (John 15:25), and for grace, by which we “are justified by his grace as a gift” (Romans 3:24). One man loved the Father perfectly with nothing in his hands: stripped and deserted, he did not curse God but said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). And Job’s sacrifices, repeated after every feast because none could finish the matter, look for the single sacrifice that did (Hebrews 10:11–12).

For us. Sooner or later every believer is asked Satan’s question: what would be left of your faith if the hedge came down? The answer does not lie in the strength of our grip but in the One who holds us, and who says to his people, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). Grief and worship can share the same breath, and the God who takes away is still the God who gave his Son.
1.theology:
The book's question is whether God deserves to be loved for himself, or only for his gifts. Satan's phrase for no reason will return in God's mouth (2:3), in Job's (9:17) and in Eliphaz's (22:6), and the gospel gives it its fullest sense (see on vv. 9-10).

God is sovereign over suffering without being the author of evil. Human wickedness, natural disaster and Satan's malice all act, and none acts outside God's permission and limit; the cross is the clearest instance of the same pattern (Acts 4:27-28).
1.examples: It is God, not Satan, who first mentions Job, and Job's trouble begins with God's delight in him. And the father who offered ten sacrifices after every feast never had the comfort of a sacrifice that was finished; Christian parents do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Man in the Land of Uz
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a single blow falls, the reader is told who Job is, so that no one can ever read his suffering as punishment. He is blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil (v. 1), a verdict God himself will repeat. He is blessed with a complete family and the greatest wealth in the east (vv. 2–3), and every item of it is about to be taken. His faith shows at home: after each round of his children’s feasts he rises early and offers a burnt offering for every one of them, in case they have cursed God in their hearts (vv. 4–5). This is the man Satan will accuse: a father whose religion reaches past his own life to the hidden hearts of those he loves.
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture's verdict on Job comes before his trouble, so that no reader can explain the trouble by some fault in him.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job was a real man whose life was whole before God and his neighbours, and the book says so first, so that no reader can take the friends’ side against him.

There was a man in the land of Uz. The book begins like a story told by the fire: “there was a man”. Uz lay outside Israel; Lamentations sets it with Edom (Lamentations 4:21). The book never mentions Israel, Abraham, the covenant, the law or the temple, and Job offers his own sacrifices as head of his family, as the patriarchs did (see the introduction). He was a real man: Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14), and James holds him up to Christians (James 5:11). His story is set outside Israel on purpose. It belongs to anyone who has ever suffered.

Blameless and upright. Then the verdict, in four parts. “Blameless” (Hebrew tam) means whole, all of a piece; the related noun is the “integrity” God will say Job still holds fast (2:3). “Upright” means straight in his dealings. He “feared God”, and the fear showed in what he did: he “turned away from evil”.

What it does not mean. Blameless does not mean sinless. Job himself will ask God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and will speak of the iniquities of his youth (13:26). It means there was no hidden life behind the visible one.

Why this matters. God will repeat the verdict word for word (v. 8; 2:3), so whatever explains Job’s suffering, it will not be his sin. That is part of why the book was given to Israel: a people who knew the law’s promises of blessing for obedience (Deuteronomy 28) and the proverbs about the flourishing of the righteous needed to learn that these are no rule for judging every sufferer.
verseByVerse.note: Uz was probably in Edom or northern Arabia, east of Israel. The story seems set in the age of the patriarchs; the book’s author and date are unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: There were born to him seven sons and three daughters. He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s family and wealth are complete, the storyteller’s way of showing how much there is to lose.

Seven sons and three daughters. Seven and three make ten, and the flocks follow the same pattern: seven thousand and three thousand, five hundred and five hundred. It is the storyteller’s way of saying complete.

The greatest of all the people of the east. The peoples east of the Jordan were famous for wealth and wisdom; when Scripture praises Solomon, it says his wisdom “surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east” (1 Kings 4:30). Job was the greatest of them.

Everything about to be taken. Keep the list in mind, for every item on it is about to be taken, the children last. At the end of the book it will be read out again (42:12–13), every number doubled except the children: ten again, not twenty. Many have seen a hint that the first ten were not lost for ever but still with God, so that Job had twenty; and the new children did not cancel the grief for the old.

verseByVerse.quote: His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job prays for hearts he cannot see: a good father, whose repeated sacrifices also show the limit of every priest before Christ.

Hold a feast in the house of each one. This is a happy family. The brothers take turns to host, each “on his day”, perhaps his birthday, and they do not leave their sisters out.

Job would send and consecrate them. When each round of feasting is over, their father gets up early and offers a burnt offering for every one of them, ten sacrifices, as head of the family in an age before priest or temple.

Cursed God in their hearts. He has no evidence. He offers for sins he cannot see, in hearts he cannot read. The Hebrew actually says “blessed” God: the writer will not put “curse God” on the page, and the ESV rightly translates the sense. The same word comes back in Satan’s mouth (v. 11) and in Job’s (v. 21), and the whole chapter turns on it.

Thus Job did continually. He had to do it again after every feast, because no sacrifice he offered could finish the matter. That is the limit of every priest before Christ: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12). The Christian parent still prays every day for children whose hearts he cannot read, but he no longer has to wonder whether the sacrifice was enough.
verseByVerse.note: “Cursed” is literally “blessed” in Hebrew, a euphemism for cursing God (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The curtain rises on a scene Job never sees, and it shows that his suffering begins not with his sin but with God’s delight in him. The heavenly beings come before the LORD, and Satan with them, back from roaming the earth (vv. 6–7). The LORD himself raises Job’s name and repeats the narrator’s verdict (v. 8). Satan answers with the question of the whole book: does Job fear God for nothing, or only because God pays well (vv. 9–11)? The LORD allows everything Job has to be touched, but sets a limit before a single blow falls: not Job himself (v. 12). Satan is real and hostile, yet he can go no further than God allows.
verseByVerse.theology: Satan is real and malicious, and he is on a leash: nothing reaches Job that did not first pass through the council of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind Job’s story stands a heavenly court where the LORD reigns, and even Satan, the accuser, has to come before him.

The sons of God. The curtain goes up on a scene Job never sees. “The sons of God” here are heavenly beings, the angels who “shouted for joy” when God laid the foundation of the earth (38:7). They come “to present themselves”, like officials reporting to a king, as Micaiah saw “the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him” (1 Kings 22:19). (Whether the same phrase means angels in Genesis 6:2 is a separate question; see the note there.)

Satan also came among them. In Hebrew the name has the article: “the satan”, the accuser or adversary. He appears in the same role in Zechariah, “standing at his right hand to accuse him” (Zechariah 3:1). The New Testament names him: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan”, “the accuser of our brothers … who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:9–10). He is real, he is hostile, and he still has to come before the LORD.

Where Christians differ: who is “the satan” here? Some scholars read him as a member of God’s court, a kind of public prosecutor, only later identified with the devil. This commentary’s view: he is the devil himself. His aim is that Job should curse God (v. 11), and that is not a servant’s aim; Zechariah 3 and Revelation 12 show the same accuser standing against God’s people before God.
verseByVerse.note: Compare the accuser of Zechariah 3:1-2, rebuked by the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan must give an account of himself to God, and his answer shows an enemy who is restless, limited and never idle.

From where have you come? God asks, not because he needs to know, but because Satan must answer to him. And the answer is restless: to and fro, up and down.

Not everywhere, and not idle. Peter takes up the picture to warn Christians: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). A creature, he is not everywhere at once; but he is not idle, and Peter’s answer is: “Resist him, firm in your faith” (1 Peter 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s trouble begins not with Job’s failure but with God’s delight in him: the LORD himself points him out.

Have you considered my servant Job? Not Satan but the LORD raises Job’s name. “Have you considered” is literally “have you set your heart on”: God points to Job the way a father points to a son he is proud of. “My servant” is the title Scripture gives to Abraham, Moses and David, and at last to the Servant in Isaiah who suffers for others (Isaiah 52:13). And God repeats the narrator’s verdict, all four parts of it, and adds that “there is none like him on the earth”.

Where Job’s trouble begins. This is an unsettling verse, and a deeply comforting one. It is not a rule for every suffering; much of our trouble we bring on ourselves, and Scripture says so. But it breaks the equation the friends will spend the debate defending, that a man in pain must be a man in the wrong. Some sufferings begin in heaven, with God’s pleasure in a servant he means to show to the world.

The beloved Son tested. The pattern reaches its height in Jesus: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and at once he is “led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1). Testing is no sign that God’s pleasure has been withdrawn.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason? Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan does not deny that Job is devout; he denies that Job’s devotion is love, and so he accuses God of being loved only for his gifts.

Does Job fear God for no reason? Here is the question of the book. “For no reason” is one Hebrew word, chinnam: for nothing, free of charge. Satan says Job’s religion is a wage: he serves God because God pays well.

A hedge around him. Satan’s own words admit that God has protected Job “on every side”. And his charge is aimed at God as much as at Job. If he is right, God is loved only for what he hands out, and no one would stay with him once the gifts stopped.

The word comes back. Watch the word as the book goes on. God turns it back on Satan: “you incited me against him to destroy him without reason” (2:3). Job uses it without knowing how true it is: God “multiplies my wounds without cause” (9:17). In Satan’s question (1:9) the Greek Old Testament renders it dōrean, “freely, as a gift”, and the New Testament uses the same word of Christ, “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25), and of us, who “are justified by his grace as a gift” (Romans 3:24). The gospel is God giving to us freely, for no reason found in us, and the faith it creates loves him back freely, for himself.

In everyday life. Every believer is asked Satan’s question sooner or later, usually by a loss: what would be left of your faith if the hedge came down? If the honest answer frightens you, take heart from the next verses. Job’s faith held because he was held, and Christ prays for his people that their faith may not fail.

Is all love self-interest in disguise? Satan’s suspicion has had a long life. Thomas Hobbes taught that every voluntary act aims at some good to the one who does it, and his friend John Aubrey tells how a clergyman, seeing Hobbes give money to a poor old man, asked whether he would have done it had Christ not commanded it. Hobbes said he would, because the man’s misery pained him, and the gift eased his own pain as well. Much modern thought shares the instinct, and turned on religion it says that faith is a bargain struck with the sky for health, success and peace of mind. A great deal of religion fits it well. The book of Job tests the charge on a real man, and its answer is that the cynic is right about the human heart left to itself, and wrong about what grace can do to it. We do not begin by loving God for nothing. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19), and a love received for nothing slowly learns to give itself the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face." And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan asks God to strike, and God allows it, but only within a limit he sets before a single blow falls.

Stretch out your hand. Satan does not ask to strike Job himself; he asks God to do it. And “curse” is again the Hebrew “bless”. Keep that word for verse 21.

Not a wager. People sometimes call this a wager, but a wager is made when the outcome is uncertain, and God has just said what Job is. It is a demonstration, before an audience in heaven, that God can be loved for himself, as Paul says that “through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10).

Only against him do not stretch out your hand. The limit is set before the first blow. Jesus told Peter the same on the night of his arrest: “Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Job did not know about the council. The Christian knows there is one, and that Jesus is in it, praying. “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Is God then responsible for the evil? He permits it and sets its limits (v. 12), and nothing happens outside his rule. But Satan and the raiders are the ones who do evil, and God is neither its author nor guilty of it. So Job can rightly say that “the LORD has taken away” (v. 21), and still not “charge God with wrong” (v. 22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On one ordinary day everything Job has is taken, and the storyteller makes us feel it as Job did, one blow landing on top of the last. While his children feast in their oldest brother’s house, four servants arrive on each other’s heels. Raiders from Sheba take the oxen and donkeys (vv. 13–15); fire from heaven burns up the sheep (v. 16); Chaldean raiders take the camels (v. 17); and a great wind brings the house down on all ten children (vv. 18–19). Men, then sky, then men, then sky: trouble comes from every side and through every kind of cause, and Job is given no time to take in one loss before the next arrives.
verseByVerse.theology: The book names four causes: wicked men, weather, the devil and God’s permission. It never lets one of them explain the others away.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them, and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What was decided in heaven arrives on earth on an ordinary day, and the first blow is plain human wickedness.

Now there was a day. The words echo verse 6. The day comes at a family meal; if the brothers hosted in order of age, the round of feasts had just begun again, in the oldest brother’s house.

The Sabeans fell upon them. The work is ordinary, ploughing and grazing; then come raiders from Sheba in Arabia, men who kill for livestock. They were not puppets: they chose their raid and will answer for it, though they came because God allowed it and Satan wanted it.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabeans came from Arabia; the Chaldeans (v. 17) from Mesopotamia.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you." While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trouble comes from the sky and from men, from every side at once, and so fast that Job cannot take in one loss before the next.

The fire of God fell from heaven. It was probably lightning, but the servant calls it “the fire of God”, the phrase used of the fire that fell at Elijah’s word (2 Kings 1:12). Even he reads it as heaven turned against his master; that is how it looked from the ground, and Job will wrestle with that appearance for the rest of the book.

The Chaldeans formed three groups. Then come raiders again, this time from Mesopotamia. Men, then sky, then men: no one explanation will cover it, and Job is given no time to look for one. “While he was yet speaking”, three times over, the next messenger arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worst blow comes last: a desert wind brings the house down on all ten children, and the book will not say that they died for their sins.

A great wind came across the wilderness. The storyteller has kept the worst till last: ten children under one roof, at the very meal their father used to pray over. A wind from the desert strikes “the four corners of the house”, every side at once, and there is nowhere to run. By the end of one day Job has ten graves to dig.

For a grieving parent. Two things must be said to a parent who reads this with a grave of his own. The book never says these children died for their sins: Bildad will say it (8:4), and the LORD will judge him and his friends for speaking what is not right (42:7). And Job’s prayers for them were not wasted; nothing suggests that a father loses his children because his prayers failed. The book refuses to explain the loss, and then shows that God can be trusted in it.

Was it just to take Job’s children for a test they knew nothing of? The book does not explain it from their side, and we should not pretend to. But the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and the manner of a death is no verdict on the one who died. Job, who had prayed and offered sacrifices for them (v. 5), never accuses God of injustice to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The LORD Gave, and the LORD Has Taken Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job meets the worst day of his life with grief and worship together, and Satan’s theory fails. He tears his robe, shaves his head and falls to the ground, the honest mourning of his time, and in the same movement he worships (v. 20). He came with nothing and will leave with nothing; the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, and Job blesses his name, using the very word Satan said would become a curse (v. 21). The narrator gives the verdict: in all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong (v. 22). To say “God did this” is not sin; to say that God was wrong to do it would have been.
verseByVerse.theology: The first round goes to God, and to the man who trusted him with nothing left in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job grieves openly and worships in the same breath, because grief and worship are not opposites.

Tore his robe and shaved his head. There are five verbs. The first four are the grief of his time, the mourning customs everyone would recognise: he rises, tears his robe, shaves his head and throws himself on the ground. Job does not pretend; there is no brave face. Then the fifth, in the same sentence: “and worshiped”, bowed down with his face to the earth.

At the graveside. A Christian at a graveside does not have to choose between weeping and trusting. “Jesus wept” at the tomb of his friend (John 11:35), and Paul does not tell the church to stop grieving, but not to grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Tears are not unbelief. Job’s were on the ground, and so was his worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job looks past every nearer cause to God, owns that all he had was God’s gift, and blesses God himself when the gifts are gone.

Naked I came from my mother’s womb. He came with nothing and will leave with nothing; everything in between was on loan. The Preacher says the same (Ecclesiastes 5:15), and so does Paul: “we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world” (1 Timothy 6:7).

The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Job does not blame the Sabeans, the Chaldeans or the weather, and he does not know about Satan. He goes straight past every nearer cause to God, and he is right to, for God will say to Satan, “you incited me against him” (2:3). This is not resignation to blind fate: his losses were in the hands not of chance but of the one who had given him everything.

Blessed be the name of the LORD. Job uses Satan’s own word. Satan said Job would “bless” God to his face, meaning curse him. Job blesses God and means it, and Satan’s theory has failed in a single verb.

The name of the LORD. When the ESV prints LORD in capitals, it stands for God’s personal name, the one he gave Moses at the burning bush: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). It speaks of the God who simply is, who depends on nothing and does not change when everything else does, and in Scripture a name is the person as he has made himself known. So Job is not thanking God for the gifts, which are gone, but praising him for who he is, the very thing Satan said no one would do. That name has since been given a human face. Jesus said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and God has “bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). The LORD who takes away is the God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). See also Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

Not a formula. This verse is not a formula to recite over someone else’s grief, and it was not easy for Job: he said it with his head shaved and his clothes torn, and in chapter 3 the same man will curse the day he was born. But it shows what a person can say when he has lost everything. Long afterwards another man was stripped, and soldiers divided his clothes among them (John 19:23–24). He had nothing left, and he did not curse God: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

In everyday life. Most of us love the gifts more easily than the Giver, and find out which we loved only when the gifts go. When something is taken from you, try praising God for one thing about him that the loss cannot touch: he is still faithful, still near, still the same.

verseByVerse.quote: In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saying that God had done this was not sin; saying that God was wrong to do it would have been, and the whole book lives between the two.

In all this Job did not sin. Read the verdict carefully, for the rest of the book depends on it. Job said that the LORD had taken away his children; what he did not do was “charge God with wrong”.

The darkest day in history. Satan, raiders, fire and wind all had their part, and over them all stood the permission and purpose of God. The same pattern appears at the cross: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Wicked men did their worst, and it was what God’s hand and plan had predetermined (Acts 4:28). If God could rule the darkest day in history for good, he rules yours too, even when you cannot yet see how.

The One who loved for nothing. Satan asked whether anyone would love God for no reason. One man did it perfectly. Jesus loved the Father with nothing in his hands and was hated “without a cause”, and because of him “the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down” (Revelation 12:10). He is worthy of such love.

Neither meaningless nor deserved. These verses are the Old Testament’s home for the question of why the righteous suffer, and they already rule out the two answers people reach for most. One says suffering simply happens, an accident in a universe that does not care, with nothing in it to understand. The other, the friends’ answer and the instinct of much popular spirituality, says suffering is always a sentence that somebody earned. Job 1 refuses both. Job’s suffering is not deserved, for God says so twice (1:8; 2:3); and it is not meaningless, for it began in heaven, with a purpose Job never learns. The philosopher Nicholas Wolterstorff, writing Lament for a Son after his son was killed in a climbing accident, said that he could not fit the death into any explanation, and that what he found instead was a God who suffers with us. That is where the whole book points. One righteous man’s suffering was the least deserved and the most meaningful in history, and because of it the suffering of those who belong to him is neither wasted nor a verdict. (For God’s answer to Job, see the note on Job 38:1–4; for the philosopher’s argument, the note on John 9:3.)

keyVerse.quote: The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is Satan’s theory answered in a single sentence. Stripped of everything, Job looks past the raiders and the weather to God, owns that all he had was God’s gift, and blesses the LORD for who he is, using the very word Satan said would become a curse. It shows what grace can make of a human heart: a love for God that does not depend on his gifts.

1.reflection:
Satan’s question is “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (v. 9). If your circumstances were stripped back as Job’s were, what do you think would be left of your faith? What does it mean that “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19)?

The reader is told twice that Job is blameless before any disaster comes (vv. 1, 8). Why does the book insist on this? How might it change the way we think, and speak, about people who are suffering?

Satan can go no further than God allows (v. 12), yet the Sabeans, the Chaldeans and Satan himself are guilty of the evil they do. How does this help us hold together God’s rule over everything and his goodness? Where else in Scripture do we see the same pattern (Acts 2:23)?

Job tears his robe and worships in the same breath (vv. 20–21). Have you found grief and worship to be opposites, or can they belong together? How would you pray, or sit, with someone who has just lost a child?

2.title: Skin for Skin
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."<sup>4</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life.<sup>5</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life."<sup>7</sup>So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.<sup>8</sup>And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.<sup>9</sup>Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."<sup>10</sup>But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.<sup>11</sup>Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.<sup>12</sup>And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.<sup>13</sup>And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
2.overview:
Where we are. This is the second and last scene of the prologue. Job has lost his wealth and all ten children, and has blessed the name of the LORD (1:21). Now the court of heaven meets again, and the test goes deeper, into Job’s own body, before the friends arrive and the long debate begins.

The message. God sets the limit even on the deepest suffering, and a believer can hold fast to him without being told why. Satan says that a man will give anything to save his own skin; Job, covered in sores and urged to curse God and die, answers that we must receive trouble from God as well as good. And the best thing anyone does for him in the whole book is the first thing his friends do: come, weep and sit silently in the dust with him.

Why it was said. Every sufferer hears two voices that this chapter answers. One says that faith has failed and it is time to let go of God; the other, soon to speak through the friends, says that suffering must be explained, and explained as punishment (see the introduction). The chapter rules out both before the debate begins.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD repeats his verdict on Job and adds that Satan incited him to destroy Job “without reason”; Satan replies, “Skin for skin!”, and is allowed to touch Job’s body but not to take his life (vv. 1–6). Job is struck with sores from head to foot and sits in the ashes; his wife says, “Curse God and die”, and he answers, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (vv. 7–10). Three friends come to comfort him, do not recognise him, weep, and sit with him seven days and nights without a word (vv. 11–13).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God shown in him. Job bears the look of the law’s curse without its guilt, so that onlookers think him struck by God; of the Servant Isaiah says, “we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4), and Christ bore the curse itself, which was ours (Galatians 3:13). Job’s face is marred beyond recognition, as the Servant’s was (Isaiah 52:14). And where the friends sat in silence for seven days, God did more: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and sat in our dust to stay.

For us. When suffering reaches the body and the voices say “let go”, faith can still say, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?”, because the limit on our trouble is set by a Father, not by our enemy. And when someone we love is on the ash heap, the first ministry is not an explanation but our presence, as Christ’s presence is ours.
2.theology:
God rules over evil without doing evil: Satan incites, and God says you incited me (v. 3). The limit on Satan moves, but it remains.

Job's sores look like the curse the law threatens for disobedience, though he has not disobeyed, so every onlooker takes him for cursed; Christ bore the curse itself, and it was ours (see on vv. 6-7).
2.examples: Job's wife turns God's own words, he still holds fast his integrity, into a despairing question, and Job, answering her, rebukes the words and spares the woman. Then three friends do the wisest thing they will ever do: they sit in silence for seven days.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Satan has lost the first round, but the test goes deeper, and God remains in full command of it. The heavenly court meets again and Satan reports, as he must (vv. 1–2). The LORD repeats his verdict on Job and adds that Job still holds fast his integrity, though Satan incited God against him “without reason” (v. 3): this suffering was not deserved. Satan answers with a cynic’s proverb, that a man will give anything to save his own skin, and asks God to strike Job’s body (vv. 4–5). God allows it, but sets a new limit before the blow: spare his life (v. 6). Satan goes out and strikes Job with sores from head to foot (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not keep his distance from Job's suffering. The evil is Satan's; the permission, and the limit, are God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD. And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan has lost the first round, and still he must come and report to the God he opposes.

To present himself before the LORD. The scene repeats chapter 1 almost word for word, with one addition. There Satan simply “came among them” (1:6); now he comes “to present himself before the LORD”, like the others. However much he roams the earth, he cannot stay away from the throne; he answers to God whether he likes it or not.

From going to and fro on the earth. The restless answer is the same as before. Nothing has changed for Satan. Everything has changed for Job, and he does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God repeats his verdict: Job has held fast, and his suffering came on him without reason.

He still holds fast his integrity. God repeats the words of 1:8 and adds two things. The first is that Job is still the blameless man of 1:1: his children are dead and his wealth gone, and he has not let go.

You incited me against him. The second is startling. God does not say that Satan did it while he looked away; he says that Satan moved him. Samuel says that the LORD “incited David” to number Israel (2 Samuel 24:1); Chronicles says that “Satan stood against Israel and incited David” (1 Chronicles 21:1). Both are true. Satan means evil by it, and God rules over it for his own ends. God takes responsibility for what has happened to Job, and still holds Satan guilty of it.

Without reason. This is Satan’s word from 1:9, handed back to him. Whatever the friends are about to argue, the LORD has already ruled that this suffering was not deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan claims that the first test did not go deep enough: touch a man’s own body, and he will show that he loves himself more than God.

Skin for skin! A proverb: a man will give anything to save his own skin. Job lost his goods and his children, Satan says, but he still has himself. Touch that, and you will see what he really loves.

All that a man has he will give for his life. Again Satan asks God to do the striking. This is the cynic’s creed: in the end everyone looks after number one. Satan has never met a love that would not save itself. He is about to watch one in Job, and one day he will watch it perfectly in Jesus, of whom the scoffers said, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42).

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of “Skin for skin” is not known. It may come from barter, one hide traded for another; it may mean that a man will give another’s skin to save his own, or one part of himself to save the rest. The next line makes the point plain whichever is right.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lets Satan touch Job’s body within a new limit, and Job is struck so that he looks like a man under God’s curse.

Only spare his life. The limit moves, but there is still a limit. Satan may touch Job’s body, not take his life. God draws the line before the blow, as he did the first time (1:12).

From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Any Israelite reader would hear one of the law’s curses on a disobedient people, word for word at its close: “The LORD will strike you on the knees and on the legs with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head” (Deuteronomy 28:35). Job has done nothing to earn that curse, but he looks exactly like a man who has, and three men are about to draw the obvious conclusion.

The curse itself, and it was ours. That is the pattern of the cross. Of the Servant the prophet says, “we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4): the onlookers were right that he bore a curse, and wrong to think it was his own. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Job bore the look of the curse without the guilt. Christ bore the curse itself, and it was ours.

Is all sickness, then, from Satan? This is a particular case, permitted and limited by God, shown to us so that we will not assume it of every illness. Sickness comes in many ways in a fallen world, and God rules over all of it.

Uncertain wording. No one knows what the illness was. The word for “sores” is used of the boils of Egypt (Exodus 9:9) and of Hezekiah’s boil (2 Kings 20:7), and Job later speaks of skin that breaks out afresh, worms, blackened peeling skin, fever and sleepless nights (7:4–5; 30:17, 30). Many diagnoses have been offered; none can be proved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job is brought as low as a man can be, and still he will not let go of God. The greatest man of the east sits in the ashes, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pot (v. 8). Then the one person left to him speaks Satan’s goal aloud: “Curse God and die” (v. 9). Job rebukes her words without rejecting her, and gives the answer of faith: if we have taken good from God’s hand without asking whether we deserved it, shall we refuse the trouble? The narrator gives the verdict a second time: in all this Job did not sin with his lips (v. 10). Satan has lost twice, and is not mentioned again.
verseByVerse.theology: The body that Satan was sure would break is the place where Job holds on. The second round goes to God as well.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest man in the east sits on the ash heap, where God’s people, and their Lord, have often been found.

A piece of broken pottery. He scrapes his sores with a shard from a broken pot, and sits in the ashes, the place of mourning. The Greek translation puts him “on the dung heap outside the city”, and that is probably the picture: the town’s rubbish and ash heap, where outcasts sat, for a man with sores like these would be kept away from others.

The poor man at the gate. Jesus told of a poor man laid at a rich man’s gate, “covered with sores”, while “even the dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke 16:20–21). God’s people have often looked like that. And their Lord did not stay away from that place: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s wife, broken by the same losses, urges him to let go of the integrity God delights in.

Do you still hold fast your integrity? Her question is God’s own sentence from verse 3 turned into a question. God said it with pride; she says it in despair, or scorn. The one thing God delights in is the one thing she wants him to let go of. And her advice is Satan’s goal to the letter: “Curse God”, and then die and be done with it.

Remember what she has lost. Readers have judged her harshly, and she has earned some of it. But she has lost ten children too, and watches her husband scraping his sores in the ashes. Hers are the words of someone who thinks faith has failed and would rather see the suffering end in death. Plenty of believers have heard such words from someone they love, or said them to themselves. Job mentions her later (19:17), but she never speaks again.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job rebukes the words but spares the woman, and refuses a faith that takes God’s good gifts and hands back the hard ones.

As one of the foolish women would speak. The fool in Scripture is not the stupid person but the one who lives as if God does not matter: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1). And Job does not call her a fool. He says she is talking like one. He rebukes the words and spares the woman.

Shall we receive good from God? “We”: he takes her into the question with him. “Evil” here means calamity, not wickedness (the ESV notes “disaster”), as when God says, “I make well-being and create calamity” (Isaiah 45:7). Job has taken God’s good gifts for years without asking whether he deserved them. Is he now to take only the good and hand back the rest? His faith is not a contract that lapses when the payments stop.

Job did not sin with his lips. In chapter 1 Job worried that his children had cursed God “in their hearts” (1:5). Here the narrator speaks of his lips, because the test was whether he would curse God aloud. And the mouth shows the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). Satan has lost twice. He is not mentioned again in the book.
verseByVerse.note: “Evil” can also be rendered “disaster” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Seven Days on the Ground
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three friends come to comfort Job, and their first response is the best thing they do in the whole book. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, wise men from the lands around Edom and Arabia, arrange to come together to show him sympathy and comfort him (v. 11). They do not recognise him at a distance; they weep aloud, tear their robes and throw dust in the air (v. 12). Then they sit with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word, because they can see how great his suffering is (v. 13). When they begin to speak, from chapter 4, they will do great harm. Their silence never needed to be forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology: When the friends begin to speak, they begin to go wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three wise men come a long way to comfort Job, and they come as true friends.

Job’s three friends. They come from the lands around Edom and Arabia. Eliphaz shares his name with a son of Esau, whose own son was called Teman (Genesis 36:10–11), and Teman was famous for its wise men: “Is wisdom no more in Teman?” (Jeremiah 49:7). Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). These are serious men from the wisdom country, and they come as friends.

To show him sympathy and comfort him. Their intentions were good: they took trouble and arranged to travel together. Keep those two verbs in mind. Job will soon call them “miserable comforters” (16:2). And at the very end, when his brothers and sisters come to eat with him, the narrator says they “showed him sympathy and comforted him” (42:11), the same pair of words. The friends came to do something the book finally sees done by others.
verseByVerse.note: Teman was a city of Edom, famous for its wise men.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends cannot recognise Job, and they grieve for him honestly and aloud.

They did not recognize him. The sores have changed his face. They weep aloud, tear their robes as he tore his (1:20), and throw dust into the air to fall on their heads: real grief, honestly shown.

So marred, beyond human semblance. Isaiah’s Servant is described the same way: “his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance” (Isaiah 52:14). There is a suffering that makes a man unrecognisable, and the Son of God went into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends sit silently in the dust with Job for seven days, the best thing they do in the whole book.

Seven days and seven nights. Joseph mourned his father seven days (Genesis 50:10), and Ezekiel sat overwhelmed among the exiles seven days (Ezekiel 3:15). The friends mourn Job as though he were already dead. They sit on the ground with him, day and night, and say nothing, because they can see that no words would be big enough for his pain. They let him speak first.

What God did for us. God did not send an explanation from a distance. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He sat in our dust, and so “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). He has been on the ground with us, and he stays.

In everyday life. This is still the right place to begin with anyone in deep grief: go, sit on the ground, and do not explain. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). When the friends open their mouths, from chapter 4 on, they will do great harm, and God will say that they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Their silence never needed to be forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Compare Ezekiel 3:15, where the prophet sits overwhelmed among the exiles seven days.

keyVerse.quote: Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?
keyVerse.note: This is Job’s answer to the voice that tells him to let go of God, and it is the heart of the prologue’s second test. Job refuses a faith that is a contract, taking God’s gifts and handing back his hard providences. It is spoken from the ash heap, not from comfort, and the narrator adds that in all this Job did not sin with his lips.

2.reflection:
God says that Satan “incited me against him to destroy him without reason” (v. 3). How does this verse hold together God’s rule over Job’s suffering and Satan’s guilt for it? Why does it matter that God says the suffering was “without reason”?

Satan’s creed is “All that a man has he will give for his life” (v. 4). Where do you see that creed in our culture, or in your own heart? How does Jesus, who would not save himself, answer it?

Job answers his wife, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (v. 10). What is the difference between this and grim resignation? What would it look like to say it honestly in a trial of your own?

The friends’ seven days of silence were their best hour (v. 13). Why is it so hard to sit with a suffering person without explaining or fixing? What has helped you most when you were grieving?

3.title: Let the Day Perish
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.<sup>2</sup>And Job said:<sup>3</sup>"Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.'<sup>4</sup>Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it.<sup>5</sup>Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.<sup>6</sup>That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months.<sup>7</sup>Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.<sup>8</sup>Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan.<sup>9</sup>Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning,<sup>10</sup>because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.<sup>11</sup>"Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?<sup>12</sup>Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?<sup>13</sup>For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest,<sup>14</sup>with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves,<sup>15</sup>or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.<sup>16</sup>Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light?<sup>17</sup>There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest.<sup>18</sup>There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster.<sup>19</sup>The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.<sup>20</sup>"Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul,<sup>21</sup>who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,<sup>22</sup>who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?<sup>23</sup>Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?<sup>24</sup>For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water.<sup>25</sup>For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me.<sup>26</sup>I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
3.overview:
Where we are. The prologue is over. For seven days and nights Job and his friends have sat in silence on the ground (2:13), and now Job is the first to speak. With his words the book changes from prose to poetry, which it will keep until 42:6, and the long debate begins.

The message. A servant of God may bring the darkest cry of his heart to God, and it is not the curse Satan wanted. Job curses the day he was born, not God; he longs for the rest of the grave and asks why life is given to those who want only to die. Scripture records this lament without tidying it, because faith sometimes has to sit in the dark for a while, and anguish spoken towards God is not unbelief.

Why it was said. The chapter is given for every believer who fears that his despair has disqualified him, and who has been offered only cheerfulness or silence (see the introduction). It also sets the debate going: Job’s word “trouble” and his longing for death are what Eliphaz will answer, and answer wrongly.

How the chapter makes its case. Job curses his birthday and the night of his conception, wishing them unmade, dark and barren, struck off the calendar because they let him be born into trouble (vv. 1–10). He asks why he did not die at birth, and pictures the grave as rest, where kings and slaves lie together and “the weary are at rest” (vv. 11–19). Then he asks why light is given to the miserable who long for death, to a man “whom God has hedged in”, and ends with no rest at all: “but trouble comes” (vv. 20–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes, and by pattern. Job looks for rest and can find it only in the grave; Christ says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). And the Son of God himself went into the dark where Job sits: “in the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone into ours “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. Do not hide your darkest words from God; say them to him, for even groans too deep for words are heard as prayer (Romans 8:26). If you long to die, tell someone today. And when others are in Job’s place, do not hurry them to the bright side; sit with them, and let Christ, who has been there, be their hope.
3.theology:
Lament is not rebellion. Job curses his day, not his God, and Scripture places the same cry in the mouth of a faithful prophet (Jer 20:14-18), lets whole psalms end in darkness, and hears the lament of Psalm 22 on Christ's own lips.

Job tries to un-create his day, and when God answers he will begin with creation. The rest Job looks for in the grave is found in Christ.
3.examples: Many of Job's words here will come back later in the book with their meaning turned: the Leviathan he wants roused, God will show him on a lead (41:1), and the man who digs for the grave as for treasure will later ask where wisdom, deeper than any treasure, can be found (ch. 28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job breaks the silence with a curse, but he curses the day of his birth, not God, and the difference is the whole difference between agony and rebellion. He wishes that the day he was born would perish and that the night which announced a boy had never spoken (vv. 1–3). He calls darkness to swallow the day, reversing God’s first word in creation, “Let there be light” (vv. 4–5). He wants the night struck off the calendar and left barren (vv. 6–7), cursed by those who know how to curse days, even by those who could rouse Leviathan, because it did not shut his mother’s womb and keep trouble from his eyes (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief this deep is not the same thing as rebellion, and Scripture keeps the two apart.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. And Job said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job breaks the silence with a curse, but on the day of his birth, not on God: the cry of a man in agony, not in rebellion.

Cursed the day of his birth. Job breaks the silence, and Satan twice predicted that Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). He does not. He curses the day he was born, and the difference is the whole difference between a man in agony and a man in rebellion.

From prose to poetry. Two things change here. The book changes from prose to poetry: from “And Job said” until 42:6 almost everything is set out in lines, like the Psalms, to be heard as the speech of a man at the end of his strength, not as a statement of doctrine. And Job seems to change: the man who said “blessed be the name of the LORD” now wishes he had never been born. It is the same man, after seven days on the ash heap. When James holds Job up to Christians, the word he uses is “steadfastness” (James 5:11): not calm, but endurance, the refusal to let go while everything in you is shouting. This chapter is part of what James meant.

Jeremiah too. Job is not the only servant of God to say this. Jeremiah, in the middle of his calling, cried, “Cursed be the day on which I was born!” (Jeremiah 20:14). Scripture prints these cries, so that the believer who has felt the same will know he is not the first, and that God has heard it before.

Must we always look on the bright side? Our culture hands the suffering two scripts. One is relentless positivity: stay strong, find the silver lining. The writer Barbara Ehrenreich, after her own diagnosis of breast cancer, described how oppressive she found the cheerful culture around the disease, which left no room for fear or anger, and went on to write a whole book against positive thinking. The other script is pure expression: let it all out. Job follows neither. He does not smile, and he does not simply vent into the void. Within a few chapters his cries are addressed to someone: “Remember that my life is a breath” (7:7); “let me know why you contend against me” (10:2). That is the difference between lament and despair: the unbeliever can rage, but there is no one to rage at, and the positive thinker can cope, but there is no one to cry to. Scripture gives a third way, and the gospel gives Christians more reason to lament, not less, because God has come that close: “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Even the groans we cannot put into sentences are heard as prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.' Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it. Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job wishes his birthday unmade, calling darkness over it as if to reverse the first day of creation.

Let the day perish on which I was born. He goes back to his birth and before that his conception, as if he could reach into the past and unmake it. The night is imagined announcing a boy; he wishes it had never spoken.

Let that day be darkness! Anyone who knows Genesis will hear it. On the first day God said, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3). Job uses the same Hebrew form in reverse: “let that day be darkness”. He wants to un-create his own day.

May God above not seek it. To “seek” a thing, in this sense, is to care for it: Israel’s was “a land that the LORD your God cares for” (Deuteronomy 11:12), where the Hebrew is the same verb. Job asks God to take his eyes off one day, so that it falls out of existence. It is the prayer of a man who still believes that nothing lasts unless God keeps it.

Gloom and deep darkness. He piles up every word for dark he has. This is what grief does to a man’s world: it runs back over his whole life and puts out the lights one by one. One of them, “deep darkness”, is the word older translations rendered “the shadow of death”, as in “the valley of the shadow of death” (Psalm 23:4). The same man who here asks the deep darkness to swallow his day will say that God “brings deep darkness to light” (12:22), and God will ask him, “have you seen the gates of deep darkness?” (38:17). The darkness Job calls on is not beyond God’s reach; God has seen its gates.

Where God will begin. When God finally answers Job, he will not start with Job’s suffering but with creation: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?” (38:4). Job has tried to undo a day. God will show him the One who made every day there is.

Uncertain wording. Three phrases in verse 5 are hard. “Claim it” translates a verb that usually means “redeem”, as the next of kin takes back what belongs to the family; a second verb spelled the same way means “defile” (hence the older “stain it”). If the ESV is right, there is a bitter irony here, for the same verb gives the book its great hope: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25). “Deep darkness” (tsalmaveth) is written in the Hebrew text as “shadow of death”, though many think it a single word for deep darkness. And “the blackness of the day” uses a rare word that may mean anything that darkens a day, such as an eclipse. The general sense is clear: every kind of darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months. Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job wants the night of his conception struck from the calendar and left barren, so deep has the wound gone.

Let that night be barren. He wants the night struck off the calendar, so that it never comes round again. And he wants it barren, with no “joyful cry”: the shout when a boy was born.

What it does not mean. He is not saying that his life was always misery; chapter 29 will show how rich it was. He is saying that if this is where it was heading, it would have been better never to begin. Deep grief can reach back and poison the happy years too; that shows not that the years were bad, but how deep the wound is.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan. Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning, because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job calls on any power that might curse his day, even the monster of chaos; but chaos too has a master.

Ready to rouse up Leviathan. The ancient world told stories of Leviathan, the monster of the sea and of chaos. Job reaches for any power at all that might undo his day, even the monster.

Leviathan again. That name will come back. God will ask Job, “Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook?” (41:1), and describe the creature Job wanted roused as something God made and holds on a lead. Scripture elsewhere uses the name for every power that opposes God: “In that day the LORD … will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent” (Isaiah 27:1). Job calls on chaos. God will show him that chaos has a master.

The eyelids of the morning. The first glimmer of dawn. He wants that night to wait for a morning that never comes, because it let him be born and so let him see trouble.

Nor hide trouble from my eyes. That word, ‘amal, is what Job calls his life now (v. 20; 7:3). And Eliphaz will seize on it in his first reply: “man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward” (5:7). Job says trouble came because he was born. Eliphaz will say that trouble is what being born means, and that its cause lies in the man himself (5:6–7). The argument of the next twenty chapters has already begun.

Uncertain wording. Those “who curse the day” are probably sorcerers thought able to blight a day. In Hebrew “day” (yom) and “sea” (yam) differ by one vowel, and some scholars suggest the line meant cursers of the Sea, which would pair with Leviathan, the sea monster. The meaning is much the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: Leviathan was a sea monster of ancient myth, a picture of chaos; God later describes it as his creature (ch. 41).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — Why Did I Not Die at Birth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since he could not be unborn, Job asks why he did not die at birth, and he pictures the grave as the rest he cannot find. Every kindness that kept the newborn alive, the knees that received him and the breasts that fed him, he now counts as a cruelty (vv. 11–12). In death he would have lain down in quiet, among kings and princes whose monuments and gold could not keep them alive (vv. 13–15), or like a stillborn child that never saw the light (v. 16). There the wicked stop troubling, the weary rest, prisoners no longer hear the slave driver, and small and great lie side by side (vv. 17–19). The Old Testament sees the grave dimly; Christ gives the longing for rest its true answer.
verseByVerse.theology: Job longs for the grave as a place of rest. The New Testament does not deny the longing; it points it to a person.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?
