verseByVerse.commentary:
Since he could not be unborn, Job asks why he did not die at birth.

Why did I not die at birth? The first “why” of the book, and there will be many. The knees may be a father’s, taking the newborn on his lap as his own; the breasts are the mother’s. Every kindness that kept the baby alive, Job now counts as a cruelty.

Not a philosopher’s question. It is the question people ask in hospital corridors and at three in the morning. The Bible does not forbid it. Job asks it, and God will answer him, though not in the way he expects.

verseByVerse.quote: For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest, with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves, or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his pain the grave looks to Job like the only rest there is, the place where even kings and princes have been made equal.

I would have been at rest. Quiet, sleep, rest: the three things he cannot have, and in his pain the grave looks like the only place to find them. He pictures himself among kings and princes who hoarded gold, whose wealth could not keep them alive. Death has made them equal, and Job would rather be equal with the dead than go on living.

A dim view of the grave. The Old Testament saints saw the grave dimly, as a place of silence, and Job speaks of it as a desperate man does, as mere relief. The New Testament gives the longing its real answer. There is a rest for the weary, and it is not the grave but a person: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Uncertain wording. “Who rebuilt ruins for themselves” is compressed: it may mean kings who restored ruined cities for their own glory, or who built monuments that now lie in ruins. Either way, their building did not save them.

verseByVerse.quote: Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light? There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest. There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job envies the stillborn child and pictures the grave as freedom, where the weary rest and slave and master lie side by side.

A hidden stillborn child. The stillborn baby is buried quietly, unnamed; the light never touches it. Job envies it.

The weary are at rest. These lines have been carved on many gravestones, and they are true as far as they go: in the grave nobody bullies anyone. The “taskmaster” is the word Exodus uses for Egypt’s slave drivers (Exodus 3:7). The weak and the powerful, the slave and his owner, lie side by side. For a man in unending pain it sounds like freedom.

Those who die in the Lord. But Scripture’s fuller word about the rest of the dead is for those “who die in the Lord”: “Blessed indeed,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors” (Revelation 14:13). The rest Job longed for in the dark is real, and it belongs to those who belong to Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s question turns from his own birth to every sufferer’s life, and at last he names God. Why is light given to the miserable, who long for death more than for buried treasure and rejoice when they find the grave (vv. 20–22)? Why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, “whom God has hedged in” (v. 23), when the hedge that once protected him now feels like a prison wall? Sighing has become his bread and groaning pours out of him like water; the thing he dreaded has come (vv. 24–25). His first speech ends with no word of hope: no ease, no quiet, no rest, “but trouble comes” (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: For the first time Job's question turns toward God. He does not doubt that God gives life. He cannot understand why God goes on giving it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures, who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks why life is given to the miserable who long for death, and he brings that longing to God instead of acting on it.

Why is light given to him who is in misery? Now the question turns from Job’s birth to everyone in misery, and it is aimed, carefully, at God, though it does not yet name him. Job still believes that God gives life. That is exactly his problem.

More than for hidden treasures. Look at the picture of digging for death “more than for hidden treasures”. In chapter 28 men will dig for treasure, and Job will ask where wisdom, dearer than all of it, can be found (28:1–13). Job is digging for the grave. What he needs lies deeper, and he has not found it yet.

For those who long for death. Some who read this will know the longing from the inside, the wish to go to sleep and not wake. Look at what Job does with it. He says it aloud, to God. And he never takes his life into his own hands; he will ask God to end it (6:8–9), because he knows it is God’s (1:21). If that is where you are, do what Job did: say it aloud, to the God who has not let go of you, and to someone who will sit with you on the ground.

Is the wish to die a sin? Job, Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (Jonah 4:3) all wished it, and God did not condemn them for saying it. But taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment; life is God’s to give and to take. Depression and despair are real, and they call for help: from God in prayer, from the church, and from a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up so that any bodily cause is found and treated; medicine, where it is needed, is no failure of faith. Anyone who is thinking of ending their life should tell someone today: a pastor, a doctor, a friend, or a crisis line, and in an emergency get help the same day. And if someone you love has died this way, this book, which records Job’s darkest words without condemning him, does not ask you to sit in judgment; leave them with the God who knows the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Job names God: the hedge that once protected him feels like a prison wall, and he cannot see where his road is going.

Whom God has hedged in. “Whose way is hidden”: Job cannot see where his road goes or why it turned. “Hedged in” is close cousin to the word Satan used when God had put a hedge around Job to protect him (1:10). Now the same hand that guarded him seems to be shutting him in.

What the reader knows. The reader knows what Job does not: that God is still guarding him, and the limit set in heaven still stands (2:6). Every believer walks, some of the time, where his way is hidden. The hedge he feels as a prison may be the very thing that is keeping him safe.

verseByVerse.quote: For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water. For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me. I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s first speech ends in the dark, with no rest, only trouble, and Scripture lets it end there, for the Son of God has been there too.

My sighing comes instead of my bread. Sighing is his food; groaning runs out of him like water from a jar. The sores, the loss and the sleeplessness have taken over the ordinary things of life.

The thing that I fear comes upon me. Some take these words to mean that Job’s fears brought the disaster on him, but chapters 1 and 2 have told us exactly how it began. Job had always known how fragile his blessings were, and rose early to pray for his children (1:5). Now the thing he dreaded has happened, and his dread did not cause it.

I have no rest, but trouble comes. Ease, quiet, rest: the words he used of the grave (vv. 13, 17–18), now each with “not” in front of it. The dead have what he lacks. And the last word of his first speech is “trouble”.

Ending in the dark. The chapter ends with no word of hope. Psalm 88 ends the same way: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). Job’s lament is not the sin Satan wanted; he has not cursed God. But it is not the whole truth either, and God will call some of his later words “words without knowledge” (38:2). Scripture lets a chapter end in darkness because some of God’s people have to sit there for a while, and the Son of God sat there too: “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and on the cross he prayed, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone into ours, “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

keyVerse.quote: Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
keyVerse.note: Here Job’s lament reaches its centre and at last names God. The hedge that once protected him (1:10) now feels like a prison wall, and his way is hidden from him. The reader knows what Job does not: the limit set in heaven still stands, and the hidden way is still in God’s hands.

3.reflection:
Job curses the day of his birth but not God (vv. 1–3). Why does that difference matter so much? What is the difference between lament and rebellion, and between lament and despair?

Our culture offers sufferers either relentless positivity or pure self-expression. How does this chapter, and the fact that God included it in Scripture, give a third way? What would it look like for you to bring your darkest words to God?

Job longs for the rest of the grave (vv. 13–19), and Jesus says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). What kind of rest does Christ give that the grave cannot?

If someone told you they felt as Job does in verses 20–22, how would you respond? What help would you make sure they had, and what would you take care not to say?

4.title: Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?<sup>3</sup>Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands.<sup>4</sup>Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees.<sup>5</sup>But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.<sup>6</sup>Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?<sup>7</sup>"Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off?<sup>8</sup>As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same.<sup>9</sup>By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.<sup>10</sup>The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken.<sup>11</sup>The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.<sup>12</sup>"Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it.<sup>13</sup>Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,<sup>14</sup>dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.<sup>15</sup>A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up.<sup>16</sup>It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:<sup>17</sup>'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?<sup>18</sup>Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error;<sup>19</sup>how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth.<sup>20</sup>Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it.<sup>21</sup>Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
4.overview:
Where we are. Job has broken the seven days of silence with his lament (chapter 3), and now his friends answer. Eliphaz, probably the eldest and certainly the most courteous, speaks first, and this chapter is the first half of his speech (chapters 4–5), which opens the first round of the debate (chapters 4–14).

The message. True things about God, wrongly applied, become false comfort. Eliphaz begins gently, then states the idea the friends will never let go: the innocent do not perish, so if you are suffering, the cause must lie in you. He backs it with a voice in the night saying that no one is right before God. Much of what he says is true, but God will say that he did not speak rightly (42:7), and the reader, who has been told twice that Job is blameless, can see where he goes wrong.

Why it was said. Every generation of God’s people is tempted to read suffering backwards, from the harvest to the seed (see the introduction). This chapter lets us watch a wise and devout man do it, so that we learn to recognise the reasoning and refuse it, and never quote the friends’ speeches as God’s verdict on a sufferer.

How the chapter makes its case. Eliphaz asks leave to speak, praises Job for having strengthened others, and then turns: now trouble has come to you, and you are dismayed; is not your fear of God your confidence (vv. 1–6)? He states the friends’ case: “who that was innocent ever perished?” Those who sow trouble reap it, and even the mighty lion perishes when God is against him (vv. 7–11). Then he tells of a spirit that glided past him in the night with a message: no mortal is right before God, and if even angels are charged with error, how much more men in houses of clay, crushed like the moth (vv. 12–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes. Eliphaz’s question, “Can mortal man be in the right before God?” (v. 17), is the question of the whole Bible, and he leaves it hanging over Job like a sword. The gospel answers it: God put forward Christ “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And Eliphaz’s rule fails at the cross, where the one truly innocent man did perish, and a Roman officer said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (Luke 23:47). Because he was raised, those who live in houses of clay have “a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

For us. Be slow to explain other people’s suffering, for sound doctrine misapplied can crush a broken man. Test every claimed word from God, however eerie or impressive, by Scripture. And bring the question no one can answer for himself to the cross, where God has answered it.
4.theology:
The friends' case, stated here for the first time, is that suffering proves sin, and God will say at the end that they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). They take a true rule (the wicked reap what they sow, Gal 6:7) and read it backwards: this man is reaping trouble, so he must have sown sin. Jesus himself refused that reasoning (Luke 13:2-5; John 9:2-3). The innocent do perish, and the cross is the proof.

The vision's question, Can mortal man be in the right before God?, is the right one, but it is asked here to crush. The gospel is its answer.
4.examples:
Watch how Eliphaz works. He quotes Job's good works back to him as a rebuke, and he turns Job's fear of God and integrity into a guarantee that nothing bad could happen. His picture of how the wicked die happens to be the way Job's children died.

Then he claims a night vision with no face and no thus says the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Strengthened the Weak Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz begins as a friend, but his gentle opening already carries the charge he will press. He asks leave to speak, apologetically, yet cannot keep silent (vv. 1–2). He pays Job a real tribute: he has taught many, strengthened weak hands, steadied stumbling feet and made feeble knees firm (vv. 3–4). Then the tribute turns. Now that trouble has come to Job himself, he is impatient and dismayed (v. 5). Surely, Eliphaz says, his fear of God and his integrity should be his confidence and his hope (v. 6). It sounds like encouragement, but it assumes that real piety is a guarantee against real loss, and God never promised that.
verseByVerse.theology: The first friend to speak is the kindest, and his courtesy is real. But a gentle voice can carry a false message.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the debate begins, the reader is told how to hear it: the friends will say many true things, but God will say they did not speak rightly of him.

The debate begins. It will run for twenty-four chapters, and before a word of it is read we should know how it ends. The LORD will say to this man by name: “My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (42:7). Everything Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar say must be read in that light. They will say many true things about God. They will be wrong about Job, and wrong about God’s ways with him.

Who can keep from speaking? Eliphaz speaks first, probably as the eldest, and he is the most courteous, asking permission almost apologetically. But “who can keep from speaking?” The friends’ seven days of silence were their best hour, as this speech is about to show.

Where Christians differ: how should the friends’ speeches be used? Many quote them as straightforward teaching, since they stand in Scripture and often sound orthodox. This commentary’s view: the book records truly what they said, but God says they did not speak rightly of him (42:7), so their speeches must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer. A single line may be true in itself, as when Paul quotes 5:13 (1 Corinthians 3:19), but their argument as a whole God rejects.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees. But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz’s real tribute turns into a rebuke: you counselled others, so take your own advice.

You have strengthened the weak hands. The tribute is real. Job had been the man others went to in trouble, and Eliphaz uses words Isaiah would later use of God’s comfort to his people: “Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees” (Isaiah 35:3). Hebrews takes up the same picture to rally tired Christians (Hebrews 12:12).

But now it has come to you. Then the tribute turns. You gave advice to others; now take it yourself. It is easier to counsel suffering than to bear it, and that much is true. But Eliphaz has not measured what has come to Job: the loss of ten children and of his health is far beyond the troubles Job used to talk people through. The comforter who says “you of all people should cope with this” has not yet understood the size of the grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz turns Job’s piety into a guarantee: if you truly fear God, you cannot come to real harm.

Is not your fear of God your confidence? These are the words of the narrator in 1:1 and of God in 2:3: Job “feared God”, and his “integrity” held. Eliphaz does not deny Job’s piety. He assumes it, and turns it into a guarantee.

What God never promised. There is truth in it: those who fear God are safe in him for ever. But Eliphaz means safe from loss and grief in this life, and God never promised that. Job’s integrity was being tested. It was never an insurance policy against loss.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the friends’ whole case, and every later speech only repeats it: the innocent do not perish, so a man who is perishing cannot be innocent. Eliphaz appeals to Job’s memory and his own experience (vv. 7–8): those who plough iniquity and sow trouble reap the same, and they perish at the breath of God’s anger (v. 9). He illustrates it with the lion, the mightiest of beasts, whose teeth are broken, who starves for lack of prey, and whose cubs are scattered (vv. 10–11). He does not say “you”; he does not need to. Scripture, and above all the cross, shows that the rule is false.
verseByVerse.theology: A true rule about the end of the wicked is turned here into a law about every sufferer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off? As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends’ whole case is that the innocent never perish, and Scripture, above all at the cross, shows it to be false.

Who that was innocent ever perished? The rest of the friends’ speeches only repeat this: the innocent do not perish; therefore, if you are perishing, you are not innocent.

Reading it backwards. Paul says something that sounds the same: “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). But Paul warns the one doing the sowing. Eliphaz reads it backwards, from the harvest to the seed: he sees trouble and concludes there was sin. “Trouble” is Job’s own word from 3:10, and the “blast” of God’s anger is the Hebrew word for the “wind” that brought the house down on Job’s children (1:19). Whether he means it or not, Eliphaz has described how Job’s children died.

The innocent do perish. Scripture answers his question on almost every page. Abel was innocent and was killed in a field. Zechariah the priest was stoned “in the court of the house of the LORD” for speaking God’s word (2 Chronicles 24:21). And a Roman officer stood at the foot of a cross and said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (Luke 23:47). Where were the upright cut off? At Golgotha. Jesus refused Eliphaz’s reasoning in so many words. Of the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by a tower: “do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others … ? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:2–5). Of a man born blind: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:3).
verseByVerse.note: The friends never move off this ground; every later speech builds on it.

verseByVerse.quote: The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken. The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The broken old lion pictures, without naming him, what Eliphaz thinks has happened to Job.

The roar of the lion. The poet uses five different Hebrew words for lion in two verses, a showpiece of his art. The most powerful beast grows old, its teeth break, it starves, and its cubs are scattered: the mighty cannot keep their strength or their children when God is against them. Eliphaz does not say “you”; he does not need to. The strong man of the east has lost his wealth, and his children are gone, and insinuation is harder to answer than accusation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz claims more than experience now: a revelation in the night, told so as to make the skin crawl. A word comes to him stealthily, amid dreams, with dread and trembling; a spirit glides past his face, a form without a face, and a voice speaks out of silence (vv. 12–16). Its message is true as far as it goes: no mortal can be right or pure before his Maker (v. 17). If God does not trust even his servants the angels, how much less frail humans in houses of clay, crushed like a moth and gone between morning and evening, unnoticed and without wisdom (vv. 18–21). Eliphaz uses a true question to condemn Job; the gospel answers it.
verseByVerse.theology: The book gives us no reason to trust where this voice came from, and the voice asks a true question only to leave a man without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it. Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake. A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz claims a revelation, but it comes by stealth and without “thus says the LORD”, and it must be tested.

A word was brought to me stealthily. Eliphaz now claims something more than experience: a revelation. It is written to make the reader’s skin crawl, and it does. But look at what is missing. There is no “thus says the LORD”. The spirit has no face. It comes by stealth. Compare the end of the book, when “the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (38:1): openly, in person, to the man himself. God does not need to creep up on anyone.

Was Eliphaz’s vision from God? The book does not say; readers have suggested a true word from God, a deceiving spirit, or a dream dressed up as revelation. What the spirit says in verse 17 is true as far as it goes: no one is righteous before God. But Eliphaz uses it to accuse Job, and God says the friends did not speak of him what is right (42:7). No vision outside Scripture binds anyone, and every claim to one must be tested by the word of God (1 John 4:1). A believer who is told “God showed me in the night what your suffering means” is right to ask what Scripture says.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice asks the true question of the whole Bible, but Eliphaz uses it to condemn, and only the gospel answers it.

Can mortal man be in the right before God? The question is true: no one can stand before God on his own merits. Job will ask it himself (9:2), and Bildad again (25:4). It is the question the whole Bible asks.

Why the friends are dangerous. That is what makes the friends dangerous: they say true things and use them to reach a false conclusion. Because no one is pure before God, Eliphaz reasons, Job’s suffering must be the fruit of Job’s sin. But the question was never meant to condemn one man above others; it is the question the gospel answers. God put forward Christ “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Eliphaz leaves the question hanging over Job like a sword. The cross answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error; how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth. Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it. Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frail humans in bodies of clay are crushed and gone unnoticed, says Eliphaz; Paul uses the same pictures and finds in Christ a house that cannot fall.

Houses of clay. If even angels fall short before God, what hope is there for men of clay? It is a picture of how frail we are: bodies of mud, founded on dust, as easily crushed as a moth. “Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it.” The body is a tent: pull up the cord and it collapses.

Jars of clay. Paul uses the same pictures, and the difference is the gospel. “We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God” (2 Corinthians 4:7). “If the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). Eliphaz’s vision ends with men dying “without wisdom”, unnoticed. Paul’s ends with a house in heaven. Same clay, same tent; the difference is Christ, raised from the dust.

Do the angels sin? Some did, and fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), but Scripture calls the rest “holy angels” and “elect angels” (Mark 8:38; 1 Timothy 5:21). Eliphaz’s point is that no creature is righteous in itself before God; he stretches it to make every creature suspect, in order to condemn Job.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “error” (v. 18) occurs only here, and its sense is guessed from the context. “Crushed like the moth” is literally “before the moth”: as easily as a moth, or sooner than one. And “tent-cord” (v. 21) can also mean what is left over or what excels (hence the older “their excellency”). Every reading makes the same point: human life is frail and quickly gone.

keyVerse.quote: Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?
keyVerse.note: This is the true question at the heart of Eliphaz’s speech, and it is the question of the whole Bible. Eliphaz uses it to condemn Job, leaving it hanging over him like a sword. The gospel answers it, for God put forward Christ “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

4.reflection:
Eliphaz begins kindly (vv. 2–4), yet God later says he did not speak rightly (42:7). How can kind words and true statements still do harm to a suffering person? What would Eliphaz have needed to know in order to comfort Job well?

“Who that was innocent ever perished?” (v. 7). Where do you see this way of reading suffering backwards, in the church, in others or in yourself? How do Luke 13:1–5, John 9:3 and the cross answer it?

Eliphaz claims a mysterious night vision to support his case (vv. 12–16). How should Christians respond when someone says God has shown them the meaning of another person’s suffering?

Eliphaz’s question, “Can mortal man be in the right before God?” (v. 17), is left hanging over Job like a sword. How does the gospel answer it (Romans 3:26), and how does that answer change the way we face our own frailty (2 Corinthians 4:7; 5:1)?

5.title: Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?<sup>2</sup>Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple.<sup>3</sup>I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.<sup>4</sup>His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them.<sup>5</sup>The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.<sup>6</sup>For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground,<sup>7</sup>but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.<sup>8</sup>"As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause,<sup>9</sup>who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number:<sup>10</sup>he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields;<sup>11</sup>he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.<sup>12</sup>He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success.<sup>13</sup>He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end.<sup>14</sup>They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night.<sup>15</sup>But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty.<sup>16</sup>So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.<sup>17</sup>"Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty.<sup>18</sup>For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.<sup>19</sup>He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you.<sup>20</sup>In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.<sup>21</sup>You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes.<sup>22</sup>At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth.<sup>23</sup>For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.<sup>24</sup>You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing.<sup>25</sup>You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth.<sup>26</sup>You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.<sup>27</sup>Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
5.overview:
Where we are. Eliphaz, the first and gentlest of Job’s three friends, is still speaking. This chapter completes the speech he began in chapter 4, the first answer anyone gives to Job’s cry of chapter 3. He has already asked who that was innocent ever perished (4:7), and claimed a night vision that no mortal can be right before God (4:17).

The message. Eliphaz’s message is simple: trouble always has its root in the sufferer, so turn to God, accept his discipline, and he will restore everything. Nearly every sentence is true and beautifully said, yet God will judge the speech as a whole wrong (42:7), because it treats Job’s suffering as a verdict on Job. Through it God shows us how true doctrine, wrongly applied, becomes a weapon against a sufferer, and that he is freer and kinder than any system that ties his blessings to our merit.

Why it was said. Job’s world, like ours, assumed that God settles accounts in this life: the good prosper and the wicked fall (see the introduction). Eliphaz speaks for that tidy wisdom, “this we have searched out” (v. 27), and the book tests it against a man the reader knows to be blameless (1:8; 2:3).

How the chapter makes its case. First a warning (vv. 1–7): no one in heaven will take Job’s side; the fool who rages is destroyed with his house and children; and trouble does not sprout from the ground but from man. Then counsel (vv. 8–16): Eliphaz would commit his cause to God, who does unsearchable wonders, lifts the lowly, catches the wise in their own craftiness and gives the poor hope. Then a promise (vv. 17–27): blessed is the one God reproves; accept his discipline, and he will keep you from every harm, give you many children and bring you to the grave like a ripe sheaf.

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need the chapter exposes. Eliphaz mocks the thought that anyone in heaven would answer for Job (v. 1), and the rest of the book is Job’s search for that someone. The New Testament names him: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). And the chapter’s truest lines find their home in him: the God who lifts the lowly raised his humbled Son, and at the cross caught the wise of this world in their own craftiness (1 Corinthians 1:20; 3:19).

For us. Hold fast to what Eliphaz says that is true: God disciplines those he loves, and he wounds in order to heal. But never hand that truth to a sufferer as a diagnosis. In Christ the punishment for our sins has been borne, so our trials are a Father’s training, not a judge’s sentence, and when we sit with someone in pain we should be slow to say, “this we have searched out”.
5.theology:
Eliphaz speaks true things falsely. God does catch the wise in their craftiness (1 Cor 3:19), does discipline those he loves (Prov 3:11-12; Heb 12:5-6), and does wound and heal (Deut 32:39). But Eliphaz applies these truths to a man God has declared innocent, and in the end the wise man caught in his own wisdom is Eliphaz himself.

A comforter must hold both what God has revealed and the limits of what he himself knows. God's works are unsearchable (v. 9), yet Eliphaz claims to have searched out Job's case (v. 27).
5.examples: Small details carry the argument. The fool's children are crushed, and so were Job's. The first Almighty in the book is on Eliphaz's lips, and so is the promise no evil shall touch you, made to a man evil has touched twice. Paul quotes one of his lines as Scripture, but turns it on the man who thinks himself wise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Man Is Born to Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s first point is that Job’s suffering has a cause, and the cause lies in Job. He opens with a taunt: no one in heaven will answer Job’s cry, not even the angels (v. 1). Then he tells a story from his own experience. He has seen a fool take root and flourish, and then seen his home cursed, his children crushed and his harvest carried off, because the fool’s own vexation destroyed him (vv. 2–5). He never says “you are the fool”, but every detail fits Job’s losses. He closes with a proverb: trouble does not grow out of the ground like a weed; man is born to it, and its root is in man (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture Eliphaz chooses of the fool's end is a picture of what has happened to Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz mocks the thought that anyone in heaven would take Job’s side; Job will spend the rest of the book looking for that someone.

To which of the holy ones will you turn? The “holy ones” are heavenly beings, the angels. If God trusts not even his angels (4:18), who in heaven would stand up for Job?

Is there anyone who will answer you? It is a cruel question, and Job will keep reaching for an answer: an arbiter between himself and God (9:33), “my witness is in heaven” (16:19), and at last “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25). Eliphaz says there is no one. The Christian knows the name of the one there is: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple. I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling. His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them. The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz tells of a fool destroyed with his home and children, and leaves Job to see himself in the story.

Vexation kills the fool. “Vexation” is exactly what Job poured out in chapter 3, and Eliphaz warns that fools die of it. Job will throw the word back: “Oh that my vexation were weighed” (6:2).

I have seen the fool taking root. Eliphaz has watched a fool prosper and then fall: his home cursed (by Eliphaz himself, where Job in chapter 1 pronounced a blessing), his harvest plundered, his children “crushed in the gate”, the town’s court, with no one to defend them. It is told as a general lesson, but Job’s children were crushed when a house fell on them, and his flocks were carried off by raiders. Eliphaz need not say “you are the fool”. The friends will work this way throughout: they describe the wicked and leave Job to recognise himself.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is obscure. “He takes it even out of thorns” may mean the hungry snatch the grain even from behind its thorn hedge. The word for “the thirsty” can also mean “a snare” (as in 18:9). The sense is clear either way: all the fool gathered is plundered.

verseByVerse.quote: For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground, but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trouble has a root, says Eliphaz, and the root is in man: Job’s trouble must have come from Job.

Man is born to trouble. The last line is often quoted as a sad truth about life, and it is true. But look at the line before. Trouble does not grow out of the ground like a weed; it has a root, and the root is in man. Eliphaz means: your trouble came from somewhere, and it came from you. “Trouble” is Job’s own word again, from 3:10.

Sin and suffering. Scripture agrees that suffering entered the world through sin (Romans 5:12). It refuses to say that each sufferer’s pain can be traced to his own sin. That is the step Eliphaz takes, and God will condemn it (42:7). The plainest proof is Jesus: no root of sin was in him, yet he was “a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3), and his trouble came from ours.

Uncertain wording. “Sparks” is literally “sons of Resheph”, a word for flame and also the name of a Canaanite plague god; some take it as soaring birds. “Sparks” is most likely, and the point stands either way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s counsel is good in itself: take your cause to God, who rules everything and loves to rescue the lowly. “As for me, I would seek God,” he says (v. 8). Then he praises the God he would seek in a short hymn. His works are beyond searching out and beyond counting; he sends rain on the fields and lifts the humble and the mourning (vv. 9–11); he turns the plans of the crafty against them, so that they grope at noon (vv. 12–14); and he saves the needy, so that the poor have hope (vv. 15–16). All of it is true, and Paul quotes a line of it. The irony is that Job will do what Eliphaz recommends, and the friends never will.
verseByVerse.theology: A true and beautiful hymn. Yet Job, not Eliphaz, is the one who will actually take his cause to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause, who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number: he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields; he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz’s advice is good: take your cause to the God who lifts the lowly. But Job, not Eliphaz, is the one who will follow it.

I would seek God. Good advice, and here is the irony of the whole debate: Job is the one who takes it. Again and again he will turn from the friends to speak to God directly, pleading, protesting, asking for a hearing. The friends never once speak to God; they only speak about him. When the LORD judges between them, that difference will matter.

He gives rain on the earth. Jesus drew a lesson from the rain that cuts straight across Eliphaz’s system: God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Rain is not a wage paid to the good; it falls on every field, out of kindness. If God’s gifts are not handed out strictly by merit, neither are the losses he sends. Eliphaz has quoted the evidence against his own case.

He sets on high those who are lowly. Mary sang it when Christ came: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). Its greatest proof is Christ himself, humbled to the cross and “highly exalted” (Philippians 2:9). God will lift this mourner too, and Eliphaz will be standing by with a sacrifice in his hands when he does (42:8).

verseByVerse.quote: He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success. He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end. They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night. But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God overturns the schemes of the clever and rescues the needy: true words, which Paul quotes, and which in the end catch Eliphaz himself.

He catches the wise in their own craftiness. Paul quotes this line: “For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness’” (1 Corinthians 3:19). It is one of only two places where the New Testament clearly quotes Job, and it quotes Eliphaz. The book records his words truly, and this sentence is true; his error was aiming it at Job. Paul aims it rightly, at the man who “thinks that he is wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18), and by the end of Job the wise man caught in his own wisdom is Eliphaz, to whom God says, “My anger burns against you” (42:7).

Grope at noonday. Groping at noonday is Deuteronomy’s curse on the disobedient (Deuteronomy 28:29), from the same chapter as the sores of 2:7. Job is sitting in the dark at noon. The friends keep reaching for the covenant’s curses to describe the wicked, and each time they fit the man in front of them.

The sword of their mouth. God rescues the needy from “the sword of their mouth”. Before long, the sword aimed at this needy man will be the friends’ own words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s promise is that if Job accepts God’s discipline, God will restore everything he has lost. He begins with a beatitude: blessed is the one God reproves, for the hand that wounds also heals (vv. 17–18). Then he paints a life of perfect safety: rescue from every trouble, from famine and sword, protection from slander, peace with the wild beasts and the stony fields (vv. 19–23), a safe home, many children, and a death like a ripe sheaf brought in at harvest (vv. 24–26). He ends with the confidence of a man who has it all worked out: “this we have searched out; it is true” (v. 27). The blessings are real, and God will give many of them; it is the reasoning that God will reject.
verseByVerse.theology: Much of it will come true for Job. None of it will come true for the reason Eliphaz gives.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty. For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does discipline those he loves and heal the wounds he gives, but Eliphaz hands this comfort to Job as a diagnosis, and for Job it is false.

Blessed is the one whom God reproves. This is the first time the book calls God “the Almighty” (Shaddai), a name it will use thirty-one times. And the sentence is true: “the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12), and Hebrews tells Christians under pressure that “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). A believer in trouble may rightly ask whether God is showing him something to put right, and he asks as a son already loved, with the Spirit to help him change. For one in Christ, discipline is a Father’s training for his good, never the punishment of sins that Christ has already borne (Romans 8:1; Hebrews 12:10).

Comfort, not diagnosis. Hebrews gives this truth to sons as comfort: your pain is no sign that you are unloved. Eliphaz gives it to Job as a diagnosis, though God has already said his suffering was “without reason” (2:3).

He wounds, but he binds up. The wounding hand is the healing hand: Moses sang it (Deuteronomy 32:39) and Hosea preached it (Hosea 6:1), and it will prove true of Job, though not by the false confession Eliphaz prescribes.

verseByVerse.quote: He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz promises safety from every harm, and one harm he names is the one he is inflicting.

He will deliver you from six troubles. Six troubles, then seven, means every trouble, however many. “Touch” is Satan’s word: “touch all that he has” (1:11), “touch his bone and his flesh” (2:5). Evil has touched Job twice, and he will cry, “Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me!” (19:21).

Perfect safety. No famine, no sword, no stones to spoil the field, no wild beast: the peace God promised Israel for obedience (Leviticus 26:6). One line stands out: Job will be hidden from “the lash of the tongue”. He is being lashed by one now.

What such promises guarantee. Such promises (Psalm 91 makes them too) are no contract that harm will never reach the faithful. Satan quoted Psalm 91 to tempt Jesus (Matthew 4:6), and the one man who fully deserved its protection was handed over to death. God guarantees something deeper: nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).

Uncertain wording. “In league with the stones of the field” probably means the stones will no longer spoil his ground, as if by treaty; some suggest a very similar Hebrew word for wild creatures of the field. Either way, all creation will be at peace with him.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz holds out a safe home, many children and a ripe old age, every one something Job has lost; and in the end God will give them freely.

Your offspring shall be many. Imagine hearing this beside ten new graves. Eliphaz means it kindly, as the reward for confession. But Job has nothing true to confess, and every line names something he has just lost.

Like a sheaf gathered up in its season. The last picture is the loveliest. A good death is a harvest, the sheaf brought to the threshing floor when it is ripe and not before. Job’s children were cut down green.

The strangest thing. And it comes true. At the end Job will have seven sons and three daughters again, and “Job died, an old man, and full of days” (42:17). Eliphaz promised the right blessings for the wrong reason. They came not as the wage for a false confession but as the free gift of a God who had vindicated Job. New children did not replace the ten he buried, and no reader who has lost a child should hear it so. God’s kindness is larger than the friends’ theology, and it does not run on their terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz claims to have searched out what he has just called unsearchable; no comforter should speak so confidently about another’s suffering.

This we have searched out. “We”: Eliphaz speaks for the three of them and for the whole tradition; the matter is settled. But in verse 9 he said God does things “unsearchable”, and in Hebrew it is the same word. God’s ways cannot be searched out, says Eliphaz; and we have searched this out, says Eliphaz. He has not noticed the contradiction.

The line Job takes up. Job will repeat the line about God’s unsearchable works almost word for word (9:10), and Paul will cry, “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). That is the right response to the God of Job. Whoever sits with a sufferer should be slow to say, “this we have searched out”. There is a proper confidence about what God has said, and a proper humility about what he has not. The friends had the first without the second.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty.
keyVerse.note: This is Eliphaz’s truest sentence and his worst mistake in one. Proverbs and Hebrews give the same truth to God’s children as comfort (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11). Eliphaz gives it to Job as a diagnosis, and the chapter teaches us the difference between a truth and its right use.

5.reflection:
Eliphaz says that trouble does not “sprout from the ground” but has its root in man (vv. 6–7). What is true in this, and where does he go wrong? Why are people, Christians included, so quick to look for a sufferer’s own fault?

Paul quotes verse 13 as Scripture, yet God says Eliphaz did not speak rightly (42:7). How can a true sentence become a false word to a particular person? Can you think of a time when you heard, or said, something true at the wrong moment?

“Blessed is the one whom God reproves” (v. 17). How does knowing that Christ has borne the punishment for our sins change the way a believer reads hard times? How would you speak of God’s discipline to a friend who is suffering without making it a diagnosis?

Eliphaz is sure: “this we have searched out” (v. 27). What should we be confident about when we sit with someone in pain, and what should we be humble about?

6.title: Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!<sup>3</sup>For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.<sup>4</sup>For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.<sup>5</sup>Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder?<sup>6</sup>Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow?<sup>7</sup>My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.<sup>8</sup>"Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope,<sup>9</sup>that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!<sup>10</sup>This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.<sup>11</sup>What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?<sup>12</sup>Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze?<sup>13</sup>Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?<sup>14</sup>"He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.<sup>15</sup>My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away,<sup>16</sup>which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself.<sup>17</sup>When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place.<sup>18</sup>The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish.<sup>19</sup>The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope.<sup>20</sup>They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed.<sup>21</sup>For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.<sup>22</sup>Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'?<sup>23</sup>Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?<sup>24</sup>"Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray.<sup>25</sup>How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove?<sup>26</sup>Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind?<sup>27</sup>You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.<sup>28</sup>"But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face.<sup>29</sup>Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake.<sup>30</sup>Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
6.overview:
Where we are. Eliphaz has finished the first speech of the debate (chapters 4–5): trouble has its root in the sufferer, so accept God’s discipline and he will restore you. Now Job answers for the first time. His reply runs through chapter 7; in this chapter he speaks to his friends, and in the next he turns to God.

The message. Job pleads to be heard honestly: weigh my pain before you judge my words, and stay loyal to me while I am going under. God lets a believer at the end of his strength say how bad it is, even that he longs to die, without counting it as unbelief. And he exposes comforters who defend their theology at the expense of their friend, for the fear of God shows itself in loyal love (v. 14).

Why it was said. The friends’ tidy belief that God always repays in this life (see the introduction) had no room for an innocent sufferer, so they heard Job’s cry of chapter 3 as rebellion. Job answers for every sufferer who has been lectured instead of loved, and the reader knows he is right (2:3).

How the chapter makes its case. Weigh the calamity (vv. 1–7): his words were rash because his grief is heavier than the sand; God’s arrows are in him; a donkey does not bray without cause, and Eliphaz’s advice has no salt in it. A request to die (vv. 8–13): his one comfort would be that he has not denied the words of the Holy One, and he has no strength left to wait. The failed friends (vv. 14–23): they have withheld loyal love, like desert streams that vanish in summer, though he asked them for nothing. A plea (vv. 24–30): teach me and I will be silent; look at me; my vindication is at stake.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the pattern it sets. Job needs a friend whose loyalty does not dry up when trouble comes, and he does not find one among men. Christ is that friend. When he was arrested, “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50), yet he laid down his life for them and called them his friends (John 15:13–15). And Job’s wish that God would “crush” him (v. 9) meets its strange answer in the Servant of whom Isaiah says, “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10): the innocent one crushed so that the guilty need not be.

For us. When someone speaks wildly out of pain, weigh the pain before the words. Be the stream that still runs in summer: stay, listen, and look at the person rather than at a theory. And if you are the one at the end of your strength, you may tell God exactly how it is; the strength to wait is not in you, but in the one who stayed loyal to you at the cross.
6.theology:
Loyal love to a suffering friend belongs to the fear of God (v. 14), and it is the friends, not Job, who are failing it. Christ is the spring that does not fail (John 4:14).

Job is right that God's hand is in his trouble and wrong about its intent. His strength is gone, but he has not denied God's word, and God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).
6.examples: Notice the order Job asks for: weigh the pain before you judge the words. He admits his words were rash, and the only time he calls God the Holy One is while asking to die. His picture of his friends is a desert wadi, full in winter and dry in summer, and all he had asked of them was their loyal company.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s first point is that his words must be weighed against his pain. If his calamity were put on the scales it would outweigh the sand of the sea, and that is why his words have been rash (vv. 1–3). And the cause of the pain is God himself: the arrows of the Almighty are in him, and their poison is in his spirit (v. 4). He does not cry out for nothing, any more than a donkey brays when it has grass (v. 5). The counsel he has just been served is like food without salt, and he cannot swallow it (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks that his pain be weighed before his words are judged. It is a fair request, and the friends never grant it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances! For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks his friends to weigh his pain before they judge his words: they were rash because his grief is so heavy.

Oh that my vexation were weighed. Eliphaz warned that “vexation kills the fool” (5:2). Job takes the word and asks them to put his trouble on the scales before they judge what he said; it would outweigh the sand of every shore. Later he will ask God for the same thing: “Let me be weighed in a just balance” (31:6).

My words have been rash. And he admits it. He does not claim that chapter 3 was measured speech: it was wild because the pain is so great. That is honesty, not defiance, as anyone who has sat with the bereaved knows. The first thing to do with rash words from a crushed person is to weigh the crushing, not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job knows that his suffering comes from God’s hand, and he feels it as the poisoned arrows of an enemy.

The arrows of the Almighty. Job says plainly who is behind it: not raiders or bad luck but “the Almighty”, an archer with poisoned arrows, and Job is the target. Lamentations says the same: “he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow” (Lamentations 3:12).

What Job gets right and wrong. Job is right that God’s hand is in it; the LORD said so in heaven (2:3). He is wrong about what the hand intends. He thinks he is God’s enemy; the reader knows he is God’s delight. Many believers have felt exactly this, and the book lets them say it, while showing what Job could not see: the arrows are not an enemy’s verdict. God’s arrows truly fell on one man, his Son, bearing our sin at the cross, and so no trial a believer suffers is God’s anger.

verseByVerse.quote: Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder? Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow? My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s cries have a cause, as a donkey’s braying does, and the advice he has been given is as tasteless as food without salt.

Why Job cries out. Animals do not complain when they are fed: when a donkey brays, something is wrong. Job’s cries have a cause, and it is not weakness of character.

Food without salt. The mallow’s juice was slimy and flavourless. Job may mean the food of suffering he is forced to eat every day, or the advice he has just been served, which has no salt in it. Either way he cannot swallow it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew words behind “the juice of the mallow” are rare and uncertain: perhaps the slimy juice of a plant such as mallow or purslane; older translations read “the white of an egg”. Either way it is tasteless and repellent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — That It Would Please God to Crush Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s one request is that God would end his life, and his one comfort is that he has not denied God’s word. He asks God to crush him and cut him off (vv. 8–9). If he died now, he would even rejoice in the pain, for he has not denied “the words of the Holy One” (v. 10). Eliphaz told him to wait in hope, but what strength has he left? He is not made of stone or bronze, and every resource has been driven from him (vv. 11–13). This is faith at the very end of its strength, not faith abandoned.
verseByVerse.theology: Even wishing to die, Job holds on to the one thing Satan tried to take: he has not denied God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off! This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks God to end his life, yet his one comfort is that he has not denied God’s word: this is faith at the end of its strength, not faith lost.

Let loose his hand and cut me off. He asks God to finish it. “Cut me off” is the picture King Hezekiah used when sick to death: “like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom” (Isaiah 38:12). Job does not reach for the knife himself. He asks God, because his life is God’s to end.

I have not denied the words of the Holy One. Here is the one thing he still has: if he died now, he would die without having denied God, which was exactly what Satan wanted (1:11; 2:5). It is the only time in the book that he calls God “the Holy One”. Even while asking to die, he names God by his holiness and clings to his word. That is not the speech of a man who has lost his faith.

That it would please God to crush me. Job was not crushed. Another was: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10), the innocent Servant, for us.

If you have prayed like this. God did not condemn Job for longing to die, but life is his to give and take (see the note on 3:20–22). If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today: a pastor, a doctor, a friend or a crisis line. Then seek a biblical counsellor, who will want a doctor to check for bodily causes; medicine is no failure of faith.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “exult” occurs only here in the Old Testament. It probably means to leap, here for joy; some take it as shrinking back. Either way, death would come as relief, with his loyalty intact.

verseByVerse.quote: What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has no strength left to wait patiently, and he is right that the strength is not in him: it must come from God.

Patient with what? Eliphaz told him to be patient. Job asks, with what? He is not made of stone or bronze, and there is nothing left in him to hold on with. He is right that the strength is not in him, and Scripture never says it should be. “They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31): the strength comes from the one waited for. Paul learned it in his own weakness: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Job has reached the end of himself. That is not the end of the road.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s charge is that his friends have failed in loyal love, and so failed in the fear of God. A friend in despair is owed kindness (v. 14). His brothers have proved like desert streams, swollen with melting snow in winter and dry in summer, so that the caravans of Tema and Sheba turn aside for water and find only disappointment (vv. 15–20). The friends have seen his calamity and are afraid (v. 21). Yet he had asked them for nothing costly: no gift, no bribe, no rescue from his enemies (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends are afraid of what Job's innocence would mean for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To withhold loyal love from a suffering friend is to abandon the fear of God.

He who withholds kindness from a friend. “Kindness” is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness that holds when holding is costly. Eliphaz told Job that his fear of God should be his confidence (4:6). Job turns it round: the man who withholds loyal love from a suffering friend is the one who has abandoned the fear of the Almighty. The friends think they are defending God, but in failing their friend they are failing him.

A test for every church. The measure of our fear of God is not how firmly we hold our doctrine while a brother suffers, but whether we stay with him. We can, because Christ stayed with us when we had nothing to give, and his Spirit gives us the love that holds on (Galatians 5:22).

Uncertain wording. The ESV’s note says one Hebrew word here is uncertain, and several translations take the verse to mean that a despairing man should have kindness from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty. Then Job says something more searching still: if his faith did falter, that is exactly when a friend’s loyalty is owed. Either way, the one going under needs love, not a verdict, most of all when his grip on God is weakest.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away, which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself. When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place. The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish. The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope. They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed. For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s friends have proved like desert streams that vanish in the heat, failing him when he needed them most, because his suffering frightens them.

Treacherous as a torrent-bed. A desert wadi roars with water in winter, when no one needs it, and is bone dry in summer, when everyone does. Traders of Tema and Sheba (the raiders who took his oxen came from Sheba, 1:15) leave their route for the stream they remember, and find stones. So are his friends: full when he prospered, dry now.

You see my calamity and are afraid. Here is the heart of it. If a man like Job can lose everything without deserving it, so can they. Their belief that the good are kept safe is their shelter, and Job’s innocence would blow the roof off, so they need him to be guilty. That is still why people blame the sufferer: it keeps them safe. In Hebrew “see” and “be afraid” sound almost the same, and a friend afraid of what your suffering means for him cannot help you with it. The Christian can afford to look, because his safety was never in having deserved his blessings. It is in Christ, and nothing that happens to a brother can take it away.

A brook that does not fail. Jeremiah once said the same thing to God himself: “Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?” (Jeremiah 15:18). God is not. Jesus offered a woman at a well “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), a spring that does not dry up in the heat.

Friends for a season. Aristotle, in his Ethics, sorted friendships into those based on usefulness, those based on pleasure, and the rarer friendship of good people who love each other for who they are; the first two, he observed, dissolve when the use or pleasure runs out. The torrent-bed is a picture of them, and modern life multiplies them: colleagues who vanish when you change jobs, contacts who stop answering after the diagnosis, hundreds of friends online and no one to sit on the ash heap. Proverbs saw it long ago: “A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). And most of us have been a dry wadi to somebody, keeping our distance from a friend’s divorce or depression because it was awkward, or because, like Job’s friends, it frightened us. The gospel does not begin by telling us to be better friends. It shows us a Friend whose loyalty never depended on what we could offer. When he was arrested, “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50); he went on to the cross for them anyway, and called them his friends (John 15:13–15). Those who have been loved like that can stay when it would be easier to leave.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'? Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job had asked his friends for nothing costly, no money, no ransom, no rescue, only their loyalty.

He asked for nothing. No gift, no bribe, no rescue from an enemy: nothing but their loyal company, which would have cost them nothing.

Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless. The last word is “redeem”. Job is not asking the friends to redeem him. He will look much higher, with a different Hebrew word, used of a near relative who rescues his kin, and find it: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — Teach Me, and I Will Be Silent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job ends by asking to be taught and to be looked at. If they can show him where he has gone astray, he will be silent (v. 24). But their reproof proves nothing, for they are correcting the words of a despairing man as if they were a lecture on doctrine (vv. 25–26), and people who treat a friend like this would gamble over orphans (v. 27). So he begs them to look him in the face and turn back before an injustice is done, because his vindication is at stake; he can still taste the difference between truth and falsehood (vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is willing to be corrected, if anyone will show him where he went wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray. How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove? Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind? You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job is willing to be shown his fault but not to have it presumed, and he asks his friends to hear a despairing man’s words as grief, not as doctrine.

Teach me, and I will be silent. Job is teachable: show me where I went wrong and I will stop talking. It is the prayer of Psalm 139 turned to his friends: “see if there be any grievous way in me” (Psalm 139:24). He does not claim to be sinless. He asks to be shown his fault, not to have it presumed.

How forceful are upright words! Honest words have force. Theirs prove nothing: they correct Job’s words as if they were a lecture on doctrine, when they were the cry of a man in despair, mere “wind”, breath forced out by pain. Bildad will throw the word back: “the words of your mouth be a great wind” (8:2). The lesson stands for every counsellor: hear grief as grief before you correct it as theology.

Cast lots over the fatherless. The harshest line in the chapter: people who can treat a suffering friend as a case to be argued would gamble over orphans. Job had been the man who “delivered … the fatherless who had none to help him” (29:12), and he will stake his life on it (31:17, 21). Before the debate is over, Eliphaz will accuse him of exactly this (22:9): the charge that fits the accusers will be laid on the accused.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face. Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake. Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job begs his friends to look him in the face and turn from injustice, because his standing as an innocent man is at stake.

Be pleased to look at me. He asks them to look at him; they have been looking at a theory. “To your face” is Satan’s phrase (1:11): Job will not curse God to his face, and he will not lie to his friends’ faces either. “My vindication” is his standing as an innocent man. That, not his health, is what he fights for from here on.

A palate that discerns. The palate that knew the mallow’s juice was tasteless (v. 6) can taste the difference between a lie and the truth. Job knows his own heart better than they do, and the reader knows he is right, because God has said so (2:3).

Vindicated. The innocent man condemned by men and vindicated by God is a pattern the gospel completes: Christ was condemned and then “vindicated by the Spirit” (1 Timothy 3:16) in his resurrection, and all who are in him share it.

keyVerse.quote: He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
keyVerse.note: Here Job turns the friends’ piety inside out. They think the fear of God means defending a doctrine; Job says it shows itself in loyal love (chesed) to a friend in trouble. It is the test every comforter, and every church, must pass, and Christ, who stayed loyal to friends who fled, is the one who passed it for us.

6.reflection:
Job asks that his calamity be weighed before his rash words are judged (vv. 1–3). How should this change the way we respond when a suffering person says something wild or bitter about God?

Job’s one comfort is that he has “not denied the words of the Holy One” (v. 10), even while he asks to die. What does this teach us about the difference between despair and unbelief? How could you help someone who feels as Job did?

Job says his friends are like desert streams that dry up in summer, because they “see my calamity and are afraid” (vv. 15–21). Why does another person’s suffering frighten us? When have you been a dry stream to someone, and what would it have taken to stay?

Christ’s friends all fled, yet he laid down his life for them (Mark 14:50; John 15:13). How does his loyalty to us free us to be loyal friends in someone else’s worst season?

7.title: What Is Man, That You Make So Much of Him?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand?<sup>2</sup>Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages,<sup>3</sup>so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.<sup>4</sup>When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn.<sup>5</sup>My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh.<sup>6</sup>My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.<sup>7</sup>"Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.<sup>8</sup>The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone.<sup>9</sup>As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up;<sup>10</sup>he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>12</sup>Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?<sup>13</sup>When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,'<sup>14</sup>then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions,<sup>15</sup>so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones.<sup>16</sup>I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.<sup>17</sup>What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him,<sup>18</sup>visit him every morning and test him every moment?<sup>19</sup>How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?<sup>20</sup>If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you?<sup>21</sup>Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
7.overview:
Where we are. Job is still answering Eliphaz (chapters 6–7). He has pleaded with his friends to weigh his pain and stay loyal to him; now he turns from them to God, and speaks to him directly for the first time since his troubles began.

The message. Job tells God the truth about human life and about his own: it is hard service, it is a breath, and it is slipping away under God’s unrelenting gaze. He cannot see why God watches so small a creature so closely, or why, if he has sinned, God does not simply pardon him. The chapter shows that honest lament addressed to God is itself an act of faith, and it lays bare two needs only God can meet: a life that does not vanish, and a pardon that takes iniquity away.
