Why it was said. Eliphaz had told Job to seek God and to accept his discipline quietly (5:8, 17). Job does seek God, but not quietly. His prayer is the voice of every believer for whom God’s nearness has come to feel like pressure rather than comfort (on the friends and their counsel, see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Life as hard service (vv. 1–6): man’s days are like a hired hand’s, and Job has been given months of emptiness, sleepless nights, broken skin and days that run out like thread on a shuttle. A breath before God (vv. 7–10): remember that my life is a breath; the one who goes down to Sheol does not come up. No more silence (vv. 11–16): Job will complain; is he the sea, that God must guard him, and frighten him even in his dreams? What is man? (vv. 17–21): why does God set his heart on man and test him every moment, and why does he not pardon Job’s sin before he is gone?

Where it leads. To Christ, by the needs the chapter exposes. Job’s “What is man, that you make so much of him?” (v. 17) turns Psalm 8 into a groan, and Hebrews answers that psalm with one man: “we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus” (Hebrews 2:9). Job’s last request, “Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity?” (v. 21), is answered at the Jordan: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). And the God whose gaze Job dreads is the God who in Christ came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

For us. You may bring God your sleepless nights and your bitterest questions; Job did, and God did not reject him. Life is a breath, but in Christ it is not a breath that simply vanishes, and the pardon Job asked for is given freely to all who trust him. When God’s attention feels like pressure, remember what the reader of this book knows and Job did not: his heart is set on you in love.
7.theology:
Job's first words to God are complaint, and they are prayer; the friends never pray at all. The Psalm 8 he turns into a groan is fulfilled, Hebrews says, in Jesus, made lower than the angels to taste death for everyone (Heb 2:6-9).

His two cries, hard service and unpardoned sin, are answered together in the gospel (Isa 40:2; John 1:29).
7.examples: Job calls life hard service, a soldier's term of duty, and watches his days run out like thread on a shuttle. Yet his first word to God is Remember, and his last line, you will seek me, carries faith inside the complaint.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Hard Service on Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that life has become for him a hard term of service with no wage and no end. All human life is like a soldier’s service or a hired labourer’s day (v. 1); yet a slave at least longs for the evening shade, and a labourer for his pay (v. 2). Job has been given only months of emptiness and nights of misery (v. 3). He lies down longing for morning and tosses till dawn (v. 4); his skin crusts and breaks open again (v. 5); and his days fly past like a weaver’s shuttle, running out of thread and of hope (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes the life of a sufferer from the inside: the long night, the body, the days that go nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand? Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages, so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s life has become hard service with no wage and no end: even a slave has the evening shade to wait for, but he has only months of emptiness.

Has not man a hard service on earth? “Hard service” is the Hebrew word for a soldier’s term of duty. A hired hand longs for his pay, a slave in the sun for shade; they at least have something to wait for. Job’s shift has no end and no wage, and the illness has gone on for months, not days.

Isaiah’s answer. Hold on to that first phrase, “hard service”, and to the last request of this chapter, “why do you not pardon my transgression” (v. 21). Isaiah was sent with a message that answers both at once: “cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned” (Isaiah 40:2). It is the gospel in one sentence, spoken to exhausted people. In Christ the service is over and the pardon is given.

verseByVerse.quote: When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn. My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh. My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job describes the sleepless nights and broken skin of long illness, and days that run out like thread on a loom, with no hope left.

The long night. Anyone who has been ill or grieving knows this night. He goes to bed longing for morning; the hours do not move; he turns over and over until grey light comes. Scripture does not think sleeplessness too small to record, and God does not think it too small to hear.

My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt. Then he describes the sores of 2:7 from the inside: crusting, cracking, weeping again, and maggots in the wounds.

Swifter than a weaver’s shuttle. The shuttle flies across the loom until the thread runs out. The Hebrew for “hope”, tiqvah, also means a cord or thread, the word for Rahab’s scarlet cord (Joshua 2:18). Job’s days come to the end of the thread, and of hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Remember That My Life Is a Breath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns to God, asks him to remember how brief a man’s life is, and refuses to keep silent. My life is a breath, he says; soon you will look for me and I will be gone, for the one who goes down to Sheol does not come up (vv. 7–10). Therefore he will speak in the anguish of his spirit (v. 11). Is he the sea, or a sea monster, that God must set a guard over him (v. 12)? Even his bed gives no rest, for God terrifies him with dreams, until he would rather die (vv. 13–15). He loathes his life and asks God to leave him alone (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is honest with God about his nights, his body and his dread of the grave. That honesty, spoken to God and not merely about him, is itself a kind of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good. The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job turns to God for the first time and asks him to remember that a man’s life is a breath, gone into the grave with no return.

Remember that my life is a breath. Here the chapter turns, and so does the book. “Remember” is spoken to God, Job’s first words to him since his troubles began, and from here on he will keep speaking to him. Eliphaz said, “I would seek God” (5:8). Job does. The friends never once will.

Remember what I am. His first prayer is: remember what I am, a breath. The psalmist says God does: “He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again” (Psalm 78:39). “Sheol” is the grave, the place of the dead. Psalm 103 says the wind passes over us “and its place knows it no more” (Psalm 103:16), and adds the comfort Job cannot yet see: “he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

Beyond the grave. Job sees no way back from the grave, only a door that closes. Later he will begin to hope past it (14:14; 19:25–27). The Christian stands where Job could not, on the far side of an empty tomb.

While your eyes are on me. God is looking at him, and he will vanish while God looks. The chapter will close the same way (v. 21): Job cannot stop believing that God’s eyes are on him; his fear is only that God will look again too late. James uses the same picture, “you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes”, and draws a different lesson: say, “If the Lord wills” (James 4:14–15). The shortness of life is a reason not to despair of God but to lean on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since life is so short, Job will not keep silent: he will pour out his complaint to God, who seems to guard him as if he were the chaos of the sea.

I will not restrain my mouth. “Therefore”: since life is this short, he will not waste it in silence. This is a decision, not an outburst. Better an honest complaint to God than a polite silence that has given up on him.

Am I the sea, or a sea monster? The ancient world pictured the sea and its monsters as chaos that God had to hold back. Job feels treated like that: watched, penned in, a danger to creation. When God answers, he will speak of exactly this: “who shut in the sea with doors” and said, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther” (38:8, 11). God does set bars for the sea, but Job is not the sea; he is a man God is holding.

What it does not mean. Not that every complaint is faith. Israel in the wilderness grumbled about God and wanted to go back to Egypt (Numbers 14:2–4); Job complains to God and will not let go of him. The difference is not how strong the words are but whom they are spoken to.

verseByVerse.quote: When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,' then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even sleep brings Job no rest, only terrors, until he loathes his life and begs God to leave him alone for a while.

You scare me with dreams. Even sleep, when it comes, is not rest. It brings nightmares, and Job lays them at God’s door too. He would rather choke than go on in this body. (On the wish to die, and where to turn with it, see the notes on 3:20–22 and 6:8–10.)

Two kinds of night visions. Eliphaz too had “visions of the night” (4:13), and came away sure of a doctrine; Job’s bring terror and teach him nothing. Neither man’s nights are a safe guide to what God is doing; God will speak openly, from the storm (38:1).

My days are a breath. “A breath” is hevel, Ecclesiastes’ word for everything that vanishes like vapour. “Leave me alone” is desperate, but he does not want God gone for good, only to stop pressing. Soon he will beg God to come near and answer (13:22; 23:3).

Uncertain wording. “Rather than my bones” is what the Hebrew says, probably meaning this body worn down to the bone; some, changing one letter, read “my pains”. The sense is the same: death would be better than this.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job ends with two questions: why does God pay such close attention to man, and why does he not simply pardon? He takes the wonder of Psalm 8, that God should care for man, and turns it into a complaint: God sets his heart on man, visits him every morning and tests him every moment, and will not look away long enough for Job to swallow (vv. 17–19). If Job has sinned, how has it harmed God, the watcher of mankind, and why make Job his target (v. 20)? Why not pardon him, before he lies in the dust and God seeks him in vain (v. 21)?
verseByVerse.theology: The answer to this complaint is a Son of Man who was tested for us, and a God who takes iniquity away.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him, visit him every morning and test him every moment? How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job turns the wonder of Psalm 8 into a groan: why does God pay such relentless attention to so small a creature?

What is man? The psalm marvels: “what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). The psalmist wonders that God pays attention to tiny man; Job groans that God will not stop. The same fact is wonder in one mouth and torment in another.

Set your heart on him. There is an echo only the reader can hear. “Set your heart on him” recalls the LORD saying, “Have you considered my servant Job” (1:8), literally “set your heart on”. Job is right that he is tested “every moment”. He does not know that God’s heart was set on him in delight.

Tested every moment, and did not fail. Hebrews takes up Psalm 8 and finds its answer in one man: “we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). What is man? The Son of Man was tested every moment, on our behalf, and did not fail.
verseByVerse.note: Job asks God to look away from him even for the moment it takes to swallow (v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you? Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks why God, if Job has sinned, does not simply pardon him; and even in protest he believes that God will come looking for him.

You watcher of mankind. Even if he has sinned, Job asks, how could that harm God, and why aim at him? “Your mark” is the archer’s target of 6:4. “Watcher” means a keeper or guard. It could be a name of comfort, but Job means that God is spying on him.

Why do you not pardon my transgression? Two things here are worth holding on to. First, Job does not claim to be sinless. He asks for pardon. His complaint is not that he has never done wrong but that nothing he has done can account for this, and that God, if he holds something against him, could forgive it.

You will seek me. Second, listen to the last line. Even in his complaint Job assumes that God will come looking for him, and grieves that he will be gone. It is the faith hidden inside the protest: he believes God cares enough to search. He was right: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). And the prayer to “take away my iniquity” was answered in almost the same words on the banks of the Jordan: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).

keyVerse.quote: Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be.
keyVerse.note: Job’s first prayer ends with the question the whole Bible answers. He does not claim to be sinless; he asks for pardon, and he still believes God will come looking for him. The answer came at the Jordan, in the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and in the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost.

7.reflection:
Job calls life “hard service” and describes his sleepless nights in detail (vv. 1–6). Why do you think Scripture records such honest descriptions of suffering? What difference does it make to a sufferer to find words like these in the Bible?

Job decides, “I will not restrain my mouth” (v. 11), and speaks his complaint to God. What is the difference between this and the grumbling of Israel in the wilderness? What stops us from being this honest in prayer?

Job turns Psalm 8’s wonder, “What is man?”, into a groan (vv. 17–19). How does Hebrews 2:6–9 answer both the psalm and Job? How does Jesus change what it means that God’s eyes are on us?

Job asks for pardon and believes God will seek him (v. 21). How has God answered that prayer in Christ, and how might you use Job’s words, and that answer, with someone who feels God has turned against them?

8.title: Does God Pervert Justice?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?<sup>3</sup>Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?<sup>4</sup>If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.<sup>5</sup>If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy,<sup>6</sup>if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation.<sup>7</sup>And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.<sup>8</sup>"For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out.<sup>9</sup>For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow.<sup>10</sup>Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?<sup>11</sup>"Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water?<sup>12</sup>While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant.<sup>13</sup>Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.<sup>14</sup>His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web.<sup>15</sup>He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.<sup>16</sup>He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden.<sup>17</sup>His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones.<sup>18</sup>If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.'<sup>19</sup>Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers.<sup>21</sup>He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting.<sup>22</sup>Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
8.overview:
Where we are. Job has answered Eliphaz (chapters 6–7), protesting his innocence to the friends and pouring out his complaint to God. Now the second friend, Bildad the Shuhite, speaks for the first time, and he is blunter than Eliphaz.

The message. Bildad defends a great truth, that God does not pervert justice, and draws from it a cruel conclusion: Job’s children died for their sins, and Job will be restored only if he is pure. Through his speech God shows us that a true doctrine of his justice can be used to wound the grieving, because God’s justice is not measured out day by day in each person’s circumstances. And Bildad’s best line, that God will not reject a blameless man (v. 20), is truer than he knows: it will be proved true of Job.

Why it was said. Bildad speaks for tradition, the settled teaching of the fathers that the godless wither and the righteous flourish (see the introduction). He cannot let Job’s words stand, because if Job is innocent, God seems unjust, and his system cannot hold both.

How the chapter makes its case. Does God pervert justice? (vv. 1–7): Job’s words are a great wind; God is just, so the children must have sinned; if Job seeks God and is pure, God will restore him and make his latter days great. Ask the fathers (vv. 8–19): we are of yesterday, so learn from earlier generations; the godless wither like papyrus without water, lean on a spider’s web, and are uprooted and forgotten like a garden plant. God will not reject a blameless man (vv. 20–22): he will yet fill Job’s mouth with laughter and clothe his enemies with shame.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God’s justice revealed in him. Bildad cannot imagine the blameless suffering while God remains just. The cross holds both. The one truly blameless man was treated as rejected and cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and God did not pervert justice but displayed it, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). In raising Christ, God vindicated him, and Bildad’s sentence becomes finally true for all who are in him: God will not reject them.

For us. Never tell a grieving person that their loss was the wage of a particular sin; Jesus refused that reasoning (Luke 13:1–5), and so does this book. Hold firmly that God is just, and humbly that his justice cannot be read off our circumstances. And take heart: the God who will not reject the blameless has clothed you in Christ’s blamelessness.
8.theology:
God does not pervert justice, but we cannot read his verdict on a person from that person's circumstances. Bildad's conclusion that Job's children died for their sins is the kind of speech the LORD rejects at the end. Tradition deserves honour, but it cannot overrule God's word.

Bildad's promises come true for the opposite of his reasons, and in the end the friends need Job's prayers.
8.examples: Bildad's speech is full of ironies he cannot see. He says we know nothing, yet claims to know why ten people died. His promise that Job's latter days will be great comes true almost word for word, and his warning that God will not reject a blameless man turns out to be good news for Job.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad’s point is that God’s justice settles the question: Job’s family suffered because they sinned. He dismisses Job’s words as a great wind (v. 2) and asks the question on which he builds everything: does God pervert justice (v. 3)? Since he does not, Job’s children must have sinned, and God handed them over to it (v. 4). If Job will seek God, plead for mercy and be pure and upright, God will rouse himself for him and restore his home, and his latter days will be greater than his beginning (vv. 5–7). Each sentence sounds devout; together they make a cruel argument.
verseByVerse.theology: God is just, and Bildad is right to say so. The error is the step he takes next.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad, the second friend, dismisses Job’s cry of pain as nothing but a great wind.

Bildad the Shuhite. His people were probably descended from Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), and lived somewhere east of Canaan.

A great wind. He has none of Eliphaz’s courtesy. Job asked them to hear “the speech of a despairing man” as “wind” (6:26), a cry and not a doctrine. Bildad turns the word into an insult. He repeats the friends’ case and adds something harder: Job’s dead children (v. 4), and the teaching of earlier generations (vv. 8–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God never perverts justice, but Bildad wrongly concludes that Job’s suffering must therefore be deserved.

Does God pervert justice? The answer is no, and Bildad is right to insist on it: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). A believer in Job’s position needs to keep hold of that.

A conclusion that does not follow. But see what Bildad does with it. God is just; Job is suffering; therefore Job deserves it. The first two are true; the third does not follow, because God’s justice is not measured out day by day in each man’s circumstances. The debate turns on this verb, “pervert”. Job will answer with the same verb turned round: “God has put me in the wrong” (19:6). Bildad reasons that God cannot pervert justice, so Job must be guilty; Job, that he is not guilty, so God seems to have perverted it. Both are trapped by the same assumption, that suffering is a verdict. The opening chapters have already told the reader it is not.

Justice at the cross. At Calvary God neither perverted justice nor ignored sin: he punished it in a substitute, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad tells a grieving father that his children died because of their sins, a baseless claim that God will reject.

If your children have sinned. This is the cruellest sentence yet. The “if” is a courtesy; Bildad means “since”. Your children are dead and God is just, so they had it coming: God simply handed them over to the consequences of their own sin.

Said to a grieving father. Say it to a father who rose early after every feast to offer a burnt offering for each of them (1:5), and who has ten graves to visit. Bildad has no evidence; his system requires it, so he says it. The LORD will name what he has done: “you have not spoken of me what is right” (42:8). Jesus refused the same reasoning about eighteen people killed when a tower fell: “do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others …? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4–5).

For the bereaved. If you have been told that someone you loved died because of their sin, or yours, hear the verdict of this book. That was Bildad’s speech, and God did not accept it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy, if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation. And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad offers restoration as a bargain for purity; God will indeed restore Job, but as a gift, after declaring Bildad wrong.

Plead with the Almighty for mercy. Be pure and upright, and God will act for you. It sounds like the gospel, but it is a bargain: be good enough and God will pay. Bildad cannot see the irony: “upright” is the narrator’s word for Job in 1:1. By Bildad’s own conditions, God should restore Job. He will.

Your latter days will be very great. Read the last chapter: “And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning” (42:12). Bildad’s promise comes true almost word for word, not because Job confessed imagined sins, but after God has declared Bildad wrong and Job right: God kept the promise and threw away the reasoning.

Psalm 44’s answer. “He will rouse himself for you”, as though God were asleep toward Job until he repented. Psalm 44 uses Bildad’s very verb and turns his theology upside down, in the prayer of people who have not sinned their way into trouble: “All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant” (Psalm 44:17); and they cry, “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). Paul quotes that psalm about Christians and answers it: “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:36–37). God never sleeps (Psalm 121:4). When the disciples woke Jesus in the storm (Mark 4:38), he had been in the boat with them all along.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad appeals to tradition: ask the earlier generations, and they will confirm that the godless perish. We are of yesterday and our days are a shadow, so learn from the fathers (vv. 8–10). Papyrus cannot grow without a marsh; cut off from water it withers before any other plant, and so do all who forget God (vv. 11–13). The godless man trusts in a spider’s web, and his house will not hold when he leans on it (vv. 14–15). He may spread like a lush plant with its roots among the stones, but once he is pulled up, his place denies it ever knew him, and others grow in his soil (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture is true of the godless. Every picture is also a portrait of Job, and that is the point of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out. For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow. Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad appeals to the wisdom of the fathers, but tradition, however old, cannot overrule what God has said or explain what he has not revealed.

Inquire, please, of bygone ages. Eliphaz appealed to experience and a vision; Bildad appeals to the fathers. “Searched out” is Eliphaz’s confident word again (5:27).

Tradition and the word of God. There is real wisdom in that: “ask your father, and he will show you” (Deuteronomy 32:7). But tradition cannot overrule what God has said; Jesus rebuked men for “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:13). And Bildad says we “know nothing”, and in the same breath knows exactly why ten young people died. David used the same words in prayer: “Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding” (1 Chronicles 29:15). In David’s mouth they lead to humble dependence on God; in Bildad’s, to a lecture.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water? While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant. Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like papyrus cut off from water, says Bildad, the godless suddenly wither, and he leaves Job to draw the conclusion about himself.

Papyrus without a marsh. The papyrus reed of the Nile grows tall and green, but only in the marsh; without water it withers before it can be harvested. So, says Bildad, is the man who forgets God: flourishing one day, dead the next.

A tree planted by water. True, and the prophets say it better: the man who trusts in the LORD “is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes” (Jeremiah 17:8). But the point of Bildad’s reed is its sudden withering, and Job has withered suddenly. What he leaves unsaid is: you must have forgotten God. Job has not. He is the one still speaking to him.

verseByVerse.quote: His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web. He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The godless man’s confidence is as flimsy as a spider’s web, and his house will not hold when he leans on it.

His trust is a spider’s web. In Hebrew it is a spider’s “house”: built with care, beautiful in the morning light, and useless when you lean on it. Isaiah says of the works of the wicked, “Their webs will not serve as clothing” (Isaiah 59:6).

He leans against his house, but it does not stand. Job’s house did not stand; it fell on his children (1:19). Bildad could hardly have chosen a sharper picture.

Two houses. Jesus’ story of two houses answers Bildad: the same storm beat on both (Matthew 7:25, 27), and the difference was not whether it came but what stood afterwards. Job’s roof fell in; his faith did not. By Jesus’ measure, he built on the rock.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “is severed” is rare and uncertain; some take it as something fragile, like gossamer threads, matching the spider’s web. Either way, what the godless trust in cannot hold them.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden. His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones. If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.' Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The godless may spread like a lush garden plant, but once uprooted he is forgotten, as if he had never been.

A lush plant before the sun. Bildad’s next plant is a creeper spreading green in the sun, its roots round the stones, looking settled. Pull it up and the garden forgets it was ever there. “This is the joy of his way” is bitter irony: this is all his flourishing came to. Job said of the dead, “nor does his place know him anymore” (7:10). Bildad agrees, and adds that the wicked deserve to be forgotten.

Not forgotten. The Christian holds a better promise than either: “whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17), and the Good Shepherd calls his own by name (John 10:3).

Uncertain wording. “He looks upon a house of stones” is obscure: perhaps the roots take hold among the stones. “This is the joy of his way” is probably irony, though some read the Hebrew differently. A few interpreters take vv. 16–19 as a well-rooted plant that springs up again, in contrast with the papyrus; the ESV’s reading, that the godless are uprooted and forgotten, fits Bildad’s flow best.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — God Will Not Reject a Blameless Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad ends with a promise and a warning in one: God will not reject the blameless, nor take the hand of evildoers (v. 20). If Job is blameless, God will yet fill his mouth with laughter and his lips with shouting, and those who hate him will be clothed with shame (vv. 21–22). Bildad means it as a challenge to repent. But every word of it will come true for Job in a way Bildad does not expect: God will vindicate Job as blameless, and the friends will need his prayers.
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad means it as a warning; it turns out to be a promise.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers. He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting. Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad’s truest sentence, that God will not reject a blameless man, will be proved true of Job, and the friends will end up needing his prayers.

God will not reject a blameless man. “Blameless” is the very word God used of Job (1:1, 8; 2:3). Bildad means it as a warning: if you have been abandoned, you are not blameless. But the sentence is simply true, the truest thing he says. God will not reject Job, because Job is exactly what Bildad doubts he is.

He will yet fill your mouth with laughter. It is the laughter of the restored, as of the returning exiles: “Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:2). It will happen. And the ones clothed with shame at the end will be Job’s friends, sent to him with seven bulls and seven rams so that he can pray for them, “not to deal with you according to your folly” (42:8). God is kinder to Bildad than Bildad was to Job.

The blameless man rejected. Once God did forsake a blameless man: Jesus, bearing our sin, cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). He was treated as rejected so that those in him never will be, but stand “holy and blameless before him” (Ephesians 1:4).

keyVerse.quote: Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?
keyVerse.note: Bildad builds his whole speech on this question, and the right answer is no. His mistake is the conclusion he draws: that a just God must be punishing Job. The book, and finally the cross, show that God’s justice is never perverted, yet cannot be read off a sufferer’s circumstances.

8.reflection:
Bildad asks, “Does God pervert justice?” (v. 3). Why is it important to say no? Where does Bildad go wrong in what he concludes from it, and how does the opening of the book (1:8; 2:3) show his error?

Bildad tells Job that his children died for their sins (v. 4). Why do people still reason like this about tragedy? How do Jesus’ words in Luke 13:1–5 and John 9:1–3 help us answer them, and comfort those who have been told it?

Bildad appeals to “the fathers” (vv. 8–10). What is the value of tradition and the wisdom of earlier generations? When does it become dangerous?

“God will not reject a blameless man” (v. 20). How is this true for Job, and how is it true for us in Christ, who was forsaken on the cross? How does that change the way you face suffering?

9.title: There Is No Arbiter Between Us
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God?<sup>3</sup>If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.<sup>4</sup>He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?—<sup>5</sup>he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger,<sup>6</sup>who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble;<sup>7</sup>who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;<sup>8</sup>who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea;<sup>9</sup>who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south;<sup>10</sup>who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.<sup>11</sup>Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him.<sup>12</sup>Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?'<sup>13</sup>"God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.<sup>14</sup>How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him?<sup>15</sup>Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser.<sup>16</sup>If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.<sup>17</sup>For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause;<sup>18</sup>he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness.<sup>19</sup>If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?<sup>20</sup>Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse.<sup>21</sup>I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.<sup>22</sup>It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'<sup>23</sup>When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent.<sup>24</sup>The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?<sup>25</sup>"My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good.<sup>26</sup>They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey.<sup>27</sup>If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,'<sup>28</sup>I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.<sup>29</sup>I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain?<sup>30</sup>If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye,<sup>31</sup>yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.<sup>32</sup>For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together.<sup>33</sup>There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.<sup>34</sup>Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me.<sup>35</sup>Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
9.overview:
Where we are. Bildad has just told Job that God never perverts justice: his children died for their own sins, and if Job were pure and upright God would restore him (8:3–6). Now Job answers, and turns the debate about his guilt into something more daring: a lawsuit with God.

The message. Job asks the question of the whole Bible, “how can a man be in the right before God?” (v. 2), and sees that no one could ever answer it by arguing his own case. God is too great to be taken to court, no one can wash himself clean, and there is no one to stand between God and man. The chapter lays bare humanity’s deepest need, and prepares us for the God who meets it himself.

Why it was said. The friends assume that God always repays in this life, so a great sufferer must be a great sinner (see the introduction). Job knows that nothing he has done explains what has happened, yet he cannot make God hear his case. He knows nothing of the heavenly council, where God himself called him blameless and his suffering “without reason” (2:3).

How the chapter makes its case. Job begins with God’s overwhelming power: he overturns mountains, seals up the stars, tramples the sea and passes by unseen (vv. 1–13). Then the conclusion: even in the right, he could only plead for mercy, for no court can summon God, and in the darkest lines he says that God destroys blameless and wicked alike (vv. 14–24). Last he turns to his own short days and his helplessness: no soap could make him clean, God is not a man, and there is no arbiter to lay a hand on them both (vv. 25–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need the chapter exposes. Job longs for a mediator who belongs to both sides, and the New Testament answers: “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). The God who is “not a man, as I am” (v. 32) became one. The God who “trampled the waves of the sea” (v. 8) walked on Galilee’s sea and said, “Take heart; it is I” (Mark 6:50). And the rod Job begged God to take away (v. 34) fell on Christ instead (Isaiah 53:5). Job is also a pattern of Christ, an innocent man wounded “without cause” (v. 17).

For us. When you cannot make sense of God’s ways, you may say so to God, as Job does, without pretending. But you need not stand in his court alone, or scrub yourself clean before you come: Christ is the arbiter Job could not find, and in him the Judge himself justifies the ungodly. And with sufferers, hear the honesty before you correct the excesses.
9.theology:
Job's cry for an arbiter who could lay a hand on God and on man describes the mediator God provided (1 Timothy 2:5). The God who walks on the sea and passes by unseen (vv. 8, 11) later walked on the sea in the flesh, and spoke (Mark 6:48-50).

Job is right that his wounds are without cause, and wrong that God mocks the innocent. No one can wash himself clean, but God washes whiter than snow.
9.examples: Job repeats Eliphaz's hymn to God's power and draws the opposite conclusion. The Rahab he names is a sea monster, not the woman of Jericho. And his bitterest question, if it is not he, who then is it?, is one the reader of chapters 1 and 2 can answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — How Can a Man Be in the Right Before God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job agrees that no one can be in the right before God, but he means it in a sense the friends never intended: no one could win a case against him. He begins with God’s wisdom and might, which no one has ever resisted and survived (vv. 1–4). Then he praises that power in a hymn: God overturns mountains, shakes the earth, commands the sun, stretches out the heavens, tramples the sea and made the stars (vv. 5–10). The hymn sounds like Eliphaz, but its point is the opposite: such a God is beyond anyone’s reach. He passes by unseen, snatches away and cannot be questioned, and even the helpers of Rahab, the monster of chaos, bow beneath him (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's hymn to God's power is as true as Eliphaz's. For Job it is not a comfort, because a God this great cannot be taken to court.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God? If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can be in the right before God, Job agrees, meaning that no one could ever win a case against him.

How can a man be in the right before God? Job begins by agreeing with the friends: “Truly I know that it is so.” It is the question Eliphaz’s night visitor asked (4:17), but Job means something sharper. “Be in the right” is courtroom language: win your case. How could anyone take God to law and win?

Once in a thousand times. God would ask a thousand questions and a man could not answer one. Job is more right than he knows. When God does speak, he will ask Job question after question (chapters 38–41), and Job will say, “I lay my hand on my mouth” (40:4).

The gospel’s answer. Every human being must still face Job’s question. Job sees only a courtroom he cannot win. The gospel announces that the Judge himself has provided the righteousness, so that he is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

The courtroom that never closes. Many people today think they stopped asking Job’s question long ago; how to be right with God sounds like a medieval worry, a monk in his cell. But watch how we live. We rehearse arguments we will never have and assemble the case for the defence after every quarrel. We need to have been reasonable, to be on the right side, to be the one who was wronged. Parents, colleagues, followers, the critic in our own head: everyone stands before some tribunal, and for most of us it sits day and night. The question has not gone away; it has only lost its address, and so it can never be settled. Job at least takes it to the right court, and the shock of the gospel is what that court does. The Judge does not wait for us to win. He sends his Son to stand in the dock in our place, and then he “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Only a verdict already given lets a person stop arguing, and admit that he was wrong without feeling that his life has ended.

verseByVerse.quote: He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?— he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger, who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble; who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job never doubts that God is almighty, and that is what makes his suffering so hard to bear.

Who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded? No one. Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his army (Exodus 14:27–28).

Who shakes the earth out of its place. God overturns mountains, shakes the earth on its pillars (the poets’ picture of the world’s foundations), and seals up the stars, as in an eclipse or a storm-dark sky. Job knows who shakes the world, and that is what makes his position so hard: a weak god could be excused, but this one could end Job’s suffering with a word.

verseByVerse.quote: who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea; who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south; who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone made the heavens, rules the sea and set the stars in place, so there is no one above him to appeal to.

Trampled the waves of the sea. God walks on the sea as a man walks on the ground. The sea, which stood for chaos and danger, is a floor under his feet. Keep that picture; it will come back in a moment (v. 11).

The Bear and Orion, the Pleiades. The constellations Job names are the ones God will name when he answers: “Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion?” (38:31). Amos praised the same Maker (Amos 5:8). The stars other nations worshipped are things he made.

Great things beyond searching out. The last line is Eliphaz’s, almost word for word (5:9). Job and the friends agree about God’s greatness; they disagree about what it means for a man in pain. For the friends it proves that everything is in order. For Job it means there is no one above God to appeal to.

Uncertain wording. The star names are rare words. “Orion” translates a word that elsewhere means “fool”, and “the Bear” may be another group of stars. “The chambers of the south” is least certain: probably the stars of the southern sky, possibly the storehouses of the south wind (compare 37:9). Either way, every star is his work.
verseByVerse.note: The Bear, Orion and the Pleiades are constellations; the identifications are probable, not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him. Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?' "God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is at work all around Job, yet Job cannot see him, stop him or question him.

He passes by me, and I see him not. Job feels the effects and never the presence. Many believers in the dark have said exactly this.

What are you doing? No one can turn God back or ask him what he is doing. Nebuchadnezzar learned the same: “none can stay his hand or say to him, ‘What have you done?’” (Daniel 4:35).

The helpers of Rahab. This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho but a sea monster, a poetic picture of chaos and of every power set against God: “Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces?” (Isaiah 51:9; compare Psalm 89:10). If the monster and its helpers bow beneath him, what hope has Job of standing up to him?

Take heart; it is I. Now put two verses together. God “trampled the waves of the sea” (v. 8), and “he passes by me, and I see him not” (v. 11). Mark’s account of one night seems to echo both. On the Sea of Galilee Jesus “came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them” (Mark 6:48). They took him for a ghost. “But immediately he spoke to them and said, ‘Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid’” (Mark 6:50). The God who passes by unseen in Job’s complaint walked the waves in a body, and was seen, and spoke. Job longed for God to come near in a form he could meet. In Christ he did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — If It Is a Matter of Justice, Who Can Summon Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If God is like that, a court case is hopeless, however innocent the man. Job could only plead for mercy from the one who seems to be prosecuting him, and would not believe he had been heard (vv. 14–16). God crushes him without cause, and no one can summon God to court (vv. 17–19). Job knows he is blameless, but fears that under God’s questioning his own mouth would condemn him (vv. 20–21). Then, in the darkest lines of the chapter, he says that God destroys blameless and wicked alike and mocks the innocent, and asks who else could be behind the world’s injustice (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is right about one thing here and wrong about another, and the reader needs to see both.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser. If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in the right, Job could only beg for mercy from the God who seems to be prosecuting him.

I must appeal for mercy to my accuser. An innocent man would normally demand justice. Before God, says Job, even the innocent could only beg for mercy. The Hebrew word behind “my accuser” can also mean “my judge”: in Job’s case the other side and the bench are the same person.

Unanswered prayer. This is the despair of unanswered prayer: even if God answered, I would not believe he had heard. And yet Job keeps summoning him. He doubts that God is listening, and still he does not stop talking to him. That is faith of a kind the friends never show: they say a great deal about God, but they never speak to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause; he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness. If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s wounds really are “without cause”, as God himself said, but Job has no court in which to prove it.

Without cause. Satan had asked, “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9), and God had said, “you incited me against him to destroy him without reason” (2:3). The words are the same in Hebrew. Job has no idea they were spoken, yet he says exactly what God said: his wounds really are without cause in him. On that point Job is right and the friends are wrong.

He crushes me with a tempest. The “tempest” that crushes him is, in Hebrew, the same word as the “whirlwind” out of which the LORD finally answers him (38:1). The storm he complains of is the storm God will speak from.

Who can summon him? No court can issue God a summons, and that is Job’s dilemma.

The language of the court. From here on, Job’s speeches are a lawsuit, in the words of a court: contend, answer, summon, in the right, arbiter. He asks less for his health than for a hearing and a verdict that he is innocent: “I have prepared my case” (13:18), “I would lay my case before him” (23:4), and at last, “Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!” (31:35). The book’s climax is that God does answer, not with a verdict on the charges but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse. I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job knows he is blameless, but fears that under God’s questioning his own words would condemn him.

I am blameless. It is God’s own word for him (1:1, 8; 2:3), and Job says it of himself. He is not claiming never to have sinned (he will speak of “the iniquities of my youth”, 13:26), but to have no hidden crime that explains his ruin. He is refusing to confess what is not true, even though a false confession might end the argument. But he fears that under God’s cross-examination he would be tripped up and made to look guilty.

I regard not myself; I loathe my life. Literally “I do not know my soul”: the exhaustion of a man who no longer cares what happens to him.

verseByVerse.quote: It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.' When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job says that God destroys blameless and wicked alike and mocks the innocent: here he says too much, though his question goes deeper than he knows.

He mocks at the calamity of the innocent. That the same disasters fall on good and bad alike is true; the Preacher says so (Ecclesiastes 9:2). But that God mocks the innocent in their calamity is not true, and God will call such talk “words without knowledge” (38:2) and ask Job, “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (40:8). A sufferer may say this in the dark, and God bears with him; but no one should build a theology on it.

The earth is given into the hand of the wicked. Unjust men rule, and God “covers the faces of its judges”, as though blindfolding them so that they cannot see what is right. Even this complaint is truer than Job knows. In the council God said to Satan, “all that he has is in your hand” (1:12), and John says of the world as a whole, “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19).

If it is not he, who then is it? The reader can answer it. It was the accuser (1:12; 2:7), acting under God’s permission and within God’s limit. Job sees only two possibilities: either God is doing this, or no one is. The opening chapters show a third that he cannot see. God rules over it all, and God does not mock.

The hand that can take it back. The hand that gave the world into the power of the wicked can take it back: “The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — There Is No Arbiter Between Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns from the world to himself: his life is rushing away, and he can find no way out of his case. His days fly like a runner, a reed boat and a swooping eagle, and forcing a cheerful face only brings the fear back (vv. 25–28). No washing could make him clean, for God would plunge him back into the pit (vv. 29–31). The real problem lies deeper: God is not a man, and there is no arbiter to lay a hand on them both (vv. 32–33). If only God would lift his rod, Job could speak without fear (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes exactly the one he needs: someone who belongs both to God and to him, and could put a hand on each.

verseByVerse.quote: "My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good. They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey. If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,' I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s life is racing away with nothing good in it, and he cannot simply cheer up.

Swifter than a runner. A royal courier, a reed boat, a diving eagle: speed on land, on water and in the air. His life is rushing past, and all of it is bad: “they see no good.”

I will put off my sad face. Every sufferer has been told to cheer up. Job has tried, and the fear comes back, because nothing has changed. Forced cheerfulness is no cure for grief, and the church should never demand it.

You will not hold me innocent. Job has stopped talking about God and begun talking to him, and for the rest of the chapter he moves between the two, as people in anguish do.

verseByVerse.quote: I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain? If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No washing could make Job clean in God’s sight, he says, for the verdict is already fixed.

If I wash myself with snow. Snow water, the cleanest there is; lye, the strongest soap. Scrub as he may, God would push him back into the filth, and his very clothes would be disgusted to wear him. Whatever he does, Job means, the verdict is fixed: “I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain?”

No one can wash himself clean. Job has stumbled on a truth bigger than his case. No one can wash himself clean before God: “Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me” (Jeremiah 2:22). But the same God who says so offers the washing himself: “Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). David prayed for it: “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7). Job cannot wash himself as white as snow. God can.

verseByVerse.quote: For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together. There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s deepest problem is that God is not a man, and there is no one who belongs to both and could bring them together.

He is not a man, as I am. This is the heart of the chapter. There is no common ground on which Job and God could meet as equals and “come to trial together”. Job needs an arbiter, an umpire who could lay one hand on God and one on Job, belonging to both and trusted by both.

There is no arbiter between us. The word “arbiter” comes from the verb God uses in Isaiah 1:18. Job thinks a hearing is impossible. God himself proposes one, “let us reason together”, and ends it with snow-white cleansing.

God, who is not a man, became one. Job has described, without knowing it, the one God would send: “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). God, who is not a man as Job is, became one, so that the hand that holds God’s throne could also be laid on us. Job cries that there is no arbiter; every Christian can answer him by name. And Job will reach higher still: to a witness in heaven (16:19), and to a Redeemer who lives (19:25).

For the sufferer. For anyone who feels that God is too high to hear, the one between us has felt our pain from the inside, “a merciful and faithful high priest”, “able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:17–18).

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament and a few Hebrew manuscripts read the line as a wish, “would that there were an arbiter between us”. Either way Job longs for one.
verseByVerse.note: The KJV's daysman is an old word for an umpire.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me. Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If only God would lift his rod, Job could speak his case without fear.

Let him take his rod away from me. It is dread, not guilt, that silences him.

The rod laid on another. The gospel does what Job asks. The rod was not simply taken away; it was laid on another: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5). And so the Christian can do what Job could not, and speak to God without dread: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Uncertain wording. “For I am not so in myself” is a compressed line. It may mean that in his own conscience Job is not the guilty man his fear makes him seem, or simply that, as things are, he cannot speak. Either way, terror silences him, not a guilty secret.

keyVerse.quote: There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.
keyVerse.note: Here Job names the need beneath all his questions: someone who belongs both to God and to man, who could bring them together. Scripture answers his cry with a name, “the man Christ Jesus”, the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5).

9.reflection:
Job’s question, “how can a man be in the right before God?” (v. 2), is the language of a courtroom. In what “courts” do people today try to win their case, and how does God’s verdict in Christ, that he “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5), set us free from them?

Job says many true things about God in this chapter, and some things God will later call “words without knowledge” (38:2), such as that God mocks the innocent (v. 23). How can we let a suffering friend speak honestly to God without agreeing with everything said in pain?

Job knows he cannot wash himself clean (vv. 30–31). Where are you tempted to scrub harder rather than receive the cleansing God offers (Isaiah 1:18)?

Job longs for an arbiter who could lay his hand on God and on him (v. 33). What does it mean to you that Jesus is both fully God and fully man, and how might it change the way you pray when God seems far away?

10.title: Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>2</sup>I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.<sup>3</sup>Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?<sup>4</sup>Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees?<sup>5</sup>Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years,<sup>6</sup>that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin,<sup>7</sup>although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether.<sup>9</sup>Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?<sup>10</sup>Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?<sup>11</sup>You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.<sup>12</sup>You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.<sup>13</sup>Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose.<sup>14</sup>If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity.<sup>15</sup>If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.<sup>16</sup>And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me.<sup>17</sup>You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.<sup>18</sup>"Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me<sup>19</sup>and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.<sup>20</sup>Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer<sup>21</sup>before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow,<sup>22</sup>the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
10.overview:
Where we are. Late in chapter 9 Job began to turn from talking about God to talking to him, and chapter 10 is almost all prayer. He has just said there is no arbiter between God and himself (9:33); now he resolves to speak to God anyway, “in the bitterness of my soul” (v. 1).

The message. This is a sufferer’s honest prayer, placed in Scripture to show that such prayer is allowed. Job cannot fit together the God who made him with such care and kept him by steadfast love (vv. 8–12) and the God who now seems to hunt him like a lion (v. 16). He takes the contradiction to God, not away from him, and holds on to one truth: he is the work of God’s hands, and a maker does not despise what he has made.

Why it was said. Like the friends, Job assumes that suffering on this scale must mean God has found something against him; unlike them, he knows there is nothing to find (v. 7). So he asks the question the book never answers for him: why? (vv. 2, 18). The reader knows of the heavenly council in chapters 1–2; Job does not (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First Job asks God to name the charge, and asks why the Maker would despise his own work or search for a sin he knows is not there (vv. 1–7). Then he sets the loving care with which God made and kept him beside the present, in which God seems to hunt him (vv. 8–17). Last he returns to the wish of chapter 3, that he had never been born, and asks only for a little relief before he goes to the land of deep darkness (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, through the character of God revealed in him and the need the chapter exposes. Job cannot see how the hands that made him can be against him. At the cross the hand of God truly was against his Son (Isaiah 53:10), so that for those in Christ it will only ever be the hand that made them and keeps them: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). And the land of deep shadow Job dreads is the land on which the great light has dawned (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16).

For us. You may pray like this. When what you feel and what God has promised seem to contradict each other, do not hide the contradiction from him: tell him, and then, as Job does, name the kindnesses he has already shown you (v. 12). In Christ the hands that made you will never despise you.
10.theology:
Job never learns the reason for his suffering, and the book shows it is possible to rest in God without it. God does not despise the work of his hands; he completes it. The care Job feels as scrutiny is the care that has preserved his spirit (v. 12).

Job's own words point beyond the grave: the God who knit him in the womb will knit the dead together again, and the land of deep darkness has seen a great light (Matt 4:16).
10.examples: Job's picture of the womb (milk, cheese, skin, flesh, bones and sinews) uses the same materials Ezekiel sees gathered again in the valley of dry bones. Even his bitterest line, about a purpose hidden in God's heart, turns out to be true in a way he could not guess.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Let Me Know Why You Contend Against Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job resolves to speak freely to God, and asks him to name the charge. He will no longer hold back his complaint, though it comes from the bitterness of his soul (v. 1), and he asks God not to condemn him without telling him why (v. 2). Then he presses three questions. Does it please God to despise the work of his own hands while the schemes of the wicked prosper (v. 3)? Does God see as limited men see, or have only a short lifetime, that he must hunt for evidence (vv. 4–6)? And why search for a sin he knows is not there, when no one could rescue Job from his hand anyway (v. 7)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks God for the charge against him, and he is right that God knows he is not guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job will no longer keep his anguish to himself: he asks God to tell him the charge.

I will give free utterance to my complaint. Not unbelief, but the boldness of a man who still believes God is there to hear; the Psalms are full of such prayers (Psalm 13; 88).

Let me know why you contend against me. He will ask for it again at the end: “Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!” (31:35).

Never told why. Job never gets his answer: not here, not from the whirlwind, not in the happy ending. He is never told about the council in heaven. He has to come to rest in God himself without ever learning why. Many believers in deep suffering live and die in the same place, and the book shows that it is possible to be at peace there.

verseByVerse.quote: Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job appeals to God’s own character: why would the Maker despise the work of his own hands?

The work of your hands. A craftsman does not smash his own best work while leaving the plans of the wicked to flourish, so why would God? Job is appealing to God’s character, and he is right to. The psalmist prays the same way: “Do not forsake the work of your hands” (Psalm 138:8). Isaiah says, “we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand” (Isaiah 64:8).

A good work completed. The New Testament gives the answer Job reaches for: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). God does not despise the work of his hands. He finishes it.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees? Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years, that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin, although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not a human investigator who must squeeze a confession out of a suspect; he already knows Job is innocent.

Have you eyes of flesh? A human investigator, short of sight and time, presses a suspect hard. But God does not see as man sees (1 Samuel 16:7), and he has all eternity. Why, then, interrogate Job?

Although you know that I am not guilty. It is exactly true; God said so himself, twice (1:8; 2:3). Job’s mistake is only in thinking that God’s hand on him means God doubts him.

None to deliver out of your hand. This echoes the song of Moses: “I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Eliphaz took up the first half (5:18); Job takes up the second. The hand that holds him is the only hand that could heal him, and Job knows it. He has nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job sets two pictures of God side by side and cannot make them fit. In the first, God is a careful craftsman: he shaped Job like clay, formed him in the womb as milk sets into cheese, clothed him in skin, knit him together with bones and sinews, and kept him by steadfast love (vv. 8–12). In the second, the same God seems to have hidden a hostile purpose all along: he watches for every sin, leaves Job unable to lift his head whether guilty or innocent, hunts him like a lion and sends fresh troops against him (vv. 13–17). That tension is the heart of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: Job remembers God's tenderness and cannot square it with his suffering. The chapter's answer is in his own words: the care that preserved his spirit has not stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether. Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job pleads as the work of God’s own hands: will the Maker who shaped him so carefully now grind him back into dust?

Your hands fashioned and made me. Job remembers where he came from. God formed man “of dust from the ground” (Genesis 2:7), and said that to dust he would return (Genesis 3:19). Job asks whether, after taking such care to make him, God will simply grind him back into dust. He pleads as the potter’s own handiwork.

verseByVerse.quote: Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made Job with a craftsman’s care and has kept him by steadfast love, and even in his complaint Job says so.

Curdle me like cheese. This is the ancient world’s picture of a child forming in the womb: something liquid set into shape, like milk thickening into cheese, then clothed in skin and flesh, then bound together with bone and sinew. It is poetry, not biology, and its point is wonder, as in the psalm: “you knitted me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13). Job knows he is not an accident. God made him, carefully, from the inside.

The loveliest line. “You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.” “Steadfast love” is chesed, God’s covenant loyalty. And “your care” comes from the same Hebrew root as the complaint of 7:18, that God would “visit him every morning and test him”. The visiting Job felt as surveillance is, in his own better words, the care that has kept his spirit alive. He has the answer in his mouth and cannot yet see it.

Knit me together with bones and sinews. There is a hope hidden in that list which Job cannot yet see. Ezekiel, looking at a valley of dry bones, heard God promise, “I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live” (Ezekiel 37:6). The same materials are gathered again: the God who knit Job together in the womb can knit him together again from the grave.

What steadfast love is. We hear “love” as a feeling; chesed is sturdier: love that has bound itself by promise and keeps faith when the other side has nothing left to give. It is the word God used when he proclaimed his own name to Moses, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Notice when Job says it: not on a good day, but on the ash heap, while every feeling in him says God has turned enemy. His feelings tell him one thing; God’s record with him tells him another, and he names the record. The New Testament shows how far that love went to keep its promise: the Word who was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) went all the way to a cross, and now nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). So on the morning you feel nothing, do what Job did: say back to God the kindnesses he has already shown you, one by one. See also Steadfast Love in the Theological Dictionary.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose. If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity. If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job suspects that God’s kindness hid a hostile plan; God did have a hidden purpose, but a good one.

Yet these things you hid in your heart. Job fears the kindness was a trap. He is half right. God did have a purpose hidden from him, settled in heaven before a single blow fell. But the purpose was not malice. It began with God saying, “Have you considered my servant Job?” (1:8). What God hid in his heart was delight in Job, and a purpose to show the world a man who would trust him for nothing in return (1:9). “For those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). A believer may be sure of that hidden purpose even when, like Job, he never sees it.

I cannot lift up my head. Job feels trapped either way. If he sins, God watches and will not acquit him; if he is guilty, he is lost; if he is innocent, he still cannot lift up his head, so covered is he in shame. But Scripture has a name for God that answers this line: “But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (Psalm 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me. You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the ash heap God looks like a hunter, a prosecutor and an attacking army at once; that is how it feels, not how it is.

You would hunt me like a lion. If he tried to stand, God would stalk him like a lion. The “witnesses” are his wasted body (16:8): everyone who sees his sores assumes his guilt.

Work wonders against me. Eliphaz praised God who does “marvelous things without number” (5:9). Now the wonders seem turned on Job. The same power that fills the psalms with praise feels, from inside the pain, like an ambush. It is the same God and the same power; what Job cannot yet see is that it is working for him.

Uncertain wording. “You bring fresh troops against me” is a compressed phrase, literally “changes and a host”. Most take it, as the ESV does, as relays of soldiers, wave after wave; either way the attack never lets up.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job ends where he began in chapter 3, wishing he had never been born, but this time he says it to God. Why did God bring him out of the womb at all? Better to have been carried straight from the womb to the grave (vv. 18–19). Since his days are few, he asks God to look away and leave him a little cheer before he goes to the land from which no one returns, a land of thick darkness and deep shadow, without order, where even the light is dark (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's land of deep shadow is not the last word about death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job returns to his wish never to have been born, but now he says it to God, and that is movement.

Why did you bring me out from the womb? In chapter 3 he cursed his day. Now he says “you”: the question has become a prayer. Job is still in the dark, but he is talking to God in it.

The deepest why. The deepest “why” ever spoken to God came from the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Jesus too prayed out of the darkness, and Scripture says “he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7). No believer’s why, prayed in faith, falls into an empty sky.

If you share this wish. Scripture does not hide that believers have wished they had never been born. But if the wish has become a thought of ending your life, tell someone today: a pastor, a doctor, a friend or a crisis line. Help from a biblical counsellor, with a medical check-up for any bodily cause, is part of God’s care, and medicine is no failure of faith (see the note on 3:20–22).

verseByVerse.quote: Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow, the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
