Job asks only for a little relief before he goes to the dark land of the dead, the very land on which, the prophets say, a great light has dawned.

Are not my days few? He asks only for “a little cheer”, the word of 9:27, the brighter face he could not put on, a short breathing space before he dies. Then he describes the grave: darkness piled on darkness, “without any order”, where even the light is dark. It is creation undone, the world before God said “Let there be light”, the dark Job wished on his birthday (3:4–5).

I shall not return. Job speaks of death as believers before Christ often did, as a land of no return. He sees dimly, but will soon reach further: “If a man dies, shall he live again?” (14:14), and at last, “in my flesh I shall see God” (19:26).

The land of darkness. Hear what the prophets say about that land: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone” (Isaiah 9:2). Isaiah’s “deep darkness” is Job’s “deep shadow”, the same Hebrew word, tsalmaveth. And Matthew says the light dawned when Jesus began to preach in Galilee: “for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned” (Matthew 4:16). The land Job dreads has been visited. Christ “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10).

keyVerse.quote: You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of his bitterest prayer Job names what God has truly been to him. His feelings say that God has turned enemy; God’s record says steadfast love, and Job holds on to the record. It is the faith of the whole book in one line, and the love it names went to the cross for us.

10.reflection:
Job says he will “give free utterance” to his complaint (v. 1), and God has put this prayer in Scripture. What is the difference between complaining to God and complaining about him? What would it look like for you to pray this honestly?

Job never learns why he suffered (vv. 2, 18). How can a believer be at peace without an answer? What has helped you, or someone you know, to trust God when the reason was hidden?

In the middle of his complaint Job says, “You have granted me life and steadfast love” (v. 12). Name, one by one, some kindnesses God has already shown you. How does remembering his record help when your feelings say he has turned against you?

Job dreads “the land of darkness and deep shadow” (v. 21). How do Isaiah 9:2 and the resurrection of Jesus change the way a Christian faces death?

11.title: Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right?<sup>3</sup>Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?<sup>4</sup>For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'<sup>5</sup>But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you,<sup>6</sup>and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.<sup>7</sup>"Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?<sup>8</sup>It is higher than heaven —what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know?<sup>9</sup>Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.<sup>10</sup>If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back?<sup>11</sup>For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?<sup>12</sup>But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!<sup>13</sup>"If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him.<sup>14</sup>If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents.<sup>15</sup>Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.<sup>16</sup>You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away.<sup>17</sup>And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.<sup>18</sup>And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security.<sup>19</sup>You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.<sup>20</sup>But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
11.overview:
Where we are. Zophar, the third friend, now speaks for the first time, answering Job’s speeches of chapters 9 and 10. Eliphaz appealed to a vision and Bildad to the wisdom of the fathers; Zophar is the bluntest of the three, and his speech closes the first round of the debate.

The message. Zophar’s message is that God is infinitely wise, has seen Job’s sin, and has given him less than he deserves; if Job repents, his darkness will turn to morning. Much of it is true, but it is spoken to the wrong man, and God will say the friends have not spoken rightly of him (42:7). Through it God shows us how truths we should confess about ourselves become cruelty when we pronounce them on someone else’s suffering, and that his mercy is never payment for a confession.

Why it was said. Zophar shares the friends’ tidy creed that God settles accounts in this life (see the introduction). He hears Job’s protests of innocence as arrogance and his laments as mockery (vv. 3–4).

How the chapter makes its case. First a rebuke (vv. 1–6): Job’s flood of words must not go unanswered; if God spoke, Job would learn that he is getting less than his guilt deserves. Then a hymn to God’s unsearchable wisdom, ending in an insult (vv. 7–12). Then an offer (vv. 13–20): if Job will set his heart right, stretch out his hands and put away his sin, his life will be brighter than noon and he will rest secure; but the wicked have no hope but death.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by an answer far beyond Zophar’s horizon. Zophar wished God would tell Job “the secrets of wisdom” (v. 6), and God did, in a way Zophar never imagined: the hidden wisdom of God is Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:7), the innocent one who received what the guilty deserve, so that the guilty might receive what they could never deserve. And the four dimensions Zophar uses to silence Job (vv. 8–9), Paul uses to measure “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:18–19).

For us. Confess about yourself what Zophar says to Job: God has dealt with you far more gently than your sins deserve, because their punishment fell on Christ. But never make that truth a verdict on someone else’s pain. When a sufferer’s words sound too long and too loud, hear them as a cry to be answered, not evidence to be used.
11.theology:
That God punishes us less than our sins deserve is a truth to confess about ourselves, not a verdict to pass on a sufferer. God had said Job suffered without reason, and in the end he condemned Zophar's speech.

God's depth and height are beyond finding out (vv. 7-9). Zophar uses them to silence Job; Paul uses the same four dimensions for the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.
11.examples: Zophar mocks Job's claim to be clean in God's eyes, which is what God himself said of him. He wishes God would speak, and God will, against Zophar. And he turns Job's own picture of the wild donkey into an insult.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — God Exacts of You Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar opens with a rebuke: Job has talked too much and too proudly, and someone must shame him. He hears Job’s laments as babble and mockery (vv. 2–3), and sums up Job’s case unfairly: “My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God’s eyes” (v. 4). Then he wishes that God would speak and show Job the secrets of his wisdom, sure that God would agree with him (vv. 5–6). His conclusion is the harshest line yet in the book: God has exacted from Job less than his guilt deserves (v. 6). The reader knows that God’s own verdict on Job was the very opposite (1:8).
verseByVerse.theology: The third friend goes further than the other two: Job, he says, is getting off lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right? Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar, the bluntest of the friends, hears Job’s laments as empty talk and mockery that someone must silence.

Zophar the Naamathite. Eliphaz appealed to a vision and Bildad to the fathers; Zophar appeals to nothing but his own certainty. What he adds to the friends’ case is harsher: Job deserves worse than he is getting.

Should your babble silence men? He hears Job’s speeches as babble, and his questions to God as mockery. That is how lament often sounds to people who are not suffering: too long, too loud, irreverent. But the man who has lost ten children has not said too much. He has said what he feels, to God, and God will take his words more seriously than Zophar does.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar sums up Job unfairly, and in mocking Job’s claim to be clean he mocks the verdict God himself has given.

My doctrine is pure. Job never claimed his doctrine was pure; he has been pleading with God, not lecturing on theology. He claimed to be innocent of anything that could explain this (9:21; 10:7). And here is the irony again: “clean in God’s eyes” is exactly what God said of him, “a blameless and upright man” (1:8). Zophar mocks as arrogance the verdict heaven has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you, and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar wishes God would speak, sure that God would tell Job he deserves even worse.

Oh, that God would speak. His wish will be granted: the LORD will speak (38:1), and when he has finished speaking to Job, he will turn to the friends and say, “you have not spoken of me what is right” (42:7).

The secrets of wisdom. The secrets of wisdom Zophar wished God would tell were told in the end, and they were not what he expected. “We impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory” (1 Corinthians 2:7), and Paul’s secret wisdom is Christ crucified, the innocent one who suffered for the guilty.

Less than your guilt deserves. You have earned more. It is true of every sinner before God. Ezra confessed, “you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved” (Ezra 9:13), and the psalmist sang, “He does not deal with us according to our sins” (Psalm 103:10). A believer may say that about himself on his knees, and should, knowing that what his sins deserved was laid on Christ. No one may say it about another person in pain. Zophar has taken a truth we confess about ourselves and made it a weapon against someone else.

Uncertain wording. “Manifold in understanding” is literally “double” in understanding, probably meaning that God’s wisdom has a hidden side as well as the side we see. The last line is unusual Hebrew: it probably means “God forgets (that is, overlooks) part of your guilt”, and the ESV’s “exacts of you less than your guilt deserves” gives that sense. Either way Zophar means that Job has got off lightly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Can You Find Out the Deep Things of God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar praises the unsearchable wisdom of God, and uses it to silence Job. No one can find out God’s limits: they are higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and broader than the sea (vv. 7–9). When God arrests a man and calls the court, no one can stop him, and he sees through worthless men even when they hide their sin (vv. 10–11). The section ends in a proverb meant as an insult: a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey’s colt is born a man (v. 12). Zophar does not notice that God’s unsearchable ways also rule out his own confident diagnosis of Job.
verseByVerse.theology: These are true words about God's greatness, used to shut a sufferer's mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven —what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s wisdom is beyond all measuring, which is true; but Zophar uses it to silence Job.

Higher than heaven. “Can you find out the deep things of God?” Up to the sky, down to the grave, out to the ends of the earth and across the sea: God’s wisdom fills every direction, and no one can measure it. This is true, and Zophar uses it to silence Job: you cannot understand God, so stop arguing with him. He does not notice that it applies to him too. If God’s ways cannot be found out, Zophar cannot find out why Job is suffering.

Paul’s four dimensions. Paul uses the same four dimensions, and uses them the other way. He prays that Christians “may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:18–19). God’s depth is not a wall to keep sufferers quiet. It is the size of the love that holds them.

verseByVerse.quote: If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back? For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it? But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can stop God when he brings a man to judgment, says Zophar, and Job is too foolish to see it.

Job’s own words thrown back. “If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back?” Job said these very things: “he passes by me” and “who can turn him back?” (9:11–12). Zophar hands Job’s words back to him: if Job admits God can do as he pleases, let him accept the verdict.

Will he not consider it? God does see what men hide, and the one thing he has seen in Job is integrity (2:3).

A wild donkey’s colt. The wild donkey born a man is a proverb for the impossible. Job had compared his cry to a wild donkey’s bray (6:5); Zophar throws the image back as an insult. When God speaks, he will talk about the wild donkey too, with pleasure, as a creature he set free (39:5). God is gentler with donkeys than Zophar is with his friend.

Uncertain wording. The proverb is hard Hebrew, with a play on words: an “empty” man will get a “heart”, that is, sense. The ESV takes it as an impossibility; some read it more hopefully, that even an empty-headed man may gain sense as a wild colt can be tamed. The ESV’s reading suits Zophar’s tone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — If You Prepare Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar ends with an offer and a warning. If Job will set his heart right, stretch out his hands in prayer and put away the sin in his hand and his tents (vv. 13–14), he will lift up his face without blemish and be free of fear (v. 15). His misery will pass like a flood that has drained away, his life will be brighter than noon, and he will lie down in hope and safety, with many seeking his favour (vv. 16–19). But the wicked will look in vain for escape, and their only hope will be death (v. 20). The promises are real gifts of God, but Zophar offers them as payment for a confession of sins Job has not committed.
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar's promises will largely come true, though not on his terms.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents. Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar’s counsel is right for a guilty man, but Job is not the man Zophar imagines.

Stretch out your hands toward him. Hands stretched out towards God is the posture of prayer. Zophar’s advice is good for anyone who has sinned: set your heart right, pray, put away what is wrong, and find the God who promised to forgive (Psalm 32:5). But it assumes what has not been shown, that Job has sinned. Job’s hands are not full of iniquity (16:17).

Without blemish. The phrase uses the word for the defect that barred an animal from sacrifice. Job will look God in the face again, but not because he confessed the sins Zophar imagined.

The face without blemish. Only one man has ever stood before God without blemish by right: Christ, offered “like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Because he was, those who trust him will be presented “blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24), their faces lifted not by their confession but by his sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away. And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning. And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security. You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar promises that repentance would turn Job’s darkness into morning; the promises are real, but they are gifts of grace, not wages.

Waters that have passed away. The misery will be like a flash flood that roared through the dry valley and is gone. Zophar reverses Job’s own words. Job described the grave as the place “where light is as thick darkness” (10:22); Zophar says that if he repents, his darkness will be like the morning. For those who belong to God it is even truer than he knew: “night will be no more … for the Lord God will be their light” (Revelation 22:5).

Because there is hope. Zophar promises hope, which Job said his days had run out of (7:6), and rest, which he could not find (3:26). As for “many will court your favor”, read the last chapter. The first to come asking for Job’s favour will be Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, with seven bulls and seven rams, needing his prayers (42:8–9).

None will make you afraid. This is the covenant blessing of Leviticus 26:6. Eliphaz reached for Deuteronomy’s curses to describe the wicked (5:14); Zophar reaches for Leviticus’ blessings to describe the repentant. Both assume that a man’s circumstances show where he stands with God. The blessings are real, and Micah sees them at last for all God’s people, “every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (Micah 4:4). But they are gifts of grace, not payment for a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked have only one hope left, to die, says Zophar, and he means Job.

Their hope is to breathe their last. The sting is in the tail. Job had said, “Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me” (6:8–9). Zophar has taken a sufferer’s cry of despair and turned it into a mark of the wicked.

A warning to every comforter. The things a person says in the worst hour are not a confession to be used against him. They are a cry to be answered. God answered Job’s, and he answers ours in Christ, who by his death came to “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15).

keyVerse.quote: Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?
keyVerse.note: Zophar asks a true question and draws the wrong conclusion. God is beyond our searching, which means that no one, Zophar included, can read his purposes in another person’s suffering. The same depths that Zophar uses to silence Job, Paul uses to measure the love of Christ (Ephesians 3:18–19).

11.reflection:
Zophar hears Job’s laments as “babble” and mockery (v. 3). Why does honest grief so often sound irreverent to people who are not suffering? How can we learn to hear it as God does?

“God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves” (v. 6) is true of every sinner, yet cruel when Zophar says it to Job. Why? How does the cross let us say it about ourselves with gratitude rather than dread?

Zophar uses the greatness of God to silence Job (vv. 7–9); Paul uses the same four dimensions to describe Christ’s love (Ephesians 3:18–19). Has God’s greatness ever felt like a wall to you? How does seeing it as the size of his love change things?

Zophar’s promises in vv. 13–19 are beautiful, but he makes them depend on Job’s confession. What is the difference between receiving God’s blessings as grace and expecting them as wages? Where do you tend to treat them as wages?

12.title: With God Are Wisdom and Might
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you.<sup>3</sup>But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?<sup>4</sup>I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock.<sup>5</sup>In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip.<sup>6</sup>The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.<sup>7</sup>"But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you;<sup>8</sup>or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you.<sup>9</sup>Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?<sup>10</sup>In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.<sup>11</sup>Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?<sup>12</sup>Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.<sup>13</sup>"With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding.<sup>14</sup>If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open.<sup>15</sup>If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land.<sup>16</sup>With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.<sup>17</sup>He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools.<sup>18</sup>He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips.<sup>19</sup>He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty.<sup>20</sup>He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders.<sup>21</sup>He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.<sup>22</sup>He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light.<sup>23</sup>He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away.<sup>24</sup>He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste.<sup>25</sup>They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
12.overview:
Where we are. Zophar has closed the first round of speeches by telling Job that he deserves worse than he is getting (11:6). Now Job begins his longest reply, running to chapter 14, and takes up the friends’ favourite theme, God’s wisdom and power, and turns it against them.

The message. Job’s message is that God’s rule is real, total and beyond anyone’s tracking. He holds every breath and overturns the wise and the mighty as he pleases. That is exactly why no one can read a man’s guilt from his circumstances. The friends know that God rules; they have not grasped that his rule is too large and too free to fit their formula, and that the wise are among those he humbles.

Why it was said. The friends have spoken as though they had wisdom to teach Job (11:6, 12), and have treated his suffering as proof of sin (see the introduction). Job, mocked by his comforters while robbers live in peace, answers that what they know is common knowledge, and that it does not prove what they think.

How the chapter makes its case. First sarcasm and complaint (vv. 1–6): I know all this too, yet I, a blameless man, am a laughingstock, while robbers live at peace. Then creation’s witness (vv. 7–12): every beast and bird knows that “the hand of the LORD has done this”, and every life is in his hand; a wise ear tests what it is told. Then a hymn to God’s wisdom and might (vv. 13–25): what he tears down no one rebuilds, and counsellors, kings, priests and whole nations are stripped and led away by him.

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly through the character of God revealed in him. The God who shuts a man in so that “none can open” (v. 14) is the God whose Son holds “the key of David, who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). The procession of the great led away stripped finds its climax at the cross, where the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, and God “put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). And the God who “brings deep darkness to light” (v. 22) will, when Christ returns, bring to light what is now hidden, including the innocence of those the world has wrongly judged (1 Corinthians 4:5).

For us. Believe that God rules everything, as Job does, but never turn his rule into a formula for reading other people’s lives: prosperity does not prove the wicked right, and suffering does not prove the sufferer wrong. Leave the judging of hearts to the Lord who will bring everything to light, and trust the hand that holds your breath (v. 10).
12.theology:
Wisdom and might belong to God, not to the aged or the learned (v. 13), and he overturns every human wisdom that thinks it has him measured (1 Cor 1:19-20). Job's one use of the covenant name in the debate is to confess that the hand of the LORD has done this (v. 9).

Because God brings deep darkness to light (v. 22), no one should pronounce judgment on another's heart before the time.
12.examples: Job meets the friends with sarcasm, wisdom will die with you, and with a sharp observation: the comfortable always despise the man who slips. Elihu will later borrow a line of this speech almost word for word, and a psalmist joins two of its lines into one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wisdom Will Die with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job answers three speeches with biting sarcasm, and then with a complaint. Wisdom, he says, will surely die with the friends; but he understands as much as they do, and what they have said is common knowledge (vv. 1–3). The real puzzle is his own position: a man who called on God and was answered, a just and blameless man, has become a laughingstock to his friends (v. 4). Those at ease always despise the one who slips (v. 5), while robbers and those who defy God live in peace and security (v. 6). If suffering proves guilt, prosperity should prove innocence, and it plainly does not.
verseByVerse.theology: Job's first answer to the friends' wisdom is to notice what it has made of him: a joke.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you. But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends have told Job nothing he did not already know; the fault in their wisdom is not that it is new to him, but that it is used on the wrong man.

Wisdom will die with you. After three speeches from three friends, Job answers with sarcasm, and then plainly: “Who does not know such things as these?” The friends have been telling Job what he taught others for years (4:3–4).

The first round closes. This speech closes the first round of the debate, and it is Job’s longest yet, running to the end of chapter 14. Here he takes the friends’ own subject, God’s wisdom and power, and shows that it cuts against them.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock. In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip. The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job, a blameless man who prayed and was answered, has become a joke to his comforters while robbers live in peace; so suffering cannot be the proof of guilt the friends suppose.

A laughingstock to my friends. The man who prayed and was answered, whom God himself called blameless (1:1), is now a joke to the men who came to comfort him.

Contempt for misfortune. Job observes sharply that contempt is always waiting for the one who stumbles. The psalmist knew it: “Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease” (Psalm 123:4). The friends are at ease, their homes standing and their children alive. It is easy, from there, to explain why someone else’s fell.

The tents of robbers are at peace. And look at the facts, says Job: plenty of wicked men are doing very well, their god their own strength, as the prophet said of Babylon, “whose own might is their god” (Habakkuk 1:11). Asaph nearly lost his faith over the same sight: “For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:3). If suffering proves guilt, prosperity should prove innocence, and it plainly does not.

Uncertain wording. Verses 5 and 6 are hard Hebrew. In v. 5 the word the ESV takes as “for misfortune” can also be read as “a torch”, which gave older versions “a lamp despised”; either way, the one who slips meets contempt. The end of v. 6 is literally “who brings God in his hand”. Most take it, as the ESV does, of men whose god is what they hold in their hand, their own strength; others read “whom God has brought into his hand”, that is, made prosperous. Both readings make Job’s point: the wicked can flourish.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns the friends’ wisdom into something any creature knows. Ask the beasts, the birds, the earth and the fish: all of them know that “the hand of the LORD has done this” (vv. 7–9), the one time in the whole debate that God’s covenant name is spoken. Every life and every human breath is in his hand (v. 10). Then Job asks his hearers to test what they are told, as the palate tastes food (v. 11), and quotes the friends’ confidence that wisdom belongs to the old (v. 12), only to answer it in the next verse: wisdom belongs to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The beasts know what the friends have missed: every life is in God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you; or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you. Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every creature knows what the friends think is their special wisdom: all that happens comes from the hand of the LORD, who holds every life and every breath.

Ask the beasts, and they will teach you. The friends claim wisdom, but every animal in the field knows as much. Creation itself testifies that everything that happens comes from God’s hand. That is not a secret the friends discovered.

The hand of the LORD has done this. Mark the name. “The LORD”, God’s covenant name, appears nowhere else in the debate from chapter 3 to chapter 37. Here, once, Job’s deepest conviction breaks through in the name God gave his people, in the very words of Isaiah: “that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it” (Isaiah 41:20). His suffering came through the LORD’s hand. That is his agony, and it is also his one firm ground: the LORD is still in charge.

In his hand is the life of every living thing. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God “gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25), and the New Testament names the Son as the one in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). Every breath Job draws on the ash heap is given by the God he argues with.

Textual note. A few Hebrew manuscripts read “God” here instead of “the LORD”.
verseByVerse.note: “The bushes of the earth” may be rendered “speak to the earth” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food? Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Test what you are told, says Job; and the friends’ boast that wisdom comes with age is answered at once: wisdom is with God.

Testing words. “Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?” Job said something like it before (6:30). The ear can tell good words from bad, as the tongue can tell good food from spoiled. Test what you are being told. Elihu will later quote this line almost word for word (34:3).

Where wisdom lies. “Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.” Taken alone it sounds like a proverb Job agrees with. But the next line answers it: “With God are wisdom and might” (v. 13). Job is probably repeating the grey-haired friends’ confidence in their years, to set it against the real source of wisdom. Elihu, the youngest man present, will say it outright: “It is not the old who are wise” (32:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — With God Are Wisdom and Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s hymn to God’s wisdom and might is the centre of the chapter, and its point is that God’s rule is beyond anyone’s tracking. What he tears down, no one rebuilds; whom he shuts in, no one releases; drought and flood are his, and so are the deceived and the deceiver (vv. 13–16). Then comes a procession of the great humbled by him: counsellors and judges, kings and priests, the trusted and the elders, princes and the strong, all stripped and led away (vv. 17–21). He brings hidden things to light, raises and destroys nations, and leaves their leaders groping like drunken men (vv. 22–25). Since God overturns the wise and the mighty, no one can read a man’s guilt from his fall.
verseByVerse.theology: Job's God overturns the wise and the powerful, and that includes any theology, the friends' among them, that thinks it has him measured.

verseByVerse.quote: "With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding. If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open. If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land. With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom and power belong to God, no one can undo what he does, and even the deceiver is under his rule.

With God are wisdom and might. This is Job’s main point: wisdom is not with the old men but with God, and the rest of the chapter is a hymn to prove it.

The key of David. “If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open.” No one reverses God. Isaiah uses similar words of a steward given the key of David’s house (Isaiah 22:22), and Jesus takes them as his own title: “the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens” (Revelation 3:7). The one who holds the keys that no one can overrule is Christ, and for his people he keeps the door open.

The deceived and the deceiver are his. Drought and flood are both his. Even deception is not outside his rule. The reader thinks of the accuser in the council, whom Revelation calls “the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9). He too is on God’s leash, going only as far as he is let.

What it does not mean. This does not make God a deceiver or the author of evil: “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). It means that no lie and no liar is beyond his rule, and none will escape his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools. He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips. He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty. He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders. He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God humbles the great of every kind, stripping counsellors, kings and priests like captives, so that the wise can claim no immunity.

He leads counselors away stripped. Job pictures a procession of the great, marched off in shame: counsellors and judges made fools, priests led away, elders who lose their judgment. God undoes the authority by which kings bound others, and ties a captive’s loincloth round their own waists. It happened whenever empires fell.

Aimed at the friends. The point is aimed at the friends: if they think wisdom guarantees their standing, God strips the wise. Paul says the same of every clever system that sets itself up against God: “Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? … Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). And the psalmist joined two of Job’s lines: “he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes” (Psalm 107:40; compare vv. 21, 24).

The procession has a victor. The picture of the great led away stripped, in shame, is the picture Paul uses for the cross. There the rulers of this age did their worst: “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). And there God “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The procession Job describes has a victor at its head, and it is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light. He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away. He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste. They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God drags hidden things into the light and raises and ruins whole nations, so no one can read a man’s guilt from his circumstances.

Brings deep darkness to light. The deep darkness Job called down on his birthday (3:5) is the very thing God drags into the daylight. It is a warning to the friends and a promise to Job. Paul turns it on everyone who judges another’s heart too soon: “do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness” (1 Corinthians 4:5). The friends have done exactly that. God will bring to light what was hidden, and what comes to light will be Job’s innocence.

He makes nations great. Whole nations rise and fall at his word, and their leaders grope in the dark like drunkards, the curse of Deuteronomy that Eliphaz used against Job (5:14). Job’s reply is that it falls on kings and nations and wise men too, and no one can read a man’s guilt from it. God rules the whole world, and that is exactly why no one can track his ways by counting who is suffering.

keyVerse.quote: With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding.
keyVerse.note: This is the thesis of Job’s hymn and his answer to the friends’ claim to wisdom. Wisdom does not belong to the old or the clever but to God, whose ways are too great for any formula. In Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), that wisdom has come to us in person.

12.reflection:
Job is “a laughingstock” to his friends, and observes that those at ease always despise the one who slips (vv. 4–5). Why is it so easy to explain other people’s troubles when our own lives are going well? How can we guard against it?

“The tents of robbers are at peace” (v. 6). How do Job’s words here, and Psalm 73, help us when we see the wicked prosper and the faithful suffer?

Job says every creature knows that “the hand of the LORD has done this” (v. 9), and that the same hand holds every breath (v. 10). How can this be both Job’s agony and his comfort? Which is it for you at present?

Job pictures the wise and the mighty stripped and led away (vv. 17–21), and Paul sees the rulers of this age shamed at the cross (Colossians 2:15). What difference does it make to you that Christ holds the keys no one can overrule (Revelation 3:7)?

13.title: Though He Slay Me
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it.<sup>2</sup>What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.<sup>3</sup>But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.<sup>4</sup>As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all.<sup>5</sup>Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!<sup>6</sup>Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips.<sup>7</sup>Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him?<sup>8</sup>Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?<sup>9</sup>Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man?<sup>10</sup>He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality.<sup>11</sup>Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you?<sup>12</sup>Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.<sup>13</sup>"Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may.<sup>14</sup>Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?<sup>15</sup>Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.<sup>16</sup>This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.<sup>17</sup>Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears.<sup>18</sup>Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right.<sup>19</sup>Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.<sup>20</sup>Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face:<sup>21</sup>withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me.<sup>22</sup>Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.<sup>23</sup>How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin.<sup>24</sup>Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?<sup>25</sup>Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff?<sup>26</sup>For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.<sup>27</sup>You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet.<sup>28</sup>Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
13.overview:
Where we are. Zophar, the bluntest of the three friends, has just told Job that God exacts less than his guilt deserves and that he must put away his iniquity (11:6, 14). Job’s answer runs from chapter 12 to chapter 14, the last speech of the first round of debate. In chapter 12 he mocked the friends’ wisdom and praised God’s sovereign power; now he turns from them to God.

The message. God does not want lies told on his behalf, and he would rather be argued with honestly than defended dishonestly. Job refuses the friends’ tidy explanations and resolves to take his case to God himself, whatever it costs: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (v. 15). The chapter shows a faith that clings to God even when God seems to be the enemy, and it leaves us longing for someone who could answer Job’s question about his sins and God’s hidden face.

Why it was said. The friends assume that God always repays in this life, so a great sufferer must be a great sinner (see the introduction). To keep that belief intact they must find guilt in Job. Job knows, as the reader does from the prologue (1:8; 2:3), that no sin of his explains what has happened.

How the chapter makes its case. First Job turns on the friends (vv. 1–12). He knows all they know; they are plasterers whitewashing a cracked wall and doctors who make the patient worse. Worse, they are lying for God, and God, who searches hearts, will rebuke them; their maxims are ashes. Then he resolves to speak, whatever comes (vv. 13–19): he will put his life in his hand, he will hope in God though God kill him, and he has his case ready. Last he speaks to God directly (vv. 20–28): lift your hand, let us talk, show me my sins, and tell me why you hide your face and treat me as your enemy, chasing a dry leaf and writing bitter things against me.

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Job’s words, “Who is there who will contend with me?” (v. 19), are taken up by the suffering Servant (Isaiah 50:8–9), and Paul gives them to every believer: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). Job asks to see the record of his sins; the gospel tells where the believer’s record went, “nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). And Job, God’s friend treated as an enemy, foreshadows the Son who was treated as God’s enemy so that real enemies could be reconciled (Romans 5:10).

For us. When God seems to hide his face, bring your complaint to him, not away from him; the honest prayer of a hurting believer honours God more than a pious lie. When you sit with sufferers, do not defend God by inventing their guilt. And when your sins accuse you, remember that in Christ the charge sheet has been cancelled and no accuser can stand.
13.theology:
God does not need lies told in his defence, and Job's warning that God will rebuke the friends for them is fulfilled at the end (42:7). Job will go to God even at the cost of his life (v. 15), and Paul borrows his words when facing death.

Job's challenge, who will contend with me?, becomes the Servant's and then the Christian's (Rom 8:33-34). The record written against us has been nailed to the cross.
13.examples: Job's pictures of his friends are vivid: plasterers smearing whitewash over cracks, and doctors who leave a sick man worse. His question Will you speak falsely for God? sums up the book's judgment on them. And when he turns to God, his deepest pain is the one the psalms know best: the hidden face.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the friends, in defending God, have lied about him, and God will hold them to account for it. He begins by refusing to be talked down to: he knows all they know, and he would rather argue his case with the Almighty than with them (vv. 1–3). Then he names their failure in two pictures: plasterers who whitewash a cracked wall, and doctors who make the patient worse; their wisest course would be silence (vv. 4–5). He presses the charge: will they speak falsely for God and plead his case with partiality (vv. 6–8)? God searches hearts and will rebuke such flattery; their maxims are ashes and their defences clay (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job tells the friends they are lying on God's behalf, and that God will hold them to account for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it. What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job knows the friends’ theology as well as they do, and he is done arguing with them: he wants to argue his case with God.

I desire to argue my case with God. “Argue my case” comes from the same Hebrew root as the “arbiter” of 9:33 and God’s own “let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18). Job wants a hearing in the highest court; the friends want to settle his case without one.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all. Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends have covered the truth with comfortable lies and made a suffering man worse; their wisest course would be silence.

You whitewash with lies. First, plasterers smearing whitewash over a crumbling wall to hide the cracks. Ezekiel used it for the false prophets who said, “Peace,” when there is no peace, and smeared a flimsy wall “with whitewash” (Ezekiel 13:10). Then, doctors who have made a sick man worse.

He does not whitewash; he heals. There is a Physician who does not fail: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17).

Oh that you would keep silent. Proverbs agrees: “even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise” (Proverbs 17:28). The friends were wisest in the seven days when they said nothing (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips. Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him? Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To defend God, the friends must invent guilt in Job, and that is speaking falsely for God, which he does not want.

Will you speak falsely for God? They plead God’s case as if he needed a lawyer, and tell lies on his behalf. Every attempt to protect God’s reputation by bending the truth about a sufferer is this sin. A pastor who says “this must be for something you did”, without knowing it, to keep his theology tidy, is speaking falsely for God.

Does faith mean pretending? Many suspect that religion survives by not looking too hard, explaining away every tragedy and defending God with any argument that comes to hand. Job’s friends are that kind of believer, and the surprise of this book is that God is against them. At the end the LORD says that Job, the man who protested, accused and demanded a hearing, spoke of him what is right, and the men who defended him did not (42:7). God does not want a faith that lasts only as long as its eyes are shut; he would rather be argued with honestly than flattered, because he is the truth. The One who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), did not meet Thomas’s doubt by sending him away, but by showing him his wounds (John 20:27). A faith that has met him can afford to look at everything, the ash heap included.

verseByVerse.quote: Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man? He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality. Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you? Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God searches hearts and will not be flattered; he will rebuke those who lie in his defence, and their maxims will blow away like ash.

Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Taking God’s side does not put God on yours. When he has finished speaking to Job, he turns to Eliphaz: “My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (42:7).

Proverbs of ashes. Job sits in the ashes, and their sayings are ash too: dry, weightless, blown away. Their defences are clay walls that crumble at a touch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he will take his case to God himself, whatever it costs him, because he hopes in God and nowhere else. He asks the friends to be quiet and lets come what may (v. 13); he will risk his life to speak (v. 14). Then come the famous words, “Though he slay me, I will hope in him”, with the resolve to argue his ways to God’s face (v. 15). His very wish to stand before God is a sign that he is not godless (v. 16). He asks them to keep listening, for his case is prepared and he is sure of the verdict; if anyone could prove a charge against him, he would fall silent and die (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Job will go to God though it kills him, sure that the godless could not come before him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may. Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job will speak to God though it may cost him his life.

Put my life in my hand. To “put my life in my hand” is to risk everything, as Jephthah did going out to battle (Judges 12:3). Bringing his case before God may cost Job his life, and he will do it anyway.

Uncertain wording. “Take my flesh in my teeth” is found only here, and its exact sense is not known. It probably says the same as the next line with another picture: an animal carrying its prey in its mouth, ready to lose it at any moment. Some translations read the verse as a statement rather than a question (“I will take my flesh in my teeth”). Either way, Job knows he is risking everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if God kills him, Job will not turn from God to anyone else: he will hope in God and bring his case to God’s face.

Though he slay me, I will hope in him. Some of the best-loved words in the book: on the ESV’s reading (and the KJV’s familiar “yet will I trust in him”), a hope that looks through death to God himself.

I will argue my ways to his face. On either reading of the first line (see the textual note below), the second half stands. Job will go to God. This is the answer to Satan’s question at its sharpest (1:9): a man with nothing left to gain from God, not even his life, who still insists on God.

Father, into your hands. The Christian says Job’s words with more light. Jesus, dying, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). The Father did let him die, and Jesus hoped in him, and was raised. Because of that, a believer can say Job’s words on his own deathbed and mean them fully.

Textual note. The Hebrew has a well-known difficulty here. The written consonants read “not”; the scribes noted in the margin that it was to be read “in him”, two words that sound the same in Hebrew. The ESV’s text follows the margin. Read the other way (the ESV’s note), it says: he will kill me; I have no hope; but I will still argue my ways to his face. Even on that darker reading, Job refuses to turn from God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative: “Behold, he will slay me; I have no hope.”

verseByVerse.quote: This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s very desire to stand before God shows that he is not godless, for no godless man would dare to come.

This will be my salvation. Job wants nothing more than a hearing before God, and that itself shows he is not godless. His “salvation” here means his rescue, his vindication.

Paul in prison. Paul, writing from prison, not knowing whether he would be executed, borrows this verse’s words as the Greek Old Testament gives them: “this will turn out for my deliverance”, and goes on to Job’s hope in the face of death, “that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death” (Philippians 1:19–20). He read himself into Job’s place: a righteous man in chains, sure of God’s vindication in life or death.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears. Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right. Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has his case ready and is sure that no charge against him will stand; in Christ every believer can say the same.

I have prepared my case. It is a bold claim, and Job will learn that being right about his innocence is not the same as being right about God (40:8). But he is not wrong that no charge will stand.

Who is there who will contend with me? These words sound again in Isaiah, on the lips of the Servant of the LORD, beaten and spat upon: “He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? … Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up” (Isaiah 50:8–9). It is the same challenge, with the same moth-eaten garment that ends this chapter (v. 28). And Paul hands the Servant’s words to every Christian: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Romans 8:33–34). Job’s lonely defiance became the Servant’s confidence, and the Servant’s confidence became ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Why Do You Hide Your Face?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he longs for a hearing with God, and cannot understand why God treats him as an enemy. He asks two things: that God would lift his crushing hand and not terrify him, so that they can speak (vv. 20–22). Then he asks to be shown his sins, and to be told why God hides his face (vv. 23–24). He feels hunted like a driven leaf, as though God were writing bitter charges against him and digging up the sins of his youth (vv. 25–26). He is a prisoner in the stocks, every step watched, and man wastes away like a moth-eaten coat (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks to see the charge sheet. The Christian knows where the record against him went.

verseByVerse.quote: Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks God to lift his crushing hand and stop terrifying him, so that they can speak together.

Only grant me two things. Now Job speaks to God, with the same two requests as at 9:34: take your hand off me, and do not overwhelm me with terror. Then they can talk.

Then call, and I will answer. God may question him, or Job may speak first. God will take the first: from the whirlwind he says, “I will question you, and you make it known to me” (38:3), and Job will find that he has nothing to answer. The hearing he longs for will not go the way he imagines; it will be better.

verseByVerse.quote: How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin. Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks God to name any sin that explains his suffering, and to say why he hides his face and treats Job as an enemy.

Make me know my transgression and my sin. If he has sinned, let God name it. Every honest believer can pray this: “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23). Job is not hiding from any sin he might have; he cannot find one that explains this.

Why do you hide your face? The hidden face is the deepest pain in the psalms: “How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). And a Hebrew reader would hear a play on words: “enemy” is oyev, and Job’s name is Iyyov. Why do you treat Job as if he were your enemy?

Count me as your enemy. The gospel turns the question round. God did count us as enemies, and we were: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). Job was not God’s enemy, and felt treated as one; Christ was not God’s enemy, and was treated as one, so that God’s real enemies could be made his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff? For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job feels hunted like a dead leaf, as though God were writing up charges against him and adding the sins of his youth; for the believer, that record has been cancelled at the cross.

Will you frighten a driven leaf? Why would the Almighty chase something as small as a dead leaf or a bit of chaff? The picture comes from the covenant curses: “The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight” (Leviticus 26:36). Again Job feels treated as one of the cursed.

The iniquities of my youth. God seems to be adding the sins of Job’s youth to the charge sheet. Job does not deny them; he asks why they are brought up now. David prayed, “Remember not the sins of my youth” (Psalm 25:7).

The record cancelled. There was a written record against us, and it was real. Paul tells us what God did with it: “canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). The bitter things written against the believer are not being added to. They have been nailed up and cancelled.

verseByVerse.quote: You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet. Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job feels like a prisoner in the stocks, every step watched, while his life rots away like a moth-eaten coat.

You put my feet in the stocks. That is how his illness feels: a prisoner whose every step is watched. Paul and Silas once sat with their “feet in the stocks” in a Philippian jail, and at midnight they were “praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:24–25). The stocks do not have the last word over God’s people.

Like a garment that is moth-eaten. Man rots like old wood and falls to holes like a moth-eaten coat, which leads into chapter 14. It is the image the Servant uses, not of himself, but of his accusers: “the moth will eat them up” (Isaiah 50:9).

Uncertain wording. “You set a limit for the soles of my feet” is obscure; the Hebrew says something like “you mark yourself on the roots of my feet”. It may mean God draws a line his prisoner cannot cross, or marks his feet like a slave’s, or traces every footprint. In verse 28 the Hebrew says “he” rather than “man”; the line seems to begin chapter 14’s lament for mankind. The overall picture is clear: Job feels hemmed in and watched.

keyVerse.quote: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.
keyVerse.note: Here is the heart of Job’s faith: he will not turn from God to anyone else, even if God takes his life. It answers Satan’s question (1:9) at its sharpest, and it finds its fullest voice in Jesus, who died committing his spirit into his Father’s hands and was raised (Luke 23:46).

13.reflection:
Job accuses the friends of speaking “falsely for God” (v. 7). In what ways are Christians tempted to defend God with explanations that are not true, and why does God not want that kind of defence?

“Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (v. 15). What does it look like to hope in God when he seems to be the cause of your pain? How does Jesus’ death and resurrection give these words a fuller meaning?

Job asks God, “Make me know my transgression and my sin” (v. 23). How can we pray Psalm 139:23 honestly without assuming that every hardship is punishment for a particular sin?

Job feels that God is writing “bitter things” against him (v. 26). How does Colossians 2:14 answer the fear that God is keeping a record of your sins?

14.title: If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble.<sup>2</sup>He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.<sup>3</sup>And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you?<sup>4</sup>Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.<sup>5</sup>Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass,<sup>6</sup>look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.<sup>7</sup>"For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease.<sup>8</sup>Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil,<sup>9</sup>yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.<sup>10</sup>But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?<sup>11</sup>As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up,<sup>12</sup>so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.<sup>13</sup>Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!<sup>14</sup>If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.<sup>15</sup>You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands.<sup>16</sup>For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin;<sup>17</sup>my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.<sup>18</sup>"But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place;<sup>19</sup>the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.<sup>20</sup>You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away.<sup>21</sup>His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not.<sup>22</sup>He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
14.overview:
Where we are. This chapter ends Job’s long reply to Zophar (chapters 12–14) and with it the first round of the debate. In chapter 13 Job turned from the friends to speak to God directly, asking why God hides his face and pursues a man who is no more than a driven leaf. Now he widens his view from himself to every human being.

The message. Human life is short, troubled and stained, and death seems final: a felled tree may sprout again, but a man lies down and does not rise. Yet in the middle of his grief Job dares to ask the question that only God can answer, “If a man dies, shall he live again?” (v. 14), and for a moment he glimpses a God who would call him out of the grave, long for the work of his hands and cover his sin. The chapter shows how deep our need is, and lets the first light of resurrection hope break into the book.

Why it was said. Job has lost his children and his health, and expects to die soon (see the introduction). The friends have promised him restoration in this life if he repents (11:13–19), but Job sees no future this side of the grave. His question is not idle speculation; it is the question of a dying man who has buried ten children.

How the chapter makes its case. First Job laments the human condition (vv. 1–6): man is few of days and full of trouble, no one born unclean can be clean, and God has fixed his limits, so let God leave him in peace for his little day. Then he compares a man with a tree (vv. 7–12): a stump sprouts at the scent of water, but a man dies and will not wake till the heavens are no more. Then hope flares (vv. 13–17): Job pictures God hiding him in Sheol until wrath is past, then calling him, longing for him and sealing his sins away. Last the hope is worn away like stone under water (vv. 18–22), and the dead man is left knowing nothing of his sons and feeling only his own pain.

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need the chapter exposes and the answer God later gives. Job’s question is not a prophecy, but the New Testament answers it with a person: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The Son of God was himself “born of woman” (Galatians 4:4), the one clean child to come out of the unclean, and in him God does what Job only imagined: he calls the dead from their tombs (John 5:28–29) and covers sin for ever.

For us. We need not pretend that death is small or grief brief; Job does not. But we grieve with a hope Job only glimpsed: our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), and the voice that will call us out of the grave is his. When hope flickers and goes out again, as it does here, do not despise the flicker; it will return.
14.theology:
No one born of woman is clean (v. 4), except the one born of woman who was holy. The first flash of resurrection hope in the book (vv. 13-17) is answered in Christ, the first to rise from the dead, whose voice all in the tombs will hear.

Job hopes to have his sin covered (v. 17), and that is exactly what God does with sin.
14.examples: Job's images stay with the reader: a flower wilting by evening, a stump sprouting at the scent of water, a lake drained in summer, a sentry waiting for his relief. Even his word for never, till the heavens are no more, turns out to have a date.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Few of Days and Full of Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that every human life is brief, troubled and unclean, so why should God watch it so closely? He begins with the frailty of all mankind: born of a woman, few of days, full of trouble, like a flower that withers and a shadow that passes (vv. 1–2). Then he asks why God should fix his eyes on such a creature and bring him to judgment, when no one born unclean can make himself clean (vv. 3–4). Since God has already set the number of a man’s days, Job pleads that God would look away and let him enjoy his short day in peace, like a hired labourer at the end of his shift (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job speaks for every human being: short-lived, troubled and unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble. He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every human being is frail and mortal, and his short life is full of trouble; the Son of God took that life on himself.

Few of days and full of trouble. Job widens his view to every human being. “Born of a woman” means weak and mortal; “few of days” means life is short; “full of trouble” picks up the last word of chapter 3 (3:26). A flower wilts by evening; a shadow slides across the ground and is gone.

He comes out like a flower and withers. Isaiah heard the same and added what Job could not yet say: “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8), and Peter tells the church that this word is the gospel (1 Peter 1:25).

Born of woman. There is a greater answer in the first phrase: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman” (Galatians 4:4). The Son of God took on the short, troubled life that Job describes, so that those born of women could be born of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you? Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God demands perfect purity, no one born of sinful parents could pass; only one clean child ever came out of the unclean.

Do you open your eyes on such a one? Why would the Almighty fix his eyes on so brief a creature and haul him into court? As in 7:17–19, God’s attention feels like prosecution.

Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Job knows that no one born of a woman is pure: sin is passed down the whole human family. David said it of himself: “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5). Job is not claiming to be sinless; he means that by that standard no human being could pass.

One clean thing did come out. Yet once, one clean thing did come out of the unclean. The angel said to Mary, “the child to be born will be called holy” (Luke 1:35), the Son of God. Job’s “there is not one” was true of every child ever born until that one, the only man who could stand God’s scrutiny, and he stood it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass, look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has fixed the length of every life, and Job asks only that he may have his few days in peace.

His days are determined. Job does not dispute God’s right to number his days; the psalmist rejoiced in it: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). His plea is that, since his days are counted and few, God would look away and let him have what a hired labourer gets at the end of his shift: a little rest before the day is over (7:1–2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — There Is Hope for a Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that a tree has more hope than a man, for a stump can sprout again but a man who dies does not rise. He describes a felled tree whose old root and dead stump bud again at the first scent of water (vv. 7–9). Then he sets a man beside it: he dies, breathes his last, and is gone, like a lake drained dry in summer (vv. 10–11). He lies down and will not wake until the heavens are no more (v. 12). Job means “never”, but Scripture will take the phrase at its word: the heavens will one day pass away, and on that day the sleepers will wake.
verseByVerse.theology: Job sees more hope for a stump than for a man. God's answer is a risen Messiah, and a day when the heavens will pass away and the sleepers wake.

verseByVerse.quote: "For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease. Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil, yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A felled tree can sprout again; Job wonders whether a man has even that much hope, and in Christ he has far more.

There is hope for a tree. “Hope” is what Job said his life had run out of (7:6); a tree has it, but has a man?

A shoot from the stump. Many Christians have set Isaiah’s stump beside it: Isaiah foresaw the royal line of David cut down to a stump, and promised, “There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1). That promise is about a royal house, not one man’s grave; but the Messiah from that stump was himself cut down and rose from the grave, and his rising answers Job’s question. There is hope for a tree; there is more for a man in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he? As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up, so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who dies seems gone for good, and will not wake “till the heavens are no more”; Scripture says that day will come.

Man breathes his last, and where is he? A man is not like the tree, but like a lake drained in summer.

Till the heavens are no more. Job means “never”. Scripture takes him at his word and gives it a date: “the heavens will pass away with a roar” (2 Peter 3:10), and John saw “a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away” (Revelation 21:1). On the day the heavens are no more, the sleepers wake. Jesus called death sleep in the same way, and meant it hopefully: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him” (John 11:11).

Do the dead sleep without awareness until the resurrection? Job speaks of what is seen at the grave. The New Testament adds what he could not yet see clearly: the believer who dies is “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), with Christ at once (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23). “Sleep” describes the body; the person is awake with God, waiting for the body’s rising.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is a daring hope: perhaps God will keep him safe in the grave and then call him back to life. He asks God to hide him in Sheol until his wrath has passed, to set a time and remember him (v. 13). Then comes the great question, “If a man dies, shall he live again?”, and his resolve to wait out his hard service like a sentry waiting to be relieved (v. 14). He imagines God calling and himself answering, God longing for the work of his hands, watching his steps kindly, and sealing up his sins and covering them for ever (vv. 15–17). It is the first light of resurrection hope in the book.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first flash of resurrection hope in the book, and Jesus will make it certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job dares to imagine the grave as a hiding place where God keeps him until his wrath is past and then remembers him.

Hide me in Sheol. Sheol is the place of the dead. Here hope breaks through: Job imagines it as a shelter where God keeps him until the storm of wrath has passed, then sets a day to come and get him. Isaiah uses the same picture for God’s people: “hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by” (Isaiah 26:20).

Hidden with Christ. The Christian knows where that hiding place is: “your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). And he knows the answer to “remember me”. A dying thief on a cross said it, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), and was told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

verseByVerse.quote: If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks whether the dead will live again, and resolves to wait in hope like a sentry for his relief; Christ’s resurrection is God’s answer.

If a man dies, shall he live again? Not a statement of doctrine, but a man daring to hope. “My service” is the soldier’s “hard service” of 7:1. There it was hopeless drudgery; here it is a sentry waiting for the change of guard.

The first sheaf of the harvest. The New Testament answers his question with a person: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20); the first sheaf of the harvest, with the rest to follow. And Paul describes that relief: “we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52). The relief Job waited for is coming, and it will come with a trumpet.

Uncertain wording. “Renewal” translates a word that means “change” or “replacement”. It is used of changes of clothing and of shifts of workers, so the ESV’s note offers “relief”, the guard who takes over the watch. Either way, Job waits for what God will bring.
verseByVerse.note: “Renewal” may be rendered “relief” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands. For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin; my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job pictures God calling him from the grave, longing for him and covering his sin for ever: his tenderest hope, and the gospel’s own.

You would long for the work of your hands. God would call to him out of the grave, and he would answer. And God would long for him, as a craftsman misses the work he made (10:3, 8). Jesus said the call would come: “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29).
