Sealed up in a bag. God would still “number my steps”, but as a father watches a child walk, not as a guard watches a prisoner. His sins would be “sealed up in a bag”, like a legal document tied, sealed and put away, never to be opened again.

You would cover over my iniquity. “Cover over” is the verb of 13:4, where Job said the friends “whitewash with lies”. The friends plaster lies over the truth about Job; Job hopes that God will cover his sin so it is seen no more. That is the gospel’s own hope: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1); “You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Destroy the Hope of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the hope he has just glimpsed seems to be worn away by God himself. Mountains crumble, rocks shift, and running water grinds stones and carries off the soil; so God destroys man’s hope (vv. 18–19). God overpowers a man for ever, changes his face in death and sends him away (v. 20). He will never know whether his sons rise to honour or sink into disgrace; he feels only his own pain and mourns only for himself (vv. 21–22). The first round of the debate ends in darkness, but the hope will return, stronger, in chapter 19.
verseByVerse.theology: The hope flickers and goes out again, but it will come back stronger.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place; the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the hope fades: as water wears away stone, so God seems to wear away man’s hope.

So you destroy the hope of man. Mountains crumble, and running water grinds stone smooth; hope is worn down the same way, slowly and completely.

How faith often moves. A flash of hope comes, like verses 13–17, and then the old grief rolls back in. The believer should not despise the flash because it did not last. Job’s hope will come back, steadier, five chapters on: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away. His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not. He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death cuts a man off from everything he loved, even news of his children; the speech ends in darkness, yet the call from the grave will come.

You change his countenance. Whatever becomes of his children, honour or disgrace, the dead man will never know; “the dead know nothing”, as the Preacher says, meaning they have no more share in what is done under the sun (Ecclesiastes 9:5–6). These are the words of a man whose sons are all dead, who would give anything for news of them.

The bleakest ending yet. But in the middle of the chapter we heard a man imagining God calling him out of the grave. That call was not imagination. Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25), and the voice that will call is his.

Uncertain wording. Verse 22 is literally “his flesh upon him has pain, and his soul upon him mourns”. It may mean that the dead feel only their own misery, or that the dying man knows only his body’s pain; the ESV takes it of the dead man’s narrowed world. Either way, Job sees in death nothing but loss; it is not his last word on the subject (19:25–27).

keyVerse.quote: If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.
keyVerse.note: Here a grieving man asks the question every human being must face, and dares to hope. The book will not answer it fully, but the New Testament does, with a person: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

14.reflection:
Job describes human life as “few of days and full of trouble” (v. 1). Why is it healthy for Christians to face honestly how short and fragile life is, and how does Galatians 4:4 change the way we see it?

“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one” (v. 4). How does this verse help us understand our need, and what does it mean to you that Jesus was the one exception?

Job asks, “If a man dies, shall he live again?” (v. 14). How would you answer that question for a friend who is grieving, and why does the resurrection of Jesus make the difference?

Job’s hope flares up (vv. 13–17) and then fades (vv. 18–22). Have you known hope to come and go like this in hard times? What helps you hold on when the hope seems to go out?

15.title: Have You Listened in the Council of God?
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?<sup>3</sup>Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good?<sup>4</sup>But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God.<sup>5</sup>For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty.<sup>6</sup>Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.<sup>7</sup>"Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills?<sup>8</sup>Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?<sup>9</sup>What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us?<sup>10</sup>Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father.<sup>11</sup>Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you?<sup>12</sup>Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash,<sup>13</sup>that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?<sup>14</sup>What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous?<sup>15</sup>Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight;<sup>16</sup>how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!<sup>17</sup>"I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare<sup>18</sup>(what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers,<sup>19</sup>to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).<sup>20</sup>The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless.<sup>21</sup>Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him.<sup>22</sup>He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword.<sup>23</sup>He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand;<sup>24</sup>distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.<sup>25</sup>Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty,<sup>26</sup>running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield;<sup>27</sup>because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist<sup>28</sup>and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins;<sup>29</sup>he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth;<sup>30</sup>he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.<sup>31</sup>Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment.<sup>32</sup>It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green.<sup>33</sup>He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree.<sup>34</sup>For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.<sup>35</sup>They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
15.overview:
Where we are. The first round of debate has ended with Job’s great question, “If a man dies, shall he live again?” (14:14). Now the second round begins (chapters 15–21), in the same order as the first, and Eliphaz, the oldest and most courteous of the friends, speaks again. The courtesy is gone.

The message. Eliphaz insists that Job’s own words prove his guilt, that the wisdom of the elders cannot be wrong, and that the wicked always live in dread and come to ruin. Through his speech God shows us how a man can claim to speak “the comforts of God” (v. 11) while wounding a sufferer, and how a theology that cannot be wrong ends up describing an innocent man as the worst of sinners. The reader knows better, for we have listened in the council of God (chapters 1–2), and what was said there was that Job is blameless.

Why it was said. The friends assume that God always repays in this life (see the introduction). Job has refused to confess sins he did not commit and has spoken boldly to God, so to Eliphaz he seems to be undermining piety itself. Eliphaz can no longer promise restoration; he can only warn. His words must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer, for God said they had not spoken rightly of him (42:7).

How the chapter makes its case. First Eliphaz attacks Job’s words (vv. 1–6): they are hot desert wind, they do away with the fear of God, and his own mouth condemns him. Then he mocks Job’s claim to wisdom (vv. 7–16): is he the first man born, has he listened in the council of God, are God’s gentle comforts too small for him? No man is pure, much less one who drinks injustice like water. Then he preaches the tradition of the fathers (vv. 17–35): the wicked man writhes in pain, the destroyer comes in his prosperity, his wealth vanishes, fire dries his shoots and his fruit falls before it ripens. Every detail fits Job’s losses; Eliphaz never needs to name him.

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the God he reveals. Eliphaz mocks the idea that anyone has listened in God’s council, but the only Son, “who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18), and the true comforts of God come through him (2 Corinthians 1:5). And the chapter’s portrait of the wicked man was one day laid on the only wholly innocent man: Jesus “was numbered with the transgressors” (Luke 22:37), treated as the guilty so that the guilty could be treated as innocent.

For us. Beware of calling your words “the comforts of God” when they wound; the test of comfort is not what the comforter calls it. Never use what a grieving person says in anguish as evidence against him. And rest in this: because Christ was counted among the wicked, no believer’s suffering is the wicked man’s portion.
15.theology:
The second round turns to one subject, the fate of the wicked (chs 15, 18, 20), and the portrait of the wicked keeps turning into a portrait of an innocent man. Eliphaz mocks the idea that Job has listened in God's council, but the reader has, and what was said there vindicates Job.

Christ, who is at the Father's side, has truly listened in God's council and has made the Father known. And he, though innocent, was counted among the wicked.
15.examples: Watch the friends' language harden. Eliphaz has moved from "no one is pure" to "you are foul", yet he calls his own speeches the comforts of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s point is that Job’s bold words prove him guilty and proud, and that he should accept the friends’ counsel as God’s comfort. He begins by dismissing Job’s speeches as hot desert wind that destroys the fear of God; Job’s own mouth condemns him (vv. 1–6). Then he mocks Job’s claim to understand: is he the first man born, older than the hills, a listener in God’s council, wiser than the grey-haired (vv. 7–10)? Why does he reject the gentle comforts of God and turn his spirit against him (vv. 11–13)? He ends by repeating his night vision: no man is pure, much less one who drinks injustice like water (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The second round begins with the courtesy gone, and with a mocking question whose answer the reader already knows.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good? But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God. For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His courtesy gone, Eliphaz calls Job’s words hot air and says his own mouth condemns him.

The second round. The friends’ case was set out in the first round (chapters 4–5, 8 and 11), and the reader should hold on to the LORD’s verdict on it: “you have not spoken of me what is right” (42:7). What is new in round two is the tone, and the subject.

Windy knowledge. In chapter 4 Eliphaz asked permission to speak. Now Job’s words are “windy knowledge”, “the east wind”, the scorching desert wind, hot and useless. Job, he says, is destroying piety itself; yet the fear of God was what God praised in him (1:1, 8).

Your own mouth condemns you. Job had said, “Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me” (9:20), meaning that God would twist his words. Eliphaz turns Job’s fear into his own verdict. It is common in any quarrel, and cruel in pastoral care, to use what a grieving person says in anguish as evidence against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills? Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself? What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us? Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father. Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you? Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz mocks the idea that Job has listened in God’s council, but the reader has, and what was said there clears Job.

Have you listened in the council of God? Here is the sharpest irony in the round. The reader has listened in the council of God: chapters 1 and 2 took us there, and what was said there was that Job was blameless and his suffering “without reason” (2:3). Eliphaz mocks the one source that could settle the argument, and it rules against Eliphaz.

Brought forth before the hills. These are the words of Wisdom: “before the hills, I was brought forth” (Proverbs 8:25). No mere man was there. Many Christians have heard in Wisdom’s words the eternal Son, and the New Testament calls Christ “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), first in rank over creation, not the first thing made: the only Son “who is at the Father’s side” (John 1:18). He has listened in the council of God, and told us what is in the Father’s heart. God himself will use Eliphaz’s irony on Job, gently: “You know, for you were born then” (38:21).

Are the comforts of God too small for you? This is what Eliphaz calls his own speeches: God’s comforts, spoken gently. Job’s answer comes in the next chapter: “miserable comforters are you all” (16:2). The test of comfort is not what the comforter calls it.

Uncertain wording. “Why do your eyes flash” uses a verb found only here. It may mean flashing in anger, or winking, or perhaps narrowing in contempt; the sense of defiance is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous? Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight; how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz repeats that no man is pure before God, and now aims the point at Job: “abominable and corrupt”.

What is man, that he can be pure? This is Eliphaz’s night vision again, in the same shape and many of the same words (4:17–19); what was said about it there applies here. What is new is where it lands: in chapter 4 it spoke of mortals in general; now the last line is aimed at Job: “abominable and corrupt”, a man who “drinks injustice like water”. Eliphaz has moved from “no one is pure” to “you are foul”. That is the whole slide of the friends’ argument in one sentence.

God puts no trust in his holy ones. The “holy ones” and “heavens” are the angels and heavenly beings: creatures, and so not pure as God is pure. Eliphaz uses this to argue that Job must be corrupt; the reasoning is his, not a revelation that the holy angels are fallen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — The Wicked Man Writhes in Pain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s point is that the wicked live in constant dread and always come to ruin, and he tells it so that every detail fits Job. He appeals to what he has seen and to the pure tradition of the fathers (vv. 17–19). The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, hears dreadful sounds and meets the destroyer in his prosperity (vv. 20–24). He has charged at God with a studded shield, grown fat and arrogant (vv. 25–27), so his wealth will not last and fire will dry up his shoots (vv. 28–30). His fruit will fall unripe and his house be barren, for the godless conceive trouble and give birth to evil (vv. 31–35).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the subject of the whole second round, and Job's own story supplies every detail.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare (what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers, to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).
verseByVerse.commentary:
No tradition, however pure, knew what had been said about Job in heaven.

What I have seen I will declare. Eliphaz appeals to his own experience and to the tradition of the fathers, handed down unmixed in a land no foreigner entered, as Bildad did (8:8–10). Tradition is not worthless; it simply could not know what God had said about this man.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless. Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him. He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword. He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand; distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man lives in dread and the destroyer comes in his prosperity, says Eliphaz, and the picture is Job’s own story.

The wicked man writhes in pain. Here begins the subject of the whole second round. All three friends will now preach the same sermon on the terrible end of the wicked (15:20–35; 18:5–21; 20:4–29). No more promises of restoration now, only warning.

In prosperity the destroyer will come upon him. Every reader of chapter 1 knows who this is: a man in prosperity, and the destroyer came. The sword fell on his servants (1:15, 17), and he is in pain every day. Eliphaz never names Job; he does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty, running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield; because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins; he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth; he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man raises his hand against God and loses everything, says Eliphaz; but Job never raised his hand against God.

Running stubbornly against him. The wicked man charges at God like a soldier with a studded shield, grown fat and arrogant, like Israel who “grew fat, and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15).

Stretched out his hand against God. This turns the opening chapters upside down. In chapter 1 it was Satan who asked God to “stretch out your hand” against Job (1:11). Job has not raised his hand against God; he has kept his hands open to him, even in protest.

Job’s story retold. The wealth that does not endure and the flame that dries his shoots, like “the fire of God” that fell on Job’s flocks (1:16), are Job’s story told as a sinner’s fate.

Uncertain wording. In verse 29 the word behind “possessions” is found only here, and its meaning is guessed from the context; some translations take it instead of roots or a harvest that will not spread. In verse 30 “the breath of his mouth” is probably God’s breath, which blows the wicked away (compare 4:9). The sense is clear: all he gained will vanish.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment. It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green. He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree. For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery. They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked lose their fruit before it ripens, says Eliphaz to a man whose children died young; one wholly innocent man was truly counted among the wicked, so that the guilty could go free.

He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine. A vine drops its grapes before they ripen, an olive tree that sheds its blossom: children lost before they grew old, a house left “barren”. He says it in front of a man whose ten children died young.

They conceive trouble and give birth to evil. True of the wicked (Psalm 7:14); not true of Job.

Numbered with the transgressors. One man was treated as everything this chapter describes, and he was wholly innocent. Jesus said, “this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors’” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12). The innocent one was treated as the man Eliphaz describes, so that the guilty could be treated as innocent.

keyVerse.quote: Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?
keyVerse.note: Eliphaz means it as mockery, but it is the key to the whole debate. The reader has listened in the council of God (chapters 1–2), where Job was called blameless, and so knows that the friends’ confident wisdom is wrong. Only the Son, “who is at the Father’s side” (John 1:18), has truly heard that council and made the Father known.

15.reflection:
Eliphaz calls his speeches “the comforts of God” and “the word that deals gently with you” (v. 11), yet Job will call him a miserable comforter (16:2). How can we tell whether our words to a suffering friend are truly comforting?

“Your own mouth condemns you” (v. 6). Why is it cruel to use what a grieving person says in anguish against them? How should we listen to someone who says hard things about God in their pain?

Eliphaz mocks Job for claiming to have “listened in the council of God” (v. 8), but the reader has heard that council (1:8; 2:3). How does it help in suffering to remember that God knows things about our situation that we do not?

Every detail of Eliphaz’s wicked man fits Job, yet Job is innocent. How does Jesus being “numbered with the transgressors” (Luke 22:37) change the way a believer should read his own sufferings?

16.title: My Witness Is in Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all.<sup>3</sup>Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?<sup>4</sup>I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you.<sup>5</sup>I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.<sup>6</sup>"If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me?<sup>7</sup>Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company.<sup>8</sup>And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.<sup>9</sup>He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me.<sup>10</sup>Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me.<sup>11</sup>God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.<sup>12</sup>I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target;<sup>13</sup>his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground.<sup>14</sup>He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.<sup>15</sup>I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust.<sup>16</sup>My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness,<sup>17</sup>although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.<sup>18</sup>"O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.<sup>19</sup>Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.<sup>20</sup>My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God,<sup>21</sup>that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor.<sup>22</sup>For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
16.overview:
Where we are. Eliphaz has opened the second round of debate by calling his speeches “the comforts of God” (15:11) and painting the dreadful end of the wicked in colours that fit Job’s losses exactly (15:20–35). Now Job answers, in a speech that runs through chapter 17.

The message. Job feels that God has torn him like a wild beast and handed him over to the wicked, though his hands are clean of violence. Yet in the same breath, with his friends scorning him, he reaches past the God who seems to be attacking him to the God who knows the truth: “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven” (v. 19). The chapter shows that a believer may feel God has become his enemy while still clinging to him as his only hope, and it points to the advocate in heaven who pleads for us.

Why it was said. The friends assume that great suffering proves great sin (see the introduction), and Job’s wasted body seems to testify against him (v. 8). No one on earth will speak for him. He expects to die soon, with his name still under a cloud (v. 22).

How the chapter makes its case. First Job dismisses the friends (vv. 1–5): they are miserable comforters, full of wind; in their place he could mock them too, or he could strengthen them, as they should be strengthening him. Then he pours out his anguish (vv. 6–17): God has worn him out, torn him in wrath, given him to the ungodly who strike his cheek, set him up as a target and run at him like a warrior; he sits in sackcloth with his face red from weeping, though there is no violence in his hands. Last he turns upward (vv. 18–22): let the earth not cover his blood; his witness is in heaven; with tears he asks that one would plead his case with God, for his years are few.

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Job’s night traces the outline of Good Friday: the gaping mouths, the blow on the cheek, the innocent man given up “into the hands of the wicked” (v. 11; compare Matthew 26:67; Acts 2:23), the one who had “done no violence” (Isaiah 53:9). And Job’s longing for a witness who pleads for a man with God is answered in Jesus, “the faithful witness” (Revelation 1:5), who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. When God seems to have become your enemy, the feeling is real but it is not God’s verdict; you may say it to him, and you may still appeal to him. You have what Job only reached for: an advocate with the Father who is speaking for you now. And when you visit someone in pain, remember how easily good people with right doctrine become miserable comforters.
16.theology:
Job's description of his suffering (vv. 9-11, 17) anticipates the language of Isaiah’s suffering Servant and of the sufferings of Christ (Matt 26:67; Acts 2:23): innocent, struck, handed over, though his hands have done no violence.

From no arbiter (9:33) Job climbs to my witness is in heaven (v. 19). Christ is that faithful witness and advocate, and his blood speaks a better word than Abel's (Heb 12:24).
16.examples: Job's phrase miserable comforters has clung to the friends ever since. Yet he knows the mouth that mocks could just as well strengthen, because his own once did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the friends have failed as comforters, and he knows what real comfort sounds like. He has heard all they have to say; they are miserable comforters, and their words are wind, the very charge Eliphaz laid against him (vv. 1–3). If they swapped places, he says, he could do what they are doing: string words together against them and shake his head in scorn (v. 4). Or he could do what they should be doing: strengthen them with his words and ease their pain (v. 5). The same mouth can wound or heal, and Job, who once comforted many (4:3–4), knows which they have chosen.
verseByVerse.theology: Job knows what real comfort would sound like, because he used to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all. Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends came to comfort and have only added to Job’s trouble.

Miserable comforters are you all. Eliphaz had called his speeches “the comforts of God” (15:11). Job answers with the description that has clung to the friends ever since: “miserable comforters”, literally comforters of trouble, the word Job has used for his life since chapter 3. They came to comfort (2:11) and have added to his trouble. And he throws back Eliphaz’s opening insult (15:2): whose words are wind now?

A word for every church. The friends were not bad men; they talked when they should have listened, and explained when they should have wept. Real comfort is passed on: the God of all comfort comforts us in our affliction so that we can comfort others with the comfort we have received (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you. I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In their place, Job could mock as they mock, or strengthen as they should; the same mouth can do either.

If you were in my place. In their place he could string sermons together and shake his head at them, or strengthen them, as he had done for others (4:3–4). Jesus put it in one sentence: “whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12).

Shake my head at you. Shaking the head is the gesture of scorn. “All who see me mock me; … they wag their heads,” says the sufferer of Psalm 22 (Psalm 22:7), and at the cross “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — He Has Torn Me in His Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that God seems to have turned against him with the violence of an enemy, though he has done nothing to deserve it. Speaking does not ease his pain, and neither does silence (v. 6). God has worn him out, stripped him of his household, and made his wasted body a false witness against him (vv. 7–8). God has torn him like a beast, and men gape at him, strike his cheek and mass against him (vv. 9–11). He was at ease, and God broke him, made him a target and charged him like a warrior (vv. 12–14). He sits in sackcloth, face red with weeping, though there is no violence in his hands and his prayer is pure (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's suffering is described in the words the prophets would use for the suffering of the Servant, and the Gospels for the passion of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me? Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company. And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither speech nor silence eases Job’s pain, and even his wasted body seems to testify against him.

If I speak, my pain is not assuaged. Talking does not help; silence does not help. Anyone in chronic pain knows the trap.

Which is a witness against me. His family gone and his friends turned, his wasted body stands up in court against him: people see how thin and sick he is and conclude that he must be guilty. That is the false witness; the true one comes at verse 19.

Uncertain wording. “Shriveled me up” translates a rare verb that may mean “seized” or “wrinkled”; either way his body is wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me. Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me. God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job feels that God has become his enemy and handed him to the wicked; the feeling is real, but it is not God’s verdict.

My adversary sharpens his eyes against me. Job believes God has become his enemy, tearing him like a wild beast. By “my adversary” Job means God, but the reader knows there is another adversary in this story, the one in the council, and God has not become Job’s enemy at all. That is a mercy for every sufferer who feels the same: the feeling is real, and Job may voice it, but it is not God’s verdict. God’s verdict was spoken in heaven before his trouble began (1:8).

The outline of Good Friday. These lines will be heard again. The gaping mouths return in Psalm 22, “like a ravening and roaring lion” (Psalm 22:13), and the blow on the cheek in Micah and Isaiah: “with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek” (Micah 5:1); “I gave … my cheeks to those who pull out the beard” (Isaiah 50:6). In the high priest’s house “they spit in his face and struck him” (Matthew 26:67). And “God gives me up to the ungodly”: Peter said Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Job’s night shows, long beforehand, the shape of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target; his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground. He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job describes his sudden ruin as an onslaught of violence, and the book lets him say it all.

I was at ease, and he broke me apart. The prosperous life of chapter 1, then, without warning, ruin. Job piles up pictures of violence: a man grabbed by the neck and smashed, a target ringed by archers (6:4; 7:20), a wall breached again and again, a soldier charging. The poet of Lamentations felt the same arrows: “He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver” (Lamentations 3:13). This is how undeserved suffering feels from the inside, and the book does not ask the reader to pretend it is anything but agony.

verseByVerse.quote: I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust. My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job mourns in the dust though his hands are clean of violence, words Isaiah would use of the Servant of the LORD.

I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin. The sackcloth is stitched on, as if grown into his skin; his “strength”, literally his horn, is in the dirt. The horn is how Scripture pictures strength and honour; Hannah sang, “my horn is exalted in the LORD” (1 Samuel 2:1). And the answer, when it came, came as a horn: God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69).

There is no violence in my hands. Job is suffering like a criminal, and he has done no violence. Isaiah uses the same words, in the same Hebrew construction, of the Servant of the LORD, led like a lamb to the slaughter: “they made his grave with the wicked … although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9). What Job could say of himself in part, the Servant could say perfectly. Job’s hands were clean of violence; Christ’s were clean of every sin, and they were nailed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Witness Is in Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that, with no one on earth to speak for him, he has a witness in heaven. He asks the earth not to cover his blood, so that his cry for justice will never be silenced (v. 18). Then comes the second great step in his hope: “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven” (v. 19). In chapter 9 there was no arbiter; now there is one on high who knows the truth. His friends scorn him, so he weeps to God, asking that someone would plead his case with God as a man pleads for his neighbour (vv. 20–21), for his time is short (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the second step up the ladder of Job's hope: from no arbiter to a witness in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place. Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my innocent blood never be hidden, says Job, for even now my witness is in heaven.

O earth, cover not my blood. Job expects to die unjustly, and asks the ground not to hide his blood but let it cry out, as Abel’s blood cried from the ground after his brother killed him: “The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Hebrews speaks of another blood that says something better: “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for vengeance; Christ’s cries for pardon.

My witness is in heaven. In chapter 9 Job said there was “no arbiter” (9:33). Now, in his darkest chapter yet, he says: even now, someone in heaven knows the truth and will speak for me. Job reached into heaven in the dark and found someone there. He was right.

Where Christians differ. Who is the witness? Many readers think Job means God himself: he appeals to God against God, to the God who knows his innocence against the God who seems to be attacking him. Others think he means a heavenly advocate distinct from God.

This commentary’s view. Job is probably appealing to God himself, as with the Redeemer of 19:25 (see the introduction), and the New Testament shows how both readings meet. God the Son, who is God, stands before the Father for us: “Jesus Christ the faithful witness” (Revelation 1:5), who “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God, that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor. For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scorned by his friends, Job weeps for someone to plead his case with God as a man pleads for his neighbour.

My friends scorn me. The friends scorn; the tears go to God.

As a son of man does with his neighbor. He wants his witness to plead for him before God as a man stands up for his neighbour in court. “As a son of man” here simply means as one human being for another; the title Jesus would use is not in Job’s mind. But the longing is plain: an advocate on God’s side of the courtroom who pleads like one of us. Jesus, God the Son made man, is exactly that: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

When a few years have come. He is running out of time and needs the witness to speak soon. The Christian’s advocate is speaking now.

Uncertain wording. The word for those who “scorn” can also mean spokesmen or interpreters, the word Elihu will use for a “mediator” (33:23). Some therefore read “my friends are my spokesmen” (bitterly, since they speak against him), or “my interpreter is my friend”, linking it to the witness of verse 19. The ESV’s “scorn” fits the context well; either way, no one on earth is speaking for Job.

keyVerse.quote: Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.
keyVerse.note: In the darkest part of his speech, abandoned by his friends, Job reaches past the God who seems to be attacking him to the God who knows the truth. It is the second step in his rising hope, from “no arbiter” (9:33) to a witness in heaven, and it is answered in Jesus, who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

16.reflection:
Job calls his friends “miserable comforters” (v. 2), yet they were sincere and their doctrines were often right. What makes the difference between comfort that helps and comfort that wounds? What have you found most comforting in your own hard times?

Job feels that God has torn him “in his wrath” (v. 9), but the reader knows God has not become his enemy (1:8). How can a believer be honest about feeling attacked by God while trusting that this is not God’s verdict?

Many details of Job’s suffering (vv. 10–11, 17) reappear in the sufferings of Jesus. What does it mean to you that Christ has walked this road before us?

“My witness is in heaven” (v. 19). How does knowing that Jesus is your advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1) change the way you pray when you feel accused or misunderstood?

17.title: Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
17.text: <sup>1</sup>"My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me.<sup>2</sup>Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.<sup>3</sup>"Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me?<sup>4</sup>Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph.<sup>5</sup>He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.<sup>6</sup>"He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit.<sup>7</sup>My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.<sup>8</sup>The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless.<sup>9</sup>Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger.<sup>10</sup>But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.<sup>11</sup>My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart.<sup>12</sup>They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'<sup>13</sup>If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness,<sup>14</sup>if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,'<sup>15</sup>where then is my hope? Who will see my hope?<sup>16</sup>Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
17.overview:
Where we are. Eliphaz has opened the second round of the debate with a long portrait of the terrors that haunt the wicked (chapter 15). Job’s reply fills chapters 16 and 17. In chapter 16 he described God as an enemy who has torn him, and yet cried that his witness is in heaven (16:19); this chapter is the second half of that speech, spoken by a man who expects to be dead within days (16:22).

The message. When no one on earth will stand up for a sufferer, the only place left to turn is God himself. Mocked and dying, Job asks God to stand surety for him with God, and he refuses to let go of his way, though he can see no hope this side of the grave. The chapter exposes a need no human friend can meet: a guarantor before God, and a hope that can survive death.

Why it was said. The friends hold that God always repays in this life (see the introduction), so they keep promising that Job’s darkness will turn to morning if only he repents. Job knows that no hidden sin explains his suffering, and he can see nothing ahead but the grave.

How the chapter makes its case. Broken and surrounded by mockers (vv. 1–2), Job asks God to give a pledge for him, since God has closed the friends’ minds and no one else will (vv. 3–5). He has become a byword, spat upon, a shadow of himself (vv. 6–7), and yet in the middle of it he says that the righteous holds to his way and grows stronger (vv. 8–10). His plans are broken off, and the friends call night day (vv. 11–12). If the grave is his only home and the worm his family, where is his hope? Will it go down with him into the dust (vv. 13–16)?

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need the chapter exposes. Job asks, “who is there who will put up security for me?” (v. 3), and the New Testament answers with Jesus, “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). By pattern too: the innocent man made a byword and spat upon foreshadows the Servant who did not hide his face “from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6), fulfilled in the high priest’s courtyard (Matthew 26:67). And Job’s last question, whether hope must go down to the bars of Sheol, is answered by the one who went down and now holds “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

For us. When no one will vouch for you, Christ has already put up the pledge, with his own life. When your spirit is broken, the grip that keeps you is God’s on you, not yours on him. And when you sit with a sufferer, do not call night day: sit with him in the night, and point him to the morning that is real, a hope that has already been through the grave.
17.theology: Job asks God to stand surety for him with God, that is, to be his guarantor (v. 3), a request the New Testament sees answered in Christ. The righteous holds to his way even when his spirit is broken (vv. 1, 9), because God holds him. And the bars of Sheol (v. 16) have been opened by the one who holds the keys of Death.
17.examples: The chapter moves between extremes: a man made a byword and spat on, who still says the righteous holds to his way; friends who call night day; and a grave pictured as a family, with the pit for a father and the worm for a mother.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he is dying, mocked and without a defender, so he must ask God himself to stand guarantor for him. His spirit is broken, his days snuffed out, the grave ready, and the mockers’ taunts never leave his sight (vv. 1–2). So he turns to God: lay down a pledge for me with yourself, for who else will shake hands on my behalf (v. 3)? God has closed the friends’ minds, so they will not triumph (v. 4), and an old proverb warns what becomes of those who inform against their friends (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks God to stand surety for him with God, because he can find no one else who will.

verseByVerse.quote: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me. Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job expects to die soon, and mockers will not let him die in peace.

My spirit is broken. Job speaks in three short, broken clauses: spirit gone, days snuffed out, the graveyard waiting. And he cannot stop seeing the mockers’ taunts. The friends came to sit with him in grief (2:11–13); now he lies awake with their words in front of his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me? Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph. He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no one on earth to vouch for him, Job asks God to stand guarantor for him before God.

Lay down a pledge for me with you. In the ancient world, when a man could not pay or could not be trusted to appear in court, someone else could stand surety for him, pledging his own property or person and sealing it with a handshake (“put up security” is literally “strike hands”, as in Proverbs 6:1). Job finds no one who will do it, so he asks God to stand guarantor for him with God, as he looked to his witness in heaven (16:19).

Christ the surety. The verb is the one Judah used when he offered himself for his brother Benjamin before their father: “I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him” (Genesis 43:9). Judah put his own life on the line for his brother, and the Son of God, of the tribe of Judah, did the same for us: “This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). Job asked who would stand surety for him with God. God answered by becoming the surety himself.

You have closed their hearts to understanding. God has shut the friends’ minds; they will not win this argument. Then Job seems to quote a proverb: when a man informs against his friends for gain, his own children pay for it. The friends have informed against Job to God, and the proverb is a warning.

Uncertain wording. The first line of verse 5 is compressed, and the word behind “a share of their property” usually means simply “portion”. The KJV reads flattery of friends; some read a man who invites friends to share his portion while his own children go hungry. The ESV’s reading fits what the friends are doing to Job, and on every reading the man’s own children pay for what he does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Righteous Holds to His Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that disgrace has not broken his hold on the right way. God has made him a byword, a man people spit at, his eye dim with grief and his body a shadow (vv. 6–7). Upright people are appalled at it, yet the righteous man holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger under the pressure (vv. 8–9). Let the friends come on again: he will still not find a wise man among them (v. 10). In the middle of his lowest words he says the very thing Satan claimed no one would say.
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of his darkest words Job says that the righteous man does not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit. My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made Job a public warning and a man people spit at, and grief has worn him to a shadow.

A byword of the peoples. A byword is a name used as a warning. It is the covenant curse: “you shall become a horror, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples” (Deuteronomy 28:37).

One before whom men spit. Men spit in his face. The Servant of the LORD would say, “I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6), and in the high priest’s courtyard “they spit in his face and struck him” (Matthew 26:67).

verseByVerse.quote: The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless. Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger. But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even at his lowest, the righteous man holds to his way, and pressure makes him stronger.

The righteous holds to his way. Suddenly, in the middle of his lowest words, comes a burst of steel. Good people look at what has happened to Job and are horrified. But the righteous man does not give up his road; he holds on, and the one with clean hands grows stronger as the pressure grows.

The perseverance of the saints. This is what the Reformed churches have called the perseverance of the saints: not that God’s people never stumble or despair, but that the one who truly belongs to God holds to his way, because God holds him and has given him his Spirit as the seal and guarantee of it (Ephesians 1:13–14). “The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day” (Proverbs 4:18). Job’s spirit is broken (v. 1) and his grip on his way unbroken, both in one chapter: exactly what Satan said could not happen (1:9–11). For the believer who feels he is barely hanging on, the grip that matters most is God’s on him, not his on God (John 10:28–29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Where Then Is My Hope?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he can see no hope this side of the grave, and he asks whether his hope must die with him. His days are past and his plans snapped off, while the friends insist that dawn is near (vv. 11–12). If Sheol is to be his house, the pit his father and the worm his mother and sister, where is his hope, and who will ever see it (vv. 13–15)? Will it go down with him through the bars of Sheol into the dust (v. 16)? The chapter ends on the question; chapter 19 will begin to answer it.
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks whether his hope will go down into the grave with him.

verseByVerse.quote: My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart. They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s plans are cut short, and the friends’ promise that dawn is near is false comfort.

My plans are broken off. Everything he meant to do, the desires of his heart, has been snapped off like thread.

They make night into day. Zophar promised that Job’s darkness would be like the morning (11:17). It is midnight, and they keep saying dawn is near, if only he will repent. It is the false comfort the prophets condemned: “They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). Real comfort does not pretend that night is day; it sits in the night, and waits for the real morning.

Uncertain wording. Verse 12 is terse, and “they say” is not in the Hebrew. Most modern versions take the line as the friends’ claim that light is near; the KJV reads it as Job’s complaint that his light is cut short by darkness. Zophar’s promise of morning (11:17) makes the ESV’s reading likely.

verseByVerse.quote: If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness, if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,' where then is my hope? Who will see my hope? Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the grave is his only home, Job asks, will his hope be buried with him?

Where then is my hope? Job has lost his house and his children; now he pictures the grave adopting him, the pit for a father and the worm for mother and sister. And he asks whether his hope will go down with him through the barred gate of Sheol, the realm of the dead, and lie in the dust beside him.

The bars of Sheol. The Bible answers with a man who went down to those bars. Jonah prayed from the belly of the fish, “I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me forever; yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God” (Jonah 2:6), and Jesus called his own death and resurrection the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39–40). The risen Christ says, “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). The bars Job feared have a key, and Christ holds it.

A living hope. So Job’s question has an answer. Where is his hope? Not in the dust: “he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). A hope that has already been through the grave and come out cannot be buried with us.

keyVerse.quote: Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me?
keyVerse.note: Here is the chapter’s deepest need, voiced as a prayer: someone to stand surety for Job before God when no one on earth will. It belongs with his longing for an arbiter (9:33) and a witness in heaven (16:19), and it is answered in Jesus, who became “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22) by putting up his own life.

17.reflection:
Job’s friends came to comfort him, yet he lies awake over their mockery (v. 2) and says they “make night into day” (v. 12). When have words meant as comfort made someone’s suffering worse? What does it look like to sit in the night with a sufferer instead?

Job asks God to stand surety for him with God (v. 3). How does knowing Jesus as “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22) change the way you come to God when you feel no one is on your side?

In one chapter Job’s spirit is broken (v. 1), and yet “the righteous holds to his way” (v. 9). How can both be true of a believer at once? Where do you most need to remember that God’s grip on you matters more than yours on him?

Job asks whether his hope will go down with him into the dust (vv. 15–16). How would you answer him from the resurrection of Jesus, and how does that answer shape the way you face your own death?

18.title: The King of Terrors
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak.<sup>3</sup>Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight?<sup>4</sup>You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?<sup>5</sup>"Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.<sup>6</sup>The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out.<sup>7</sup>His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down.<sup>8</sup>For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh.<sup>9</sup>A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him.<sup>10</sup>A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.<sup>11</sup>Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels.<sup>12</sup>His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling.<sup>13</sup>It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs.<sup>14</sup>He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.<sup>15</sup>In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation.<sup>16</sup>His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above.<sup>17</sup>His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street.<sup>18</sup>He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world.<sup>19</sup>He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.<sup>20</sup>They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east.<sup>21</sup>Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
18.overview:
Where we are. Job has just ended his reply to Eliphaz by asking whether his hope must go down with him into the dust (17:16). Now Bildad speaks for the second time. He has nothing new to say about God; instead he paints the end of the wicked man in darker colours than before, and nearly every stroke is aimed at Job.

The message. The chapter is a warning about how true words can be used falsely. It is true that those who reject God come at last to ruin, and that death is a terror to those without him. But Bildad reads that truth backwards from one man’s suffering, and so calls the man God praised a man “who knows not God” (v. 21). The reader is meant to grieve at such comfort, and to long for someone who can overthrow the king of terrors.

Why it was said. Bildad holds the friends’ fixed belief that God always repays in this life (see the introduction). Job has treated them as stupid cattle and found no wise man among them (12:7; 17:10), and he will not confess a hidden sin, so Bildad answers with wounded pride and a sharper picture.

How the chapter makes its case. Bildad first resents Job’s scorn and asks whether the world must be rearranged for him (vv. 1–4). Then comes his portrait. The wicked man’s lamp goes out, and his own feet carry him into nets and snares (vv. 5–10). Terrors chase him, disease devours his skin, and he is marched to the king of terrors (vv. 11–14). His tent is burned with sulfur, his roots dry up, and his name and his children perish (vv. 15–19). East and west are appalled, for this is the place of the man who does not know God (vv. 20–21). Almost every line fits Job: the lamp that once shone on him (29:3), his ruined skin, his dead children.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by pattern. Bildad’s picture of death as a king who rules by fear is true for those without God, and no one in the book can overthrow him. Christ shared our flesh “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” and set free those enslaved by its fear (Hebrews 2:14–15). And the pattern of Job runs on to him: Jesus too was condemned as one who did not know God, and died young and childless, cut off from the land of the living; yet of the Servant it was promised, “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10).

For us. Be slow to read anyone’s suffering as God’s verdict on him: the true doctrine of judgment becomes cruel when it is aimed by guesswork. If you fear death, look to the King who conquered the king of terrors. And if your hope rests on being remembered, rest it instead on being known and kept by God.
18.theology:
Bildad's rule that wickedness ends in ruin is true at the last judgment. His error is to work backwards from one man's suffering in this life and conclude that Job is wicked and does not know God.

Death, the king of terrors, has been dethroned: Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death and freed those enslaved by its fear.
18.examples: Bildad packs six traps into three verses. Then he aims his lines: a disease that eats the skin, said to a man with a skin disease, and no posterity, said to a father of ten dead children.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Are We Counted as Cattle?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad’s point is that Job has insulted the friends and must not expect the world to bend to his grief. He opens with impatience: how long will Job hunt for words, and why does he treat them as stupid cattle (vv. 1–3)? Job has said that God tore him; Bildad says that Job tears himself in his anger. Shall the earth be abandoned and the rock moved from its place for his sake (v. 4)? There is truth in it, for God does not rearrange his world to suit a sufferer; but Bildad has not considered that God’s order may be larger than his account of it.
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad's pride is hurt, and he tells Job that the world will not be rearranged to suit him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak. Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight? You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stung by Job’s scorn, Bildad tells him the world will not be rearranged for his sake.

Bildad takes it personally. His case from chapter 8 has not changed; what is new is mostly wounded pride. “How long will you hunt for words? … Why are we counted as cattle?” Job told them to ask the animals for wisdom (12:7) and said he could not find a wise man among them (17:10).

You who tear yourself in your anger. Job said God had torn him (16:9); Bildad says he tears himself. And he throws back Job’s own words, “the rock is removed from its place” (14:18): do you expect the way God runs the world to be changed for your sake? Bildad is right that God does not rearrange the world to please a sufferer. He has not considered that God’s order might be larger than his account of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–21 — The Light of the Wicked Is Put Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad’s point is that the wicked are always caught and destroyed in this life, and he means Job. The wicked man’s lamp goes out (vv. 5–6), and his own feet carry him into trap after trap (vv. 7–10). Terrors chase him, a deadly disease eats his skin, and he is dragged from his tent to death, the king of terrors (vv. 11–14). His home is burned, his roots and branches wither, his name is forgotten and he leaves no children (vv. 15–19). West and east are appalled, for such is the place of one who does not know God (vv. 20–21). Each picture is drawn from Job’s own losses.
verseByVerse.theology: Every line of Bildad's portrait of the wicked describes Job, down to the final verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: "Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine. The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out. His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down. For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh. A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him. A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man’s light goes out and his own feet walk him into the trap, says Bildad, and he means Job.

The light of the wicked is put out. A burning lamp was the sign of a living household. Proverbs says it too: “the lamp of the wicked will be put out” (Proverbs 13:9). Job will remember the days “when his lamp shone upon my head” (29:3). Bildad says that lamp has gone out because Job is wicked.

Cast into a net by his own feet. Six traps in three verses, and the wicked man walks into them by his own steps. It is true of the wicked: “in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught” (Psalm 9:15). But Job did not set these nets. He is caught in something he cannot see, and the reader knows who laid it.

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels. His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling. It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs. He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terror, disease and death hunt the wicked down, says Bildad, and he aims it at Job’s skin.

The firstborn of death. Here Bildad goes further than before. The wicked man, he says, dies of a disease that eats his skin, “the firstborn of death”, and he says it to a man whose skin is crusting and breaking (2:7; 7:5). It is no longer a general warning but a diagnosis. Christians still do this, reading a friend’s cancer or a child’s death as the sign of some hidden sin. Jesus refused that reasoning (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3), and so must we; the LORD rebuked exactly this kind of sermon (42:7).

The king of terrors. Death is pictured as a king, the lord of every fear, and the wicked are marched before him. It is a terrible and true picture of death for those without God. But the New Testament shows the king of terrors dethroned. Christ shared our flesh “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26). The believer is not marched before the king of terrors; he is welcomed by the King who conquered him.

Uncertain wording. “The firstborn of death” is found only here. Most take it as the deadliest disease, death’s eldest son; some hear an echo of the way Israel’s neighbours pictured Death as a god with servants. On any reading, death is at work in the man’s body.

verseByVerse.quote: In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation. His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above. His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street. He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world. He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man’s home, children and name are wiped out, says Bildad to a bereaved father; but Job’s name did not perish.

Sulfur is scattered over his habitation. Strangers move into his house; burning sulfur falls on it, as on Sodom (Genesis 19:24). Root and branch, nothing is left.

He has no posterity. The wicked man, says Bildad, leaves no children and no one to carry his name, and he says it to a father whose ten children are in their graves. It is the cruellest turn of his speech, and it is false. Job’s name did not perish: Ezekiel named him as a righteous man (Ezekiel 14:14), James held him up to the church (James 5:11), and his story is read wherever the Bible is read. “The righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever” (Psalm 112:6).

Cut off, yet with offspring. Jesus died young and childless, numbered with the transgressors. Yet of the Servant it was promised, “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10), and every believer is one of the children God has given him (Hebrews 2:13).

Can we live on in our legacy? Bildad’s threat still has teeth, because for many modern people being remembered is the only afterlife left. If there is nothing beyond the grave, a name or a reputation is the one way to outlast death, so we build, post and plan our legacy with almost religious seriousness. Woody Allen once joked that he did not want to achieve immortality through his work; he wanted to achieve it by not dying. Being remembered is a pale kind of life, and it fades: within a few generations most of us are a name on a document. Job did win a lasting name, but that was never his hope. His hope, in the very next chapter, is a Redeemer who lives and a God he will see in his own flesh (19:25–26). The gospel does not offer to keep our memory alive; it offers to keep us alive, known by name to the God who says, “I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:16). That frees us to work hard without needing our work to rescue us from being forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east. Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad’s verdict is that Job does not know God, and Job’s next speech proves him wrong.

Him who knows not God. Bildad’s last line is his verdict on Job. The LORD will say otherwise, and Bildad will be among the three he rebukes (42:7–9). Job’s very next speech reaches its peak with the words Bildad has just denied him: “For I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25). The man Bildad says does not know God is about to say one of the best-known sentences of faith in the Old Testament.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew words behind “they of the west” and “them of the east” can also mean “those who come after” and “those who went before”, which is how the KJV takes them. Either way, everyone everywhere is appalled at his end.

keyVerse.quote: Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God.
keyVerse.note: The whole speech drives towards this verdict, and it is aimed at Job. As a description of the end of those who reject God it is true; as a verdict on Job it is false, and God will say so (42:7). Job’s answer comes in the next chapter, from the depths: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25).

18.reflection:
Much of Bildad’s description of the wicked is true in general, yet it is cruel when aimed at Job. How can true doctrine be used wrongly? How can we warn about sin without reading someone’s suffering as proof of it?

Bildad pictures death as “the king of terrors” (v. 14). What fears about death do you carry, and how does Hebrews 2:14–15 speak to them?

Bildad says the wicked man’s memory perishes and he leaves no children (vv. 17–19). Why do so many people today look to their legacy to outlast death? Why is being known by God better than being remembered by people?

Bildad calls Job a man “who knows not God” (v. 21), yet Job’s next speech says, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25). What does it mean to know God, and how can a person know him even in deep suffering?

19.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words?<sup>3</sup>These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?<sup>4</sup>And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself.<sup>5</sup>If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me,<sup>6</sup>know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice.<sup>8</sup>He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.<sup>9</sup>He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head.<sup>10</sup>He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.<sup>11</sup>He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary.<sup>12</sup>His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.<sup>13</sup>"He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me.<sup>14</sup>My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.<sup>15</sup>The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes.<sup>16</sup>I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.<sup>17</sup>My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother.<sup>18</sup>Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me.<sup>19</sup>All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.<sup>20</sup>My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.<sup>21</sup>Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me!<sup>22</sup>Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?<sup>23</sup>"Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!<sup>24</sup>Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!<sup>25</sup>For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.<sup>26</sup>And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God,<sup>27</sup>whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!<sup>28</sup>If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,'<sup>29</sup>be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
19.overview:
Where we are. Bildad has just painted the end of the wicked man and aimed every line at Job, ending with the verdict that he is one “who knows not God” (18:21). This chapter is Job’s reply, in the middle of the second round of the debate. It goes lower than any chapter before it, and then climbs higher than any.

The message. Faith can say its greatest words from the bottom of the pit. Abandoned by God, as it seems, and by everyone he loves, Job still knows that he has a living Redeemer, a divine kinsman who will stand up for him at the last, and that after death he will see God with his own eyes, not as a stranger. The man Bildad said does not know God says, “I know” (v. 25).

Why it was said. The friends have made Job’s disgrace the proof of his guilt (v. 5), because they believe God always repays in this life (see the introduction). Job cannot answer them by pointing to any change in his circumstances; nothing has changed. So he looks past death to God himself.

How the chapter makes its case. Job begins with the friends: how long will they crush him with words and use his disgrace against him, when it is God who has done this (vv. 1–6)? Then he describes God as an enemy who has walled up his way, stripped his crown, uprooted his hope like a tree and besieged his tent (vv. 7–12). Next he counts, circle by circle, the people who have abandoned him: brothers, friends, guests, servants, his wife, even children in the street, until he is skin and bone and begs the friends for pity (vv. 13–22). Then the turn. He wishes his words were cut in rock for ever (vv. 23–24), because he knows that his Redeemer lives and will stand upon the dust, and that in his flesh he will see God (vv. 25–27). He ends by warning the friends that there is a judgment (vv. 28–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise as much as anywhere in the book, and by the need it exposes. Job’s Redeemer is most likely God himself; but a redeemer must be a kinsman, and the Son of God became one, sharing “in flesh and blood” to set his brothers free (Hebrews 2:14). The risen Christ calls himself “the first and the last, and the living one” (Revelation 1:17–18), the living Redeemer who stands at the last. Job’s loneliness is the path Christ walked, deserted by his friends; his crown stripped away is the crown of thorns; and his hope of seeing God in his flesh is made good by Christ’s bodily resurrection, the firstfruits of ours.

For us. You do not have to wait for the dark to lift before you say, “I know that my Redeemer lives.” Faith does not rest on how things look but on who God is. When everyone has gone, a believer is not alone: the kinsman who rose from the dust will stand on it again, and you will see him for yourself, as one who belongs to him.
19.theology:
A go'el is the near relative who rescues a family member in trouble, and Scripture uses the word above all of God (Isa 41:14). The risen Christ takes Job's words as his own: he is the last and the living one (Rev 1:17-18). This is the summit of the book's longing for someone to stand between Job and God (9:33; 16:19).

After the destruction of his body Job will see God with his own eyes, and not as a stranger: the hope of the resurrection of the body (1 Cor 15:42-44) and of seeing God.
19.examples: Job's lowest point and his highest stand fifteen verses apart. In between he wishes his words were cut in rock, and they were written somewhere more lasting still: in Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — How Long Will You Torment Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the friends have tormented him by treating his suffering as proof of his guilt, when the hand behind it is God’s. He begins in exhaustion: how long will they break him with words, after so many reproaches, and feel no shame (vv. 1–3)? Even if he has erred somewhere, that is between him and God (v. 4). If they insist on making his disgrace an argument against him, let them know that God has put him in the wrong and closed his net about him (vv. 5–6).
