Job did not walk into a trap, as Bildad said; it was spread for him.
verseByVerse.theology: Job names what the friends have been doing: using his suffering as evidence. He knows the suffering came from God's hand, not from his own feet walking into a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words? These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s friends, who came to comfort him, have instead crushed him with words again and again, and they feel no shame.

Break me in pieces with words. Bildad has just told Job that he does not know God (18:21). Job’s reply begins in exhaustion: how long? Their words have been hammers. “Ten times” is not a count, for the friends have spoken five times so far. It means “over and over again”, as Jacob said Laban had changed his wages “ten times” (Genesis 31:7).

Are you not ashamed? The friends came “to show him sympathy and comfort him” (2:11). They have wronged him, and they do not blush. This chapter goes deeper into the dark than any before it, and then climbs higher than any. It begins here, with a man broken by the words of his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself. If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me, know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if Job has sinned somewhere, the friends have no right to use his disgrace as proof of guilt, for it is God, not Job’s own feet, that has brought this on him.

Even if it be true that I have erred. If he has sinned somewhere, says Job, “my error remains with myself”: it has not harmed them, and gives them no right to stand over him.

Make my disgrace an argument against me. This is exactly what the friends have done: they have taken his disgrace, his ruined body and his dead children, and made them evidence. They have the cause wrong. It was not his sin that did this, but God.

God has put me in the wrong. Listen to the two words he chooses. “Put me in the wrong” is the verb of Bildad’s first question, “Does God pervert justice?” (8:3). And “his net” answers Bildad’s last speech, where the wicked man “is cast into a net by his own feet” (18:8). No, says Job, I did not walk into this; God spread the net. He is right that God’s hand is in it (2:3). He is wrong, and will be told so, to think that God has done him wrong (40:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — He Has Walled Up My Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that God seems to have become his enemy, and will not answer him. He cries “Violence!” and no one comes; there is no justice (v. 7). God has walled up his road and darkened his paths (v. 8), stripped him of his honour and his crown (v. 9), broken him down and pulled up his hope like a tree (v. 10). He feels God’s anger and counts himself treated as an adversary, a single tent besieged by a whole army (vv. 11–12). It is the lowest point his hope reaches in the book, and it comes just before the highest.
verseByVerse.theology: Job's picture of God is still of an enemy besieging him. It will not stay that way to the end of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice. He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job cries for help and gets no answer, and God seems to have walled him in.

I call for help. A man attacked in the street shouts for help, and no one comes. Habakkuk would pray almost the same: “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you ‘Violence!’ and you will not save?” (Habakkuk 1:2). God did answer Habakkuk, and he will answer Job, but not yet; the waiting is part of the trial.

He has walled up my way. In chapter 3 God had “hedged” him in (3:23). Now it is a wall. Lamentations knew it: “He has walled me about so that I cannot escape” (Lamentations 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head. He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has stripped Job of his honour and torn up his hope by the roots.

Taken the crown from my head. The honour Job once had, the respect of his city (29:7–11), is gone, as if God had pulled the crown from his head in public.

A crown of thorns. That is exactly what men did to Christ, in mockery: “they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head” (Matthew 27:28–29). And that is the road by which he came to be “crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). The glory stripped from Job will be given back; the glory Christ laid down was taken up again, for us.

My hope has he pulled up like a tree. In chapter 14 Job said, “there is hope for a tree” (14:7). Now even that hope has been torn out by the roots. It is the lowest point his hope has reached, and it comes fifteen verses before the highest.

verseByVerse.quote: He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary. His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job feels that God treats him as an enemy and has laid siege to him.

His troops come on together. Job pictures God as a general and himself as a besieged town: a whole army against one tent, one sick man. “Counts me as his adversary” is the complaint of 13:24 again. The reader knows God said the opposite: “there is none like him on the earth” (1:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Have Mercy on Me, O You My Friends
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he has been abandoned by everyone, and he begs his friends at least to show him mercy. He counts the circles of desertion: brothers and acquaintances (vv. 13–14), guests and maidservants who treat him as a foreigner, and a servant who will not answer (vv. 15–16). His wife cannot bear his breath, his brothers find him loathsome, children jeer, and his closest friends have turned against him (vv. 17–19). He is skin and bone, alive by the skin of his teeth (v. 20). So he pleads twice for pity, since God’s hand has struck him, and asks why they hunt him as God does (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the loneliness of the sufferer, described from the inside, and the Son of God knew it.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me. My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s family and friends have abandoned him, and he lays even this at God’s door.

He has put my brothers far from me. Now the attack reaches his own household. Job counts, circle by circle, the people who have abandoned him, and says that God has put them far from him. When a man is ill and disgraced, people stop coming, some embarrassed, some afraid, some having drawn their own conclusions.

verseByVerse.quote: The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes. I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his own house Job has become a stranger, and the master must beg his servant.

I have become a foreigner in their eyes. The guests he once fed and the maids who served him treat him as a foreigner. The master calls his servant, and the servant does not come; the master has to beg. The world of chapter 1 has been turned upside down.

Count me as a stranger. Keep the word “stranger”. It will come back at the summit of the chapter, in verse 27.

verseByVerse.quote: My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother. Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me. All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even his wife, his brothers and his dearest friends recoil from him, and Christ walked this lonely road before us.

Those whom I loved have turned against me. His wife cannot bear his breath; his own brothers find him disgusting; his closest friends have turned their backs. His wife, who told him to curse God and die (2:9), cannot come near him. He does not curse her. He grieves that she has gone from him too.

Even young children despise me. Set them beside chapter 29: “the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood” (29:8). Now children jeer when he struggles to his feet. There is no one left.

A path Christ walked. The psalms know this loneliness: “I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s sons” (Psalm 69:8). The New Testament applies the next verse of that psalm to Jesus (John 2:17), and he lived the whole of it. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). In Gethsemane, “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50). Whoever reads this chapter alone, abandoned by family and friends, may know that the Son of God has stood exactly there, and does not abandon his own.

Uncertain wording. “The children of my own mother” is literally “the sons of my womb”. Since Job’s children are dead, the ESV takes it as the sons of the womb that bore him, his brothers (compare “my mother’s womb”, 3:10). Some think it means his own children or grandchildren; the point, rejection by his nearest family, is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job is wasted to skin and bone and only just alive, as God allowed and no further.

My bones stick to my skin. He is skin and bone, wasted to nothing, barely alive, and barely is enough. God said to Satan, “only spare his life” (2:6), and his life has been spared, just.

Uncertain wording. “By the skin of my teeth” has passed into English as the phrase for the narrowest escape, but what Job meant is not certain. Teeth have no skin, and that may be the point: he has escaped with nothing at all, or he has only his gums left. Either way, he is barely alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me! Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the only time in the debate, Job begs his friends for pity, since God’s hand is on him, and asks them not to hunt him too.

Have mercy on me. Twice he pleads. He is not arguing now. “Touched” is the word Satan used (2:5). Job knows nothing of Satan; he knows that the hand on him is God’s, and he asks his friends not to add their hands to it.

Why do you, like God, pursue me? They are hunting him as he feels God hunts him, and devouring him with accusations.

Where mercy was found. Here is a man with a skin disease crying for mercy and getting none. Centuries later ten men with a skin disease stood at a distance from Jesus “and lifted up their voices, saying, ‘Jesus, Master, have mercy on us’” (Luke 17:13), and he did. The friends had no mercy for the man whose skin was rotting; the Lord had nothing but mercy for such men.

Uncertain wording. “Not satisfied with my flesh” is probably an idiom for slander. In the Aramaic of Daniel, to “eat the pieces” of a man means to accuse him maliciously (Daniel 3:8, where the ESV has “maliciously accused”). It may also simply picture hunters who will not stop until they have eaten their prey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — I Know That My Redeemer Lives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he knows, beyond death, God will vindicate him and he will see God. He wishes his words were engraved in rock for ever (vv. 23–24), and then says what he wants on record: his Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth (v. 25). After his skin is destroyed, yet in his flesh he will see God for himself, with his own eyes and not as a stranger, and his heart faints with longing (vv. 26–27). Then he turns back to the friends: if they keep pursuing him, let them fear the sword, for there is a judgment (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: From the bottom of the pit, the summit of the book's faith: a living Redeemer, standing at the last on the dust where Job will lie, and Job seeing God with his own eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sure that he will die unvindicated, Job wants his testimony on permanent record, and God gave him more than he asked.

Oh that my words were written! The chapter turns. Job wants what he is about to say cut into rock with an iron chisel and filled with lead, like the royal inscriptions on cliff faces, to outlast him and the friends.

A wish granted. His words were written in a book, and that book is Scripture. They have been read in more languages and by more people than any inscription ever cut into a cliff. The man who thought his voice would die with him is still speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the bottom of the pit, Job declares that he has a living Redeemer, God himself as his kinsman and defender, who will stand up for him at the last. It is the summit of the book’s faith.

I know that my Redeemer lives. Bildad said Job was a man “who knows not God” (18:21). Job says, “I know”. Not I hope, not I wish. And what he knows is that he has a Redeemer, and his Redeemer is alive.

My Redeemer. The Hebrew word is go’el, your nearest kinsman, whose duty was to rescue you when you could not rescue yourself. If you sold your land in debt, he bought it back (Leviticus 25:25). If you were sold as a slave, he redeemed you (Leviticus 25:48–49). If you were murdered, he avenged your blood (Numbers 35:19), which is why Job cried, “O earth, cover not my blood” (16:18). Boaz was Ruth’s go’el (Ruth 3:9). But the word belongs above all to God: “your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 41:14). Job has no kinsman left who will stand up for him (vv. 13–19). He knows he has one who will.

At the last. The word is acharon, and Isaiah puts Job’s two words, Redeemer and last, side by side: “Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer … I am the first and I am the last” (Isaiah 44:6). The Redeemer is the Last.

He will stand upon the earth. The earth is, in Hebrew, “dust” (ESV note): the dust of the grave, where Job feared his hope would go down (17:16). His Redeemer will stand up on that very dust, over the place where Job lies, like a kinsman rising in court to speak for the dead.

God became our kinsman. A go’el has to be a kinsman, one of the family. How can God be that? The New Testament answers. The Son of God “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and “since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things” (Hebrews 2:14). God became our kinsman so that he could be our Redeemer. And the risen Christ took Job’s words as his own titles: “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore” (Revelation 1:17–18). As he said it, John writes, “he laid his right hand on me”. Job had cried that there was no arbiter “who might lay his hand on us both” (9:33), and many Christians have heard an echo of that cry in the hand laid on John. Christ went down into the dust of the grave and rose from it, and he will stand upon the earth again at the last day. Job’s words reached further than he could see.

Spoken from the depths. This sentence does not come after Job has been healed or answered. Nothing has changed. Fifteen verses ago God had torn up his hope like a tree (v. 10). The harshest things Job says about God and the greatest thing he says about him stand in the same speech. That is how faith often speaks in real suffering. It does not wait for the dark to lift before it says “I know”, because it rests not on how things look but on who God is. A believer who can only say today, “he has walled up my way”, is still allowed to say in the next breath, “my Redeemer lives”. Job did.

Where Christians differ: who is Job’s Redeemer? Many readers, from the early church to Handel’s Messiah, have heard the verse as a direct prophecy of Christ. Others take the Redeemer to be a heavenly figure distinct from God, a mediator or witness standing between Job and God (compare 16:19; 33:23), and some think Job hopes only to be vindicated before he dies. This commentary’s view: Job most likely means God himself. The God who seems to be his enemy in verses 6–12 is the God he appeals to as his kinsman and defender, appealing to God against God, as in 16:19. Job did not know how God could be his kinsman, but the New Testament shows it in the Son, so that the Christian reading is not forced on the verse but grows from it.
verseByVerse.note: A go'el was the near relative who stood up for a family member who could not help himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
After death Job will see God with his own eyes, in his flesh, and not as a stranger: the hope of the resurrection of the body.

In my flesh I shall see God. Job expects his skin to be destroyed, and yet he will see God for himself. “My eyes shall behold”: eyes belong to a body. The Christian reads here the resurrection of the body: “It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:43). The wasted flesh on the ash heap will be raised, and with those eyes Job will see his God.

And not another. This means not as a stranger. His own household counts him a stranger (v. 15), but when he looks at God, it will not be as a stranger. He will see God face to face, as one who belongs to him. “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

My heart faints within me! This is not calm doctrine. It is a man overwhelmed by what he has just said. Every believer who has stood by a grave and said these words knows the feeling. And Job will taste the first of it before he dies: “now my eye sees you” (42:5).

Uncertain wording. These are among the hardest verses in the book. “In my flesh” can also be read “without my flesh” (ESV note), and some take Job to mean that he will see God as a spirit after death. The King James Version’s “though after my skin worms destroy this body” supplies “worms” and “body” (printed in italics), and the Greek Old Testament reads the line as God raising up Job’s skin. On every reading Job will see God for himself, and “my eyes” points to a bodily hope.
verseByVerse.note: “In my flesh” may be rendered “without my flesh” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,' be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job warns the friends that if they keep hunting him, they themselves will face God’s judgment.

That you may know there is a judgment. Job turns back to the friends. “The root of the matter is found in him” is their case in a sentence: the cause of all this lies in Job himself. If there is a Redeemer who will stand up at the last, there is also a judgment, and it may fall on them. It did: “My anger burns against you and against your two friends” (42:7). And the man they condemned would pray for them (42:8).

Saved by the one condemned. That is the shape of the gospel. We who condemned Christ were saved by the one we condemned, who died for us and prayed for us: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Job’s Redeemer lives, and he lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25).

keyVerse.quote: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the book’s longing for someone to stand between Job and God (9:33; 16:19), spoken from its lowest point. Job has a living kinsman-redeemer who will stand on the dust of his grave. The Son of God became that kinsman in our flesh, died, and rose as “the living one” (Revelation 1:18).

19.reflection:
The friends made Job’s disgrace “an argument against” him (v. 5). How do people today still treat suffering as evidence against the sufferer, and how can we be better comforters than Job’s friends?

In verses 13–19 Job is abandoned by family, friends and servants. How does it help a lonely or rejected believer to know that Jesus was deserted by his own (John 1:11; Mark 14:50)? Who around you might be feeling like Job?

A go’el was a near kinsman who rescued family members in trouble. What does it mean for you that Jesus became your kinsman in order to be your Redeemer (Hebrews 2:14)?

Job says, “I know that my Redeemer lives” when nothing in his circumstances has changed. How can a believer say “I know” in the dark? How does the hope of seeing God “in my flesh” (v. 26) shape the way you grieve and face death?

20.title: The Wicked Man's Portion
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me.<sup>3</sup>I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.<sup>4</sup>Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth,<sup>5</sup>that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment?<sup>6</sup>Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,<sup>7</sup>he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?'<sup>8</sup>He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night.<sup>9</sup>The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him.<sup>10</sup>His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth.<sup>11</sup>His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.<sup>12</sup>"Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue,<sup>13</sup>though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth,<sup>14</sup>yet his food is turned in his stomach; a bronze arrow will strike him through.<sup>25</sup>It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him.<sup>26</sup>Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.<sup>27</sup>The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.<sup>28</sup>The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath.<sup>29</sup>This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
20.overview:
Where we are. Job has just confessed, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25), and warned the friends that there is a judgment (19:29). Now Zophar answers for the second and last time, closing the second round of the debate. He ignores the confession and hears only the warning.

The message. Zophar’s speech is true about sin and false about Job. It is true that the joy of the wicked is short, that sin sweet in the mouth turns to poison, and that greed cannot keep what it swallows. But Zophar insists that this always happens quickly and visibly in this life, and he aims it at a man God called blameless. The chapter warns against both the sweetness of sin and the cruelty of tidy explanations, and leaves us asking who could ever bear the wicked man’s portion in another’s place.

Why it was said. Zophar holds the friends’ fixed belief that God always repays in this life (see the introduction), and Job’s warning (19:28–29) has stung him. Since Job will not confess, Zophar now hints for the first time at a specific crime: oppressing the poor (v. 19).

How the chapter makes its case. Stung by the insult (vv. 1–3), Zophar appeals to what has been known since man was placed on earth: the triumph of the wicked is short (vv. 4–5). Though he reach the clouds, he perishes like his own dung and vanishes like a dream (vv. 6–9); his children beg from the poor, and his strength lies down in the dust (vv. 10–11). Then comes the speech’s one new picture: evil sweet in the mouth turns to cobra venom in the stomach, and God makes the greedy man vomit up the riches he swallowed (vv. 12–19). The man never satisfied will be filled at last with God’s burning anger, struck by arrows and consumed by a fire no one lit (vv. 20–26). Heaven reveals his guilt and earth rises against him: this is the wicked man’s portion from God (vv. 27–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the character of God revealed in the gospel. Zophar can describe the portion God gives the wicked, but he cannot imagine anyone else bearing it. At the cross the one man who was not wicked received it: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Because he took the wicked man’s portion, those who trust him receive his, and God himself becomes their portion (Psalm 73:26). And the heavens did reveal the truth in the end, but it was Job’s innocence, not his guilt (42:7).

For us. Take Zophar’s true warning seriously: the sin you hold under your tongue will turn to poison, so run from it to the mercy that forgives. But do not copy his method, for a true doctrine aimed by guesswork at a sufferer becomes a lie. And when an argument stings you, listen again for the sentence you may have missed: it may be the one that could change everything.
20.theology:
Zophar's last speech ignores Job's confession of a living Redeemer and turns Job's own hope against him. Its one new picture is a true warning: sin is sweet in the mouth and deadly in the stomach (vv. 12-16; James 1:14-15).

Christ received the wicked man's portion though he knew no sin, and so the believer's portion is God himself.
20.examples: Zophar never speaks again after this, and his parting line, the wicked man's portion, is one Job will quote back at him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Exulting of the Wicked Is Short
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar’s point is that the triumph of the wicked has always been brief, and he means Job’s. He speaks because he feels insulted by Job’s rebuke (vv. 1–3). Since man was placed on earth, he says, the joy of the godless has lasted only a moment (vv. 4–5). However high the wicked man climbs, he perishes like his own dung and vanishes like a dream, so that those who knew him ask where he is (vv. 6–9). His children must seek the favour of the poor, his hands give back what he took, and his youthful strength lies down with him in the dust (vv. 10–11). Line after line echoes Job’s own losses.
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar has heard only the warning aimed at him, not the hope that came just before it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me. I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar speaks because he feels insulted, and he has heard only Job’s warning, not Job’s great confession of faith.

Zophar the Naamathite answered. This is Zophar’s last speech. As the text stands, he will say nothing at all in the third round (some scholars think part of chapter 27 was once his). His case was set out in chapter 11, and the round’s subject, the end of the wicked, in chapter 15; what follows repeats both. What is new is what he does not say.

What Zophar did not hear. Job has just said, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25), the highest confession of faith in the book so far. Zophar does not mention it. What he heard was the warning that judgment might fall on the friends (19:28–29), “censure that insults me”. It is a very human failure: people in an argument often hear only the sentence that stings them, and miss the one that could have changed everything.

Uncertain wording. Verses 2–3 are hard in Hebrew. “Because of my haste within me” probably means his inner agitation, and “out of my understanding a spirit answers me” his own mind prompting him to reply. The sense is clear enough: Zophar is upset and cannot keep quiet.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth, that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar appeals to the wisdom of the ages: the joy of the wicked has always been short-lived.

Do you not know this from of old? Zophar appeals to what everyone has always known, “since man was placed on earth”, that is, since Adam. Like Bildad before him (8:8–10), he rests on the wisdom of the ages rather than on what he has seen. Long tradition deserves a hearing, but a general truth can be wrongly applied, and here it is turned into a rule without exceptions.

The exulting of the wicked is short. That is true in the end, and the psalms say it: “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end … How they are destroyed in a moment” (Psalm 73:17–19). But Zophar means that it is always short in this life, and Job will spend the next chapter showing that it often is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds, he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?' He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night. The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However high the wicked man rises, says Zophar, he will vanish like a dream, utterly and for ever.

Though his height mount up to the heavens. The proud man who climbs to the clouds, like the king of Babylon who said, “I will ascend to heaven” (Isaiah 14:13), ends on the dung heap and vanishes like a dream. Job said the same of every man (7:8–10); Zophar says it only of the wicked.

He will perish forever like his own dung. The coarse picture is deliberate: the man who rose highest ends as the lowest and most worthless thing, swept away and forgotten. He is gone so completely that those who saw him ask, “Where is he?”, like a dream gone on waking: “Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms” (Psalm 73:20).

verseByVerse.quote: His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth. His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man’s children are left begging, his stolen wealth is handed back, and he dies in his prime: once more the lines are drawn from Job’s own life.

His hands will give back his wealth. What he took he must return, probably to the very people he robbed; Zophar makes that charge plainer in v. 19 (see the note on vv. 12–19).

It will lie down with him in the dust. His bones are full of youthful vigour, and all his strength goes into the grave with him. The point is not that he grows old and weak, but that death cuts him off while he still feels strong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–29 — The Wicked Man's Portion from God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar’s point is that wickedness, however sweet, carries its own punishment from God, and that this is the portion God has decreed for the wicked. Evil is a sweet held under the tongue that turns to cobra venom in the stomach; God makes the greedy man vomit up his riches, and he never enjoys the streams of honey and curds, because he crushed the poor (vv. 12–19). The man who was never satisfied will be filled with God’s anger, pierced by arrows and consumed by a fire no one fanned (vv. 20–26). Heaven and earth will witness against him: this is his heritage from God (vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar turns Job's hope into his doom, and God will turn the verdict back on Zophar.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth, yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him. He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly. He will suck the poison of cobras; the tongue of a viper will kill him. He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds. He will give back the fruit of his toil and will not swallow it down; from the profit of his trading he will get no enjoyment. For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is sweet in the mouth and poison in the stomach, says Zophar, and that is true; but his hint that Job crushed the poor is false.

Evil is sweet in his mouth. This is the one new picture in the speech, and it is a true one. The sinner rolls sin round his tongue like a sweet, cannot bear to let it go, and swallows it, and in the stomach it turns to snake venom. “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel” (Proverbs 20:17). James traces the same course: “desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:15). Every believer should hear the warning, and run from the sweet poison to the mercy that forgives and the Spirit who gives new desires (Galatians 5:16).

He swallows down riches and vomits them up again. God makes the greedy man bring his riches back up, like the rich fool who heard, “This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). “Streams flowing with honey and curds” is plenty at its richest, like the land “flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), and the greedy man will never enjoy it.

He has crushed and abandoned the poor. Here, for the first time, a friend hints at a specific charge; Eliphaz will say it outright (22:6–9). It is false. Job was the man who “delivered the poor who cried for help” (29:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him. There was nothing left after he had eaten; therefore his prosperity will not endure. In the fullness of his sufficiency he will be in distress; the hand of everyone in misery will come against him. To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body. He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through. It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him. Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who was never satisfied will be filled at last, says Zophar, with God’s wrath, and he paints it in Job’s own pictures of his pain.

To fill his belly to the full. The man always hungry for more will be filled at last, with God’s burning anger. Zophar pictures sickness in the body as anger rained down from heaven, and he is looking at Job’s body when he says it.

Job’s picture turned against him. Job had described his suffering in exactly these terms: God’s archers, and “he pours out my gall on the ground” (16:13). Zophar takes Job’s picture of his own pain and makes it the death of the wicked. “A fire not fanned” is one no human hand lit, as none lit the “fire of God” that fell on Job’s flocks (1:16).

Uncertain wording. Several lines here are obscure in Hebrew. Verse 20 may mean, as the ESV takes it, that the greedy man lets nothing he delights in escape his grasp, or that he will not be able to save anything he delights in. In verse 23, “into his body” can also be read “as his food”, so that God rains his anger on the glutton as his meal. On each reading the greedy man’s appetite is answered by judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar turns Job’s own hope into his doom; but heaven’s real verdict vindicated Job, and Christ bore the wicked man’s portion.

The heavens will reveal his iniquity. Here Zophar answers Job directly, and cleverly. Job had cried, “O earth, cover not my blood”, and “my witness is in heaven” (16:18–19); and just now, that his Redeemer “will stand upon the earth” (19:25). Zophar turns all three round: heaven will witness against you, and the earth will “rise up”, the same verb as “stand”, not for you but against you. Job’s hope is thrown back at him as his doom.

The wicked man’s portion from God. Zophar’s last words are a verdict: this is the share God deals out to the wicked. Job will quote the line back almost word for word (27:13).

What heaven did reveal. The heavens did reveal the truth in the end, and it was not Job’s iniquity: God said that Job had spoken rightly and Zophar had not (42:7). And there was one man who received the wicked man’s portion from God though he was not wicked: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Because he took that portion, the believer’s portion is God himself: “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

keyVerse.quote: This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God.
keyVerse.note: Zophar’s whole speech drives to this verdict, and he means it for Job. It is true that God apportions judgment to the wicked, but false that Job is the wicked man. The gospel goes further than Zophar could: the one man who was not wicked took this portion at the cross (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that God himself is the portion of all who trust him (Psalm 73:26).

20.reflection:
Zophar passes over Job’s confession, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25), and hears only the words that stung him (vv. 2–3). When have you heard only the part of someone’s words that hurt you? How can we listen better, especially to people in pain?

Zophar says that evil is sweet in the mouth but turns to poison within (vv. 12–16). Where have you seen this happen? How does the gospel help us when a sin still tastes sweet?

Much of what Zophar says about the end of the wicked is true, yet it is false about Job. How can we hold firmly to God’s justice without turning it into a rule that every sufferer must be guilty?

Zophar calls ruin “the wicked man’s portion from God” (v. 29). How does 2 Corinthians 5:21 change what the believer’s portion is, and what difference does it make to say with the psalmist that God is “my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26)?

21.title: Why Do the Wicked Live?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort.<sup>3</sup>Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.<sup>4</sup>As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient?<sup>5</sup>Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth.<sup>6</sup>When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.<sup>7</sup>Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?<sup>8</sup>Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes.<sup>9</sup>Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.<sup>10</sup>Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry.<sup>11</sup>They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance.<sup>12</sup>They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe.<sup>13</sup>They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.<sup>14</sup>They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.<sup>15</sup>What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'<sup>16</sup>Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>17</sup>"How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger?<sup>18</sup>That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?<sup>19</sup>You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it.<sup>20</sup>Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty.<sup>21</sup>For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?<sup>22</sup>Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high?<sup>23</sup>One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure,<sup>24</sup>his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist.<sup>25</sup>Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity.<sup>26</sup>They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me.<sup>28</sup>For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?'<sup>29</sup>Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony<sup>30</sup>that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?<sup>31</sup>Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done?<sup>32</sup>When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb.<sup>33</sup>The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable.<sup>34</sup>How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
21.overview:
Where we are. Zophar has just finished the second round of debate with the darkest sermon yet on the fate of the wicked (chapter 20). Job now answers the whole round, not with lament but with facts.

The message. The friends’ rule, that the wicked always suffer in this life, is simply not true, and anyone who has looked at the world knows it. Many who tell God to depart live long and die in comfort. Through Job’s honesty God teaches that faith does not need to pretend, that justice is not always visible on this side of the grave, and that a theology which ignores the facts can only offer “empty nothings” (v. 34).

Why it was said. All three friends have preached the same sermon on the end of the wicked (15:20–35; 18:5–21; 20:4–29), aimed at Job. Their case rests on the belief that God always repays in this life (see the introduction). Job answers it at its root.

How the chapter makes its case. Job first asks simply to be heard: his quarrel is with God, and what he is about to say makes him shudder (vv. 1–6). Then he paints the prosperous wicked, long-lived, their children dancing, though they tell God, “Depart from us!” Yet he refuses their counsel (vv. 7–16). He asks how often the lamp of the wicked is really put out, rejects the idea that God punishes their children instead, and sets two deaths side by side under the same worms (vv. 17–26). Finally he appeals to any traveller: the evil man is often spared and buried with a guard of honour, so the friends’ comfort is vapour and their answers falsehood (vv. 27–34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by the God who answers it. If death were the end, Job’s two corpses under the same worms would mean there is no justice at all. Christ’s resurrection is God’s proof that there is: he “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). And the chapter’s strange reversal, the evil man spared in the day of wrath (v. 30), finds its deepest answer at the cross, where God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The repentant are spared because judgment fell on him.

For us. Be honest about the world; God does not need us to pretend that the wicked never prosper. When their prosperity tempts you to envy, look to the day God has fixed, and hold on to God himself, who is better than all they have. And with those who suffer, begin as Job asks: listen.
21.theology:
Job answers the second round with the facts: the wicked often prosper and die in peace. Scripture agrees (Jer 12:1; Ps 73) and places the reckoning beyond death: after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27; Luke 16:25). The friends' neat system is empty nothings, and God will say so (42:7).

The wicked reject God because prayer brings no profit (v. 15). Satan accused Job of serving God for profit (1:9), yet Job goes on serving God when it has cost him everything.
21.examples: Some of the chapter's phrases are worth carrying away. Let this be your comfort tells every visitor to the sick and the grieving that listening is itself a gift. What profit do we get if we pray to him? is the wicked man's reason for refusing God, the opposite of Job, who serves him at a loss. And How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? takes Bildad's own picture and asks how often anyone has actually seen it happen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Lay Your Hand over Your Mouth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he argues, Job asks to be heard, because listening is the comfort his friends have not yet given. He asks them to bear with him to the end of his speech, and then they may mock (vv. 1–3). His complaint is not with any man but with God, which is why he cannot simply be patient. What he is about to describe should make them fall silent with their hands over their mouths, and it makes him shudder to think of it (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The best comfort the friends could have given was to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort. Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks his friends for the one comfort they have not given him: to listen to the end, and then mock if they must.

Keep listening to my words. Zophar has made his last speech, and Job answers with something new: not a lament, but an argument from the facts. He begins with a request every comforter should hear: “let this be your comfort”.

The rarest ministry. The friends came to comfort (2:11) and have done everything but listen. The ministry Job asks for is the cheapest there is and the rarest.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient? Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth. When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s quarrel is with God, not with any man, and what he is about to say should silence them, as it terrifies him.

Is my complaint against man? A man can shrug off a human critic, but not the Almighty. That is why Job cannot simply calm down: “Why should I not be impatient?”

Lay your hand over your mouth. Look at me and be silent. When God has spoken from the whirlwind, Job himself will say, “I lay my hand on my mouth” (40:4). The silence he asks of the friends before his suffering, he will give to God before his glory.

When I remember, I am dismayed. He is going to describe the world as it actually is, and it does not fit what anyone has been taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Why Do the Wicked Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the wicked often flourish to the end, the plain opposite of what the friends have preached. They live to old age, their children are settled around them, and no rod of God touches their houses (vv. 7–9). Their herds breed, their children dance to tambourine and pipe, and they die in peace (vv. 10–13). All this while they tell God to depart, since prayer brings no profit (vv. 14–15). Yet Job, who has lost everything they still have, refuses their counsel (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the whole second round with plain facts. And he refuses the wicked's creed even though it seems to work.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes. Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job states plainly what the friends have denied: the wicked often live long, grow powerful and keep their families safe, untouched by God’s rod.

Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Zophar said “the exulting of the wicked is short” (20:5). Then why do so many live to a ripe old age with their grandchildren around them, untouched by the “rod of God”? Job knows the rod; it is on him (9:34).

Jeremiah’s question. Jeremiah asked the same: “Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” (Jeremiah 12:1). Both hold that God is righteous and bring the question to him. Faith does not require pretending that the wicked never prosper.

verseByVerse.quote: Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry. They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance. They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe. They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked enjoy thriving herds, happy children and a peaceful death, everything Job has lost; but a peaceful death is not the end of the story.

Their children dance. Herds that breed; little boys let out to play like lambs; children dancing to tambourine and pipe. Every line hurts, because Job’s own children once feasted together in their brother’s house (1:4). The children of the wicked dance; his are in the ground.

In peace they go down to Sheol. No long illness, no ash heap. Jesus’ story of the rich man and Lazarus answers this line: “remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish” (Luke 16:25).

verseByVerse.quote: They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?' Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prosperous wicked tell God to go away because religion does not pay, yet Job, who has lost everything, will not take their advice.

Depart from us! Religion does not pay, they say, and here the first chapter is turned inside out. Satan accused Job of serving God for profit: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9). The wicked reject God because serving him brings no profit; Job serves him when it has brought him nothing but loss. And their “Depart from us” will be answered in their own words at the last: “I never knew you; depart from me” (Matthew 7:23).

The counsel of the wicked is far from me. Job wants no part of their philosophy, however well it seems to work. The Psalter opens by blessing the man who makes the same refusal (Psalm 1:1), and Eliphaz will quote Job’s line back at him word for word (22:18).

When the wicked do well. Watching them, we are tempted not only to doubt God but to envy them. Asaph nearly slipped on exactly this, and found his footing only when he saw that what he had was God himself: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). Job has lost everything the wicked still have, and he would rather have God with nothing than their prosperity without him.

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 reads literally as a statement, that their prosperity is not in their hand. The ESV takes it as a question (they seem to hold it securely); others take it as it stands (their prosperity is God’s gift, not their own doing). The last line is clear either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — How Often Is the Lamp of the Wicked Put Out?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that in this life the judgment of the wicked cannot always be seen, so the friends cannot read guilt from suffering. How often, he asks, is the lamp of the wicked really put out (vv. 17–18)? If the friends say God punishes their children instead, that is no justice to a man who no longer cares (vv. 19–21). No one may teach God how to judge, and the grave takes the comfortable and the bitter alike (vv. 22–26). The reckoning must lie beyond death.
verseByVerse.theology: In this life the lamp of the wicked often burns to the end. The book's answer, and the gospel's, lies beyond the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger? That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How often has anyone actually seen the wicked snuffed out? Job does not deny that God judges, only that the judgment can always be seen in this life.

How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? Bildad said, “the light of the wicked is put out” and “his lamp above him is put out” (18:5–6) (the lamp left burning all night in a home). Job takes his words and asks: how often do you actually see it? The wicked truly “are like chaff that the wind drives away” (Psalm 1:4), but how often do we watch it happen in time to prove the friends’ argument?

verseByVerse.quote: You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it. Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty. For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the friends say God punishes the children of the wicked instead, Job replies that justice must reach the guilty man himself.

God stores up their iniquity for their children. Job anticipates the reply (the ESV supplies “You say” to show that he is quoting it). But what does the wicked man care for his house once he is dead? If justice means anything, it must reach the man himself, as Ezekiel would later say in God’s own word: “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20). And Job has heard where that argument leads, for Bildad said Job’s own children died for their sins (8:4).

Let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty. Job wants the guilty to drink the cup of wrath themselves (Jeremiah 25:15). One day an innocent man would pray in a garden for that cup to pass from him, and then drink it for others.

verseByVerse.quote: Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high? One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure, his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist. Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can teach God how to judge, and the grave treats the comfortable and the bitter alike, so the reckoning must lie beyond death.

Will any teach God knowledge? The friends are telling God how his justice must work, as if he were bound to run the world by their system. “Who taught him the path of justice?” asks Isaiah (Isaiah 40:14), and Paul, “who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34). (“Those who are on high” are probably heavenly beings.) No one teaches God. That cuts against the friends’ neat system, and it will cut against Job’s demands too when God speaks.

They lie down alike in the dust. Two deaths: one well fed and comfortable to the last, the other bitter all his days. And the grave makes no distinction; the worms take both. If this life were all, there would be no justice. The New Testament answers where Job’s argument points: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “pails” (v. 24) occurs only here. It may mean milk pails or a part of the body (the KJV has “breasts”, others “flanks” full of fat). Either way the man is well fed and vigorous to the day he dies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that common experience refutes the friends, so their comfort is empty. He knows that their pictures of the ruined house of the wicked were aimed at his own (vv. 27–28). But anyone who travels the roads can testify that the evil man is often spared in the day of calamity (vv. 29–30). No one dares rebuke him; he is buried with honour and a guard at his tomb, and crowds follow his funeral (vv. 31–33). So the friends’ answers are vapour and betrayal (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Job sums up the friends' comfort as vapour and treachery.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me. For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?' Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job knows that the friends’ ruined “house of the wicked” means his own, and he answers that any traveller knows better.

Where is the house of the prince? Job knows exactly whose house they mean. His own lies in ruins. They have been describing it for three chapters.

Have you not asked those who travel the roads? Anyone who has seen the world knows that disaster often passes the evil man by. Job appeals to common experience against a theory that ignores it.

Spared in the day of calamity. The gospel shows how the guilty can be truly spared at the last: God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The day of wrath fell on him, so that those who trust him are rescued in it.

Uncertain wording. A small Hebrew word in verse 30 can mean “in” or “for”. The ESV has the evil man spared “in” the day of calamity, which suits Job’s argument; the KJV has him “reserved to the day of destruction”, kept for judgment to come. The ESV is probably right here, but the other reading is also true.

verseByVerse.quote: Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done? When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb. The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable. How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powerful wicked man is never confronted and goes to an honoured grave, so the friends’ answers are vapour and betrayal.

Who declares his way to his face? No one dares tell him the truth or repay him for what he has done.

Watch is kept over his tomb. A grand funeral, a guard of honour at the grave (see burial customs), the earth lying lightly on him, crowds in the procession. Christians may remember another guarded tomb, watched for a very different reason. The authorities “made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard” (Matthew 27:66), to keep the Righteous One in. It could not.

Nothing left of your answers but falsehood. Verse 34 is Job’s verdict on the friends’ whole case. “Empty nothings” is hevel, vapour, the word of Ecclesiastes; “falsehood” is the word for unfaithfulness, used again and again in Chronicles of unfaithfulness to God. God will give the same verdict at the end: “you have not spoken of me what is right” (42:7).

keyVerse.quote: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?
keyVerse.note: This question drives the whole chapter and answers the whole second round, in which all three friends insisted that the wicked always come to ruin. Job will not pretend about the world, yet he asks his question of God and still refuses the counsel of the wicked (v. 16). The answer lies beyond the grave, on the day God has fixed for judgment by the man he raised from the dead (Acts 17:31).

21.reflection:
Job begins, “let this be your comfort”: simply listen (v. 2). Why is listening so hard when someone is suffering? What would it look like to listen well to a friend this week?

Job insists that the wicked often prosper and die in peace (vv. 7–13). Why is it important that faith does not pretend about the world? How do Jeremiah 12:1 and Psalm 73 help us bring this question to God rather than away from him?

The wicked say, “what profit do we get if we pray to him?” (v. 15), while Job keeps serving God at a loss. Where are you tempted to measure God by what he gives you? What would it mean to want God himself?

Two men die, one at ease and one in bitterness, and “the worms cover them” (v. 26). How do Christ’s resurrection and the coming judgment (Hebrews 9:27; Acts 17:31) change the way we look at the unfairness we see now?

22.title: Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.<sup>3</sup>Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless?<sup>4</sup>Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?<sup>5</sup>Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities.<sup>6</sup>For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing.<sup>7</sup>You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.<sup>8</sup>The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it.<sup>9</sup>You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.<sup>10</sup>Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you,<sup>11</sup>or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.<sup>12</sup>"Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are!<sup>13</sup>But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness?<sup>14</sup>Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'<sup>15</sup>Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod?<sup>16</sup>They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away.<sup>17</sup>They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?'<sup>18</sup>Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>19</sup>The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them,<sup>20</sup>saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'<sup>21</sup>"Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.<sup>22</sup>Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.<sup>23</sup>If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents,<sup>24</sup>if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed,<sup>25</sup>then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.<sup>26</sup>For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.<sup>27</sup>You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows.<sup>28</sup>You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.<sup>29</sup>For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly.<sup>30</sup>He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
22.overview:
Where we are. Job has just shown that the wicked often prosper and die in peace, and called the friends’ comfort “empty nothings” (21:34). Now the third and last round of debate begins (chapters 22–27), and Eliphaz, the oldest friend, speaks for the last time. He no longer hints; he accuses.

The message. Eliphaz’s speech shows where a theology that cannot be wrong finally goes: when the facts do not fit, it invents them. With no evidence, he charges the man God called blameless with cruelty to the poor. Yet God overrules even this. Eliphaz’s best line, “the Almighty will be your gold” (v. 25), is true, and his last line, that God “delivers even the one who is not innocent” through someone else’s clean hands (v. 30), comes true on Eliphaz himself.

Why it was said. The friends believe that God always repays in this life (see the introduction), and Job has just argued that experience proves otherwise. Eliphaz cannot answer the argument, so he answers the man: if Job suffers so greatly, his sins must be great. His words must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer, for God said they had not spoken rightly of him (42:7).

How the chapter makes its case. First Eliphaz argues that God gains nothing from a man’s righteousness, so he cannot be punishing Job for his piety; it must be for “abundant” evil, and he lists sins Job never committed: stripping the poor, refusing bread to the hungry, sending widows away empty (vv. 1–11). Then he accuses Job of thinking God too far away to see, and of walking the old path of the wicked, borrowing Job’s own words to do it (vv. 12–20). Finally he pleads with Job to agree with God, return to him and make the Almighty his gold; then his prayers will be heard and he will even deliver others (vv. 21–30).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the gospel Eliphaz speaks without knowing it. The innocent Job is falsely accused, as Jesus would be. And Eliphaz’s closing words come true in chapter 42, when the guilty Eliphaz is spared through the prayer of the man he accused. That is the shape of the gospel: “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The guilty are delivered through the clean hands of another, hands that were pierced for them.

For us. Never invent sins to explain someone’s suffering; a counsellor who “knows” without evidence is doing what Eliphaz did. Make God your treasure, now, before trouble takes the rest. And rest your hope not on your own clean hands but on Christ’s, who prays for those who wronged him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s point is that Job’s suffering must be the punishment for great sin, and he supplies the sins himself. He begins with a half-truth: God gains nothing from a man’s goodness, so he cannot be reproving Job for his piety (vv. 1–4). It must therefore be for abundant evil, and Eliphaz lists the crimes of a cruel rich man: taking pledges for nothing, stripping the naked, refusing water and bread, sending widows away empty, crushing orphans (vv. 5–9). That, he says, is why snares, terror, darkness and flood surround Job now (vv. 10–11). Every charge is false.
verseByVerse.theology: With no evidence, Eliphaz invents Job's crimes. They are the opposite of what the narrator and God have said of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless? Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz argues that God gains nothing from Job’s goodness, so he cannot be punishing him for it; he has asked the question the whole book turns on, and got the answer backwards.

The last round. Eliphaz speaks for the last time, and now he stops hinting and starts inventing.

Can a man be profitable to God? Eliphaz’s answer is no: God gains nothing from us. Half of that is true. God needs nothing, and Paul asks, “Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35), quoting this very book (41:11). But the other half is false. God does take pleasure in the righteous; he said so in heaven: “Have you considered my servant Job?” (1:8). “He will rejoice over you with gladness” (Zephaniah 3:17). Eliphaz’s God is too remote to care.

Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you? Eliphaz means it as sarcasm: surely God is not punishing you for being godly! The reader, who has seen the scene in heaven (chapters 1–2), knows the answer. It was precisely because of Job’s fear of God that the trial came: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities. For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry. The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it. You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed. Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you, or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no evidence, Eliphaz invents Job’s crimes against the poor, the very sins Christ will name at the last judgment, and God will call his speech false.

Is not your evil abundant? With no evidence, Eliphaz supplies it: Job must have taken the cloak of a poor man as security for a debt and left him naked (the law required a pledged cloak to be returned by nightfall, Exodus 22:26; see clothing), refused water to a traveller and bread to the hungry, turned widows away and trampled orphans. None of it is true. Job will answer every item: “I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him” (29:12); no one perished “for lack of clothing”, for each was “warmed with the fleece of my sheep” (31:19–20). And the charge about orphans turns back on him one that Job made against the friends (6:27).

For nothing. The Hebrew is chinnam, Satan’s word: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9). God said Job’s suffering was “without reason” (2:3). The word that marks Job’s innocence is now used to accuse him.

The sins of the goats. The list is the very list by which Christ will judge the nations: “For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink … naked and you did not clothe me” (Matthew 25:42–43). Eliphaz has charged Job with the sins of the goats, the people condemned in that scene (see sheep and goats). Job belonged with the sheep. And Jesus himself would one day stand before religious leaders who, having no evidence, looked for false witnesses (Matthew 26:59).

Therefore snares are all around you. When the facts will not fit the friends’ theology, the facts are invented. A counsellor who “knows” what a sufferer must have done, without evidence, is doing what Eliphaz did, and God will call it what he called it (42:7).

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is hard to place. It may describe Job as the man of power who seized the land for himself, or it may accuse him of favouring the powerful while he turned the poor away. Either way it belongs to the same false charge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s point is that Job thinks God too remote to see, and is walking the old road of the wicked. He sets God high above the stars, then puts in Job’s mouth the wicked man’s words: God cannot see through the clouds (vv. 12–14). He warns Job against the path of the ancient wicked, swept away before their time, who said to God, “Depart from us,” though he had filled their houses with good things (vv. 15–18). The righteous, he says, rejoice to see their fall (vv. 19–20). He borrows Job’s own words to make the charge.
verseByVerse.theology: Eliphaz puts the words of the wicked in Job's mouth, and borrows Job's own words to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are! But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness? Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz accuses Job of thinking God too high and far away to see, the very opposite of what Job has complained.

Is not God high in the heavens? Eliphaz begins with a truth no one in the book denies: God is higher than the highest stars. Then he imagines Job reasoning that a God so high must be too far away to see, peering down through “deep darkness” and “thick clouds” as he “walks on the vault of heaven”, the dome of the sky. Scripture draws the opposite conclusion from God’s height: “Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?” (Psalm 113:5–6). Being high above all things is what lets him see all things.

What does God know? Eliphaz puts words in Job’s mouth, and they are the wicked man’s words: “How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Psalm 73:11). Job has said the opposite all along. His complaint is that God sees too much: he said God would “watch all my paths” (13:27) and “test him every moment” (7:18). Eliphaz is not listening; he is answering the man his theory needs Job to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away. They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?' Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me. The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them, saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz warns Job off the old road of the wicked, and does it by taking Job’s own words and making them his.

The old way that wicked men have trod. Probably the generation of the flood, swept away with their foundations (2 Peter 2:5). Their “Depart from us” is Job’s own description of the wicked (21:14), and “the counsel of the wicked is far from me” is Job’s own sentence, word for word (21:16). Eliphaz sets it in his own mouth: I, Eliphaz, am the one far from the wicked. He has turned Job’s confession into his accusation.

Yet he filled their houses with good things. Their prosperity came from God, which only made their ingratitude worse: they said “Depart from us” to the God who had filled their houses. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and they took it as proof that they did not need him.

The innocent one mocks at them. The righteous are glad, and the fire consumes what the wicked left, as it consumed Job’s flocks (1:16). There is a right gladness when God puts down evil (Psalm 58:10), but laughing over the ashes comes close to gloating, and Proverbs warns against it: “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls” (Proverbs 24:17). The friends, sure that Job is the wicked man, are standing over him in just this way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–30 — Agree with God, and Be at Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz’s point is that if Job returns to God, all will be restored, and his appeal contains some of the loveliest words in the book. Agree with God, receive his words, put away injustice, treat gold as gravel, and the Almighty himself will be Job’s gold (vv. 21–25). Then Job will delight in God, pray and be heard, and light will shine on his way; God saves the lowly, and will even deliver the guilty through Job’s clean hands (vv. 26–30). The offer is conditional and aimed at the wrong man, yet its last line comes true on Eliphaz himself (42:7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: These are the loveliest words Eliphaz ever speaks, and his last. Their final line comes true in a way he never meant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents, if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz calls Job to return and make God his treasure: lovely words, true in themselves, but offered as a condition to a man who has never left God.

Agree with God, and be at peace. Elsewhere these would be the gospel’s own invitation: “be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). But Eliphaz makes Job’s return the condition: return, and then you will be built up. The gospel’s invitation rests on what God has already done: “in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them” (2 Corinthians 5:19). And Job has not been disagreeing with God, only with Eliphaz about God. He has already done what Eliphaz demands: “I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food” (23:12). In the end God will say which of them agreed with him (42:7).

The Almighty will be your gold. It is true, and beautiful, whatever the speaker’s motives, and Paul lived it: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Job has already lost all his gold. He is about to prove that God is his treasure without it.

Gold in the dust. To “lay gold in the dust” and the “gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed” is to treat one’s treasure as gravel, thrown away because something better has been found. Ophir was the far-off source of the finest gold, where Solomon’s ships went (1 Kings 9:28); its site is uncertain, probably in Arabia or East Africa.

For us. Eliphaz’s order is wrong, but his treasure is right: we do not make God our gold in order to be restored; restored in Christ, we can hold every other gold loosely.

verseByVerse.quote: For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows. You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways. For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly. He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eliphaz’s last words prophesy more than he knows: God does deliver the guilty through another’s clean hands, and the guilty man turns out to be Eliphaz.

He will hear you. Every word of this comes true. Job will pray and God will hear, but the prayer God hears will be Job’s prayer for Eliphaz.

Delivered through the cleanness of your hands. Eliphaz means that a repentant Job will be able to rescue other sinners by his prayers. In chapter 42 God, angry with Eliphaz, sends him with seven bulls and seven rams to Job and says, “my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer not to deal with you according to your folly” (42:8).
