The one who was “not innocent” was Eliphaz. The clean hands were Job’s. Eliphaz was delivered through the prayers of the man he had accused.

The gospel in Eliphaz’s words. That is the gospel in a sentence Eliphaz spoke without knowing it. “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Who has “clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:4)? Only one man fully, and he prayed for those who wronged him (Luke 23:34) and “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). The guilty are delivered through the clean hands of another, hands that were pierced for them.

Uncertain wording. Verses 29–30 are among the hardest lines in the chapter. In verse 29 the Hebrew is compressed, and the KJV reads it quite differently (“When men are cast down, then thou shalt say, There is lifting up”). In verse 30 “the one who is not innocent” uses an unusual word for “not”; the KJV took it as “island”, and some scholars change it slightly to read “the innocent”. The ESV’s reading is well supported and fits the chapter’s end, where the guilty are spared through Job’s prayer.

22.theology:
When the facts do not fit the friends' system, Eliphaz invents them (vv. 5-9), and God judged the speech false (42:7). Yet his sarcastic question, whether God reproves Job for his fear of God (v. 4), is answered yes by the book’s opening chapter (1:8-9).

Eliphaz's last words (v. 30) are fulfilled on himself: the one who was not innocent is delivered through Job's intercession (42:8), as the guilty are saved through the clean hands of Christ.
22.examples: Eliphaz is a warning to every comforter. He answers the man his theory needs rather than the man in front of him, and even borrows Job's own words to accuse him. Yet he also speaks the chapter's loveliest line, the Almighty will be your gold, which is true whatever the speaker's motives: God is the treasure that remains when everything else has gone.

keyVerse.quote: He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.
keyVerse.note: These are Eliphaz’s last words in the book, and they come true on Eliphaz himself: in chapter 42 the guilty friend is spared through the prayer of the innocent man he accused (42:8). Without knowing it, Eliphaz has described the gospel, in which the unrighteous are brought to God through the righteous one who suffered for them (1 Peter 3:18).

22.reflection:
With no evidence, Eliphaz lists sins Job never committed (vv. 5–9). Why are we tempted to assume we know why someone is suffering? What does this chapter warn us about when we try to help?

Eliphaz imagines that a God so high cannot see (vv. 12–14), but Psalm 113:5–6 says his height is what lets him see everything. When have you felt that God was too far away to notice you, and how does this truth answer that feeling?

“The Almighty will be your gold” (v. 25) is true even on Eliphaz’s lips. What does it look like to treat God as your treasure in ordinary life? What “gold” would you find hardest to lay in the dust?

Eliphaz was delivered through the prayers of the man he wronged (v. 30; 42:8). How does this picture what Christ has done for us? Is there someone who has wronged you whom you could pray for this week?

23.title: He Knows the Way That I Take
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.<sup>3</sup>Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat!<sup>4</sup>I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments.<sup>5</sup>I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.<sup>6</sup>Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me.<sup>7</sup>There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.<sup>8</sup>"Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him;<sup>9</sup>on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.<sup>10</sup>But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.<sup>11</sup>My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside.<sup>12</sup>I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.<sup>13</sup>But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does.<sup>14</sup>For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.<sup>15</sup>Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him.<sup>16</sup>God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me;<sup>17</sup>yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
23.overview:
Where we are. Eliphaz has just accused Job of crimes he never committed and urged him to return to God (chapter 22). Job will answer the charges in chapters 29–31; here he turns away from Eliphaz altogether and speaks about God: where he is, and what he knows.

The message. God may be hidden from the sufferer, but he is never absent and never ignorant. Job cannot find God in any direction, “but he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold” (v. 10). The chapter gives believers in the dark both an honest longing and a sure hope: the God who cannot be seen sees us, his fire is a refiner’s and not an executioner’s, and what he has appointed he will complete.

Why it was said. Eliphaz told Job to return to God and receive his words (22:21–23), as if Job had left him. Job answers that he has never left God’s way; his trouble is that God seems to have left him. The friends think suffering means God is against him (see the introduction); Job holds on to God while feeling both his absence and his terrifying power.

How the chapter makes its case. Job longs to find God’s seat and lay out his case, and he now believes God would listen and acquit him (vv. 1–7). He searches forward, backward, left and right and cannot see him, yet he rests on the fact that God knows his way, and that he himself has kept God’s way and treasured his words (vv. 8–12). Then fear returns: God is unchangeable and will complete what he has appointed, and Job is terrified; yet the darkness has not silenced him (vv. 13–17).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by pattern. Job could not find the way to God’s seat; Christ has opened “the new and living way” (Hebrews 10:20), so that we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). Job was acquitted in the end through his innocence; we are acquitted through Christ’s. And Job’s tested faithfulness, holding to God’s words “more than my portion of food” (v. 12), was fulfilled in Jesus, who in his hunger answered the tempter that “man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4)

For us. When God seems silent, keep speaking to him: he knows your way even when you cannot see his. Read your trials as a refiner’s fire, not a sentence. And let God’s unchangeable purpose steady you rather than frighten you, for in Christ what he has appointed for you is your salvation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh, That I Knew Where I Might Find Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he longs to meet God face to face, and now believes God would hear him fairly. His complaint is still bitter (vv. 1–2), but his desire is not to escape God but to find him: to come to his seat, lay out his case and hear God’s answer (vv. 3–5). In chapter 9 he feared God would crush him; now he is sure God would pay attention, and that an upright man could reason with him and be acquitted for ever (vv. 6–7). Job longs to stand in the court he once feared.
verseByVerse.theology: Job now longs to stand in the court he once feared.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s suffering is unchanged and his complaint still bitter, but he turns from Eliphaz to speak about God.

Today also my complaint is bitter. Nothing has changed. Eliphaz has just accused him of crimes he never committed (22:5–9), and Job does not answer the charges yet. The rest of this chapter is about God: where he is, and what he knows.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew “my hand is heavy” is obscure (perhaps he presses his hand on his groaning to hold it in). Some translations read “his hand”, God’s hand on Job (compare 19:21). Either way he groans under a weight he cannot lift.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat! I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job longs not for an explanation from a friend but for a hearing from God himself, and the way he could not find has now been opened in Christ.

Oh, that I knew where I might find him. Few prayers in the Bible are more honest. Job does not doubt that God exists; he does not know where to find him. He wants to come “even to his seat”, God’s judgment seat, and hear God’s own answer.

The way Job did not know. The Christian knows the way Job did not. “We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us” (Hebrews 10:19–20). “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). The seat Job longed for is now “the throne of grace”, and we may draw near to it “with confidence” (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me. There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job now believes that God, if he could reach him, would listen rather than crush him, and acquit him for ever.

No; he would pay attention to me. In chapter 9 Job was sure that God would simply overpower him: “How then can I answer him?” (9:14). Now he says God would not crush him with his strength; he would listen. Something has changed in Job, not in his circumstances: he has longed for an arbiter (9:33), claimed a witness in heaven (16:19) and confessed a living Redeemer (19:25), and he has come to believe that God, if he could only reach him, would be fair.

Acquitted forever by my judge. That is the verdict every believer has in Christ: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Job hoped for it through his own innocence. We receive it through Christ’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — He Knows the Way That I Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that although he cannot find God, God has never lost sight of him. He searches in every direction, forward and back, left and right, and cannot see God at work (vv. 8–9). Yet God knows the way he takes, and the testing is a refiner’s fire: Job will come out as gold (v. 10). He can say this because he has kept God’s way without turning aside, and treasured God’s words more than his daily food (vv. 11–12). Hidden is not the same as absent.
verseByVerse.theology: Job cannot find God, and God has never lost sight of Job. The fire is a refiner's, and he will come out as gold.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job searches every direction and cannot find God, yet the God he cannot find is the God no one can escape.

He is not there. Forward and backward, left and right (in Hebrew idiom also east, west, north and south), and God is nowhere to be found. Job knows God is at work, “when he is working”, but he cannot see him. Many of God’s people have known seasons exactly like it.

Beside Psalm 139. There the psalmist tries every direction too, and cannot get away from God: “If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!” (Psalm 139:8). Job spoke of making “my bed in darkness” in the grave (17:13); the psalm answers that God is there too. Hidden is not the same as absent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job cannot see God, but God sees him, and the fire he is in is a refiner’s fire from which he will come out as gold.

He knows the way that I take. Job has lost sight of God; God has not lost sight of Job. It is the first psalm’s promise: “the LORD knows the way of the righteous” (Psalm 1:6). The believer who cannot find God in the dark is still completely known.

When he has tried me, I shall come out as gold. Job has spoken of testing before: God would “test him every moment” (7:18), and there it was a complaint. Now he sees that it is a refiner’s fire, not an executioner’s. Gold goes into the furnace to lose what is not gold. Eliphaz had promised that “the Almighty will be your gold” (22:25) if Job repented; Job answers that he will come out as gold because God is testing him, not punishing him.

The refiner. Malachi pictures the Lord who “will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3), and Peter writes to suffering Christians of “the tested genuineness of your faith”, “more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:7). The refiner sits beside the furnace and watches. Job came out as gold (42:10–17), and so will every believer whose faith is in Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that every trial means something in us is especially impure; Job was blameless (1:8), and testing proves faith as well as purifying it. Nor that we will feel refined at the time: Job says this in the middle of the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside. I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has kept God’s way and treasured his words more than food, the very faithfulness Christ showed when he was hungry and tempted.

I have kept his way. Job’s claim is not boasting. It is the testimony God himself gave of Job (1:8). And the last line answers Eliphaz, who told him to “receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart” (22:22): Job already has, more than his daily bread.

More than my portion of food. That is exactly the answer Jesus gave when he was tested, hungry, in the wilderness: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). Job held on to God’s word when he had nothing else; Christ held on to it when the devil offered him everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — What He Desires, That He Does
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that God’s unchangeable will both terrifies him and cannot silence him. God is one, and no one can turn him back; what he desires he does, and he will complete whatever he has appointed for Job (vv. 13–14). That is why Job is in dread of his presence, his heart faint before the Almighty (vv. 15–16). Yet the darkness has not stopped his mouth (v. 17). The same sovereignty that frightens Job is, for the believer who knows God’s purpose in Christ, the ground of hope.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty frightens Job, and it is also the ground of his hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does. For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is unchangeable and will carry out all he has appointed; Job says it with a shiver, but in Christ it is the believer’s comfort.

What he desires, that he does. Then the fear returns. The psalm says it as praise: “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). Job says it with a shiver, not knowing what God has appointed for him.

He will complete what he appoints. The Christian hears the same truth and is steadied by it, because he knows what God has appointed: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). The God who will complete what he appoints is exactly the God you want if what he has appointed is your salvation. Job could not yet see that God was completing his refining, not his ruin.

Uncertain wording. “He is unchangeable” renders a compressed phrase, literally “he is in one”: either God is one, without rival, or his mind is made up. Both fit “who can turn him back?”

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him. God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me; yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swings from trust to terror, yet he keeps speaking to God in the dark, and that is still faith.

Therefore I am terrified at his presence. Trust in verse 10 and terror in verse 15, in the same man and the same speech: real faith under pressure is not a steady glow but swings between confidence and dread.

Yet I am not silenced because of the darkness. He goes on praying, arguing, hoping, into the dark. Isaiah gives the word for such a person: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). A believer who can only keep talking to God, without feeling anything, is still walking by faith. Christ himself prayed in the dark of Gethsemane and on the cross, and the Father heard him (Hebrews 5:7).

When the darkness does not lift. Long seasons of feeling nothing can sometimes be depression, which is suffering, not sin. Keep praying, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and have a medical check-up; medicine, where needed, is no failure of faith.

Uncertain wording. Verse 17 is hard. The ESV reads defiance: the darkness has not silenced him. Others read a complaint, that he was not cut off before the darkness came (so the KJV), or that the darkness has undone him. The ESV suits the chapter’s movement.

23.theology: God may be hidden from the sufferer but is never absent (vv. 8-10), and trials are a refiner's fire from which faith comes out as gold (v. 10). The same unchangeable will that terrifies Job (vv. 13-16) is the believer's assurance, for what God has appointed he will complete. And the way to the seat Job longed for has been opened in Christ (Heb 10:19-22).
23.examples: This chapter has been a lifeline for believers who feel God has gone silent. It gives them words for the longing (Oh, that I knew where I might find him), a reason to hold on when they cannot see him (he knows the way that I take), and permission to keep praying when they feel nothing (yet I am not silenced because of the darkness).

keyVerse.quote: But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter and one of the great sentences of faith in the book. Job cannot find God anywhere, yet he rests on the fact that God knows him, and he reads his suffering as a refiner’s fire rather than a sentence. Peter writes the same hope to suffering Christians, whose tested faith is “more precious than gold” (1 Peter 1:7).

23.reflection:
“Oh, that I knew where I might find him” (v. 3). Have you known a season when God seemed absent? What helped you to keep seeking him, and how does Hebrews 10:19–22 speak to that longing?

Job cannot see God, “but he knows the way that I take” (v. 10). Why is it a comfort to be known by God even when we cannot sense him? How might that change the way you pray in hard times?

Job sees his suffering as a refiner’s fire (v. 10). What is the difference between being refined and being punished? Where have you seen God use a trial to strengthen faith, in your life or someone else’s?

God’s unchangeable purpose terrifies Job (vv. 13–15), but Philippians 1:6 makes it a comfort. Why does knowing what God has appointed for us in Christ make all the difference?

24.title: Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
24.text: <sup>1</sup>"Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?<sup>2</sup>Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them.<sup>3</sup>They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge.<sup>4</sup>They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.<sup>5</sup>Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children.<sup>6</sup>They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man.<sup>7</sup>They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.<sup>8</sup>They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.<sup>9</sup>(There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.)<sup>10</sup>They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves;<sup>11</sup>among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst.<sup>12</sup>From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.<sup>13</sup>"There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths.<sup>14</sup>The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.<sup>15</sup>The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me'; and he veils his face.<sup>16</sup>In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light.<sup>17</sup>For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.<sup>18</sup>"You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards.<sup>19</sup>Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned.<sup>20</sup>The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'<sup>21</sup>"They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow.<sup>22</sup>Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life.<sup>23</sup>He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways.<sup>24</sup>They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain.<sup>25</sup>If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
24.overview:
Where we are. Job’s reply to Eliphaz, begun in chapter 23, continues. Having spoken of his own case, he now lifts his eyes to the whole suffering world, and asks why God seems to let injustice run on unchecked.

The message. Job asks the question every believer asks who reads the news: “Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty?” (v. 1). The strong rob orphans and widows, the poor shiver on the mountainside, and God seems to charge no one with wrong. Yet Job does not deny God’s justice: God watches the mighty and cuts them off at last like heads of grain. The chapter teaches that judgment delayed is not judgment denied: God keeps his own times, and his patience is not blindness.

Why it was said. Eliphaz has accused Job of stripping the naked and crushing the fatherless (22:6–9). Job answers by describing the poor with a compassion no oppressor could feel, and by showing that the world is not as tidy as the friends’ theology (see the introduction). The wicked do fall, but on God’s timetable.

How the chapter makes its case. Job asks why God does not hold court on fixed days (v. 1). He describes the crimes of the strong: moving boundary stones, seizing the orphan’s donkey and the widow’s ox (vv. 2–4). He paints the poor, naked in the cold, clinging to the rock for shelter, harvesting food they may not eat, while the wounded cry out (vv. 5–12). He turns to those who rebel against the light: the murderer, the adulterer and the burglar who love the dark (vv. 13–17). Finally, the wicked are swept away (vv. 18–20); God lets the mighty stand a little while and then cuts them off like grain at harvest. Let anyone prove him a liar (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by the God he reveals. Job’s question is answered in the gospel: the delay is God’s patience, “not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9), and the day is fixed, with the Judge already named and raised from the dead (Acts 17:31). Until then the wheat and the weeds grow together (Matthew 13:30). And the Judge himself came among the poor this chapter describes: the Son of Man had “nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and the one who was rich “became poor” for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Bring your outrage at injustice to God in prayer, not cynicism. Do not take God’s patience for indifference: the harvest is certain. And let the chapter’s compassion for the poor become your own, for the Judge who is coming will ask what we did for the hungry and the naked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the oppressed suffer while God seems to do nothing, and he asks why. He opens with the question itself: why does the Almighty not keep set times of judgment, so that those who know him see him act (v. 1)? Then he gives the evidence. The strong steal land, flocks, the orphan’s donkey and the widow’s ox, and push the poor off the road (vv. 2–4). The poor scavenge in the wasteland, sleep naked in the cold and shelter against rocks (vv. 5–8). Children are seized for debt, and workers starve while harvesting others’ grain and oil (vv. 9–11). The dying groan, yet God charges no one with wrong (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's question widens from his own suffering to the suffering of the poor. He is asking what the prophets and James will ask: when will God judge?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job asks why God does not hold court on fixed days to put things right, and the gospel answers that the day is fixed and the delay is mercy.

Why are not times of judgment kept? Chapter 23 was about Job’s own case; now he looks beyond himself. Why does God not hold court on set days, like a king, so that those who know him see him act? It is the question of every believer who reads the news, and of the martyrs in heaven: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10).

Why God waits. The New Testament gives two answers and holds them together. The delay is mercy: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). And the day is fixed: “he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). The times of judgment are kept on God’s calendar, and the Judge has already been named and raised from the dead.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says literally that times are not “stored up” by the Almighty; the ESV’s “times of judgment” is a fair reading.

verseByVerse.quote: Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them. They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge. They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strong steal land and livestock from the weakest and push the poor out of sight, the very sins Eliphaz falsely charged to Job.

Some move landmarks. They shift the boundary stone to steal a neighbour’s land, which the law cursed: “Cursed be anyone who moves his neighbor’s landmark” (Deuteronomy 27:17). They drive off an orphan’s only donkey, and take a widow’s ox as security for a debt, when the law forbade even taking her garment (Deuteronomy 24:17). They shove the poor off the road until they hide.

Job’s answer to Eliphaz. These are the very sins Eliphaz accused Job of (22:6–9). Job has not done them. He has seen them done, and he is asking why God lets them go on.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children. They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man. They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold. They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job describes the homeless poor with a compassion no oppressor could feel, which is his real answer to Eliphaz.

They lie all night naked. Eliphaz said Job had “stripped the naked of their clothing” (22:6). Here is Job describing the naked poor: scavenging in the wilderness like wild donkeys to feed their children, picking over the leftovers in a rich man’s vineyard, lying all night without a blanket, soaked by mountain storms, pressing themselves against a rock for shelter. No man who had done this to them could describe them like this.

Of whom the world was not worthy. Hebrews describes God’s faithful people in almost the same terms: “destitute, afflicted, mistreated”, people “of whom the world was not worthy”, “wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Hebrews 11:37–38). And the Son of God himself shared their lot: “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20). The poor on the mountainside are not forgotten by God, even when they seem to be.

verseByVerse.quote: (There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.) They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves; among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst. From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Workers starve while harvesting others’ plenty and the dying cry out, yet God seems to charge no one with wrong; but the cries reach God’s ears.

Hungry, they carry the sheaves. A baby taken from its mother’s breast as security for a debt; men carrying armfuls of grain while they starve, pressing olive oil they will never taste, treading the winepress with parched throats. The law let even an ox eat while it threshed: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9). These men are treated worse than animals.

The cries reach God. James, who holds Job up to the church (James 5:11), writes in the same chapter: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts” (James 5:4). Job heard those cries. So does God.

God charges no one with wrong. The phrase uses the word of the book’s opening: “In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong” (1:22). Now he complains that God does not charge the oppressors with wrong. It is the complaint of a man who still believes God is just, and cannot see the justice being done. God will answer it, not with a timetable, but with himself (chapters 38–41).

For us. Those who buy, employ and invest share in how workers are treated; the God who hears the harvesters asks his people to hear them too.

Uncertain wording. By reading the same Hebrew letters with different vowels, a few translations read “God pays no attention to their prayer”. The ESV keeps the Hebrew, which links the line to 1:22.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Those Who Rebel Against the Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that some sinners love the darkness because they think it hides them. They rebel against the light and refuse its paths (v. 13). The murderer is up before dawn to kill the poor and prowls like a thief at night (v. 14). The adulterer waits for twilight, sure that no eye will see him, and covers his face (v. 15). Burglars dig through house walls in the dark and hide by day (v. 16). For all of them deep darkness is their morning, and its terrors are their friends (v. 17). But no darkness hides anything from God.
verseByVerse.theology: Evil loves the dark because it thinks the dark hides it. It does not (Ps 139:12; John 3:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: "There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths. The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief. The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me'; and he veils his face. In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light. For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Murderers, adulterers and burglars love the dark because they think it hides them, but nothing is hidden from God.

Those who rebel against the light. Job turns from the oppressor in daylight to the criminal who rebels against the light itself, “not acquainted with its ways” (v. 13).

The murderer rises before it is light. The killer is out before dawn; the adulterer waits for dusk, as in Proverbs, “in the twilight, in the evening” (Proverbs 7:9), and covers his face; the burglar tunnels through a mud-brick wall at night, the picture Jesus used for “thieves” who “break in and steal” (Matthew 6:19).

Deep darkness is morning to all of them. For them the night is the working day. Jesus said it exactly: “people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19). The light they hate has a name; he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And they are wrong that “no eye will see”: “even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day” (Psalm 139:12).

In everyday life. Every sin that needs the dark, the private screen or the hidden account, makes the adulterer’s mistake. The way out is to bring it into the light, where Christ forgives (1 John 1:7–9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the wicked do fall at last, but at God’s harvest and not on the friends’ timetable. Verses 18–20 describe the wicked swept away like debris on the water, their land cursed, swallowed by the grave and forgotten (vv. 18–20). They prey on the childless woman and the widow, yet God prolongs their life for a time and watches their ways (vv. 21–23). Then, exalted a little while, they are gone, cut off like heads of grain (v. 24). Job challenges anyone to prove him wrong (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The wicked do fall at last, but on God's schedule and not the friends'.

verseByVerse.quote: "You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards. Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned. The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
These verses picture the wicked swept away, cursed and forgotten; whoever is speaking, they agree that the wicked perish at last.

Swept away and forgotten. The wicked are like debris on a flood; Sheol swallows them as heat swallows the snow waters; even the womb that bore them forgets them, and wickedness is broken like a tree.

Uncertain wording. These verses are one of the hard places in the book. They sound like the friends, and the Hebrew has no “You say”; the ESV adds it, taking the lines as Job quoting the friends’ view before he answers it. Others think Job himself is saying the wicked come to a bad end at last, which he never denied; others, that a piece of a friend’s speech has been misplaced here. The first two readings come to the same place: the wicked do perish, but not on the friends’ timetable, and not in a way that lets anyone read a man’s guilt from his troubles. The opening line of verse 18 is also obscure, probably picturing flotsam carried off by the current.

verseByVerse.quote: "They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow. Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life. He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways. They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain. If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lets the mighty stand a while and watches their ways, then cuts them off like grain at harvest; the delay is patience, and the harvest is certain.

God prolongs the life of the mighty. The powerful who prey on the childless and the widow are kept alive by God’s power; when they seem to be dying, they recover. “His eyes are upon their ways”: God is watching them, as he is watching Job (23:10). He is not blind. He is patient.

Cut off like the heads of grain. In the end they die like everyone else, like ears of wheat at harvest. That is Job’s real answer to his own question in verse 1. Judgment does come, but in God’s time, at harvest.

The wheat and the weeds. Jesus told a parable that fits this chapter exactly. An enemy sowed weeds in a man’s field (see wheat and tares), and his servants wanted to pull them up at once. “No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matthew 13:29–30). That is why the times of judgment seem not to be kept: God is protecting the wheat. The harvest is certain.

Who will prove me a liar? Job’s challenge to the friends: prove me wrong. They cannot. Bildad will try, with six verses (chapter 25), and then the friends fall silent for good.

24.theology: The delay of judgment is God's patience, and the day is fixed and the Judge named (2 Pet 3:9; Acts 17:31). Until then God lets the wheat and the weeds grow together (Matt 13:30). Job's complaint is the complaint of a man who still believes God is just and cannot yet see the justice being done.
24.examples: Job's portrait of the poor clinging to the rock in the rain is the best answer to Eliphaz's charge: no one who had stripped them could describe them with such compassion. It also gives every believer who reads the news a prayer to pray, Why are not times of judgment kept?, and the parable of the wheat and weeds to hold on to while waiting for the answer.

keyVerse.quote: Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter is the evidence for this question, and Job asks it as a believer, not a sceptic. Scripture answers it without denying it: God’s delay is patience (2 Peter 3:9), and his day is fixed, with Christ appointed as Judge (Acts 17:31). Until then the wheat and the weeds grow together, and the harvest is certain.

24.reflection:
Job asks, “Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty?” (v. 1). Where do you find yourself asking that question today? How do 2 Peter 3:9 and Acts 17:31 help you hold on while you wait?

Job describes the poor with deep compassion (vv. 5–12), which answers Eliphaz’s charge that he had oppressed them. What does our attitude to the poor reveal about our hearts? How might your church or household hear the cries of the vulnerable around you?

The adulterer says, “No eye will see me” (v. 15). Why does sin love the dark? What would it mean for you to bring hidden things into the light (John 3:19–21; 1 John 1:7–9)?

God lets the mighty stand “a little while” and then cuts them off like grain at harvest (vv. 22–24). How does Jesus’ parable of the wheat and the weeds (Matthew 13:24–30) change the way you see God’s patience with evil?

25.title: How Can Man Be in the Right Before God?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven.<sup>3</sup>Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?<sup>4</sup>How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?<sup>5</sup>Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes;<sup>6</sup>how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
25.overview:
Where we are. The third and last round of debate (chapters 22–27) is ending. Eliphaz has invented crimes for Job (chapter 22), and Job has answered that God is hidden from him and that the wicked often go unpunished in this life (chapters 23–24). Now Bildad speaks for the last time, in six verses, and after him none of the friends will speak again.

The message. Bildad says something true: God is great beyond measure, and no human being can stand in the right before him by his own purity. But he says it to silence a sufferer, not to help him, and he ends by calling man a maggot and a worm. The chapter shows true doctrine used as a weapon and left without grace, until it has nothing left to say. It asks the right question, “How then can man be in the right before God?” (v. 4), and has no answer.

Why it was said. The friends hold that God always repays in this life (see the introduction), and Job’s last speech, that the wicked often prosper and die in peace, has left them without a reply. Bildad cannot refute Job, so he retreats to God’s majesty and man’s smallness. His words must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer, for God said the friends had not spoken rightly of him (42:7).

How the chapter makes its case. Bildad first praises God’s rule: dominion and awe belong to him, he keeps peace in heaven, his armies cannot be counted and his light rises on everyone (vv. 1–3). Then he draws his conclusion: if even the moon and the stars are not pure in God’s sight, how can man be, who is a maggot and a worm (vv. 4–6)? There the speech, and the friends’ part in the debate, simply stops.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes. Bildad’s question is the question of the whole Bible, and the gospel answers it: sinners “are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24). And the word Bildad uses to crush man, worm, the Messiah took on his own lips: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 22:6). The God who makes peace in his high heaven made peace on earth “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

For us. It is possible to say only true things about God and still be no comfort at all. Bildad’s question deserves an answer, not a sermon that ends in contempt, and we give it when we point the guilty and the hurting to Christ, who was scorned as a worm for us so that we might be counted righteous before God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Man, Who Is a Maggot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad’s point is that God is too great and man too small for anyone to be in the right before him, so Job should stop protesting. He sets out God’s majesty: rule and awe belong to God, he keeps peace among the powers of heaven, his armies are beyond number, and his light shines on all (vv. 1–3). Then he asks the question the whole book has been circling, how man can be right before God (v. 4), and answers only by setting man beside the moon and stars: a maggot, a worm (vv. 5–6). After this the friends never speak again.
verseByVerse.theology: The friends' last words ask the right question, but ask it to crush, and offer no answer. God gives the answer, and when he calls his people worms he also calls himself their Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven. Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad praises God’s rule truly, and the peace God keeps in heaven points to the peace Christ made on earth.

He makes peace in his high heaven. It is true: God keeps the heavenly powers in order. The New Testament hears a deeper peace in those words. God was pleased through Christ “to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). The God who makes peace in heaven made it on earth, at a cross.

The friends’ last words. This is the last time any of the friends speaks. Bildad manages six verses, Zophar none, and the cycle that began so confidently in chapter 4 has run out of breath. Some scholars think the third round was disturbed in copying and parts of chapters 26–27 were once Bildad’s and Zophar’s; possibly, but as the text stands the friends simply run out of words. The LORD’s verdict on everything they said still stands: “you have not spoken of me what is right” (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad asks the right question, how anyone can be right with a holy God, but only to silence Job, and he has no answer.

How then can man be in the right before God? Eliphaz’s night visitor asked it (4:17), Job asked it (9:2), and now it is the friends’ last question. It is the question every human being must face before a holy God. Bildad asks it to shut Job’s mouth, and leaves it hanging.

The answer came in a person. The book of Job does not answer it in so many words. The answer came later, in a person: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:23–24). “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). The question Bildad used as a club, the gospel answers as good news.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes; how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad calls man a worm in contempt; God uses the same word to redeem, and Christ took it on himself.

Man, who is a maggot. If the moon and stars look dim beside God’s holiness, what is a human being? A maggot, Bildad says, to a man whose flesh is “clothed with worms” (7:5).

The worm God calls his own. But Scripture uses the word worm in two places that change everything. God himself calls his people worms, and says it tenderly: “Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 41:14). The God who sees how small we are calls himself our Redeemer, the word of Job’s great confession (19:25). And in the psalm fulfilled at the cross the sufferer says, “But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people” (Psalm 22:6). Bildad called man a worm to crush him. The Son of Man became the worm, scorned and despised, to lift us. God’s last word is redemption.

What it does not mean. Not that we are worthless: small and stained before God, but made in his image and crowned with glory (Psalm 8:5).

25.theology: The friends' debate collapses. Their last question, how man can be right before God (v. 4), is the right one, and they cannot answer it; the gospel does (Rom 3:23-24; 5:1). Bildad calls man a worm in contempt (v. 6), but God uses the same word tenderly of his people, and the sufferer of Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, takes it on himself.
25.examples: Bildad shows how a true doctrine can be used as a club. Human smallness before a holy God is real, but he says it with contempt, to a man whose sores are full of worms. Scripture says the same truth with tenderness, and anyone who speaks to sufferers should learn to say it that way.

keyVerse.quote: How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?
keyVerse.note: This is the friends’ last question, and the right one: the question every human being must face before a holy God. Bildad asks it to silence Job and has no answer. The gospel answers it: sinners are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24).

25.reflection:
Everything Bildad says about God’s greatness in verses 2–3 is true, yet his speech brings Job no comfort. How can true things about God be said in a way that wounds? What makes the difference?

“How then can man be in the right before God?” (v. 4). How would you answer Bildad’s question from the gospel? Why do you think the book of Job leaves it hanging here?

Bildad calls man a worm to crush him (v. 6), but God calls his people “you worm Jacob” in order to help them (Isaiah 41:14), and Christ says “I am a worm” on the cross (Psalm 22:6). What does it mean to you that the Lord knows how small you are and still calls himself your Redeemer?

The friends end the debate in silence, having run out of answers. When have neat answers run out for you, or for someone you were trying to help? What did you, or they, need instead?

26.title: The Outskirts of His Ways
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength!<sup>3</sup>How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge!<sup>4</sup>With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?<sup>5</sup>The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants.<sup>6</sup>Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.<sup>7</sup>He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing.<sup>8</sup>He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them.<sup>9</sup>He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud.<sup>10</sup>He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.<sup>11</sup>The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke.<sup>12</sup>By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab.<sup>13</sup>By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.<sup>14</sup>Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
26.overview:
Where we are. Bildad has just made the friends’ last speech, six verses that end with man as a maggot and a worm (chapter 25). Job answers him briefly and bitingly, and then, instead of arguing further, praises God’s power in some of the most splendid poetry in the book.

The message. Job knows God’s greatness better than his comforters do, and he knows something they have forgotten: all that we see of God’s power is only the edge of it. The grave, the sky, the clouds and the sea lie open to him and obey him, yet what we hear of him is “a whisper”. A God this great cannot be mapped by anyone’s formula, the friends’ or ours.

Why it was said. Bildad lectured Job on God’s greatness and man’s smallness (25:2–6), as if Job needed the lesson and as if it settled his case. Job shows that he does not need it, and that God’s greatness, rightly seen, undercuts the friends’ confident theology (see the introduction) rather than supports it.

How the chapter makes its case. Job first thanks Bildad, with heavy irony, for his help to the helpless, and asks where his words came from (vv. 1–4). Then he climbs through creation. The realm of the dead lies bare before God (vv. 5–6). He hangs the earth on nothing, holds water in the clouds, veils the moon and draws the horizon (vv. 7–10). The mountains tremble at his rebuke, and he masters the sea and its monsters (vv. 11–13). Then the turn: all this is only “the outskirts of his ways”, a whisper; who could understand his thunder (v. 14)?

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him. The God who stills the sea is the one the disciples watched rise from sleep in a sinking boat, rebuke the wind and say to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39). The God who hangs the earth on nothing is the Son who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). And the thunder Job could not yet hear, God has spoken at last: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

For us. When life falls apart, we are tempted either to shrink God to the size of our explanations or to doubt that he is there at all. Job does neither. He praises a God far greater than his questions, and the gospel lets us go further: the hands that hold up the earth are the hands that were pierced for us, and they hold up those who have nothing left under them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — How You Have Helped Him Who Has No Power!
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that Bildad’s lecture on God’s greatness has been no help at all to a man who needed help. With biting irony he thanks Bildad for rescuing the powerless, strengthening the feeble arm and counselling the man without wisdom (vv. 1–3), as if Bildad had brought him anything. Then he asks the question every comforter must answer: whose help did you have, and whose breath was speaking through you (v. 4)? Bildad has told a broken man that he is a worm, and Job wants to know whether God sent that message.
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the friends' last speech with sarcasm. Six verses about worms have helped no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength! How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge! With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job tells Bildad, with bitter irony, that his lecture has helped no one, and asks whose breath was speaking through him.

How you have helped him who has no power! Bildad’s six verses told Job he was a maggot (the “you” is singular). Job’s reply drips with sarcasm: what a help you have been to the weak! They came to comfort him (2:11), and have told him he is a worm; “plentifully declared sound knowledge” mocks a speech six verses long.

Whose breath has come out from you? Not God’s, Job implies; perhaps the spirit that “glided past” Eliphaz’s face in the night (4:15), whose message Bildad has just repeated (4:17–19; 25:4–6). A counsellor should ask himself Job’s question before he speaks: whose breath is this? Am I speaking God’s word, or only my own certainty?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — He Hangs the Earth on Nothing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that God’s power is greater than Bildad imagines, and that even what we can see of it is only the edge. He moves from the depths upward: the dead tremble beneath the waters, and the grave lies open before God (vv. 5–6). God hangs the earth on nothing, binds the waters in the clouds, veils the moon and draws the horizon on the sea (vv. 7–10). The mountains tremble at his rebuke, and he masters the sea and strikes down its monsters (vv. 11–13). Then Job steps back: all this is the outskirts of his ways, a whisper; who could grasp his thunder (v. 14)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job outdoes the friends in praising God's power, and ends where all theology must: we have heard only a whisper.

verseByVerse.quote: The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants. Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world of the dead, hidden from every human eye, lies wide open before God. For the friends that is a threat; for Job it is a hope.

Sheol is naked before God. The dead, far down beneath the waters, tremble before him. “Sheol” is the grave; “Abaddon” means destruction, the place of ruin. Neither is hidden from him: “Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!” (Proverbs 15:11).

Naked and exposed. Hebrews says the same of every one of us: “no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13). If even the grave is naked before God, then Job’s innocence is not hidden from him either.

Uncertain wording. “The dead” is rephaim, used elsewhere for the shades of the dead (Isaiah 14:9) and for an ancient people of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11); here it means the dead. The rest of verse 5 is compressed: probably the dead tremble beneath the waters and all that live in them.

verseByVerse.quote: He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing. He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them. He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud. He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth and the sky hang on nothing but God, who holds every cloud and draws every horizon.

He hangs the earth on nothing. The ancient world usually pictured the earth resting on pillars or on the back of something. Job says God hangs it on nothing. It is poetry, not a science lesson, but the point is exact: nothing holds the world up except God. “The void” is the word for “without form” in Genesis 1:2.

The cloud is not split open under them. Tons of water carried in a cloud that does not burst; the moon veiled; the horizon drawn like a compass line on the sea, the edge of day and night. Wisdom says it too: “when he drew a circle on the face of the deep” (Proverbs 8:27). Everything Job points to is ordinary and astonishing at once.

The hands that hold. The New Testament names the one who does it: the Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3); “in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). The same hands that hold up the earth hold up the believer who has nothing left under him.

Uncertain wording. “The north” (tsaphon) may be the northern sky, or the sacred mountain of the north where Israel’s neighbours placed their gods (compare Isaiah 14:13); either way it rests only on God. In verse 9 the word read “the full moon” could also be read “his throne” (so the KJV); the sense is much the same.

verseByVerse.quote: The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke. By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab. By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mountains, the sea and its monsters, everything the ancient world feared, bow to God’s rebuke; and in the Gospels a man in a boat does what only God does.

By his power he stilled the sea. The mountains, the pillars on which the sky seemed to rest, shake at his rebuke. “Rahab” is the sea monster of 9:13, and “the fleeing serpent” is Leviathan, whom Isaiah calls “Leviathan the fleeing serpent” (Isaiah 27:1), the monster Job once wanted roused against the day of his birth (3:8). The powers of chaos are nothing to God.

The man in the boat was God. Then read the Gospel. A storm on the lake, the boat filling with water, and Jesus asleep. “And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mark 4:39). The disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Job has told us. Only God stills the sea. The man in the boat was God.

Does the Bible endorse pagan myths of sea monsters? No. Job borrows the imagery of the nations’ stories, in which gods fought chaos monsters, to say that the true God rules what they feared, with no battle and no rival. Rahab is also a poetic name for Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 30:7).

Uncertain wording. The verb for “stilled” can also mean “stirs up”, as in Isaiah 51:15; either way the sea is in God’s hand. In verse 13 “made fair” renders a rare word meaning clearness or beauty, probably the sky swept clear by his wind after a storm.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of God’s power that we can see is only the fringe of who he is, which humbles every confident explanation of his ways.

These are but the outskirts of his ways. After all that, Job says: this is only the edge, the fringe of God’s garment, a faint whisper of who he is. If this is the whisper, who could stand the thunder?

Every neat explanation judged. This verse judges every neat explanation of suffering, the friends’ and ours. They thought they had God’s ways mapped: sin brings trouble, righteousness brings blessing, and Job’s case can be read off the chart. Job says: we have heard a whisper. Paul says the same of the Christian’s knowledge now: “For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Humility is not a lack of faith; it is faith that knows how big God is.

The thunder of his power. And the thunder is coming. In twelve chapters the LORD will answer Job out of the whirlwind (38:1), and Job will hear more than a whisper. It will not explain his suffering; it will show him God.

26.theology: The God who holds up the world with nothing beneath it and stills the sea by his rebuke is the God made known in the Son, who upholds the universe and calmed the storm on the lake. Yet all that can be seen of him is the outskirts of his ways (v. 14), and no theology, the friends' or ours, has him mapped.
26.examples: Job's question to Bildad, Whose breath has come out from you?, is one every preacher and counsellor can ask before speaking. And the picture of the earth hung on nothing comforts anyone who feels there is nothing left under them: the same hands hold them up.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?
keyVerse.note: After describing God’s power over the grave, the earth, the sky and the sea, Job says that all of it is only the edge. The verse humbles every tidy explanation of God’s ways, including the friends’, and prepares for the moment when the LORD himself speaks out of the whirlwind (38:1).

26.reflection:
Job asks Bildad, “whose breath has come out from you?” (v. 4). When you try to help someone who is suffering, how can you tell whether you are speaking God’s word or only your own certainty?

Job says God “hangs the earth on nothing” (v. 7), and Hebrews 1:3 says the Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power”. What difference does it make to know that the one who holds up creation is Jesus? Where do you feel you have nothing left under you?

The disciples asked of Jesus, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). How does Job 26:12 help answer their question?

Job calls all he has described “but the outskirts of his ways” (v. 14). How should knowing that we hear only “a whisper” of God shape the way we speak about suffering, our own or other people’s?

27.title: I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter,<sup>3</sup>as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,<sup>4</sup>my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.<sup>5</sup>Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me.<sup>6</sup>I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.<sup>7</sup>"Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous.<sup>8</sup>For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?<sup>9</sup>Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?<sup>10</sup>Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?<sup>11</sup>I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal.<sup>12</sup>Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?<sup>13</sup>"This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty:<sup>14</sup>If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread.<sup>15</sup>Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.<sup>16</sup>Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay,<sup>17</sup>he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver.<sup>18</sup>He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes.<sup>19</sup>He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.<sup>20</sup>Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off.<sup>21</sup>The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place.<sup>22</sup>It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight.<sup>23</sup>It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
27.overview:
Where we are. Bildad has spoken his last, Zophar never takes his turn, and Job has answered with a hymn to God’s power (chapter 26). Now, with the friends silent, Job “again took up his discourse” (v. 1), beginning a closing statement that runs, with the poem on wisdom in the middle, to the end of chapter 31.

The message. Job will not lie to end his pain. On oath, by the very God he feels has wronged him, he refuses to confess sins he has not committed or to let go of his integrity, the thing God boasted of in heaven and his wife urged him to abandon (2:3, 9). He still believes that God judges the wicked; what he denies is that every sufferer is wicked. What separates him from the godless is not what has happened to him but where his hope is.

Why it was said. The friends have made a confession the price of restoration (22:21–23; see the introduction). To give one would be easy, and false. Job’s oath is his answer to their whole case, and to Satan’s question whether he fears God only for what he gets (1:9).

How the chapter makes its case. Job swears by the living God that while he has breath he will not speak falsehood, will not say the friends are right, and will hold fast his righteousness (vv. 1–6). He wishes on his accusers the lot of the wicked, whose hope dies with them, who neither delight in God nor call on him, and he offers to teach the teachers (vv. 7–12). Then he describes the wicked man’s portion from God: children for the sword, silver heaped like dust and shared by the innocent, a house as flimsy as a moth’s, and a night wind that carries him away (vv. 13–23).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Job holds fast his integrity under false accusation and will not save himself with a lie; Jesus, falsely accused, “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Yet Job’s integrity is not sinlessness, and a clear conscience is not the final verdict (1 Corinthians 4:4). Only Christ was whole all the way through, and he was counted a sinner for us, “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For us. Refuse false confessions as firmly as you make true ones: integrity means being one person all the way through, not saying whatever will make the pain or the pressure stop. And measure your safety not by what is happening to you but by where your hope rests. The wicked man’s hope ends when God takes his life; hope in a living Redeemer does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he will not lie to end his suffering, not even to satisfy his friends. With Zophar silent, Job takes up his discourse again (v. 1) and swears by the living God, the God he feels has taken away his right and embittered his soul, that while he has breath his lips will speak no falsehood (vv. 2–4). He will never say the friends are right; he will hold fast his integrity until he dies, and his heart does not reproach him for any of his days (vv. 5–6). It is his answer to the question asked in heaven and by his wife (2:3, 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Job swears by the God he is protesting to.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zophar does not take his turn, so Job speaks again, beginning a closing statement that runs to the end of chapter 31.

And Job again took up his discourse. A new heading marks the change: Job “took up his discourse”, his mashal, a word for a weighty, measured speech. From here to chapter 31, with the great poem on wisdom in the middle, Job speaks alone. What follows is his closing statement.

verseByVerse.quote: "As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter, as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears by the God he feels has wronged him, bringing his complaint to God rather than away from him, and he will not use the breath God gave him to lie.

As God lives. Job swears an oath, the most solemn there was, and he swears it by God: by the God “who has taken away my right”, who has “made my soul bitter”. Job is protesting against God and swearing by him in the same breath. That is the way for every sufferer: bring the complaint to God, not away from him.

My soul bitter. Scripture puts the same verb and the same name for God in the mouth of a widow who came home from Moab with nothing: “call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me” (Ruth 1:20). And Naomi’s story ends with a kinsman-redeemer, Boaz, a near relative whose duty was to rescue the family, a go’el, the very word of Job’s great confession (19:25). Naomi and Job were both being led, without knowing it, to a redeemer.

As long as my breath is in me. Every breath he uses to speak is God’s gift (12:10), and he will not use it to lie. As at the beginning, “Job did not sin with his lips” (2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me. I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears he will never confess to sins he has not committed but will hold fast his integrity until he dies, exactly what God saw in him from the start.

I will not put away my integrity. Here is the answer to a question asked in chapter 2. God said, “He still holds fast his integrity” (2:3). Job’s wife said, “Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die” (2:9). Now Job answers, on oath, with the same word and the same verb: “I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go.” A false confession would end the argument, and he will not tell that lie.

What integrity is. We hear “integrity” as honesty or a clean record; the Hebrew word is closer to wholeness: being one person all the way through, the same on the ash heap as at the city gate, the same before God as before men. It is not sinlessness; Job has asked for pardon (7:21). It is an undivided heart, the prayer of the psalm, “unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11). The pressure on Job is on all of us: to say whatever will stop the pain, keep the peace, and win approval. Job would rather be misjudged than become two people.

My heart does not reproach me. John writes, “if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:21). But Paul adds a caution: “I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4). A clear conscience is a gift, not the final verdict. Job’s defence of his innocence is true, and it will be vindicated (42:7). But Elihu will accuse him of justifying himself rather than God (32:2), and God will ask him, “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (40:8). Holding fast to one’s integrity is right; using it to put God in the wrong is not.

The one who was whole. Only one man has ever been whole all the way through: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). And he was counted a sinner for us, “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Our confidence before the Judge rests on his record, not ours: “not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9). So we are free both to confess real sin without hiding and to refuse false guilt without fear.

In everyday life. This week that may mean not nodding along to something you do not believe just to end an awkward conversation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Let My Enemy Be as the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the friends’ own doctrine of judgment should frighten them, not him. Let his accusers have the lot of the wicked (v. 7), for the godless have no hope when God takes their life: God will not hear their cry, and they never delighted in the Almighty or called on him (vv. 8–10). Each question quietly describes the opposite of Job, who hopes, cries out and keeps calling on God. Then he turns teacher: he will instruct them about the hand of God, for they have seen the same world he has, so why their empty talk (vv. 11–12)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job does not deny that God judges the wicked. He denies that he is one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous. For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life? Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job turns the friends’ doctrine on them: the godless have no hope when God takes their life, and Job is plainly not godless.

Let my enemy be as the wicked. The friends have risen up against him like false witnesses, and the law said a false witness should receive what he meant for his brother (Deuteronomy 19:18–19).

What is the hope of the godless? Every one of these questions is a quiet claim about Job. He has hope (19:25); he cries to God and expects to be heard (23:3–7); Eliphaz told him to “delight yourself in the Almighty” (22:26), and he has never stopped calling on God. That is not how a godless man behaves.

Is Job cursing his friends? It is a solemn warning more than a curse, and not his last word: in the end Job prays for them, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:44), and the LORD restores him “when he had prayed for his friends” (42:10).

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “cuts him off” can also mean to make a profit, often a dishonest one, hence the KJV’s “though he hath gained”. Either way, the godless man’s hope comes to nothing when God takes his life.

verseByVerse.quote: I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal. Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job will teach the teachers, for they have seen the same world he has and their answers do not fit it.

I will teach you concerning the hand of God. They have seen the same world he has, the wicked prospering and the righteous suffering. Why then have they become “altogether vain”? The words are built from hebel, the “vanity” of Ecclesiastes, a breath or vapour; Job has already called their comfort “empty nothings” (21:34), the same word. Their answers do not fit what their own eyes have seen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Portion of a Wicked Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the wicked man’s end is real and terrible, though it cannot be read off every sufferer’s troubles. Echoing Zophar’s own words (20:29), he describes the portion God gives the oppressor: children multiplied for the sword, survivors buried by plague, widows who do not mourn (vv. 13–15); silver heaped like dust and clothing piled like clay, all of it worn and shared by the innocent, a house as flimsy as a moth’s, and riches gone overnight (vv. 16–19); and at last terror like a flood and a night wind that hurls him away, clapping and hissing (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Job holds the same truth about the wicked as the friends; he refuses their use of it against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty: If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread. Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job affirms that God does judge the wicked; what he denies is that every sufferer is wicked.

The portion of a wicked man. Verse 13 is almost exactly Zophar’s last line (20:29), and the paragraph that follows sounds like the friends: the wicked man’s children fall by the sword, his survivors die of plague, his widows do not mourn him. It fits what Job has just said: “let my enemy be as the wicked” (v. 7). Job has never denied that God judges the wicked. He believes this portion is real, and he warns the men who have falsely accused him that it is theirs to fear.

If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword. It is hard to read these words from a man whose children are dead. Job does not turn them round and apply them to himself. That was the friends’ mistake: reasoning backwards from a man’s troubles to his guilt.

Is Job now contradicting chapter 21? In chapter 21 he spoke of this life; here he speaks of the end, when God settles accounts. Both are true, and Psalm 73 holds them together: the wicked prosper, “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17).

Who is speaking? Some readers think verses 13–23 are Zophar’s missing third speech, misplaced in copying; others think Job is quoting the friends back to them. But the text gives the words to Job, and they fit what he has said.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay, he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver. He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes. He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man’s wealth is as flimsy as a moth’s house: he goes to bed rich and wakes with nothing, and others enjoy what he heaped up.
