The innocent will divide the silver. Clothing was a form of wealth in that world, and the righteous wear what the wicked heaped up. “The sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous” (Proverbs 13:22). Job himself will one day be given money and gold by those who come to him (42:11).

He builds his house like a moth’s. Like a moth’s cocoon, or the shelter of branches a watchman put up in a vineyard at harvest: flimsy things that vanish in a season. Moths also eat the clothes he hoards, as Jesus warned of treasures on earth, “where moth and rust destroy” (Matthew 6:19). The rich man goes to sleep secure and wakes up with nothing, like the man in Jesus’ parable who heard, “This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off. The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight. It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man’s end is a storm in the night, real and from God; but not everyone a storm has struck is wicked.

In the night a whirlwind carries him off. Terrors overtake him like a flood; the hot east wind from the desert picks him up and throws him away, then claps its hands and hisses at him, the gesture of scorn passers-by made at ruined Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:15). A great wind took Job’s children (1:19), and the friends concluded that they had sinned (8:4). The storm is real, Job says, but that does not make every man it strikes wicked.

Where hope lies. The difference between Job and the wicked man is not what has happened to them. It is where their hope is. The wicked man’s hope ends when God takes his life (v. 8). Job’s does not: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25). For all who trust that Redeemer, the storm of God’s judgment has already broken on someone else, on Christ at the cross.

Uncertain wording. Verse 23 does not name who claps and hisses: the east wind, as the ESV takes it, or onlookers (“Men shall clap their hands at him”, KJV). Either way his end is public and scorned.

27.theology: Job holds fast his integrity and will not buy peace with a false confession. Yet a clear conscience is a gift, not the final verdict: God will vindicate Job's honesty and also correct his self-justification. Job affirms the judgment of the wicked while denying that suffering proves wickedness, and the difference between him and the wicked lies in where their hope is when God takes a man's life.
27.examples: Job shows a sufferer how to complain rightly: he protests to God and swears by him in the same breath, bringing the bitterness to God rather than away from him, as Naomi did. And he shows a costly honesty: he would rather go on suffering than make a false confession to end the argument.

keyVerse.quote: Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me.
keyVerse.note: This is Job’s answer, on oath, to the question asked in chapter 2: God said he “still holds fast his integrity” (2:3), and his wife urged him to let it go (2:9). A false confession would have ended the argument, but Job would rather be misjudged than lie. Only Christ was wholly without deceit (1 Peter 2:22), and in him believers are free both to confess real sin and to refuse false guilt.

27.reflection:
Job complains against God and swears by God in the same breath (v. 2). What does this teach about bringing our pain to God rather than away from him? What would that look like for you this week?

Job refuses to confess sins he has not committed just to end the pressure (vv. 4–6). Where are you tempted to say what others want to hear rather than what is true? How does resting on Christ’s righteousness, rather than our own, free us both to confess real sin and to refuse false guilt?

Job says his heart does not reproach him (v. 6), but Paul says a clear conscience does not acquit him (1 Corinthians 4:4). How do you hold these two truths together?

Job believes God judges the wicked (vv. 13–23) but denies that every sufferer is wicked. Why is it so tempting to reason backwards from someone’s troubles to their guilt? How can we warn of judgment without doing that?

28.title: Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
28.text: <sup>1</sup>"Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine.<sup>2</sup>Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.<sup>3</sup>Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness.<sup>4</sup>He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.<sup>5</sup>As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire.<sup>6</sup>Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.<sup>7</sup>"That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it.<sup>8</sup>The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.<sup>9</sup>"Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots.<sup>10</sup>He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing.<sup>11</sup>He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.<sup>12</sup>"But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>13</sup>Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.<sup>14</sup>The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'<sup>15</sup>It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price.<sup>16</sup>It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.<sup>17</sup>Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.<sup>18</sup>No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls.<sup>19</sup>The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.<sup>20</sup>"From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>21</sup>It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air.<sup>22</sup>Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'<sup>23</sup>"God understands the way to it, and he knows its place.<sup>24</sup>For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.<sup>25</sup>When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure,<sup>26</sup>when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder,<sup>27</sup>then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.<sup>28</sup>And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
28.overview:
Where we are. The debate is over. The friends have fallen silent, and Job has sworn to his integrity (chapter 27). Before his last defence (chapters 29–31), the book pauses for a quiet poem, with no accusation and no complaint, that asks the question underneath the whole debate: where is wisdom?

The message. Human beings can find almost anything: they tunnel into mountains and bring hidden treasure to light. But the wisdom to understand God’s ways cannot be dug up, bought, or found anywhere in creation; only God knows where it is. And he has told us what wisdom is for us: not to understand everything, but to fear the Lord and turn away from evil.

Why it was said. The friends claimed wisdom from visions, tradition and long experience, and used it to explain Job’s suffering; Job has demanded that God explain himself (see the introduction). The poem gently corrects both, and prepares for the moment when God himself speaks (38:1). By its definition, the man on the ash heap who “feared God and turned away from evil” (1:1) was wise all along.

How the chapter makes its case. Men know where silver, gold, iron and copper lie, and go where no falcon has looked and no lion has walked to bring hidden things to light (vv. 1–11). But where shall wisdom be found? Not in the land of the living, not in the deep or the sea; no gold or jewel can buy it, and Destruction and Death have heard only a rumour of it (vv. 12–22). God alone understands the way to it. He saw it and established it when he weighed the wind and made a way for the lightning, and he said to man: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom (vv. 23–28).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the wisdom of God revealed in him. The wisdom by which God made the world is the Word through whom “all things were made” (John 1:3). The treasure no miner could reach is in Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The wisdom no one could dig out of the earth came down to it in a person, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and to fear the Lord now is to trust him.

For us. We live in the age of the miner, with more knowledge than any generation before us, and it has not made us wise. Wisdom is given, not extracted. When there is no explanation for what you are going through, the poem offers not an answer but a way to live: hold God in awe, keep turning from evil, trust Christ, and leave the understanding with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem’s point in its first part is that human beings can find almost anything hidden in the earth. There are mines for silver and gold, and iron and copper are dug out and smelted (vv. 1–2). Miners carry their lamps into deep darkness and swing on ropes in lonely shafts (vv. 3–4), breaking with fire the rock beneath fields of grain to reach sapphires and gold dust (vv. 5–6). No falcon has seen their path, no lion walked it (vv. 7–8). They overturn mountains, cut channels through rock, dam streams and bring hidden things to light (vv. 9–11). The question is coming: can wisdom be found that way?
verseByVerse.theology: Human beings can get treasure out of the heart of a mountain. The poem admires it, and is about to ask what they cannot get.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine. Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice changes to a quiet poem, and it begins underground: men know exactly where to find silver and gold.

A quiet poem. After twenty-five chapters of argument there is no accusation in this chapter, no complaint, no raised voice. It asks the question underneath the whole debate: where is wisdom?

A mine for silver. It begins underground. Men know where treasure is, and how to get it out: silver mined, gold refined, iron dug from the earth and copper smelted from the ore, as in the land “whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper” (Deuteronomy 8:9).

Who speaks it? The chapter runs straight on from Job’s discourse (27:1), and the ESV sets it as his. But its calm is so unlike the speeches around it, and chapter 29 begins again with “And Job again took up his discourse” (29:1), that many readers take it as the author’s own interlude, a pause between the debate and Job’s last defence. Either way, it stands in the middle of the book like a hinge. Everything before it has been men claiming wisdom. Everything after it will lead to God speaking.
verseByVerse.note: The poem pictures ancient mining: men tunnelling for silver, gold and gems.

verseByVerse.quote: Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness. He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miners go on purpose into the deepest darkness, and hang on ropes in lonely shafts, risking their lives for silver.

Gloom and deep darkness. The miner carries his lamp into “gloom and deep darkness”, the very words Job called down on his birthday (3:5). Here men go into that darkness on purpose, looking for something precious. The verb matters: he “searches out” the ore, the word the poem will use at the end, where God “searched it out” (v. 27). Man can search out silver to the end of the seam. Only God can search out wisdom.

They hang in the air. Shafts sunk in lonely valleys, far from anyone, and the miners let down on ropes, swinging in the dark. Human beings will risk their lives for silver.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 is one of the hardest verses in Job. The ESV’s picture of shafts in remote valleys and miners swinging on ropes is a likely reading, but the Hebrew is obscure and translations vary widely. The point of the passage is clear either way.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire. Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same ground that grows bread on top hides treasure beneath, and man has learned to get at both.

Out of it comes bread. On the surface, a quiet wheat field. Underneath, men are breaking the rock with fire, splitting it open to reach the sapphire and the gold dust. Job once said the suffering “dig for” death “more than for hidden treasures” (3:21). This poem goes down into the same mines, and asks what is more precious than any of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it. The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man goes where the sharpest-eyed bird and the boldest beast have never been, yet even he cannot find wisdom.

That path no bird of prey knows. The falcon sees a mouse from the sky and has never seen a mine. The lion goes anywhere it likes and has never walked these tunnels. Wisdom will be “concealed from the birds of the air” too (v. 21), and hidden from the miner.

The proud beasts. Literally “the sons of pride”, a phrase found only once more, where God ends his description of Leviathan: “he is king over all the sons of pride” (41:34). The proud creatures that never found the miner’s path are the creatures God will parade before Job, and he is their Master.

Uncertain wording. The word behind “pride” is rare, and its exact sense is uncertain: perhaps proud, perhaps majestic or fierce. Either way it means the great wild beasts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots. He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing. He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There seems to be nothing man cannot do with the earth: he overturns mountains and brings hidden things to light, but his sight stops at the sapphire.

He overturns mountains by the roots. Flint, mountains, channels cut through stone, underground streams dammed so the miners can work. “The thing that is hidden he brings out to light.” Job said that about God: “He uncovers the deeps out of darkness” (12:22). Man can do something like it with rock and ore.

His eye sees every precious thing. The eyes in this poem tell the story. Man’s “eye sees every precious thing” in the rock (v. 10). Wisdom is “hidden from the eyes of all living” (v. 21). And God “sees everything under the heavens” (v. 24). Human sight reaches the sapphire and stops. Only God’s reaches wisdom.

Uncertain wording. “He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle” is literally “he binds the rivers from weeping”, a vivid but obscure phrase; it may mean that miners stop the water seeping into their tunnels, or that they search out where rivers rise. Either way, man masters even the hidden waters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem’s point here is that wisdom cannot be found anywhere in creation or bought at any price. The question is asked (v. 12): man does not know its worth, it is not in the land of the living, and the deep and the sea both say it is not with them (vv. 13–14). Gold, silver, the gold of Ophir, onyx, sapphire, glass, coral, crystal, pearls and the topaz of Cush: none can buy it (vv. 15–19). The question comes again (v. 20). Wisdom is hidden from every living eye, and even Destruction and Death have only heard a rumour of it (vv. 21–22). One place is left to look.
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing that matters most cannot be dug up or bought. It has to be given.

verseByVerse.quote: "But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the question the whole book has been asking: where can anyone find the wisdom to understand God’s ways? Not by digging deeper, and not among the living.

Where shall wisdom be found? The friends thought they had found it: in visions (4:12), in the fathers (8:8), in their own long experience (15:10). Job has searched for it too, and for God. Men can find silver in a mountain. Where can they find the wisdom to understand God’s ways with a suffering man? We do not even know its worth, and it is nowhere among the living. The question will come again in almost the same words (v. 20), like a refrain.

We have never known more. We have done what the miner did and far more: split the atom, read the genome, put the sum of human learning in a pocket. If wisdom were a matter of digging deeper, we would be the wisest generation that ever lived, and few people think we are. T. S. Eliot asked in 1934, in The Rock, “Where is the wisdom we have lost in knowledge? Where is the knowledge we have lost in information?” Job’s poem draws the same line. Knowledge tells you how to get the sapphire out of the rock. Wisdom tells you what a human life is for, and what to do when it falls apart, and no shaft goes down that far.

Wisdom is given. That humbles the modern mind, and the religious mind too: the friends had their own mine of tradition and experience, and came up empty. Wisdom is given, not extracted, and the gospel adds that it was given in a form no one expected: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the deepest places in the world, which no miner could reach, say that wisdom is not there.

It is not in me. The poem sends the question to the deep and the sea, the places beyond any shaft, and they answer: not here. Wisdom is not a matter of digging deeper.

verseByVerse.quote: It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price. It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom cannot be bought: all the silver and the finest gold in the world are worthless as its price.

It cannot be bought for gold. If it cannot be dug up, can it be bought? No. Silver was weighed out on scales in a sale, and there is not enough silver in the world for this. “The gold of Ophir” was the finest gold there was. Onyx and sapphire, the treasures the miners risked their lives for (v. 6), are worthless as payment.

The gold of Ophir. Eliphaz had told Job to lay “gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed”, and God would be his gold (22:24–25). He was right that God is more precious than Ophir’s gold. The poem adds what Eliphaz forgot: so is wisdom, and Eliphaz did not have it either.
verseByVerse.note: “Sapphire” may be lapis lazuli (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls. The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole jeweller’s window cannot equal wisdom; what matters most is worth more than everything else.

The price of wisdom is above pearls. Glass was a luxury in that world, as precious as jewellery. Coral from the sea, rock crystal, pearls, topaz from far-off Cush: the poem piles them all up and says, do not even mention them. Proverbs says the same: “She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her” (Proverbs 3:15).

The pearl of great value. Jesus told of a merchant who, “on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). The parable is about the kingdom, not this poem, but it makes the same point: what matters most is worth more than everything else. The friends had plenty of learning. They did not have this.

Uncertain wording. Several of these precious things cannot be identified with certainty. The word for “pearls” may mean coral or red gems, and “topaz” may be another yellow-green stone; “sapphire” in verse 16 may be lapis lazuli. The poem’s point does not depend on the names: the costliest things on earth cannot buy wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: "From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air. Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one in all creation, living or dead, holds wisdom; there is only one place left to look.

From where, then, does wisdom come? The refrain again: hidden from every living eye, even the falcon’s (v. 7).

We have heard a rumor of it. The poem goes below the sea, to Destruction and Death themselves, the places Job said lie naked before God (26:6). Death knows many secrets, and not this one. Not the living, not the dead, not the deep, not the sky: no one in all creation holds it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — The Fear of the Lord, That Is Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem’s point is that wisdom belongs to God alone, and that he has told man what wisdom is for him. God understands the way to it, for he sees to the ends of the earth (vv. 23–24). When he gave the wind its weight, measured out the waters and set a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning, he saw wisdom, declared it, established it and searched it out (vv. 25–27). And to man he said: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding (v. 28). By that definition Job, who feared God and turned away from evil (1:1), was the wise man all along.
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom belongs to God, and man's share in it is to fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "God understands the way to it, and he knows its place. For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is not lost; it is with God, who knows the way to it because he sees everything, and any wisdom we have must come from him as a gift.

God understands the way to it. He knows the road to wisdom and where it lives, because he looks to the ends of the earth. What man cannot find by digging, God has always known.

The book’s turning point. The friends spoke as if they had wisdom and could apply it to Job’s case. Job spoke as if he could summon God to court and argue with him as an equal. Both were looking for wisdom in the wrong place, in themselves. It belongs to God, and any wisdom a human being will ever have must come from him: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5), written by the same James who holds Job up to the church (James 5:11).

verseByVerse.quote: When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure, when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder, then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is the pattern God built into creation when he weighed the wind and made a way for the lightning, and the New Testament gives that wisdom a name: the Son.

Then he saw it and declared it. When God made the world he weighed the wind, measured out the seas, gave the rain its law and the lightning its path, and at that moment, the poem says, he looked at wisdom, spoke it and set it in place. Proverbs pictures Wisdom present at the making of the world, a poetic figure rather than a second person beside God: “The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old” (Proverbs 8:22). Yet the New Testament gives the wisdom by which God made the world a name and a face: “In the beginning was the Word … All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3). The wisdom by which God made the world is the Son by whom he made it.

He gave to the wind its weight. God’s wisdom measures everything exactly, even the wind, which seems to weigh nothing: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand … and weighed the mountains in scales” (Isaiah 40:12)? A God who weighs the wind has weighed Job’s trouble too, to the ounce. Job asked for his calamity to be “laid in the balances” (6:2). It had been, by the only one who could.

A way for the lightning of the thunder. Two phrases here reach across the book. This is the same Hebrew phrase God himself will use from the whirlwind, “a way for the thunderbolt” (38:25): when God speaks, he will speak about exactly this. And “searched it out” is the friends’ proud word: Eliphaz’s “this we have searched out; it is true” (5:27), and Bildad’s “what the fathers have searched out” (8:8). They claimed to have searched it out. Only God has.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man cannot possess God’s wisdom, but God has told him what wisdom is for him: to fear the Lord and turn away from evil, a way to live when there is no explanation.

The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. After the mines, the jewels, the deep and death itself, the answer is short. Not to understand everything, but to reverence the one who does, and to live accordingly. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 111:10; compare Proverbs 1:7). It is the only place in the book where God is called “the Lord” in the sense of Master, and it is fitting: wisdom begins with knowing who is Master.

Job, the wise man. Turn back to the first verse of the book: “that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil” (1:1). By the definition God gives here, Job was the wise man all along: not the three wise men from Teman, Shuah and Naamah with their visions and traditions, but the man on the ash heap who feared God and would not let go of him. Jesus thanked his Father that he had “hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children” (Matthew 11:25).

Where the treasure is. The New Testament tells us where the hidden treasure finally is. The miners dig and cannot find wisdom; Paul points to Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), “who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). The wisdom no one could dig out of the earth came down to it, in a person. To fear the Lord now is to trust the Son in whom God has given that wisdom. And the Spirit who rested on him, “the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2), now works that fear in his people.

For someone in Job’s place. The fear of the Lord is not terror; it is the reverent trust of a creature who knows God is God: “In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence” (Proverbs 14:26). It is not an explanation of suffering, and the poem does not pretend it is. It is a way of living when there is no explanation: hold God in awe, keep turning from evil, and leave the understanding with him. That is exactly what Job did on the first day of his troubles, before any friend had spoken, when he fell on the ground and worshipped (1:20). He did not understand then either. He was wise.

28.theology: Wisdom belongs to God alone: man cannot dig it out or buy it, and only God has searched it out (v. 27). Man's share in it is to fear the Lord and turn from evil (v. 28), which makes the man on the ash heap the wise man of the book. Its hidden treasures are in Christ, and God gives wisdom to those who ask.
28.examples: The poem's pictures stay in the mind: miners swinging on ropes in the dark where no hawk has looked, a wheat field on the surface and fire in the rock beneath, and Death admitting it has only heard a rumour of wisdom. Each says the same thing. Our cleverness reaches a long way, but the wisdom to live well before God is something we receive, not something we dig out.

keyVerse.quote: And he said to man, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.’
keyVerse.note: This is the answer to the poem’s question, “Where shall wisdom be found?” (v. 12), and the hinge of the whole book. Man cannot possess God’s wisdom, but he can fear the Lord and turn from evil, as Job did from the first verse (1:1). It is not an explanation of suffering but a way to live without one, and it leads to Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Colossians 2:3).

28.reflection:
Verses 1–11 celebrate what human beings can do: tunnel into mountains and bring hidden things to light. Why does all our knowledge not make us wise? Where do you see the difference between knowledge and wisdom in your own life or in our culture?

The friends looked for wisdom in visions, tradition and experience (4:12; 8:8; 15:10), and Job looked for it by summoning God to court. Where are you tempted to look for the wisdom to understand your circumstances?

“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (v. 28). What is the difference between this fear and terror? How does it give “strong confidence” (Proverbs 14:26) to someone who has no explanation for their suffering?

Paul says that in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). How does the poem’s search for hidden treasure help you see the worth of Christ? What would it mean to treasure him above silver and gold this week?

29.title: Oh, That I Were as in the Months of Old
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me,<sup>3</sup>when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,<sup>4</sup>as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent,<sup>5</sup>when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me,<sup>6</sup>when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!<sup>7</sup>When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square,<sup>8</sup>the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood;<sup>9</sup>the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth;<sup>10</sup>the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.<sup>11</sup>When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved,<sup>12</sup>because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him.<sup>13</sup>The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.<sup>14</sup>I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban.<sup>15</sup>I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.<sup>16</sup>I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know.<sup>17</sup>I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.<sup>18</sup>Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand,<sup>19</sup>my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches,<sup>20</sup>my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'<sup>21</sup>"Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel.<sup>22</sup>After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them.<sup>23</sup>They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain.<sup>24</sup>I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down.<sup>25</sup>I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
29.overview:
Where we are. The debate with the three friends is over: Bildad’s last speech was six verses long (chapter 25), Zophar never spoke a third time, and Job has answered them for the last time (chapters 26–28). Now Job makes his closing defence, three chapters long. In chapter 29 he looks back, in chapter 30 he looks at the present, and in chapter 31 he swears his innocence before God.

The message. Job remembers the days when God watched over him, and what he misses first is not his wealth but God himself: God’s lamp on his head, God’s friendship over his tent. Out of that friendship came a life of real goodness: he was eyes to the blind, a father to the needy and a comforter of mourners. The chapter teaches that a godly life flows from nearness to God, and it honestly voices the grief of a believer who remembers a closeness he no longer feels.

Why it was said. Eliphaz had accused Job of stripping the naked, sending widows away empty and crushing the fatherless (22:6–9), and the friends had assumed that his suffering proved such hidden sins (see the introduction). Job does not argue the charges point by point. He describes the life he actually lived, and lets it answer them.

How the chapter makes its case. Job longs for the months when God watched over him, his children were around him and his life overflowed (vv. 1–6). He remembers the city gate, where young and old, princes and nobles, fell silent when he came (vv. 7–10), and gives the reason: he rescued the poor and the fatherless, wore righteousness like a robe and broke the jaws of the oppressor (vv. 11–17). He expected to die old in his own nest, a tree with roots by the water (vv. 18–20), and he ends where he began, with men waiting for his words like rain and the light of his face cheering the discouraged, “like one who comforts mourners” (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by pattern. Job at the gate is the righteous ruler Israel longed for, who “delivers the needy when he calls” (Psalm 72:12), and the comforter of mourners whom Isaiah promised (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus is that ruler and comforter in full: he did not only lead the blind, he gave them sight (Matthew 11:5). The chapter also prepares for the deepest pattern of all. Job falls from the honour of chapter 29 to the shame of chapter 30, through no sin of his own; the Son of God left a glory far greater, of his own will, and “emptied himself” for us (Philippians 2:7). And it exposes a need: even righteousness as real as Job’s cannot be the ground on which a man stands before God (40:8), so we need another’s righteousness to wear.

For us. If you remember a season when God felt near and now he feels far, you may say so to him, as Job does; feeling his absence is not the same as his absence. Let your standing rest on the Father’s verdict in Christ, not on your title or your record, so that losing either cannot take away who you are. And use whatever influence you have the way Job did, for those who have no one to speak for them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Days When God Watched Over Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Job misses first in his suffering is God himself. Before he mentions his honour, his wealth or even his children, he remembers the days “when God watched over me” and his lamp shone on Job’s head, so that he could walk through darkness unafraid (vv. 2–3). He was in his prime, with God’s friendship over his tent (v. 4). Only then does he name the other gifts: his children all around him (v. 5), and a life so rich it seemed washed in butter, with oil flowing from the rock (v. 6). The order is the point. The gifts were sweet because the Giver was near.
verseByVerse.theology: What Job misses most is not his wealth but God's nearness, and his children.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said: "Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Job longs for first is not his wealth but the days when God watched over him.

When his lamp shone upon my head. The friends have nothing more to say, and Job speaks alone. He misses “the days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head”. The words sound like the blessing Israel’s priests pronounced: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:24–25). Job had lived under that blessing, kept and shone upon, and with God’s lamp over him he could walk through dark places unafraid: “For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness” (Psalm 18:28).

When God seemed close. Many believers know this ache: the memory of a season when God seemed close, set against a present in which he seems far. Job does not pretend the memory is not there. But the reader knows something Job does not: God has not stopped watching over him. The limit God set on Satan, “only spare his life” (2:6), is God’s watch still being kept. Feeling God’s absence is not the same as God’s absence.

verseByVerse.quote: as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent, when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me, when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job remembers God’s friendship over his home, his children around him and a life that overflowed.

As I was in my prime. Literally, in the autumn of his days: the season of harvest, the ripe and fruitful years.

The friendship of God. The Hebrew word means intimate counsel, and it is the word Eliphaz used when he mocked Job for thinking he had “listened in the council of God” (15:8). Job says: I had God’s friendship once, over my own tent. “The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him” (Psalm 25:14). Jesus gives it to his disciples: “I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

When my children were all around me. “Your children will be like olive shoots around your table” (Psalm 128:3), and his were, and they are gone. Then the abundance: paths so rich they seemed washed in butter, and olive oil flowing even from the rock (compare Deuteronomy 32:13). His life overflowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — I Was Eyes to the Blind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job was honoured because he was good, and his goodness was for the weak. At the city gate, where justice was done, young men stepped aside, old men stood, and princes and nobles fell silent when he came (vv. 7–10). Verses 11–13 give the reason: he delivered the poor who cried for help and the fatherless who had no helper, so that the dying blessed him and widows sang. He wore righteousness like a judge’s robe, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, investigated the stranger’s case properly and tore the victim from the oppressor’s jaws (vv. 14–17). This is Job’s answer to Eliphaz’s charges, and a portrait of the ruler Israel longed for.
verseByVerse.theology: Every charge Eliphaz invented is answered by the life Job actually lived. It is a portrait of the King the psalms long for, and Christ is that King.

verseByVerse.quote: When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square, the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood; the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth; the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the city gate everyone fell silent when Job arrived: the honour he has lost, and a warning not to build our identity on standing.

The gate of the city. The city gate was the court, the council chamber and the town square of an ancient city, where the elders sat to judge and decide. When Job came, the young men stepped back respectfully, the old men got to their feet, and even princes stopped talking. Now, by contrast, children despise him when he rises (19:18).

Laid their hand on their mouth. The great men of the city did before Job what Job will do before God. When the LORD has spoken from the whirlwind, Job will say, “I lay my hand on my mouth” (40:4). Respect for a man silences the princes. The glory of God silences the man.

Who are we when the title goes? Few chapters describe so exactly what we now call a career, and Job grieves its loss without apology. So do we, more than we admit. For many people work is no longer only what they do but who they are, which is why redundancy, retirement or a public failure can feel less like losing a job than losing a self. Respect is a good gift, and Job used his well (vv. 12–17). But notice what he mourned first: “the friendship of God” (v. 4). An identity built on achievement has to be earned again every day, and one bad year can take it. The gospel gives one that comes the other way round. Before Jesus had preached a sermon or done a miracle, the Father said over him, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Those who are in him receive that verdict first, as a gift, and then go to work: not to become somebody, but because they already are.
verseByVerse.note: Elders sat in the city gate to judge cases.

verseByVerse.quote: When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved, because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him. The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job was honoured because he rescued the poor, the fatherless and the dying, and his life answers Eliphaz’s false charges.

I delivered the poor who cried for help. Dying men blessed him; widows sang because of him. This is the answer to Eliphaz, who said, “You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed” (22:9). Job does not argue the charge. He describes his life, and the life answers it.

Is this boasting? Job is answering false charges with the truth, as Paul answers his critics (2 Corinthians 11). His good deeds are not his ground of acceptance with God; the danger lies in the use he will make of them, to put God in the wrong (40:8).

verseByVerse.quote: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know. I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job wore righteousness like a judge’s robe, serving the helpless and rescuing victims, a portrait of the king fulfilled in Christ.

I put on righteousness, and it clothed me. He wore it every day, as a judge wears his robe. And “I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know”: when a stranger’s case came before him, he investigated it properly. “Searched out” is the verb Eliphaz used for his confident conclusions (5:27). Job used it for the hard work of finding out the truth about a stranger, which is exactly what the friends never did for him.

I broke the fangs of the unrighteous. The oppressor is pictured as a wild beast with a victim in its jaws, and Job as the man who wrenched the victim out. It is what the psalmist asks God to do: “you break the teeth of the wicked” (Psalm 3:7). Job’s justice was God’s justice at work through a human judge, which is what earthly authority is for.

The king Israel longed for. This is the picture of the king Israel longed for: “he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper.… From oppression and violence he redeems their life” (Psalm 72:12, 14). It is the picture of God himself, who “put on righteousness as a breastplate” (Isaiah 59:17). And it is Christ. When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus answered, “the blind receive their sight and the lame walk” (Matthew 11:5). Job was eyes to the blind. Christ gave the blind their sight.

For us. For anyone with influence today, at work, in a church or in a family, the pattern is concrete: notice who has no one to speak for them, take the trouble to hear their side properly, and use what standing you have to protect them rather than yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Like One Who Comforts Mourners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job expected his blessing to last, and he ends where he began, with a life that gave to others what it received from God. He thought he would die old in his own nest, a tree with roots by the water and dew on its branches, his strength always fresh (vv. 18–20). It was the natural hope of a godly man, and in the end it came true (42:16–17). Then he returns to the gate: men waited for his counsel like farmers for rain, his smile gave courage to the discouraged, and he led like a king, “like one who comforts mourners” (vv. 21–25), the very thing his friends could not do for him.
verseByVerse.theology: Job had been the comforter the friends failed to be. The comforter of all who mourn is the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand, my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches, my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job expected to die old and secure at home, a natural hope that, after the fire, came true.

I shall die in my nest. He expected to die at home, old and surrounded by his family, like a bird in its nest. He pictured himself as a tree with roots in the water and dew on its branches every night, the blessed man of the first psalm, “like a tree planted by streams of water” (Psalm 1:3), with his strength, his “bow”, always new in his hand. It was not pride to expect it. Any godly man might have.

It came true. The strange thing is that it did: “And after this Job lived 140 years.… And Job died, an old man, and full of days” (42:16–17). The tree he thought uprooted (19:10) put down its roots again. But not before he had been through the fire.

Uncertain wording. The word for “sand” (v. 18) normally means sand, a common picture of countless numbers. An old Jewish tradition read it as the phoenix, the legendary long-lived bird reborn from its nest, which would suit “my nest”, and some translations adopt it. Either way Job expected a very long life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel. After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them. They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain. I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down. I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People waited for Job’s counsel like dry ground for rain, and he comforted mourners, as his friends failed to comfort him and as Christ comforts in full.

Men listened to me. People waited for his advice the way a dry field waits for rain, and when he spoke there was no more to be said. Moses prayed, “May my teaching drop as the rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2). Job’s counsel was like that.

The light of my face. When others lost heart, his smile gave them courage. At the start of the chapter God’s lamp shone on Job (v. 3); here Job’s face shines on the discouraged and frightened. He passed on what he received. That is the believer’s calling still: “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Like one who comforts mourners. The last line of the chapter is pointed. The friends came “to comfort him” (2:11). Job had been, for years, the man who comforted mourners, and they could not do for him what he had done for others. The Messiah’s mission is described in the same words: the Spirit of the Lord is upon him “to bind up the brokenhearted… to comfort all who mourn” (Isaiah 61:1–2), and Jesus read the opening of that passage in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in him (Luke 4:18–21). The comforter Job was, Christ is, to everyone who mourns.

Uncertain wording. Verse 24 is compressed. The ESV takes it that Job’s smile encouraged those who had lost confidence; it may mean that people could hardly believe he smiled on them, so great was the honour. “The light of my face they did not cast down” probably means nothing could darken his favour. Either way, his kindness lifted others.

29.theology: What Job misses most is God's watching care and friendship (vv. 2-4), though in fact God had not stopped watching (2:6). His past life answers Eliphaz's invented charges and sketches the righteous King who delivers the needy (Ps 72:12-14), the King whom Christ fulfils as the comforter of all who mourn.
29.examples: This chapter gives words to anyone who remembers a better season: a time when God seemed close, the family was whole, and their work did good. Job neither pretends the memory away nor lets it be the last word. And his picture of a life spent as eyes to the blind and feet to the lame is still a pattern for anyone with influence over others.

keyVerse.quote: Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me,
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of Job’s longing: before he mentions his honour, his wealth or even his children, he misses God’s watchful care. It shows what Job had always loved most, which answers Satan’s question (1:9). And the reader knows what Job cannot see: God is watching over him still.

29.reflection:
Job’s longing begins with “the days when God watched over me” and “the friendship of God” (vv. 2–4), not with his wealth. If you lost the gifts God has given you, what would you miss first? What does that reveal about what you love most?

Have you known a season when God felt close and then seemed far away? How does it help to know that the reader can see God’s watch over Job that Job himself could not?

Job was “eyes to the blind and feet to the lame” and “searched out the cause of him whom I did not know” (vv. 15–16). Who around you has no one to speak for them, and how could you use your influence, however small, on their behalf?

Much of Job’s grief is for lost standing at the city gate (vv. 7–10). How much of your sense of who you are rests on your work, title or reputation? How does the Father’s word over Jesus (Matthew 3:17), given to those who are in him, change that?

30.title: But Now They Laugh at Me
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock.<sup>2</sup>What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?<sup>3</sup>Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation;<sup>4</sup>they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food.<sup>5</sup>They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief.<sup>6</sup>In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks.<sup>7</sup>Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together.<sup>8</sup>A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.<sup>9</sup>"And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them.<sup>10</sup>They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me.<sup>11</sup>Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence.<sup>12</sup>On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction.<sup>13</sup>They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them.<sup>14</sup>As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on.<sup>15</sup>Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud.<sup>16</sup>"And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me.<sup>17</sup>The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest.<sup>18</sup>With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic.<sup>19</sup>God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes.<sup>20</sup>I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me.<sup>21</sup>You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me.<sup>22</sup>You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm.<sup>23</sup>For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.<sup>24</sup>"Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help?<sup>25</sup>Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy?<sup>26</sup>But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came.<sup>27</sup>My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me.<sup>28</sup>I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.<sup>29</sup>I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches.<sup>30</sup>My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat.<sup>31</sup>My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.
30.overview:
Where we are. This is the second part of Job’s closing defence (chapters 29–31). Chapter 29 remembered the days when God watched over him and the city honoured him. Chapter 30 answers it with three blunt words, “but now” (vv. 1, 9, 16), and sets the present beside the past.

The message. Job has fallen from the top of society to below the bottom of it: mocked by outcasts, spat on, attacked, and, worst of all, met by silence from God. The chapter gives believers words for the darkest kind of suffering, where pain, disgrace and unanswered prayer come together, and shows that such words may be spoken to God. It also lets us see the worst of Job as well as the best: suffering brings his pride to the surface, and he charges God with cruelty. Scripture records it honestly, and God will answer it.

Why it was said. The friends have insisted that God never treats the upright like this, so Job must be guilty (see the introduction). Job lays out exactly how he is being treated, by men and by God, so that no one can pretend his suffering is light, and he still brings his complaint to God rather than away from him.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the mockers: young men from a brood of outcasts, driven from society to live in gullies and eat roots, now laugh at the man they once feared (vv. 1–8). Second, the attack: he has become their song and byword; they spit at him and pour through his broken defences, because God has loosed his cord (vv. 9–15). Third, the silence: his life drains away, pain gnaws his bones at night, and when he cries to God there is no answer, only a gaze he feels as cruel (vv. 16–23). Last, the lament: he wept for others in trouble, but when he hoped for good, evil came, and his lyre plays only funeral music (vv. 24–31).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need exposed. Job’s descent from honour to contempt is traced again, further down and of his own will, by the Son of God: he “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7), was despised by the lowest, spat upon at his trial (Matthew 26:67) and mocked on the cross. He prayed Job’s darkest prayer, the cry of Psalm 22, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and was truly not answered, so that those who belong to him never will be finally unanswered. And where Job answered his mockers with contempt, Christ “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). Job needs, as we do, a sufferer better than himself.

For us. When pain, shame and the silence of God come together, you may pray this chapter; honesty before God is not unbelief. Do not take your darkest feelings about God for the truth about him: the reader knows God was watching Job with love. And because Christ went lower still for you, your night is not the last word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — But Now They Laugh at Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he has fallen below the bottom of society. “But now”, he says, answering the honour of chapter 29: young men laugh at him whose fathers he would not have set with his sheepdogs (v. 1), men so broken they are of no use to anyone (v. 2). Verses 3–8 describe them: starving outcasts gnawing the desert by night, eating saltwort and broom roots, driven out of the towns with shouts like thieves, living in gullies and holes, braying in the scrub, a nameless brood whipped out of the land. Even they now look down on Job. The scorn in his description, so unlike his compassion in 24:5–8, shows what suffering is drawing out of him.
verseByVerse.theology: The man before whom princes fell silent is mocked by outcasts. And the bitterness of it shows in how he speaks of them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock. What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job is now mocked by the lowest of men, and in his pain he answers with a contempt that is not the best of him.

But now they laugh at me. Chapter 29 was then. This chapter answers it three times: “But now” (v. 1), “And now” (v. 9), “And now” (v. 16). The man before whom princes fell silent is laughed at by young men whose fathers he would not have trusted with his sheepdogs.

Harsh words. These words sit badly beside the Job of chapter 29, “a father to the needy” (29:16), or the Job who described the homeless poor with such compassion (24:5–8). Suffering has done what suffering often does: it has brought pride to the surface. The mockers are cruel, and Job is right that they are, but the contempt in his reply is not the best of him. Job is a real man with real faults, not a flawless model, and the book lets us see it.

Another answer. The one mocked by the lowest of men and answered differently is Christ: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation; they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food. They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief. In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks. Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together. A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s mockers are starving, nameless outcasts, and even they look down on him.

A senseless, a nameless brood. These are men driven out of the towns, living in dry riverbeds and caves, eating salty desert plants and the bitter roots of the broom bush, chased off with shouts like thieves, huddling in the scrub like animals. Even they despise Job now: he has fallen below the bottom of society.

Among the bushes they bray. Compare 24:5, where Job described the homeless poor “like wild donkeys in the desert”, scavenging for their children, and wrote with tenderness. Here the same kind of men bray among the bushes, and he writes with scorn. The picture is the same; the heart has changed, because now they are mocking him. Every reader should hold that mirror up to himself: how we speak of the poor can change the moment they turn on us.

Despised by the despised. It is the depth of social disgrace, and the Son of God went there too. The men who spat on him, the passers-by who shook their heads at the cross, the criminal who mocked him as he hung there: he was despised by the despised. He came down further than Job, and he came down on purpose.

Uncertain wording. Several words in verses 2–4 are rare. “Gnaw the dry ground” may mean they chew whatever the desert offers, or that they flee into it. Broom roots were bitter and usually burnt for charcoal (Psalm 120:4), so some, changing one word, read “to warm them” for “for their food”. The picture of starving outcasts is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — I Have Become Their Song
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that, because God has humbled him, the contempt of men has broken loose. He has become their song and byword; they keep away from him and do not hesitate to spit at him (vv. 9–10). The reason is that “God has loosed my cord”: with his strength and standing gone, men no longer restrain themselves (v. 11). Then the mob attacks like an army storming a city, pushing him off his path, promoting his ruin and rolling through the breach (vv. 12–14). Terrors turn on him, and his honour and prosperity blow away like wind and cloud (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: He is a joke and a song among the lowest of men, as the sufferer of Psalm 69 was, and as Christ was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them. They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me. Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has humbled Job, men no longer hold back: he is their song, their byword, a face to spit at.

I have become their song. They make up songs about him. Psalm 69, a psalm of innocent suffering which the New Testament applies to Christ, says the same: “I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me” (Psalm 69:12). He is a byword (a name people use as a taunt), a joke, a face spat on (compare 17:6). The spitting will come again at the trial of Jesus (Matthew 26:67).

God has loosed my cord. God has cut his tent-rope (compare 4:21), or unstrung his bow (compare 29:20); either way, his strength and standing are gone, and people who once feared him feel free to do as they like. Job traces even their insolence back to God’s hand. He is right that God’s hand is in it (2:3), and still does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction. They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them. As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on. Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mob storms Job like an army through a breach, and his honour and wealth blow away.

On my right hand the rabble rise. The picture of a siege returns from 19:12, but now it is a mob, not an army: rabble pushing him off the path, pouring through the breach in his defences, rolling on amid the crash. “My honor is pursued as by the wind”, and his wealth is gone like a cloud that crosses the sky and is not there any more.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 12–14 is difficult, and translations vary in detail, especially “they need no one to help them” (v. 13). The picture of a breached wall overrun is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Cry to You and You Do Not Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that the worst of his suffering is not men’s contempt but God’s silence. “And now”, the third time: his life is poured out, and the night racks his bones with pain that never rests (vv. 16–17). His garment clings to him, and God has thrown him into the mire, so that he is like dust and ashes (vv. 18–19). Then he speaks straight to God: I cry and you do not answer; I stand and you only look; you have turned cruel and persecute me; you toss me in the storm and will bring me to death (vv. 20–23). It is the darkest prayer in the chapter, and it is still a prayer.
verseByVerse.theology: These are the words of Psalm 22, and of the cross. God did not answer yet, but he would.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me. The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest. With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic. God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s life drains away in pain that gives no rest, and God has thrown him in the mire: words Scripture gives sufferers to pray.

My soul is poured out within me. The third “now”, and the deepest. His life drains out of him like water from a jar. At night the pain is in his bones, gnawing, never resting. It is the language of Psalm 22, the psalm of the cross: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint” (Psalm 22:14).

God has cast me into the mire. His clothes cling to his sores; he is thrown in the mud. “Dust and ashes”: Abraham used the words of himself before God, “I who am but dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27), and Job will use them once more, at the very end, when he has seen God: “I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (42:6). Here they are the words of humiliation. There they will be the words of worship.

In chronic pain. Anyone living with chronic pain, or with depression that will not lift, may find their own nights in these verses. Scripture gives such words to pray, and praying them is not unbelief. The God who let Job say all this, and then came to him, does not turn away from the same prayer now.

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 is obscure. The ESV takes it that Job’s garment is disfigured and clings to him, perhaps to his sores; others read that God seizes him by the collar, leading into verse 19. Either way he cannot get free.

verseByVerse.quote: I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me. You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me. You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm. For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job cries to God and meets only silence and a gaze he feels as cruel, a silence Christ entered for his people.

You do not answer me. One of the loneliest lines in Job’s prayers, and many believers have prayed into the same silence. The psalm of the cross prays it: “O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer” (Psalm 22:2). And on the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The Son of God entered the silence Job describes, so that for those who belong to him it would never be the last word.

You only look at me. Job feels God’s gaze as cold, a spectator watching him suffer. But he said himself, in a better hour, “he knows the way that I take” (23:10). God’s eyes on Job were never the eyes of indifference. They were the eyes that had looked at him in the heavenly court and said, “there is none like him on the earth” (1:8).

You have turned cruel to me. This is Job’s hardest charge, and it is not true; the reader must not take it as true. God will ask Job, “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (40:8). But Job says it to God, and God does not strike him for it. God can bear his children’s worst words spoken to his face, and he will speak to Job out of the storm (38:1). The grave, “the house appointed for all living”, is coming for everyone (Hebrews 9:27). Job expects to go there unanswered. He will not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — My Lyre Is Turned to Mourning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he showed others the compassion no one now shows him, and his hope has turned to darkness. Even a man in ruins may stretch out his hand and cry for help (v. 24); Job himself wept for those whose day was hard and grieved for the needy (v. 25). Yet when he hoped for good, evil came, and when he waited for light, darkness (v. 26). He describes his turmoil, his blackened skin and burning bones, his cry for help in the assembly, and his only companions, the jackals and ostriches of the wilderness (vv. 27–30). His lament ends with music turned to mourning (v. 31). But the book is not over.
verseByVerse.theology: This is Job's closing lament. The God who turns mourning into dancing has not finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help? Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy? But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job wept for others in trouble, yet no one weeps for him, and his hope of light met darkness.

Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Surely a man buried in the rubble may reach out his hand and shout for help. And Job had always helped others who cried: he wept for people whose day was hard, he grieved for the poor. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). He did it for others. Why will no one do it for him?

When I waited for light, darkness came. The prophet confessed the same for a whole people: “we hope for light, and behold, darkness” (Isaiah 59:9). It is the experience of disappointed hope, and Scripture does not pretend it never happens to the faithful.

Uncertain wording. Verse 24 is very hard, and translations differ. The ESV reads a question: does not even a man in ruins cry for help? Others read that no one raises a hand against a ruined man, yet Job is attacked. The ESV fits verse 25 well.

verseByVerse.quote: My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me. I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help. I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches. My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat. My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job ends diseased and alone, his music turned to mourning, but neither the book nor God is finished.

I go about darkened, but not by the sun. His skin is blackened, not by sunburn but by the disease. His only kin now are jackals and ostriches, the creatures of ruined places whose wailing in the night was proverbial; Micah would say, “I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches” (Micah 1:8). When God speaks, he will talk about the ostrich (39:13–18), with something like a smile: the creature Job named as his companion in misery, God describes as his own handiwork.

My lyre is turned to mourning. His music has changed: the lyre and pipe that should play at feasts play funeral songs. The wicked still “rejoice to the sound of the pipe” (21:12). Job’s pipe weeps.

Not the end. But the book is not over, and neither is God. “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Psalm 30:11). Job has sewn sackcloth upon his skin (16:15). God will loose it.

30.theology: Job's lament uses the words of Psalms 22 and 69, the psalms Christ fulfilled in his suffering. His charge that God is cruel (v. 21) is false and God will correct it, yet God receives it without striking him. And suffering exposes pride even in the godly (vv. 1-8), whereas Christ, when he was reviled, did not revile in return.
30.examples: This is a chapter for the long nights of pain and the prayers that seem to meet only silence. Job gives the sufferer honest words, and the book does not rebuke him for using them. It also shows, gently, how suffering can sour the way we speak of others, and it ends with a lyre turned to mourning that God has promised to turn back to dancing.

keyVerse.quote: I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me.
keyVerse.note: This is the lowest point of the chapter: worse than the mockery of men is the silence of God. Yet Job still speaks to God, and the reader knows that God’s gaze was never indifferent (1:8). Christ prayed the same kind of prayer on the cross (Matthew 27:46), so that for his people silence is never the last word.

30.reflection:
Job contrasts “the months of old” (29:2) with “but now” (30:1, 9, 16). Have you known a sudden reversal like this? What helped you, or would have helped you, to keep speaking to God through it?

Job wrote of the homeless poor with tenderness in 24:5–8, but here with scorn, because they mock him (vv. 1–8). How can suffering or hurt change the way we speak of others? What does 1 Peter 2:23 show us about a better way?

“I cry to you for help and you do not answer me” (v. 20). Why do you think God allows Scripture to include prayers like this, and even charges like “You have turned cruel to me” (v. 21)? How should we pray when God seems silent?

Jesus was spat upon, mocked and cried out on the cross, “why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). How does knowing that Christ went lower than Job change the way you face your own darkest seasons, or sit with someone else in theirs?

31.title: Here Is My Signature
31.text: <sup>1</sup>"I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?<sup>2</sup>What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high?<sup>3</sup>Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?<sup>4</sup>Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?<sup>5</sup>"If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit;<sup>6</sup>(Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!)<sup>7</sup>if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands,<sup>8</sup>then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.<sup>9</sup>"If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door,<sup>10</sup>then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her.<sup>11</sup>For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges;<sup>12</sup>for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.<sup>13</sup>"If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me,<sup>14</sup>what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him?<sup>15</sup>Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?<sup>16</sup>"If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail,<sup>17</sup>or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it<sup>18</sup>(for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow),<sup>19</sup>if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering,<sup>20</sup>if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,<sup>21</sup>if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate,<sup>22</sup>then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket.<sup>23</sup>For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.<sup>24</sup>"If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence,<sup>25</sup>if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much,<sup>26</sup>if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor,<sup>27</sup>and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand,<sup>28</sup>this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.<sup>29</sup>"If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him<sup>30</sup>(I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse),<sup>31</sup>if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?'<sup>32</sup>(the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),<sup>33</sup>if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart,<sup>34</sup>because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—<sup>35</sup>Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!<sup>36</sup>Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown;<sup>37</sup>I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.<sup>38</sup>"If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together,<sup>39</sup>if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last,<sup>40</sup>let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
31.overview:
Where we are. This is the end of Job’s closing defence (chapters 29–31), and the last words he speaks before God answers him. He has remembered his past (chapter 29) and lamented his present (chapter 30). Now he takes an oath before God on the whole of his life.

The message. Job swears that he has not done the sins his suffering is supposed to prove, and his oath reaches far beyond outward crimes: to the look of the eyes, the secret trust of the heart, the treatment of servants and the hungry, gloating over an enemy and hiding his own faults. The chapter shows what real godliness looks like, from the inside out, and it is among the highest pictures of a righteous life in the Old Testament. Yet Job ends by demanding that God answer him, as if the case could be settled by his own record; the God who will answer is not one we can summon.

Why it was said. Eliphaz had invented crimes for Job: stripping the naked, starving the hungry, crushing widows and orphans (22:5–9). In the ancient world a man accused without proof could clear himself by an oath, calling God’s judgment down on himself if he lied (see the introduction). Job does exactly that, sin by sin.

How the chapter makes its case. He begins with purity: a covenant with his eyes, honesty in his dealings and faithfulness to his neighbour’s wife, because God sees every step (vv. 1–12). He turns to justice and mercy: he heard his servants’ complaints, because the same God made them in the womb, and fed, clothed and protected the orphan and the poor (vv. 13–23). Then the hidden sins: trusting in gold, secretly worshipping the sun and moon, gloating over an enemy, closing his door to the traveller, and concealing his own faults for fear of others (vv. 24–34).
