He signs his defence and demands the written charge, which he would wear as a crown (vv. 35–37), adds a last oath about his land (vv. 38–40), and falls silent: “The words of Job are ended.”

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by the gospel it prepares. Measured by this chapter, few readers can say what Job says, and no one but Christ could swear it all without a flaw. He alone lived this life perfectly, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Job longed to wear his indictment as a crown because he was innocent; Christ was crowned with thorns, with a charge nailed over his head, and carried “the record of debt that stood against us” to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Because he did, we may approach God with the confidence Job longed for (Hebrews 4:16).

For us. Let this chapter search your eyes, your wallet, your table, your treatment of those under you and your reaction when an enemy falls. Where it finds you guilty, do not hide your sin “as others do” (v. 33), but confess it to the God who forgives in Christ. Then, clothed in his righteousness rather than your own, walk the way Job walked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Covenant with My Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that his purity reached beyond his actions to his eyes and heart, because God sees every step. He begins not with adultery but with the look before it: he made a covenant with his eyes (v. 1), knowing that God punishes the wicked and numbers his steps (vv. 2–4). He swears he has not walked with deceit, let his heart follow his eyes or let any stain cling to his hands, and asks to be weighed in an honest balance (vv. 5–8). He swears he has not lain in wait at his neighbour’s door, for adultery is a crime for the judges and a fire that burns a man’s whole life to the root (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's innocence begins where Jesus' teaching begins: not only with the deed, but with the look.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high? Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity? Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s purity began with his eyes, because he knew God sees every step.

The oath of clearance. Job’s last speech takes a form every ancient reader would have recognised: “If I have done this, then let that happen to me.” Calling God’s judgment down on himself if he lies, Job goes through life sin by sin. It answers Eliphaz’s invented charges more thoroughly than any argument could.

I have made a covenant with my eyes. He starts not with adultery but with the look before it: his eyes would not linger on a young woman with desire. Jesus would teach the same: “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Job’s righteousness went down to where he let his eyes go.

Does not he see my ways? Job kept his covenant because he knew God watched and numbered every step, and that calamity is the portion of the unrighteous (vv. 2–4). That is not fear of being caught. It is the fear of the Lord, which is wisdom (28:28).

A covenant with the eyes today. It is a decision made beforehand, not in the moment, not to look at another person, or an image on a screen, in order to desire them. A passing glance is not the sin; the second look, kept and fed, is. Keeping the covenant means guarding what you allow before your eyes, removing what you know will draw you in (Matthew 5:29), and bringing every failure to Christ, who forgives and cleanses. Nor is it kept by willpower alone: “walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit; (Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!) if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands, then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears he never gained by deceit, and asks to be weighed on an honest scale.

If I have walked with falsehood. Deceit in business, dishonest gain, the heart following wherever the eyes lead (Numbers 15:39), a stain on his hands: if so, let someone else eat his harvest.

Let me be weighed in a just balance. A dishonest trader kept false scales; Job asks God to use true ones, as in his first reply (6:2). A king of Babylon was once weighed by God and “found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). Job asks to be weighed, because he believes the scales will show his “integrity”, the word God used of him (2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door, then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her. For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears he never plotted adultery, a crime for the courts and a fire that burns everything.

If my heart has been enticed toward a woman. If he had waited at his neighbour’s door for the husband to go out, then let his own wife become another man’s servant and worse. It is one of the harshest curses in the chapter, and to a modern reader it seems unjust to his wife; the reader is right to feel it. Job is not asking for it to happen to her; he uses the shame-language of a world where a man’s household shared his disgrace, to say how unthinkable the sin is to him. Scripture elsewhere insists that each bears his own guilt (Ezekiel 18:20).

A fire that consumes as far as Abaddon. Adultery is more than a crime for the judges: it is a fire that burns everything a man has, down to Abaddon, “destruction”, a name for the realm of the dead. “Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned?… So is he who goes in to his neighbor’s wife” (Proverbs 6:27, 29). Job knew it, and did not touch the fire.

Uncertain wording. “Grind for another” (v. 10) means at least turning another man’s millstone as a slave, the lowest household work (Exodus 11:5). Because of the next line, many think it is also a veiled reference to sexual use. Either way it is utter shame.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Did Not He Who Made Me Make Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he treated the powerless with justice and mercy, because God made them as he made Job. He heard his servants’ complaints, knowing that he too must answer to God, who fashioned master and servant alike in the womb (vv. 13–15). He swears he never withheld what the poor needed, ate alone while the orphan went hungry, or let anyone shiver without clothing while his sheep had wool; from his youth he was a father to the fatherless (vv. 16–20). He never used his influence at the gate against the orphan, because he stood in awe of God’s majesty (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Master and servant were made by the same God in the same way. Job lived as if that were true.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me, what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him? Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job heard his servants’ complaints because the same God made master and servant alike.

The cause of my manservant. In Job’s world a servant had no rights against his master. Job listened to his servants’ complaints anyway, because he knew he had a Master too, who would one day ask him how he had treated them.

Did not he who made me in the womb make him? Here is the reason. The same God made master and slave, in the same way, in their mothers’ wombs. Neither is more human than the other. “Has not one God created us?” asks Malachi (Malachi 2:10). Paul tells Christian masters to treat their servants well, “knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (Ephesians 6:9). The dignity of every human being rests here: not on what he can do or what he owns, but on the fact that God made him.

Does this mean the Bible approves of slavery? Job had servants, as every household of means did in his world (see slavery in the ancient world), and Scripture regulates that world’s institutions before it overturns them. But this verse lays an axe at the root of treating any person as property or as less than human, and the law put to death anyone who kidnapped a man to sell him (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow), if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering, if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job swears he fed, clothed and fathered the poor and the orphan, the very works of the last judgment.

If I have withheld anything that the poor desired. Job answers on oath every item of Eliphaz’s charge (22:6–9). He never ate alone while an orphan went without; orphans grew up in his house as if he were their father; he never let a poor man freeze while his own sheep had wool. The poor man’s body “blessed” him, warm under Job’s fleece.

Pure religion. It is the religion James describes: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). And it is the religion of the sheep in Jesus’ judgment, who fed the hungry and clothed the naked (Matthew 25:35–36). The list Eliphaz threw at Job is the list of the last judgment, and Job’s life stands on the right side of it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 is compressed in Hebrew and does not name the fatherless or the widow; the ESV supplies them, rightly. The sense is that caring for the helpless was part of Job’s life as far back as he could remember.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate, then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket. For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job never used his power at the gate against the helpless, because he feared God more than any man.

If I have raised my hand against the fatherless. Wronging an orphan would have been easy: he had no one to speak for him at the city gate, where the elders were Job’s friends and Job himself sat as judge (29:7). Job could have raised his hand against the helpless and won. If he had, let that arm be torn from its socket. He did not, because he was in terror of God’s judgment and could not have faced his majesty (v. 23). Power over the defenceless is the real test of a man, and Job passed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–34 — If I Have Made Gold My Trust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he was faithful even in the sins no one else could see. He swears he never trusted in gold or rejoiced in wealth (vv. 24–25), nor secretly worshipped the sun and moon, which would have been false to God above (vv. 26–28). He never gloated over an enemy’s ruin or cursed his life (vv. 29–30). His table fed everyone and his door was open to every traveller (vv. 31–32). And he did not hide his sins, as others do, out of fear of what people would think (vv. 33–34). This last oath is not a claim to be sinless, but to be honest about his sins.
verseByVerse.theology: The inward sins, greed, idolatry, spite, secrecy, are the ones a man could hide. Job swears he did not hide them.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence, if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much, if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job never trusted in his gold or secretly worshipped the sun and moon, either of which would be unfaithfulness to God.

If I have made gold my trust. Now the sins no one could see. Job was the richest man in the east, and he swears his confidence was never in his gold. That is why he could lose it and still bless God (1:21). Paul calls greed what it is, “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5), and tells the rich not “to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God” (1 Timothy 6:17).

My mouth has kissed my hand. The worship of the sun and moon was the religion of most of the ancient world, and Moses warned Israel against it (Deuteronomy 4:19). To “kiss the hand” was to blow a kiss of worship toward the sky. Job never did it, even secretly. Either sin, trusting in gold or bowing to the heavens, “would have been false to God above”. Idolatry is unfaithfulness to the one true God, and Job was faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him (I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse), if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?' (the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job never gloated over an enemy or cursed him, and his door was always open to the stranger.

If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me. He did not gloat when an enemy fell, and he never asked for an enemy’s life with a curse. “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls” (Proverbs 24:17). Jesus went further: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). In 27:7 Job said of his accusers, “Let my enemy be as the wicked”; that was an appeal for justice against false witnesses, not a curse on a man’s life, and here he holds to the same standard.

I have opened my doors to the traveler. His household could say there was no one who had not been filled at his table, and no traveller ever had to sleep in the street (see hospitality). “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers” (Hebrews 13:2). Job’s door was always open.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart, because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job does not claim to be sinless, but swears he never hid his sins for fear of others.

If I have concealed my transgressions. What Job swears here is not that he had no sins but that he did not hide the sins he had, or keep quiet about his faults out of fear of what the neighbours would think. Adam, when he sinned, “hid” himself (Genesis 3:10). Job did not hide.

The way of the gospel. “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). The fear of people is what makes us hide, and “the fear of man lays a snare” (Proverbs 29:25). Job feared God, and so he did not need to hide from anyone.

The one who kept it perfectly. No one but Christ could swear this whole chapter without a flaw. He kept it perfectly, in our place, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). So the failures this chapter exposes in us are not the end: the way back is the confession Job did not hide from, and the mercy God has promised.

Uncertain wording. “As others do” (v. 33) translates a word that can mean “as man does” or “as Adam did”, and the ESV notes the second. Either reading fits: hiding sin is what people do, and it is what the first man did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job’s point is that he has nothing left to say: let God answer. He signs his defence like a statement in court and demands that his accuser write out the charge, which he would wear proudly as a crown, approaching God like a prince (vv. 35–37). Then he adds a last oath, about the land: if he gained his fields by fraud or killed their owners, let thorns and weeds grow instead of grain (vv. 38–40). “The words of Job are ended.” He will not speak again until God has spoken, and then he will say very little.
verseByVerse.theology: Job signs his defence and rests his case. The next voice he hears will be God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown; I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job signs his defence and demands the written charge, which he would wear as a crown, words that find their deepest meaning at the cross.

Here is my signature! Job ends his defence like a man in court signing his statement. In Hebrew it is “here is my mark”, using the name of the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script was written as a simple cross-mark. Now let God answer.

I would bind it on me as a crown. He asks for the charge sheet: let my accuser write out the case against me. He would wear the indictment proudly, because he knows it would prove nothing, and he would walk into God’s presence with his head up, “like a prince”. It is magnificent, and it is also the edge of presumption: God will not be summoned to answer Job’s record (40:2, 8).

He wore our indictment. Read those words beside the cross. Christ was crowned, with thorns, and “over his head they put the charge against him, which read, ‘This is Jesus, the King of the Jews’” (Matthew 27:37). He carried a written charge that was no crime, and he carried ours, which were real: the “record of debt that stood against us”, which God set aside, “nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). Job wanted to wear his indictment as a crown because he was innocent. Christ wore ours because we were not. And because he did, we can do what Job longed to do, and approach God with confidence (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together, if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last, let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s last oath is that he never gained his land by fraud, and then he falls silent.

If my land has cried out against me. If he had got his fields by fraud, eaten their yield without paying, and brought their owners to their death, the soil would cry out against him, as Abel’s blood cried from the ground (Genesis 4:10) and as the unpaid wages of the harvesters “are crying out against you” (James 5:4). If so, let the curse of Eden fall on his fields: “thorns and thistles” (Genesis 3:18), thorns instead of wheat and stinking weeds instead of barley.

The words of Job are ended. He has nothing more to say to the friends, and he has made his last appeal to God. The next time Job opens his mouth it will be to God, and it will be short: “Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth” (40:4). Between here and there, a young man will speak, and then the LORD himself.

31.theology: Job's oath describes righteousness from the heart outward: the eye, the servant made by the same God, the orphan and widow, the heart that does not trust in gold, the enemy not cursed, sin confessed and not hidden. Only Christ kept it all, and he wore the charge and the crown because we were guilty.
31.examples: Read slowly, this chapter is a searching examination of conscience: what we let our eyes rest on, how we treat those who work for us, whether our money has quietly become our trust, whether we hide our faults. No reader passes it as Job did, and the chapter itself points to the confession and mercy that meet us where we fail.

keyVerse.quote: Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!
keyVerse.note: This is the climax of Job’s whole defence: he signs his oath and calls on God to answer. It is the cry of a man sure of his integrity, and also the edge of presumption, for God will answer, but not on Job’s terms (38:1–3). At the cross Christ carried a written charge for us, so that we may come to God not on our record but on his.

31.reflection:
Job begins with “a covenant with my eyes” (v. 1). What would it look like for you to make that kind of decision beforehand, about screens, images or a second look? Why does it help to remember that God sees “all my steps” (v. 4) and that the Spirit gives strength (Galatians 5:16)?

“Did not he who made me in the womb make him?” (v. 15). How should the truth that God made every person shape the way you treat those who work for you, serve you or have less power than you?

Job swears he never trusted in gold, gloated over an enemy or hid his sins for fear of others (vv. 24–34). Which of these hidden sins most searches your own heart? What does Proverbs 28:13 promise to those who confess rather than conceal?

No one but Christ could swear this whole chapter without a flaw. How does it change the way you read a chapter like this to know that Christ kept it in your place and carried “the record of debt that stood against us” to the cross (Colossians 2:14)?

32.title: I Am Young in Years
32.text: <sup>1</sup>So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.<sup>2</sup>Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God.<sup>3</sup>He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong.<sup>4</sup>Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he.<sup>5</sup>And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.<sup>6</sup>And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you.<sup>7</sup>I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.'<sup>8</sup>But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand.<sup>9</sup>It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right.<sup>10</sup>Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'<sup>11</sup>"Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say.<sup>12</sup>I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words.<sup>13</sup>Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.'<sup>14</sup>He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.<sup>15</sup>"They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say.<sup>16</sup>And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more?<sup>17</sup>I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion.<sup>18</sup>For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me.<sup>19</sup>Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst.<sup>20</sup>I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.<sup>21</sup>I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person.<sup>22</sup>For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
32.overview:
Where we are. “The words of Job are ended” (31:40). The three friends have given up, and Job has signed his defence and called on God to answer. Instead of God, a voice we have not heard before speaks: Elihu, a young man who has been listening all along. His speeches run from chapter 32 to chapter 37, and this chapter is his introduction.

The message. Elihu is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and angry with the friends for condemning Job without being able to answer him. He insists that wisdom does not come with grey hair but from “the breath of the Almighty” (v. 8), and he promises to speak without partiality or flattery. The chapter teaches that true understanding is God’s gift, not the property of age or status, and it sets the reader listening for whether this new voice will finally speak rightly of God.

Why it was said. The debate has ended in deadlock. The friends’ theory, that suffering is always punishment, has failed to convict Job, yet Job’s defence has begun to put God in the wrong (see the introduction). Elihu sees both failures, and the book lets him speak before the LORD himself answers.

How the chapter makes its case. A short prose introduction tells us why the friends stopped, and four times says that Elihu “burned with anger”: at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for finding no answer (vv. 1–5). Elihu then explains why he, the youngest, dares to speak: understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from years (vv. 6–10). He has listened carefully, and none of the friends refuted Job, so he will not use their arguments (vv. 11–14). He is full of words, like new wineskins ready to burst, and he must speak (vv. 15–20), without partiality or flattery, as before his Maker (vv. 21–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need it exposes. Old men and young have now spoken, and none of them can give the last word on Job’s suffering. Only God can, and he will. In these last days God has spoken his last word “by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Elihu promises to show no partiality and to speak by the Spirit; even Jesus’ enemies had to admit of him, “you are not swayed by appearances” (Matthew 22:16), and on him the Spirit of wisdom rested without measure (Isaiah 11:2).

For us. Do not despise a word from God because the speaker is young, nor trust one because the speaker is old; test it by Scripture. When you speak into someone’s suffering, ask whether you are angry for God’s honour or full of your own words. And keep listening for the voice that has the last word: God’s, in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The point of these verses is that the debate has failed on both sides, and a new speaker is angry with both. The three friends stop answering, because Job is righteous in his own eyes (v. 1). Then Elihu, introduced with a full family line, burns with anger: at Job, because he justified himself rather than God (v. 2), and at the friends, because they condemned Job without finding an answer (v. 3). He had held back because they were older, but when he saw they had nothing left to say, his anger burned again (vv. 4–5). Four times in four verses the narrator speaks of his anger.
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator does not tell us whether Elihu is right. The end of the book gives a clue by its silence: God rebukes the friends, commends Job, and says nothing of Elihu.

verseByVerse.quote: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends give up because Job is righteous in his own eyes, their complaint and also a real warning.

Righteous in his own eyes. The debate is over, and the narrator tells us why, from the friends’ point of view: they could not move him. The reader knows that Job was righteous in God’s eyes too (1:8). But the phrase is a warning as well. There is a way of holding on to one’s innocence that begins to look like self-righteousness, and the next speaker will say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God. He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong. Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he. And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu is angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer: he is half right.

Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite. A new voice, and one the reader has not been told was there. Elihu is the only speaker in the book given a family line. Buz was the brother of Uz in the family of Abraham’s brother Nahor (Genesis 22:21), so Elihu’s clan and Job’s homeland carry the names of two brothers. His own name means “He is my God”.

He burned with anger. The narrator says it four times in four verses. He is angry at Job “because he justified himself rather than God”. That is a real charge, and it is not the friends’ charge. The friends said Job had sinned before his suffering; Elihu says Job is going wrong in how he speaks now, defending himself at God’s expense. God himself will put the same question to Job: “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (40:8).

Although they had declared Job to be in the wrong. The friends condemned Job and could not prove it. Elihu sees that too.

The anger that burns. At the end of the book the LORD will say to Eliphaz, “My anger burns against you and against your two friends” (42:7), the same expression. Elihu’s anger burns against Job and the friends. God’s burns against the friends alone. Elihu is half right.
verseByVerse.note: Elihu was from Buz, a name linked with Abraham’s family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–22 — I Am Young in Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that wisdom comes from God’s Spirit, not from age, so he, the youngest, must now speak. He was timid and waited, expecting days and years to teach wisdom (vv. 6–7), but understanding is the gift of “the breath of the Almighty”, and the old are not always wise (vv. 8–10). He listened carefully to the friends, and none of them refuted Job; they must not claim that only God can deal with him, and Elihu will not repeat their speeches (vv. 11–14). Now they are silent, and he is full of words, bursting like new wineskins (vv. 15–20). He will speak without partiality or flattery, as one answerable to his Maker (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right that wisdom is God's gift and not the property of the old. Whether he has it is what the next five chapters will show.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you. I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.' But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand. It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right. Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from age.

I was timid and afraid. He has kept quiet out of respect, expecting the old men to show their wisdom. They did not.

The breath of the Almighty. It is this that makes a man understand: not grey hair but God’s Spirit, the breath God breathed into man at the beginning (Genesis 2:7). Job had quoted the friends’ proverb, “Wisdom is with the aged” (12:12), and answered it: “With God are wisdom and might” (12:13). Elihu agrees.

A true word for the church. Paul told a young pastor, “Let no one despise you for your youth” (1 Timothy 4:12), and said that he spoke of God’s things in words “not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:13). Age deserves respect. It does not guarantee wisdom, and youth does not rule it out. But Elihu’s claim cuts both ways: if wisdom comes from God, the young man’s words must be tested like anyone else’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say. I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words. Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.' He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu has seen that the friends lost the argument, and he promises a fresh answer.

While you searched out what to say. The friends’ favourite verb once more (5:27; 8:8). They searched and searched for what to say, and none of them actually answered Job. Elihu noticed what they never admitted: they lost the argument.

Beware lest you say. Do not retreat into saying, “only God can deal with him.” Elihu promises a fresh approach: he will not recycle their arguments. How far he keeps that promise is the question of the next chapters. At times he says new and true things. At times he sounds exactly like them.

Uncertain wording. Verse 13 is compressed. The ESV takes “God may vanquish him, not a man” as the friends’ excuse: only God can refute him. It may instead be Elihu’s own warning that God, not man, will defeat Job’s arguments. Either way, Elihu refuses to hide behind their failure.

verseByVerse.quote: "They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say. And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more? I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion. For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu is bursting to speak, whether by the pressure of God’s Spirit or of his own words.

Like new wineskins ready to burst. He is bursting to speak, like new wine fermenting in a sealed wineskin. Jesus used the picture: “new wine is put into fresh wineskins” (Matthew 9:17). A prophet described the same compulsion: “there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).

Where Christians differ. Some hear in this preface God’s spokesman, pressed by his Spirit and preparing for the voice from the whirlwind. Others hear another mistaken friend in love with his own words: seventeen verses about how much he has to say before he says any of it. Both readings have something in the text to stand on, and the end of the book gives the clue: the LORD rebukes the three friends and commends Job, and says nothing about Elihu at all (42:7–9).

This commentary’s view. Elihu speaks partly truly and partly not, and the book gives no verdict on him (see the introduction). He rightly says that God can use suffering to teach and that God cannot be unjust, and his speech of the storm prepares for God’s answer out of the whirlwind. But he still assumes that Job’s suffering must have a cause in Job. God passes over him because God himself now speaks; Elihu’s words are neither a rival to his nor the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person. For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu promises to speak without partiality or flattery, the right spirit for anyone who speaks for God.

I will not show partiality to any man. He will not take sides for anyone’s sake, and he will not flatter, for his Maker would soon take him away. “God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34), and his servants should not either. Job had accused the friends of showing partiality to God, lying in his defence (13:8). Elihu promises to tell the truth to Job and friends alike. The best test of it will be whether he can tell the difference between Job’s words, which were sometimes wrong, and Job’s life, which was not.

32.theology: Elihu is right that understanding is the Spirit's gift and not the property of the old (vv. 8-9; 1 Cor 2:12-13), and right that Job has begun to justify himself at God's expense (v. 2). But his anger burns against Job and the friends, while God's burns against the friends alone: he says true things and is not the last word.
32.examples: Elihu is an encouragement to the young believer who hesitates to speak among older Christians: wisdom is God's gift, not the reward of grey hair. He is also a caution, since he burns with anger four times in four verses, and zeal that is half right can still wound. It is wise to listen as long as he did before speaking, and then to speak with less heat.

keyVerse.quote: But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand.
keyVerse.note: This is Elihu’s reason for speaking, and it is true: understanding is God’s gift, not the prize of age. It also sets the test for Elihu himself, whose words must be weighed like anyone’s. And it points to Christ, on whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding rests in full (Isaiah 11:2).

32.reflection:
Elihu says, “It is not the old who are wise” (v. 9), but “the breath of the Almighty” that gives understanding (v. 8). How should a church honour the wisdom of older believers while still listening to the young? How do we test any speaker’s words, whatever their age?

Elihu is angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer (vv. 2–3). When is anger on God’s behalf right, and when does it become something else?

Elihu says he is “full of words” and must speak (vv. 18–20). When you sit with someone who is suffering, how can you tell whether you need to speak or to keep listening?

None of the human speakers in Job can give the last word; only God can. How does it help you to know that God has spoken his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2)?

33.title: I Have Found a Ransom
33.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words.<sup>2</sup>Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks.<sup>3</sup>My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely.<sup>4</sup>The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.<sup>5</sup>Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay.<sup>7</sup>Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.<sup>8</sup>"Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words.<sup>9</sup>You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me.<sup>10</sup>Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy,<sup>11</sup>he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'<sup>12</sup>"Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man.<sup>13</sup>Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?<sup>14</sup>For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it.<sup>15</sup>In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds,<sup>16</sup>then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings,<sup>17</sup>that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man;<sup>18</sup>he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.<sup>19</sup>"Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones,<sup>20</sup>so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food.<sup>21</sup>His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out.<sup>22</sup>His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.<sup>23</sup>If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him,<sup>24</sup>and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;<sup>25</sup>let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor';<sup>26</sup>then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.<sup>27</sup>He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me.<sup>28</sup>He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'<sup>29</sup>"Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man,<sup>30</sup>to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life.<sup>31</sup>Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak.<sup>32</sup>If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you.<sup>33</sup>If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
33.overview:
Where we are. Job and his friends have fallen silent, and a younger man, Elihu, has explained why he must speak (chapter 32). Now he turns to Job himself. This is the first of four speeches that run to the end of chapter 37.

The message. Job has said God will not answer him. Elihu says God has been speaking all along: in warnings in the night and in pain that brings a man to the edge of the grave, not to destroy but to rescue. And Elihu glimpses how the rescue happens: a mediator speaks for the dying man and says, “I have found a ransom”, and the man is brought back into the light, confessing that he sinned and was not repaid as he deserved.

Why it was said. Job had cried, “I cry to you for help and you do not answer me” (30:20), and ended his defence by demanding that the Almighty answer him (31:35). Elihu, angry with both sides (32:2–3), offers a different account of suffering, one the book neither simply endorses nor rejects (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Elihu begins gently, as one creature of clay to another (vv. 1–7). He quotes Job’s complaint and says Job is wrong to claim that God does not answer, for God is greater than man (vv. 8–13). God speaks in more than one way: in dreams that turn a man from his pride (vv. 14–18), and in sickness that wastes him almost to death (vv. 19–22). Then the turning point: a mediator, a ransom, and a restored man who prays, sees God’s face and sings of grace (vv. 23–28). God does this again and again (vv. 29–30), and Elihu ends by saying he wants Job justified (vv. 31–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the pattern it sketches. Elihu does not say who the mediator is or what the ransom is; the psalmist knew that “no man can ransom another” (Psalm 49:7). The New Testament puts Elihu’s two great words into one sentence: “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6). Elihu’s messenger finds a ransom; Christ is the ransom. And the “light of life” Elihu promises (v. 30) is the light Jesus gives (John 8:12).

For us. When God seems silent, he may be speaking in ways we have not yet learned to hear, and pain can be his call to turn back to him, though not every pain is a rebuke. Whatever we have done, the song of the ransomed is open to us: “I sinned… and it was not repaid to me” (v. 27), because Christ paid what we owed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Too Was Pinched Off from Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that he comes to Job not as a judge but as a fellow creature. He addresses Job by name, which the friends never did, and promises to speak sincerely what he knows (vv. 1–3). He grounds his right to speak in the Spirit of God who made him and the breath of the Almighty who keeps him alive (v. 4). Then he invites Job to answer him and take his stand, for he is clay like Job, pinched from the same lump, and Job need not fear that his hand will be heavy (vv. 5–7). It is the kindest opening any of Job’s counsellors has made, and a faint picture of the go-between Job longed for (9:33).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu offers to meet Job as an equal. It is a kinder start than the friends', and a faint picture of the Mediator Job wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words. Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks. My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely. The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu speaks to Job personally and sincerely, as one whose life comes from God’s Spirit.

Hear my speech, O Job. Elihu addresses Job by name, which the three friends never once did. His opening is roundabout, but he promises to say what he truly believes, and grounds that promise where he grounded his right to speak: the Spirit of God made him, and the breath of the Almighty keeps him alive (32:8; Genesis 2:7). Whatever else is true of Elihu, he knows where his life comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand. Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu invites Job to answer him as an equal, a fellow creature of clay.

I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Job had asked God, “let not dread of you terrify me” (13:21), and complained that God “is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him” (9:32). Elihu steps forward almost as if to meet that wish: I am clay too, pinched off the same lump as you (compare 10:9), so you need not be afraid of me. It is gracious, and a kinder beginning than the friends made.

Only clay. But Elihu cannot be what Job needs, because he is only clay. The arbiter Job longed for had to be able to lay his hand on God as well as on man (9:33). Only one person has ever been both God and man. Elihu’s gentleness is a faint outline; Christ is the portrait.

Uncertain wording. “I am toward God as you are” (v. 6) is literally “like your mouth toward God”: most take it as the ESV does; some read it as I am the spokesman you asked for. “My pressure” (v. 7) translates a word found only here, probably a heavy hand (compare 13:21). Either way, Elihu will not overwhelm him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — In This You Are Not Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that Job is wrong to say God will not answer him. He shows he has listened: he quotes Job’s claim to be clean and his complaint that God treats him as an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks and watches all his paths (vv. 8–11). Most of it is Job’s own words, though Elihu sharpens Job’s claim of innocence into a claim of sinlessness. Then comes the charge: in this Job is not right, for God is greater than man (v. 12). A God so great is not obliged to answer on our terms, and Job’s complaint that he answers nothing (v. 13) is mistaken, as the next verses will show: God has been speaking.
verseByVerse.theology: God has not been silent, Elihu says; Job has not been hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words. You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me. Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy, he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu quotes Job’s complaint fairly, except that he makes Job claim to be sinless.

I am pure, without transgression. Most of this is Job’s own words: God counts him as his enemy (13:24) and “you put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths” (13:27). Job had said, “I am blameless” (9:21), but he never claimed to be sinless; he asked God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and spoke of “the iniquities of my youth” (13:26). What he denied was sin that could explain this suffering. Elihu, like the friends, blurs that distinction a little; but he has heard far more than they did.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu’s charge is that Job is wrong to say God has refused to answer him.

In this you are not right. Job had said, “I cry to you for help and you do not answer me” (30:20), as if God owed him an answer and had withheld it. Elihu replies that God is greater than man and is not bound to answer on our terms; the LORD himself will soon make the same point far more overwhelmingly (38:2–4). And God has not been silent. Job has not been hearing him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — God Speaks in One Way, and in Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God speaks to people in more than one way, and always to rescue them. The first way is in the night: dreams and visions that alarm a man, turn him from what he planned, cut short his pride and keep his soul from the pit (vv. 14–18). The second way is pain: sickness on his bed, aching bones, appetite gone, flesh wasting until the bones show, and death drawing near (vv. 19–22). Elihu is plainly describing Job. Here he moves beyond the friends, who saw only punishment, to see suffering as God’s warning and discipline. It is a true word, but it is not the reason for Job’s suffering (2:3).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Elihu's real contribution, true in itself though it does not explain Job's case.

verseByVerse.quote: For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds, then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks in more than one way, first in night warnings that turn a man from pride before it destroys him.

God speaks in one way, and in two. That is, in more than one way (compare 40:5). This is the heart of what Elihu adds. First, dreams that frighten a man away from what he was about to do, cut his pride short before it ruins him and keep him from the grave. Eliphaz’s night vision gave him a doctrine to use against Job (4:12–17); Elihu’s night warnings are rescues.

Spoken by his Son. Hebrews opens with the same thought and brings it to its end: “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). Everything God has to say to us is finally in him.

Does God still speak in dreams? In Elihu’s day, before the Scriptures were complete, God did. Now that he has spoken finally in his Son, a dream may stir the conscience or prompt prayer, but no believer should treat one as a message from God. Faithful Christians differ on whether God still gives such dreams, and many who think he may agree that any dream must be tested by Scripture; this commentary holds, with the historic Reformed churches, that Scripture is now sufficient for all we need to know and do (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Uncertain wording. “Conceal pride” (v. 17) probably means put pride away, cut it off. The word for “sword” (v. 18; also 36:12) may instead mean a channel, so some translate crossing the river of death. Either way the point is rescue from death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones, so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food. His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out. His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second way God speaks is pain, which can be his discipline, meant to rescue rather than repay.

Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed. Illness, aching bones, no appetite, flesh wasting until the bones stick out, death coming near: Elihu is describing Job (compare 19:20; 30:30), and he says that this too can be God speaking.

Beyond the friends. The friends asked what Job had done to deserve it; Elihu asks what God might be saying through it. Scripture agrees: “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word”; “It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes” (Psalm 119:67, 71). God “disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). A believer in pain may, and should, ask what God is teaching, but need not find the answer to be faithful: Job never learned the reason for his trial, and was God’s servant all through it.

The limit of this truth. It is not why Job suffered; God himself said it was “without reason” (2:3). Elihu has found a true word about suffering, but he is applying it to a man whose case it does not fit. Pain can be discipline. Not all pain is.

What it does not mean. Not that sickness calls only for soul-searching. Seeing a doctor and taking medicine are no failure of faith; prayer and treatment belong together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — I Have Found a Ransom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God’s purpose in warning and pain is to bring a man back from the pit into the light of life. A mediator, one of the thousand, takes the dying man’s part and declares, “I have found a ransom” (vv. 23–24). The man is restored to the vigour of his youth; he prays, God accepts him, he sees God’s face with joy and is given back his righteousness (vv. 25–26). His song confesses that he sinned and was not repaid as he deserved (vv. 27–28). God does all this again and again (vv. 29–30). Elihu ends by inviting Job to speak, because he wants to justify him; if not, Job should listen and learn wisdom (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the clearest picture in the book of a mediator who pays a ransom. The New Testament names him: one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

verseByVerse.quote: If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him, and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A heavenly messenger pleads for the dying man and declares that a ransom has been found.

An angel, a mediator, one of the thousand. A man lies near the pit; a messenger takes his part, shows him the way back to God (“what is right for him”) and pleads for his life. This is the high point of Elihu’s speeches, and one of the brightest glimpses of the gospel in the book.

Two words. A mediator (Hebrew melits, the word for the interpreter between Joseph and his brothers, Genesis 42:23) stands between and speaks for another, what Job’s friends should have been and were not (16:20). A ransom is the price paid to set a condemned life free. Elihu does not say what the ransom is, and the psalmist knew that no human being can pay it: “Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly” (Psalm 49:7–8).

The price no man could pay. Elihu’s messenger finds a ransom; the New Testament’s Mediator is the ransom. “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6): both of Elihu’s words in one sentence. “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The price no man could pay, God paid.

Where Christians differ: who is this mediator? Many older interpreters read him as the Son of God himself, as the angel of the LORD; others, a created angel; some, a human messenger, perhaps Elihu himself. This commentary’s view: Elihu speaks of a heavenly messenger and says no more, so the passage is not a direct prediction of Christ. But it describes a need only Christ meets: no angel can pay a ransom for a man, and the one mediator between God and men is a man who is also God (1 Timothy 2:5).

Uncertain wording. “One of the thousand” may mean one among God’s countless angels (Daniel 7:10), or a rare one in a thousand (compare 9:3).
verseByVerse.note: Elihu imagines a mediator who finds “a ransom”, a hope fulfilled in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor'; then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ransomed man is restored in body and accepted by God, who gives him back his righteousness.

Let his flesh become fresh with youth. His skin becomes fresh as a child’s, as Naaman’s did when he was cleansed in the Jordan: “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2 Kings 5:14).

He sees his face with a shout of joy. All this will happen to Job: the LORD will accept his prayer (42:9), Job will see God (42:5), and he will be restored. And it happens to every believer in Christ, whose ransom has been paid: accepted, given a righteousness not his own, and one day raised with a body that will never wear out.

verseByVerse.quote: He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescued man’s song confesses that he sinned and was not treated as he deserved.

I sinned and perverted what was right. I sinned; I twisted what was right; and I did not get what I deserved. “I acknowledged my sin to you… and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). It is the prodigal’s “Father, I have sinned” (Luke 15:21), met by a father running down the road. And God “redeems your life from the pit” (Psalm 103:4).

Not innocent, but ransomed. Elihu’s gospel is not “you were innocent all along” but “you were not, and you were ransomed.” That is closer to the truth about every human being than anything the friends said, and it is the truth Job will come to when he sees God (42:6).

Uncertain wording. “It was not repaid to me” is literally “it was not equal to me”: probably I was not punished as I deserved, though older versions read “it profited me not”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life. Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak. If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you. If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God works again and again to bring a man back into the light, and Elihu wants Job shown in the right.

Twice, three times. God does not give up after one warning. Again and again he works to bring a man back from the edge, and the goal is “the light of life”, the very phrase Jesus used of himself: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

I desire to justify you. Unlike the friends, Elihu wants Job vindicated. His manner is lecturing, and he will go on for four more chapters; but his heart, at least here, is for Job.

33.theology: Suffering can be God's speech, a warning and discipline meant to rescue (vv. 14-22; Heb 12:10-11). That is Elihu's real advance on the friends, though it is not the reason for Job's suffering (2:3). And the mediator who finds a ransom (vv. 23-24) is fulfilled in Christ: no man can ransom another, and God did.
33.examples: Elihu models some good habits for anyone who comes alongside a sufferer: he uses Job's name, meets him as one creature of clay to another, and quotes him fairly. His best word is that pain may be God speaking to rescue us, and his ransom points to the one Mediator who gave himself (1 Timothy 2:5-6). Held with its limit, that can help a sufferer ask what God is teaching without concluding that the pain is a punishment.

keyVerse.quote: and he is merciful to him, and says, ‘Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom
keyVerse.note: This is the high point of Elihu’s speeches and one of the brightest glimpses of the gospel in Job. Elihu sees that a dying sinner needs someone to plead for him and a price to set him free, though he cannot say who or what. The New Testament answers both at once: Christ is the one Mediator, who “gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6).

33.reflection:
Elihu addresses Job by name and meets him as one “pinched off from a piece of clay” like himself (vv. 1–7). What can we learn from him about speaking to someone who is suffering, and about avoiding the friends’ mistakes?

Elihu says God speaks “in one way, and in two” (v. 14), including through pain (vv. 19–22). Has God ever used a hard time to turn you back to him? Why does it matter to add that not every suffering is a rebuke?

Psalm 49:7 says “no man can ransom another”. How does 1 Timothy 2:5–6 answer Elihu’s picture of a mediator who finds a ransom (vv. 23–24)? What does it mean for you that Christ is himself the ransom?

The restored man sings, “I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me” (v. 27). Why is confession part of the song of joy rather than its opposite? How might your own praise sound more like this?

34.title: Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know;<sup>3</sup>for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.<sup>4</sup>Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good.<sup>5</sup>For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right;<sup>6</sup>in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'<sup>7</sup>What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water,<sup>8</sup>who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men?<sup>9</sup>For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'<sup>10</sup>"Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong.<sup>11</sup>For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him.<sup>12</sup>Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.<sup>13</sup>Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world?<sup>14</sup>If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath,<sup>15</sup>all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.<sup>16</sup>"If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say.<sup>17</sup>Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty,<sup>18</sup>who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,'<sup>19</sup>who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands?<sup>20</sup>In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.<sup>21</sup>"For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps.<sup>22</sup>There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves.<sup>23</sup>For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.<sup>24</sup>He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place.<sup>25</sup>Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed.<sup>26</sup>He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see,<sup>27</sup>because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways,<sup>28</sup>so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted—<sup>29</sup>When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?—<sup>30</sup>that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.<sup>31</sup>"For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more;<sup>32</sup>teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'?<sup>33</sup>Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know.<sup>34</sup>Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say:<sup>35</sup>'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.'<sup>36</sup>Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men.<sup>37</sup>For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
34.overview:
Where we are. This is Elihu’s second speech. He has spoken to Job directly (chapter 33); now he turns to the wise men listening and, in effect, puts Job on trial before them.

The message. God cannot do wrong. He holds his authority from no one, every creature’s breath is his to give or take back, he treats king and pauper alike, he sees every step in the dark, and he hears the cry of the poor. So when he is silent, no one can condemn him. That is true, and Job needed to hear it. But Elihu wraps it in a harsh verdict on Job that God himself will not share.

Why it was said. Job had said that God had taken away his right (27:2) and put him in the wrong (19:6). Elihu hears this as an attack on God’s justice and rises to defend it. In doing so he slides back into the friends’ argument, which he had promised not to repeat (32:14; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Elihu calls the wise to test Job’s words as the palate tests food (vv. 1–4). He quotes Job fairly, then accuses him of keeping company with the wicked (vv. 5–9). He insists that God does no wickedness: he repays everyone, answers to no one and sustains every breath (vv. 10–15); he rebukes kings and shows no favour to the rich (vv. 16–20). God sees everything, needs no court hearing, overthrows oppressors in public and hears the cry of the poor, and his silence is no injustice (vv. 21–30). Finally Elihu presses Job to submit, and declares that Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin (vv. 31–37).

Where it leads. To Christ, through the character of God that the chapter defends and the question it leaves open. If God never perverts justice and repays everyone according to his work (vv. 11–12), how can any sinner stand? The cross answers: there God showed his righteousness, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And there is a pattern too. Elihu counts innocent Job among “wicked men” (v. 8); Jesus, who had no sin at all, “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), so that the guilty might be counted righteous.

For us. Hold fast to God’s justice when life looks unjust: his silence is not his absence, and the full reckoning belongs to the last day, not to this week’s fortunes. And learn from Elihu’s slide. Answer what a sufferer actually said, and do not let sound doctrine about God become a harsh verdict on the person in front of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — What Man Is Like Job?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that Job’s words must be tested, and he believes they fail the test. He appeals to the wise who are listening: the ear tests words as the palate tastes food, so let them choose together what is right (vv. 1–4). He quotes Job’s claim that he is in the right and God has taken away his right, which is fair (vv. 5–6). Then he turns harsh: Job drinks up scoffing like water, keeps company with evildoers, and says it does a man no good to delight in God (vv. 7–9). That last saying was never Job’s, and here the young man who promised something new begins to sound like the friends.
verseByVerse.theology: Here Elihu starts to sound like the friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu answered and said: "Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know; for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good. For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right; in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.' What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu calls the wise to test Job’s words, then slides into the friends’ harsh voice.

The ear tests words as the palate tastes food. That is Job’s own line, almost word for word (12:11). “Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good” is a sound instinct: test the arguments and keep what is true, as Paul says, “test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). And “Job has said, ‘I am in the right, and God has taken away my right’” is fair: Job said it (27:2). The trouble is what Elihu does next.

Where Elihu goes wrong. Job, he says, “drinks up scoffing like water”, which is Eliphaz’s picture of a man “who drinks injustice like water” (15:16). He “travels in company with evildoers”, which is the friends’ old charge. And the last sentence, “It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God”, is not Job’s at all. Job described the wicked saying, “What profit do we get if we pray to him?” (21:15), and said their counsel was far from him. Elihu has put the wicked’s words into Job’s mouth, exactly as Eliphaz did (22:13, 17). The young man who promised not to answer Job “with your speeches” (32:14) is doing just that.

Counted with the wicked. Blameless Job is placed among evildoers. Jesus, wholly sinless, was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19) and at the last “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). He bore the false charge so that we, who deserve the true one, might go free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God cannot do wrong, and he gives reasons. God repays everyone according to his work and never perverts justice (vv. 10–12). He holds his authority from no one, and every breath in every creature is his to withdraw (vv. 13–15). A God who hated justice could not rule the world, yet he tells kings to their face that they are worthless, shows no favour to princes over the poor, and brings down the mighty in a moment (vv. 16–20). All of this is true, and Job, who had said God wronged him, needed to hear it. The God who gives every breath is just, and owes no one an explanation.
verseByVerse.theology: This is true, and Job needed it: the God who gives every breath is just and owes no one an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong. For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him. Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice. Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world? If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God cannot do wrong: he repays justly, answers to no one, and holds every breath in his hand.

Far be it from God that he should do wickedness. Bildad said the same (8:3), and it is true: “Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!” (Romans 9:14). Job needed to hear it, because he had said that God “has put me in the wrong” (19:6) and “You have turned cruel to me” (30:21). God is not unjust, however things look from the ash heap.

Who gave him charge over the earth? No one handed God the world to run, so he answers to no one. Every breath in every creature is his, lent moment by moment: “when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created” (Psalm 104:29–30). A God like that is no one’s debtor.

He will repay him. “According to the work of a man he will repay him” (v. 11) is true, and the New Testament says it as plainly: “He will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6); “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). The question has never been whether God repays, but when. The friends, and Elihu here, expected the repayment to be visible now, in each man’s health and wealth. Scripture places the full reckoning at the last day. Say that God always repays in this life, and a true doctrine becomes a lie about the sufferer in front of you.

Proved at the cross. How can a just God let the guilty go? Paul answers that God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath, to show his righteousness, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Sin was not overlooked; it was punished, in the Son. Far be it from God to do wickedness: at Calvary he forgave without doing any.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say. Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty, who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,' who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands? In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A God who rebukes kings and treats rich and poor alike cannot be unjust to Job.

Shall one who hates justice govern? Could a God who hated justice rule the world? He tells kings to their face what they are, and treats rich and poor alike, “for they are all the work of his hands”. That was Job’s own argument about his servants: “Did not he who made me in the womb make him?” (31:15). Elihu turns it on Job: if God is impartial with kings, will he be unjust to you?

In a moment they die. The great fall overnight at his word, “taken away by no human hand”, as Egypt learned at another midnight (Exodus 12:29).

Uncertain wording. Older versions read v. 18 as a question: is it fitting to say to a king, “Worthless one”? Either way, God judges those no human dares to judge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God knows all, judges rightly in his own time, and that Job has spoken wrongly. God sees every step, and no darkness hides the wicked, so he needs no court hearing (vv. 21–23). He shatters the mighty suddenly because he already knows their works (vv. 24–25). He strikes oppressors in public, for they turned from him and made the poor cry out, and he heard them; his silence for a time is no injustice (vv. 26–30). Then Elihu turns on Job: God will not repay to suit him (vv. 31–33), Job speaks without knowledge, and he adds rebellion to his sin (vv. 34–37). Elihu is right about Job’s words and wrong about Job’s heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right about Job's words and wrong about Job's heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps. There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves. For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees everything, so he needs no court hearing; that he gives Job one anyway is grace.

God has no need to consider a man further. He sees every step, and no “deep darkness” hides anyone (v. 22). This answers Job’s great demand for a day in court (13:18; 23:4; 31:35): God needs no inquiry, for he knows everything already. And yet in a few chapters God will grant Job the audience he asked for (38:1). He did not owe it. He gave it. That is grace.

There is no gloom or deep darkness. Evildoers count on the dark, and for God it does not exist. David found that truth first frightening and then a comfort: “even the darkness is not dark to you” (Psalm 139:12). It warns the man who sins where no one sees, and comforts the one whose wrongs no one else has noticed: God has seen them (Hebrews 4:13).

Uncertain wording. Verse 23 is compressed in Hebrew; with a small change to one word, some translate God does not appoint a time for a man to come before him in judgment. Either way, God is not summoned to court on our schedule.

verseByVerse.quote: He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place. Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God overthrows the mighty suddenly but never carelessly, because he already knows their works.

Without investigation. Not that God judges carelessly, but that he needs no inquiry, because he is already “knowing their works” (v. 25). Human courts must gather evidence; God has it all. What looks to onlookers like a sudden, unexplained fall is a verdict already fully weighed.

He sets others in their place. The mighty whom God shatters, he replaces. Daniel praised the same God: “he removes kings and sets up kings” (Daniel 2:21). History is not a machine running on its own. Every throne is held at his pleasure, and he takes it back when he chooses, often suddenly, “in the night” (v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see, because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways, so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted— When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?— that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God publicly judges oppressors who turned from him and crushed the poor, and his silence for a time is no injustice.

In a place for all to see. God’s judgments on oppressors are often public, so that others may learn. Elihu names the cause: they “turned aside from following him”, and it showed in how they treated the weak, until “the cry of the poor” came up to God. Turning from God and crushing the poor go together, as the prophets would say again and again (Isaiah 3:14–15; Amos 2:6–7).

He heard the cry of the afflicted. God hears the poor; that answers Job’s complaint that the dying groan and God does nothing (24:12). “When he is quiet, who can condemn?” Job took God’s silence as proof that God was against him (30:20). Elihu is right that silence proves nothing of the kind.
