That a godless man should not reign. God may be quiet for a time, yet he removes the godless ruler so that he will not “ensnare the people”. His overthrow of tyrants is mercy to the people they would trap, and those who suffer under cruel rulers may pray in that hope.

Uncertain wording. Verses 29–30 are among the hardest Hebrew in the book, and translations differ over how the lines connect. The ESV’s sense is clear enough, and most versions agree on its two points: God’s silence is beyond our condemning, and he acts so that the godless will not rule over his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more; teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'? Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know. Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say: 'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.' Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men. For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu is right that Job spoke without knowledge, and wrong to accuse him of rebellion.

Teach me what I do not see. Elihu wants Job to say this. Job had said something very like it long before: “Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray” (6:24).

Will he then make repayment to suit you? God does not adjust his justice to our preferences. That is a fair word to Job, and to the friends, who each wanted God’s ways to fit their expectations.

Job speaks without knowledge. Here Elihu is right, and God will say the same in almost the same words: “Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2). Job had spoken about things he did not understand.

He adds rebellion to his sin. And here Elihu is wrong. He wishes Job more suffering, calls his answers those of the wicked, and assumes a sin to which Job has added rebellion. That is the friends’ verdict, and God will overturn it: “you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (42:7). In two verses Elihu is right about Job’s words and wrong about Job’s heart. It is a warning to every critic, however sound his doctrine: it is possible to be right about what a sufferer said and wrong about who he is.

Tried to the end. Elihu wished Job “tried to the end” (v. 36). Jesus was: condemned as a blasphemer though “there was no deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9), he bore the full trial in our place.

Uncertain wording. Verses 31–33 are very obscure in Hebrew, and translations vary widely. The general sense: God will not change his justice to suit Job, and Job, not Elihu, must decide how to respond.

34.theology: God cannot do wrong, every breath is his, and his silence is not injustice (v. 29). He owes no one a hearing (v. 23), and grants Job one as grace. Elihu, sliding into the friends' voice, is half right: Job spoke without knowledge, but he did not add rebellion to sin.
34.examples: Elihu's slide is easy to recognise in ourselves. He begins by fairly quoting Job, then puts words in his mouth that Job never said. Anyone arguing with a hurting person needs the discipline to answer what was actually said, and to remember that sound doctrine about God does not license a harsh verdict on the person in front of us.

keyVerse.quote: Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.
keyVerse.note: This is the conviction at the centre of Elihu’s second speech, and it is true even where he applies it wrongly to Job. God’s justice is not in doubt, however things look from the ash heap. The cross shows how far God’s justice goes: he did not pervert it to save sinners, but satisfied it in his Son (Romans 3:26).

34.reflection:
Elihu calls the listeners to test words “as the palate tastes food” (v. 3), yet he then puts words in Job’s mouth that Job never said (v. 9). Why is it so easy to misquote someone we disagree with, especially someone who is suffering? How can we guard against it?

“Far be it from God that he should do wickedness” (v. 10). When have you been tempted to doubt God’s justice? How does the cross, where God is “just and the justifier” (Romans 3:26), help you hold on to it?

Elihu says God sees every step and that no darkness hides the wicked (vv. 21–22). How is that truth both a warning and a comfort? To whom would you want to say it this week?

Elihu is right that Job spoke “without knowledge” (v. 35), but wrong about Job’s heart (v. 37). What does that teach us about correcting a fellow believer? How did Jesus, “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), bear the false verdict for us?

35.title: Songs in the Night
35.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,'<sup>3</sup>that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?'<sup>4</sup>I will answer you and your friends with you.<sup>5</sup>Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you.<sup>6</sup>If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him?<sup>7</sup>If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.<sup>9</sup>"Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty.<sup>10</sup>But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,<sup>11</sup>who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'<sup>12</sup>There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men.<sup>13</sup>Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it.<sup>14</sup>How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!<sup>15</sup>And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression,<sup>16</sup>Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
35.overview:
Where we are. This is Elihu’s third and shortest speech. He has defended God’s justice before the listening wise men (chapter 34); now he takes up two more things he has heard in Job’s words: that righteousness has brought Job no advantage, and that God does not answer.

The message. God is far above us: our sin cannot damage him and our goodness cannot make him richer, so no one can strike a bargain with him. And when people cry out in suffering and hear nothing, it is often because they want relief rather than God; the God worth seeking is the Maker “who gives songs in the night”. Elihu’s questions are searching, though he aims them unfairly at Job.

Why it was said. Job had said that God “destroys both the blameless and the wicked” (9:22), and that he could not find God anywhere (23:3, 8–9). Elihu hears in this the voice of a man who served God for what he could get, the very charge Satan made in the heavenly court (1:9; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Elihu accuses Job of claiming to be in the right before God while asking what his righteousness has gained him (vv. 1–4). Look at the sky: God is higher than the clouds, untouched by our sin or our goodness, which affect only other people (vv. 5–8). The oppressed cry out, but do not seek their Maker, who gives songs in the night and makes us wiser than the beasts (vv. 9–11); God does not hear an empty, proud cry, much less, Elihu says, a complaint like Job’s (vv. 12–14). Because God has not punished him, Job multiplies words without knowledge (vv. 15–16).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God that the chapter half sees. Elihu is right that our goodness cannot pay God: “who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35). He is right that our sin cannot damage God’s being. But the God who could not be harmed chose to be wounded: in Christ “he was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). And on the darkest night of all, before he went out to be betrayed, Jesus sang a hymn with his disciples (Matthew 26:30), so that his people are never left without a song in theirs.

For us. Ask yourself Elihu’s question honestly: in trouble, do I want relief, or do I want God? Do not try to bargain with him, as if your goodness put him in your debt. And if you are still waiting for him to answer, take heart: waiting for the LORD is not sin but faith (Psalm 27:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that Job cannot bargain with God, for God is too high to be harmed or helped by us. He challenges Job’s claim to be in the right before God, when in the same breath Job seems to ask what advantage his righteousness has brought him (vv. 1–3), and he promises an answer for Job and his friends together (v. 4). Let Job look up at the heavens and the clouds far above him (v. 5). If Job sins, God is not damaged; if Job is righteous, God receives nothing he lacked (vv. 6–7). Wickedness and righteousness touch other people, men like Job himself (v. 8). Half of this is true: God needs nothing. But he is not indifferent to what his people do.
verseByVerse.theology: God is not harmed by us and needs nothing from us, but that does not mean he does not care.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu answered and said: "Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,' that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?' I will answer you and your friends with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu hears Job asking what his righteousness has gained him, as if faith were a bargain.

What advantage have I? Elihu puts this question in Job’s mouth, but Job never said it in those words. He said God “destroys both the blameless and the wicked” (9:22), and he quoted the wicked asking, “What profit do we get if we pray to him?” (21:15). Satan said Job served God for profit (1:9). If Job now asked what profit his goodness had brought him, Satan would have won. The whole point of Job’s faith is that it is not a bargain.

I will answer you and your friends with you. Elihu will correct all four of them.

Uncertain wording. “It is my right before God” (v. 2) may also be read, as in older versions, my righteousness is more than God’s (compare 32:2). Verse 3 is also compressed, but the sense is clear: what good has my innocence done me?

verseByVerse.quote: Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you. If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him? If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand? Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is far above us: our sin cannot harm him, our goodness cannot enrich him, and what we do touches other people.

Look at the heavens, and see. God is higher than the clouds, and your sin cannot damage him nor your goodness add to him. Eliphaz said the same (22:2–3), and half of it is true: God needs nothing and cannot be harmed. But he is not indifferent. He can be grieved by his people’s sin, “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30), and he delights in his servants: “Have you considered my servant Job?” (1:8). A God who could not be harmed and did not care would not be the God of this book. And it is true that our sin and goodness land on our neighbours: “your wickedness concerns a man like yourself”.

The God who chose to be wounded. The God who could not be harmed took flesh and let our sin wound him, “pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). He needed nothing from us, and gave everything for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God. Under oppression people cry for help, but none asks for God his Maker, who gives songs in the night and has made human beings wiser than the beasts and birds (vv. 9–11). So they cry and are not answered, because of their pride: God does not listen to an empty cry (vv. 12–13). How much less, Elihu says, will he listen to Job, who complains that he cannot see God and is waiting for his case to be heard (v. 14). Because God has not punished him, Job multiplies empty words (vv. 15–16). Elihu is right about the proud, but wrong about Job, who has been seeking God himself.
verseByVerse.theology: Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God himself, and Job, for all his faults, has been seeking God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty. But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many cry out for relief without seeking God himself, who gives songs in the dark.

Where is God my Maker? This is the one new thing in the chapter. People who are crushed cry out, of course. But crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God. Many want the pain gone, but do not want him. Yet he made us able to know him, wiser than the beasts (v. 11); to cry in pain like an animal, without turning to the Maker, wastes his gift.

Who gives songs in the night. In the dark he gives his people something to sing: “at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8); “let me remember my song in the night” (Psalm 77:6). In a Philippian prison, “about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:25).

A rebuke that does not fit. Elihu means this as a rebuke to Job, and it does not fit him. Job has not only cried out for relief; he has cried for God: “Oh, that I knew where I might find him” (23:3).

He sang on the darkest night. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus sang a hymn with his disciples (Matthew 26:30), probably the Passover psalms. He sang on the darkest night any man has faced, and walked into it for us; because he did, his people are never left in their own dark nights without a song.

Relief, or God? Every sufferer may ask it: am I seeking relief, or him? Whoever seeks God himself may find a song in the night before he finds the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it. How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not answer the proud cry that wants his gifts without him, but Elihu is wrong to fault Job for waiting on God.

He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. God does not answer the proud, who want his gifts without him: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3). This is not about the weak, stumbling prayer of a believer in pain; God hears that, and his Spirit helps us in it (Romans 8:26).

You are waiting for him! Elihu faults Job for saying he cannot see God and is waiting for his case to be heard. But waiting for God is not sin; it is faith. “Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!” (Psalm 27:14). Job’s case was before God, and God was about to answer it (38:1). Here Elihu is simply wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression, Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu says Job has abused God’s patience with empty talk: right about the words, wrong about the man.

He multiplies words without knowledge. Because God has not struck Job down, Elihu says, Job has taken advantage of God’s patience and piled up “empty talk”, hevel, vapour, the word that runs through Ecclesiastes. And “words without knowledge” is exactly the phrase God will use: “Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2). On that, Elihu and God agree. What Elihu missed, God will not: the man who spoke those words was still his servant, and had spoken of God what is right (42:7).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “transgression” (v. 15) occurs only here; many take it as the ESV does, others as folly or arrogance. Either way, God has seemed to overlook Job’s words.

35.theology: God cannot be harmed by our sin nor enriched by our goodness (vv. 6-7), yet he is grieved and delighted by his people. Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God, who gives songs in the night (v. 10). Elihu faults Job for waiting on God (v. 14), but waiting on God is faith, and God will answer.
35.examples: The question Elihu leaves with every sufferer is worth asking honestly: am I seeking relief, or am I seeking God himself? Many believers have found that when they seek him, he gives songs in the night before the morning comes. And anyone who is still waiting for God to answer may take heart: waiting is faith, not sin.

keyVerse.quote: But none says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night
keyVerse.note: This is the one new and lasting word in Elihu’s third speech. Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God himself, and the God worth seeking is the one who gives his people a song before he gives them the morning. Jesus sang on the darkest night of all (Matthew 26:30), so that his people would never be without one.

35.reflection:
Satan claimed that Job served God for what he got (1:9), and Elihu hears Job asking, “What advantage have I?” (v. 3). In what ways are we tempted to treat faith as a bargain with God? How does Romans 11:35 change that?

Elihu says our sin cannot harm God and our goodness cannot enrich him, but that both affect “a man like yourself” (vv. 6–8). Yet Scripture also says we can grieve the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:30). How do these truths fit together, and what do they mean for how we treat others?

“Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night” (v. 10). When you are in trouble, do you find yourself seeking relief, or seeking God himself? Has God ever given you a song in a dark time?

Elihu faults Job for “waiting for him” (v. 14), but Psalm 27:14 calls waiting for the LORD faith. What helps you keep waiting on God when his answer is slow?

36.title: He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
36.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu continued, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf.<sup>3</sup>I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker.<sup>4</sup>For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding.<sup>6</sup>He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right.<sup>7</sup>He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted.<sup>8</sup>And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction,<sup>9</sup>then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly.<sup>10</sup>He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity.<sup>11</sup>If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness.<sup>12</sup>But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.<sup>13</sup>"The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them.<sup>14</sup>They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes.<sup>15</sup>He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity.<sup>16</sup>He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.<sup>17</sup>"But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside.<sup>19</sup>Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength?<sup>20</sup>Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place.<sup>21</sup>Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.<sup>22</sup>Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him?<sup>23</sup>Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'?<sup>24</sup>"Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung.<sup>25</sup>All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar.<sup>26</sup>Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.<sup>27</sup>For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain,<sup>28</sup>which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly.<sup>29</sup>Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion?<sup>30</sup>Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea.<sup>31</sup>For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance.<sup>32</sup>He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark.<sup>33</sup>Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
36.overview:
Where we are. Elihu’s fourth and last speech begins here and runs through chapter 37. He gathers his teaching on affliction into one great sentence, then turns from argument to praise as a storm gathers.

The message. God is mighty and despises no one, and his purpose in affliction is to rescue: “He delivers the afflicted by their affliction” (v. 15). The very thing that crushes can be the means of deliverance, opening ears, humbling pride and calling his people back. And this God is greater than all our knowing, so the right answer to him is not argument but praise.

Why it was said. Job had come to see in his suffering only God’s hostility (19:6; 30:21), and had longed for death (7:15). Elihu wants him to see that affliction may be God’s instruction, and to beware of turning to scoffing or sin to escape it. His teaching is true of how God often works, though it is not the reason for Job’s trial (2:3; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Elihu asks for patience and claims to speak with perfect knowledge on God’s behalf (vv. 1–4). God watches over the righteous and exalts them; when they are bound in affliction he shows them their pride and calls them back, and their response decides their end (vv. 5–12). The godless nurse their anger and die young, but God delivers the afflicted by their affliction, and would lead Job too into a broad place (vv. 13–16). Elihu warns Job against scoffing, longing for death or choosing sin over suffering (vv. 17–21). Then he turns to praise: God is the great Teacher, his greatness seen in rain, cloud, thunder and lightning, whose crash declares his presence (vv. 22–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the pattern the chapter’s great sentence describes. God delivered the world by the affliction of his Son: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), and “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The mighty God who “does not despise any” (v. 5) is seen in the Servant of whom it was said, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3). And Elihu’s claim that one “perfect in knowledge” stood before Job (v. 4) is true only of the Son, who alone knows the Father and makes him known (Matthew 11:27).

For us. Suffering carried in Christ is never wasted: God can bring rescue through the very thing that hurts. Ask what he is teaching you, refuse the way out that sin offers, and if you find yourself longing for death, tell someone today. Then lift your eyes from your own case to the greatness of God, and praise him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — God Is Mighty, and Does Not Despise Any
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God, who despises no one, uses affliction to call his people back from pride. Elihu asks Job to bear with him, for he has more to say on God’s behalf, and he claims to speak with perfect knowledge (vv. 1–4). God is mighty in strength and in understanding; he does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right, and he keeps his eyes on the righteous and sets them with kings (vv. 5–7). If they are bound in the cords of affliction, he shows them their arrogance and commands them to turn back (vv. 8–10). Those who listen end their days in peace; those who refuse perish without ever learning (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu restates his teaching that affliction is God's instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu continued, and said: "Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf. I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker. For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu sets out to defend God’s righteousness, but claims for himself a perfect knowledge that belongs to God alone.

Ascribe righteousness to my Maker. In his last speech, two chapters long, Elihu will defend God, and that is a good aim. But the last line gives pause: “one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.” He means himself. In the next chapter he uses exactly this phrase of God: “the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge” (37:16). Without noticing, Elihu has claimed for himself the title that belongs to God alone. Every preacher who speaks “on God’s behalf” should feel the warning.

The one who knows. Only one person has ever spoken for God with perfect knowledge: “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding. He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right. He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mighty God despises no one: he gives the afflicted their right and lifts up the righteous.

Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any. A lovely line: the mighty God despises no one, however small. “A bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3), said of the Servant who is Christ.

He gives the afflicted their right. This answers Job’s charge that God “has taken away my right” (27:2): it is God’s way, Elihu says, to give the afflicted their right. And his eye on the righteous is not a watch for faults but a care that lifts them up: “with kings on the throne he sets them”, as Hannah sang, “He raises up the poor from the dust… to make them sit with princes” (1 Samuel 2:8). “The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous” (Psalm 34:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly. He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s people are bound by affliction, he uses it to show them their pride and call them back.

The cords of affliction. This is Elihu’s teaching of chapter 33 again: affliction as God’s instruction, opening the ear and calling a man back from pride (33:14–30). What was said there stands, including its limit: it is true of how God often deals with his people, and it is not the explanation of Job’s suffering (2:3).

That they are behaving arrogantly. The sin affliction most often uncovers in God’s people is not some gross crime but pride. The chains and cords do not only hurt; they humble, and God uses them to show people “their work and their transgressions” and call them back. Manasseh is the classic case: bound in chains and taken to Babylon, he “humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” (2 Chronicles 33:11–13).

verseByVerse.quote: If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness. But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who listen to God’s instruction find peace; those who refuse perish without learning.

If they listen and serve him. Two ways open before the afflicted, as Moses set life and death before Israel (Deuteronomy 30:15–20). Those who listen end their days in peace; those who refuse “perish by the sword and die without knowledge”, without ever learning what the affliction was meant to teach. The promise of prosperity is a general rule, with the limit noted on vv. 8–10.

Will I listen? The first question for a believer under trial is not, Why has this happened? but, What is God teaching me, and will I listen? Discipline “yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

Uncertain wording. “Perish by the sword” uses the same word as 33:18, which some translate as crossing the river of death. Either way it means an early death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it, so Job must not be turned aside. The godless nurse their anger, never cry to God when he binds them, and die young in shame (vv. 13–14). But God delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears through adversity, and he longs to bring Job out of distress into a broad place, with a full table (vv. 15–16). So Elihu warns him: do not let the judgment you are preoccupied with drive you to scoffing, do not be turned aside, do not long for the night of death, and do not choose sin as a way out of suffering (vv. 17–21).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Elihu's best sentence: God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them. They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes. He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity. He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it.

The godless in heart cherish anger. The godless nurse their resentment and never turn to God, even in chains. The “cult prostitutes” of v. 14 were men and women who sold their bodies as part of pagan worship (Deuteronomy 23:17; 1 Kings 14:24). Elihu says the godless die young, in the shameful company of the vice they chose.

He delivers the afflicted by their affliction. This is the one truly new thought in Elihu’s last speeches, and one of the weightiest sentences in the book. God does not only rescue his people from affliction; he rescues them by it. The suffering itself becomes the means of deliverance: it opens their ears, loosens their grip on the world, drives them to God. In Hebrew the words for “afflicted” and “affliction” are almost the same, as if to say: the thing that crushes is the thing that saves.

Into a broad place. God wants to bring Job out into open country, with a full table. “He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me” (Psalm 18:19). Elihu does not know how true that last phrase is of Job (1:8).

The pattern of Christ. Paul knew this truth: “suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4); “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). And it is the pattern of Christ himself: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). God delivered the world by the affliction of his Son, so the believer may trust that his own affliction is not wasted.

Is a painless life the good life? Most of us quietly assume so: comfort is the measure of a good day, and suffering looks like pure loss, to be removed as fast as possible and forgotten. Elihu’s sentence will not fit that assumption, nor will the testimony of some who suffered most. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, looking back on his years in Stalin’s camps, wrote in The Gulag Archipelago, “Bless you, prison,” because of what had happened to his soul there. He knew how many the camps destroyed, and so should we; this is never a word to say glibly to someone in pain. But affliction can do what comfort almost never does: loosen our grip on the things we were secretly worshipping, and send us to God for God’s own sake. The gospel goes further than any survivor’s testimony: God saved the world through the suffering of his Son, so no affliction carried in him is wasted. “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 is very difficult Hebrew. Most, like the ESV, take it as God’s wish to draw Job into freedom and plenty; a few read it as a warning.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you. Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside. Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength? Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place. Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu warns Job not to let anger drive him to scoffing, to longing for death, or to sin.

The greatness of the ransom. Elihu warns Job that he is so taken up with the judgment he thinks the wicked deserve, and with his own case, that he may be tempted to scoff at God. “Ransom” is the same word as in 33:24. Whatever exactly Elihu meant, the one ransom that could set a man free was still to come.

Do not long for the night. That is, the death that swallows whole nations; Job had longed for it since chapter 3 (7:15). Anyone who longs for death today should tell someone at once: a pastor, a friend, a doctor; and if you are in danger, call emergency help the same day. Job’s longing was heard by God, not punished, and he lived to see good days again (42:12).

Do not turn to iniquity. Do not choose sin as a way out of suffering. That is a real temptation for every sufferer, and Elihu is right to name it, though he is wrong to say Job had chosen it.

Uncertain wording. Verses 17–20 are among the most obscure lines in the book, and translations differ widely. In v. 18 “ransom” can also mean a bribe, so the line may mean, do not let the great cost of your suffering turn you away, or, do not think a great payment could buy your way out. The overall warning is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — God Is Great, and We Know Him Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu’s point is that God is great beyond all our knowing, and is to be praised rather than argued with. God is exalted in power and is the Teacher no one can instruct or correct (vv. 22–23). So remember to extol his work, which all mankind has seen, if only from afar; his years are beyond counting (vv. 24–26). Elihu points to the weather: God draws up the drops and pours down rain on mankind (vv. 27–28); he spreads the clouds, sends the thunder of his pavilion and scatters his lightning, by which he both judges and feeds the peoples (vv. 29–32). The thunder’s crash declares his presence (v. 33). A storm seems to be gathering, and God will speak from it.
verseByVerse.theology: As Elihu praises, a storm begins to gather, and God will speak from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him? Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'? "Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar. Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu turns from argument to praise: God is the great Teacher, beyond correction and beyond our knowing.

Who is a teacher like him? Elihu’s voice changes. God is the great Teacher, and no one teaches him: “what man shows him his counsel?” (Isaiah 40:13). No one can tell God he has done wrong. That is the answer to Job’s worst charges (19:6; 30:21), and God will make it himself (40:8).

Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. The right response to God is not argument but praise: “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty!” (Revelation 15:3). “We know him not”: he is greater than all our understanding. His years are “unsearchable”, the word Eliphaz used at the start (5:9) and the psalmist sings: “his greatness is unsearchable” (Psalm 145:3). The friends claimed to have searched God out. The book keeps saying that no one can.

verseByVerse.quote: For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain, which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly. Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion? Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea. For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance. He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark. Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rain, cloud, thunder and lightning display God’s power and presence, as a storm gathers.

He draws up the drops of water. God draws them up into the clouds and sends them down as rain. “All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full” (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Ordinary weather is God at work.

The thunderings of his pavilion. Clouds spreading like a tent over the sky, thunder, lightning thrown like a spear at its target. The same rain can destroy a nation’s harvest or fill its barns; God “did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17). And “its crashing declares his presence”: the thunder announces that God is near.

A storm coming up. Many readers have noticed that Elihu seems to be describing a storm that is actually coming up as he speaks. The cattle sense it; the thunder rolls. Keep watching the sky. Soon the storm will break, and the LORD will speak out of it (38:1).

Uncertain wording. In v. 31 “judges” differs only slightly in Hebrew from a word meaning nourishes, which would match “he gives food in abundance”. Verse 33 is among the most obscure lines in Job; the ESV’s reading is one reasonable guess. Either way the storm announces God.

36.theology: God delivers the afflicted by their affliction (v. 15): suffering can be the means of rescue (Rom 5:3-5), as it was for Christ, who learned obedience through what he suffered. God is great beyond our knowing (v. 26), and those who speak for him must not claim the knowledge that is his alone.
36.examples: For a believer in a long trial, he delivers the afflicted by their affliction is a word to hold on to: the suffering is not wasted. It does not explain any particular pain, and it does not make pain good in itself, but it says God can bring rescue through the very thing that hurts.

keyVerse.quote: He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity.
keyVerse.note: This is Elihu’s best sentence and one of the weightiest in the book. God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it, so that the very thing that crushes becomes the means of deliverance. It is the pattern of the cross, where God delivered the world by the affliction of his Son (Hebrews 5:8).

36.reflection:
Elihu claims that “one who is perfect in knowledge is with you” (v. 4), a title he later gives to God (37:16). How can those who speak for God, in a pulpit or over coffee, avoid claiming more knowledge than they have?

“He delivers the afflicted by their affliction” (v. 15). Can you think of a time when God used something painful to rescue you from pride or draw you to himself? Why must we be careful how we say this to someone who is suffering now?

Elihu warns against choosing sin “rather than affliction” (v. 21). What are the ways out of suffering that tempt people today? What would it look like to refuse them, and to tell someone if the longing for death grows strong?

Elihu ends by pointing to the rain and the storm (vv. 27–33). How does looking at God’s greatness in creation help a sufferer? How does Christ, who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), show us that our affliction is not wasted?

37.title: The Almighty: We Cannot Find Him
37.text: <sup>1</sup>"At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place.<sup>2</sup>Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth.<sup>3</sup>Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth.<sup>4</sup>After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard.<sup>5</sup>God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.<sup>6</sup>For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour.<sup>7</sup>He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it.<sup>8</sup>Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens.<sup>9</sup>From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds.<sup>10</sup>By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast.<sup>11</sup>He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning.<sup>12</sup>They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world.<sup>13</sup>Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.<sup>14</sup>"Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God.<sup>15</sup>Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine?<sup>16</sup>Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge,<sup>17</sup>you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind?<sup>18</sup>Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror?<sup>19</sup>Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness.<sup>20</sup>Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?<sup>21</sup>"And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them.<sup>22</sup>Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty.<sup>23</sup>The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate.<sup>24</sup>Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
37.overview:
Where we are. Elihu is ending the last of his speeches (chapters 32–37). He has begun to describe God’s greatness in the autumn rains (36:26–33), and as he speaks a real storm seems to be gathering over the ash heap. His is the last human voice before God speaks.

The message. The God who rules thunder, snow, ice and cloud is too great for us to search out, and he sends each storm for his own purposes, “whether for correction or for his land or for love” (v. 13). Since we cannot see what he is doing, we cannot put him on trial; we must stop, consider his works and fear him. And the chapter ends where Job’s search ended, “we cannot find him” (v. 23), on the edge of God’s coming to find Job.

Why it was said. Job has demanded a hearing and accused God of injustice, and the friends have read every storm in his life as punishment (see the introduction). Elihu answers both.

How the chapter makes its case. Elihu trembles at the thunder, God’s voice (vv. 1–5). Snow, rain and ice come at God’s word and halt the work of men (vv. 6–10). The clouds wheel at his direction, for correction, for the land, or for love (vv. 11–13). Then Elihu questions Job: does he know how God works the lightning or balances the clouds? No one can draw up a case against God in such darkness (vv. 14–20). The sky clears, golden splendour comes out of the north, and Elihu ends with God’s majesty and justice, and a warning to the wise in their own conceit (vv. 21–24).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by the character of God it reveals. Elihu is right that we cannot find God. Yet the next words of the book are “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (38:1), and the gospel has the same shape: God comes to us. The voice Elihu heard as thunder once spoke from heaven about the Son (John 12:28–29), and in Jesus the majesty no one could look at came near enough to touch, for “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

For us. When a storm breaks over your life, do not assume you know which of God’s purposes it serves, and never read other people’s storms as punishment. Stop and consider his works, fear him, and do not be wise in your own eyes. The God we could never find has come and found us in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Thunder of His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules every kind of weather and sends each for his own purposes, so no one can read his intentions off the sky. Elihu trembles at the thunder, which he hears as God’s voice going out to the ends of the earth, doing great things we cannot comprehend (vv. 1–5). Snow and downpour come at his command, halting the work of every man and sending the animals to their dens, and by his breath the waters freeze (vv. 6–10). The loaded clouds wheel at his direction to do whatever he commands, and he sends them for correction, for his land, or for love (vv. 11–13). That last verse undoes the friends’ single explanation of suffering.
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu hears the storm as God's voice.

verseByVerse.quote: "At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place. Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth. Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth. After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thunder is God’s voice, and it shows works too great for us to understand.

At this also my heart trembles. The storm gathering at the end of chapter 36 is breaking, and Elihu’s heart is pounding as the thunder rolls and the lightning flashes to the corners of the earth: “God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend” (v. 5).

The voice of the LORD. Scripture often hears God in the thunder: “The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders” (Psalm 29:3). And once, when the Father spoke from heaven about his Son, “the crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered” (John 12:29). Elihu is right to tremble. In a few moments God will speak from this storm in words.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour. He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it. Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens. From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds. By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Snow, rain and ice come at God’s command, and when they halt our work they show who is in charge.

To the snow he says. Snow and heavy rain come at his word. When they do, work in the fields stops; every man’s hand is “sealed up”, forced to rest, “that all men whom he made may know it” (v. 7). The animals take shelter in their dens. Even winter is his breath: “By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast” (v. 10). An illness that stops a working life can carry the same lesson.

Preparing for God’s speech. Elihu’s winter scene prepares for the LORD’s, which asks Job, “Have you entered the storehouses of the snow” and “From whose womb did the ice come forth” (38:22, 29). There God takes up the same weather, not to explain it, but to show Job how little he knows of it.

verseByVerse.quote: He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning. They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world. Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God steers every cloud and sends storms for different purposes, so no one can read his reasons off the weather.

They turn around and around by his guidance. The clouds heavy with rain, and the lightning they scatter, wheel across the sky, but not at random. The word for “guidance” probably comes from steering a ship (it is used of wise counsel in Proverbs 1:5): God pilots the clouds “to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world”. Every shower falls where he sends it.

For correction or for his land or for love. Here is the wisest thing Elihu says. Sometimes “for correction”, as judgment on sin. Sometimes “for his land”, because the earth needs rain. Sometimes “for love”: the word is chesed, God’s covenant love, the “steadfast love” Job once saw in God’s care for him (10:12). The friends knew only the first reason, and read every storm as punishment. The same weather that judges one man waters another’s field and is a gift of love to a third. A believer caught in a storm cannot tell from the storm itself which of the three it is, but he can know the God who sends it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — God Is Clothed with Awesome Majesty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Job cannot understand even the weather, he cannot put God on trial; he must stop, consider and fear. Elihu calls Job to stand still and consider God’s wonders, and questions him as God soon will: does he know how the lightning shines or how the clouds hang balanced, and can he spread out the sky (vv. 14–18)? No one can draw up a case against God in such darkness, and to demand a hearing would be like asking to be swallowed up (vv. 19–20). Then the sky clears, golden splendour comes from the north, and Elihu’s last words confess a God we cannot find, great in power and perfect in justice, who regards no one who is wise in his own conceit (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu ends by saying no one can find God. In the next verse, God finds Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine? Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge, you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind? Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror? Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness. Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job cannot explain even the clouds, so he cannot argue his case against God; he should stop and consider.

Stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Stop talking; look. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). It is the right advice, and God is about to give Job the fullest possible opportunity to take it.

Do you know how God lays his command upon them? Elihu’s questions are a foretaste of how God will speak in the next chapter. And “him who is perfect in knowledge” is now said of God, where Elihu had said it of himself (36:4). The title has found its right owner.

Hard as a cast metal mirror. Ancient mirrors were polished bronze. When the south wind blows and Job’s very clothes are hot on him (v. 17), the sky stands over him like burnished metal. He cannot even cool himself; can he spread out that sky?

We cannot draw up our case because of darkness. No one can draw up a legal case against God; we are in the dark. Who would ask to be summoned before him, when it would be like being swallowed alive? Job had asked exactly that (31:35). He is about to get it, and he will not be swallowed up.

Uncertain wording. The second half of v. 20 is difficult Hebrew. The ESV takes it as a question; others read a statement, that a man who spoke against God would surely be swallowed up. Either way, to press a complaint before God would overwhelm the one who brought it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them. Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty. The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s majesty is too bright to look at; we cannot find him, but we must fear him.

God is clothed with awesome majesty. The wind sweeps the clouds away, the sky blazes too bright to look at, and from the north comes a golden glory. Ezekiel saw God come the same way: “behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually” (Ezekiel 1:4). Elihu may be describing, without knowing it, the approach of God himself.

We cannot find him. These are Elihu’s last words, and they echo Job’s: “Oh, that I knew where I might find him” (23:3). Elihu is right: no one can find God by searching. And the very next line of the book is “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (38:1). Job could not find God, so God came and found Job. That is the whole shape of the gospel: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

Justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. The God too great to be found is not too great to be just. Job had feared power without justice; Elihu holds the two together, as the cross does.

Wise in their own conceit. The last line is a warning to everyone in the book: God “does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit”. Not the friends, nor Elihu, who called himself perfect in knowledge, nor Job, who demanded that God answer him. “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:7): fearing God and turning from evil are the two things said of Job on the first page (1:1) and called wisdom in the poem (28:28). Now God speaks.

Uncertain wording. In v. 22 the Hebrew says simply “gold” comes out of the north. Most, like the ESV, take it of golden light as the sky clears. Some think of gold mined in the north: men can dig out gold (28:1), but God’s majesty is beyond their reach. On any reading, God comes in splendour.

37.theology: God sends storms, and sufferings, for different ends (v. 13), so no one can read his purpose off the weather, and the friends' single explanation fails. Thunder is his voice, and his coming is glory (v. 22). And though man cannot find God (v. 23), God at once comes to Job: the shape of the gospel, in which God seeks the lost.
37.examples: Verse 13 is a steadying word for anyone in a hard season: the storm may be correction, or provision, or love, and from inside it we often cannot tell which. What we can know is the God who sends it, and the chapter ends with him coming near.

keyVerse.quote: Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge between all the human talk in the book and the voice of God. Elihu’s best counsel is not another argument but a call to stop and look, and God himself will take it up in the next chapter with question after question about his works. The sufferer who stops and considers God’s works finds, in the end, the God who comes to him.

37.reflection:
Elihu says God sends storms “whether for correction or for his land or for love” (v. 13). Why is it dangerous to assume we know which reason lies behind a hardship, our own or someone else’s?

Snow and rain stop men’s work so “that all men whom he made may know it” (v. 7). Has an interruption in your life, such as illness, delay or loss, ever turned your attention to God? What did you learn?

Elihu tells Job to “stop and consider the wondrous works of God” (v. 14). What would it look like for you to do that this week, and why does it help a troubled heart?

Elihu’s last words are “we cannot find him” (v. 23), and the next verse in the book is God answering Job. How does the coming of Jesus show that God is the one who seeks us?

38.title: Where Were You?
38.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:<sup>2</sup>"Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?<sup>3</sup>Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.<sup>4</sup>"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.<sup>5</sup>Who determined its measurements—surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it?<sup>6</sup>On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone,<sup>7</sup>when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?<sup>8</sup>"Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb,<sup>9</sup>when I made clouds its garment and thick darkness its swaddling band,<sup>10</sup>and prescribed limits for it and set bars and doors,<sup>11</sup>and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?<sup>12</sup>"Have you commanded the morning since your days began, and caused the dawn to know its place,<sup>13</sup>that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it?<sup>14</sup>It is changed like clay under the seal, and its features stand out like a garment.<sup>15</sup>From the wicked their light is withheld, and their uplifted arm is broken.<sup>16</sup>"Have you entered into the springs of the sea, or walked in the recesses of the deep?<sup>17</sup>Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?<sup>18</sup>Have you comprehended the expanse of the earth? Declare, if you know all this.<sup>19</sup>"Where is the way to the dwelling of light, and where is the place of darkness,<sup>20</sup>that you may take it to its territory and that you may discern the paths to its home?<sup>21</sup>You know, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great!<sup>22</sup>"Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you seen the storehouses of the hail,<sup>23</sup>which I have reserved for the time of trouble, for the day of battle and war?<sup>24</sup>What is the way to the place where the light is distributed, or where the east wind is scattered upon the earth?<sup>25</sup>"Who has cleft a channel for the torrents of rain and a way for the thunderbolt,<sup>26</sup>to bring rain on a land where no man is, on the desert in which there is no man,<sup>27</sup>to satisfy the waste and desolate land, and to make the ground sprout with grass?<sup>28</sup>"Has the rain a father, or who has begotten the drops of dew?<sup>29</sup>From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who has given birth to the frost of heaven?<sup>30</sup>The waters become hard like stone, and the face of the deep is frozen.<sup>31</sup>"Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion?<sup>32</sup>Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth in their season, or can you guide the Bear with its children?<sup>33</sup>Do you know the ordinances of the heavens? Can you establish their rule on the earth?<sup>34</sup>"Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that a flood of waters may cover you?<sup>35</sup>Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go and say to you, 'Here we are'?<sup>36</sup>Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind?<sup>37</sup>Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can tilt the waterskins of the heavens,<sup>38</sup>when the dust runs into a mass and the clods stick fast together?<sup>39</sup>"Can you hunt the prey for the lion, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions,<sup>40</sup>when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in their thicket?<sup>41</sup>Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God for help, and wander about for lack of food?
38.overview:
Where we are. Thirty-five chapters of human voices have ended. Elihu’s last words were “we cannot find him” (37:23), and now the LORD himself answers Job out of the whirlwind. This is the first of God’s two speeches (38:1–40:2; 40:6–41:34).

The message. God answers Job not with an explanation but with himself. He says nothing of the heavenly court and accuses Job of no sin; he asks question after question about the making and running of the world, until Job sees how little he knows and how great, wise and caring the Maker is. The God who laid the earth’s foundations to songs of joy, sets limits to the sea, commands each dawn and feeds the young ravens can be trusted with what Job cannot understand.

Why it was said. Job had demanded that God answer him (31:35) and had spoken of God’s purposes as cruel and unjust, while the friends insisted his suffering was punishment (see the introduction). God comes, rebukes Job for darkening counsel “by words without knowledge” (v. 2), and by saying nothing of punishment lets the friends’ theory fall.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD summons Job to answer like a man (vv. 1–3). Where was Job when the earth was founded and the morning stars sang (vv. 4–7), or when the sea was born and given its limits (vv. 8–11)? Has he commanded the dawn that exposes the wicked (vv. 12–15), or seen the depths of the sea, the gates of death and the homes of light and darkness (vv. 16–21)? Can he open the storehouses of snow, send rain on empty deserts, father the dew or freeze the deep (vv. 22–30), lead out the stars (vv. 31–33), or command the clouds and the lightning (vv. 34–38)? Can he feed the lion and the young ravens (vv. 39–41)? Every question turns Job’s eyes from himself to God.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him. The one who laid the earth’s foundation is the Son: “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning” (Hebrews 1:10). The God who would not be summoned by Job later let himself be put on trial before Pilate for us. The gates of death God asks Job about, Christ has opened (Revelation 1:18), and the God who feeds the ravens is the Father Jesus taught his disciples to trust (Luke 12:24).

For us. When suffering comes without explanation, God offers something better than a reason: himself. Let his questions humble your verdicts on him, and let his care for deserts, dawns and raven chicks assure you that you are not forgotten.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers at last, not to explain but to question. After all the human voices, the LORD speaks to Job by his covenant name, out of the storm (v. 1). His first words rebuke Job for darkening God’s plan with words spoken in ignorance, yet they charge him with no sin and say nothing of punishment, so the friends’ theory falls without a word (v. 2). Then God tells Job to brace himself like a man, for God will ask the questions and Job must answer: the hearing Job asked for, though not on Job’s terms (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asked for a hearing, and God comes. He does not come to explain; he comes to question, and in coming he gives Job what he most needed: himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After thirty-five chapters of human voices, the LORD himself speaks to Job, and that he comes at all is grace.

Then the LORD answered Job. Elihu has just said “we cannot find him” (37:23), and the next words are “Then the LORD answered Job”. Job could not find God; God found Job.

The LORD. The narrator uses God’s covenant name, not heard since the opening chapters: the God of the heavenly court who called Job “my servant” (1:8) now speaks. In chapters 1 and 2 God spoke only to Satan; these are his first words to Job in the whole book. Job had asked again and again for a hearing (13:22; 23:3; 31:35). Elihu was right that God owes no one a trial (34:23); he came anyway.

Out of the whirlwind. God comes in storm, as he came at Sinai: “his way is in whirlwind and storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3). And it was “a great wind” from the wilderness that brought the house down on Job’s children (1:19). The kind of thing that broke his life is where God meets him. Many believers have found the same: the place of their deepest loss became the place where God spoke.
verseByVerse.note: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, not with an explanation but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rebukes Job for speaking of God’s plan without knowing it, yet brings no charge of sin, and calls him to stand up and answer.

Who is this that darkens counsel? God’s first sentence is a rebuke, and a precise one. “Counsel” is God’s plan, his purpose. Job has spoken of God’s purposes as if he understood them, calling God cruel, an enemy, unjust, and so has made God’s plan look dark. “Without knowledge”: he did not know of the scene in heaven, Satan’s challenge, or God’s delight in him. Job will take these words on his own lips at the end (42:3).

No word of punishment. God does not say that Job is wicked, or that his suffering was punishment. The friends’ whole theory falls without a word.

Dress for action like a man. Literally, gird up your loins: tuck up your robe for hard work or a fight. “Man” is the same Hebrew word as in “A man is conceived” (3:3), the night Job cursed. The man Job wished had never been conceived, God treats as a man fit to be questioned. And he takes Job at his word: Job had said, “Then call, and I will answer” (13:22). Now God calls.
verseByVerse.note: “Dress for action like a man” is literally “gird up your loins” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job came late into a world he did not make, so he is in no position to judge how it is run. God asks where Job was when he laid the earth’s foundations and cornerstone while the morning stars sang and the angels shouted for joy (vv. 4–7). He tells how he wrapped the newborn sea in cloud and set it limits it cannot pass (vv. 8–11). He asks whether Job has ever commanded the dawn, which shakes the wicked out of the earth each morning (vv. 12–15), or seen the springs of the sea, the gates of death and the dwellings of light and darkness (vv. 16–21). The gentle irony of v. 21 makes the point: Job was not there.
verseByVerse.theology: God answers Job's questions with his own, and every one of them is about God. The Maker of the world has not lost control of it, and he still sets limits to the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who determined its measurements—surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job was not there when God built the world, so he cannot sit in judgment on how God runs it.

Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Job has been judging how God runs the world; where was he when it was built? God pictures himself as the builder who drew the plan and stretched the measuring line. “If you have understanding” is pointed: the wisdom poem said that for man “to turn away from evil is understanding” (28:28). Job has that. What he lacks is the architect’s understanding, and he has been speaking as if he had it. The point is not to humiliate Job but to put him in the place of every creature: he came late to a world already made, and does not have the plans. We see a few feet of a building whose architect saw the whole.

Who is speaking? Hebrews applies a psalm about God laying the earth’s foundation to the Son: “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands” (Hebrews 1:10). The voice from the whirlwind is the voice of the one through whom all things were made, who would one day stand on that earth in flesh.

Why does God answer with questions? To a modern reader it can sound like evasion, a powerful being changing the subject when asked to account for himself. But look at the assumption underneath. C. S. Lewis observed, in an essay called “God in the Dock”, that ancient people came to God as the accused come before a judge, while modern people have reversed the roles: we are the judge, and God is in the dock. Job in his pain had drifted into the modern position, and so do we, assuming we stand outside the universe with a clear view and a fair standard. We arrived late, have seen a few feet of the building, and have been grading the architect. Yet here is the reversal no one in the book foresaw. One day God did go into the dock. He stood before Pilate, was questioned, mocked and condemned, and gave almost no answer, so that we who put him there could be acquitted. The God who would not be summoned by Job let himself be summoned for Job. (On why God permits suffering at all, see the notes on Job 1:20–22.)

verseByVerse.quote: On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone, when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth was founded amid the joyful shouts of heaven: creation began in delight, not in anger.

Who laid its cornerstone. The earth is a building, its foundations sunk and its cornerstone laid, and when the cornerstone went in there was music: the morning stars singing, “all the sons of God” shouting for joy. The “sons of God” are the heavenly council of 1:6, glimpsed now not as a courtroom but at a celebration.

The morning stars. They and the sons of God are angels, joined to the stars in poetry, as in Psalm 148:2–3. They were there, singing, when the earth was founded, so the poem implies they were made before it, though it does not say when.

For a man in pain. The world was not made in anger. It was made to shouts of delight, and the God who made it that way has not changed. The New Testament uses the same builder’s picture for God’s new building, with “Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20): the Son through whom the first world was founded (Hebrews 1:10) is the foundation of the second.

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb, when I made clouds its garment and thick darkness its swaddling band, and prescribed limits for it and set bars and doors, and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea, the ancient picture of chaos, is to God a newborn he swaddled and set within limits, and he sets the same limits on every power that breaks over his people.

Who shut in the sea with doors. The sea, the ancient symbol of chaos, bursts out like a baby from the womb, and God wraps it in swaddling bands of cloud and thick darkness, as a mother wraps her infant. The chaos that terrifies men is, to God, a baby he dressed.

Thus far shall you come, and no farther. And he set it limits: bars and doors, a line in the sand. Jeremiah heard the same: “I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea… though they roar, they cannot pass over it” (Jeremiah 5:22). Job had asked, “Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?” (7:12). God answers: I do set a guard over the sea.

The same kind of limit. The reader has met these limits before: “Only against him do not stretch out your hand” (1:12); “only spare his life” (2:6). God set the same kind of limit on Satan that he sets on the waves. The chaos that broke over Job came so far and no farther, because God said so. That is what God was doing all along, while Job thought he had lost control.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you commanded the morning since your days began, and caused the dawn to know its place, that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it? It is changed like clay under the seal, and its features stand out like a garment. From the wicked their light is withheld, and their uplifted arm is broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands every dawn, and every dawn exposes the wicked and breaks the arm raised against the weak.

Have you commanded the morning? Each morning the dawn takes hold of the edges of the earth like a blanket and shakes it, and the wicked who have worked in the dark fall out. Job complained that the murderer, the adulterer and the thief love the night and are never caught (24:13–17). God answers: I send the dawn every day, and every day it exposes them.

Their uplifted arm is broken. Job swore that if he had ever raised his hand against the fatherless, his arm should “be broken from its socket” (31:21–22). God answers that he breaks the arm raised against the weak, every day, and the dawn is his witness.

Since your days began. Job tried to curse one day out of existence: “Let that day be darkness!” and “let it not come into the number of the months” (3:4, 6). God asks whether Job has commanded even one morning “since your days began”. Job tried to unmake a single day; God makes every one.

The great dawn. God commanded the dawn every morning of Job’s life, including the mornings on the ash heap. And the Bible’s great dawn was still to come: “the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:78–79), words Zechariah sang at the birth of his son John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ.

Uncertain wording. The pictures in v. 14 are compressed. Clay takes on shape when a seal is pressed into it, and so the earth, shapeless in the dark, takes on form at dawn. “Its features stand out like a garment” may picture colours appearing as in a dyed cloth, or the folds of the land showing like a robe held up to the light. The sense is plain either way: the dawn gives the world its shape again.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you entered into the springs of the sea, or walked in the recesses of the deep? Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness? Have you comprehended the expanse of the earth? Declare, if you know all this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has never seen the depths of the sea or the gates of death, but God has, and Christ holds their keys.

The gates of death. Down to the bottom of the ocean, where its springs rise; further still, to the gates of death. “Deep darkness” is what Job called down on his birthday (3:5), and the grave he dreaded was “the land of darkness and deep shadow” (10:21). Has he seen its gates? God has.

The keys of Death and Hades. Jesus spoke of those gates too: “on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). And the risen Christ says, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). The gates God asks Job about, Christ has opened from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: "Where is the way to the dwelling of light, and where is the place of darkness, that you may take it to its territory and that you may discern the paths to its home? You know, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light and darkness have homes only God knows, and his gentle irony reminds Job how recently he arrived.

The dwelling of light. Light and darkness are pictured as living in houses, going out and coming home each day. Does Job know the road to their homes? God knows where darkness lives, and keeps it there.

You know, for you were born then. Gentle irony. Eliphaz once mocked Job, “Are you the first man who was born?” (15:7). God uses the same irony in a different tone: Eliphaz wanted to shut Job up; God is bringing him to see.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — The Storehouses of the Snow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The weather and the stars obey God, not Job, and God’s care reaches places no person will ever see. God keeps snow and hail in storehouses for his purposes and knows the path of every wind (vv. 22–24). He cuts channels for the rain and sends it on deserts where no one lives (vv. 25–27). He alone is the Father of rain and dew, ice and frost (vv. 28–30). He leads out the constellations and fixes the laws of the heavens (vv. 31–33). The clouds, the lightning and the wisdom in a creature’s mind answer to him, and he tips the waterskins of heaven to turn the dust to mud (vv. 34–38).
verseByVerse.theology: Weather and stars are all under God's hand, and his care reaches places no human eye will see.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you seen the storehouses of the hail, which I have reserved for the time of trouble, for the day of battle and war? What is the way to the place where the light is distributed, or where the east wind is scattered upon the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps snow and hail like weapons in an armoury, and knows where every wind comes from and where it goes.

The storehouses of the snow. God keeps snow and hail in storerooms, ready for the day he needs them, “for the time of trouble, for the day of battle and war” (v. 23). He has used them: hail on Egypt (Exodus 9:23), and in Joshua’s battle at Beth-horon “there were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword” (Joshua 10:11).

Where the east wind is scattered. The east wind was the hot desert wind, and the great wind that killed Job’s children came across the wilderness (1:19). God knows where every wind comes from, and where it is going.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who has cleft a channel for the torrents of rain and a way for the thunderbolt, to bring rain on a land where no man is, on the desert in which there is no man, to satisfy the waste and desolate land, and to make the ground sprout with grass?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends rain on deserts where no one lives, because his care for his world reaches far beyond human interests.

A way for the thunderbolt. The phrase echoes the wisdom poem (28:26), which pointed ahead to this moment. Then something striking: God sends rain on a desert where no one lives. No farmer will harvest that grass; no human eye will see it grow. God waters it anyway, because he delights in his world for its own sake.

On the desert in which there is no man. Job has thought of the world as if everything in it must be about him and his case. God’s care is much wider: he tends places no one will ever visit. If it reaches the empty desert, it reaches Job, even where Job cannot see it, and the lonely places in every believer’s life that no one else knows about.

A vast universe is not a silent one.
