Modern people often feel the size of the cosmos as a verdict on us: billions of galaxies, and here we are, specks on a speck; surely no one out there is paying attention. Pascal felt it in the seventeenth century, looking at the night sky: “The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me.” God’s speech makes the same discovery and turns it round. Creation is far bigger than Job and mostly has nothing to do with him. And yet it is a speech: the immensity comes with a voice, and the voice is talking to one sick man on an ash heap. The size of the world was never the measure of God’s indifference; it is the measure of his care, which reaches the deserts and the ravens and therefore Job. The psalmist looked at the same sky and asked, “what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). The full answer came when the Maker of the stars came to this small planet himself, as a man.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has the rain a father, or who has begotten the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who has given birth to the frost of heaven? The waters become hard like stone, and the face of the deep is frozen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rain and dew, ice and frost have no father or mother but God.

Has the rain a father? Father and mother pictures again: who fathered the rain? Out of whose womb came the ice? No one’s but God’s. James calls God “the Father of lights”, from whom “every good gift and every perfect gift” comes down (James 1:17). The Father who begets the dew and brings the frost is the Father of every believer, and he gives good gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth in their season, or can you guide the Bear with its children? Do you know the ordinances of the heavens? Can you establish their rule on the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stars move by God’s laws, not Job’s, and their fixed order is a pledge of God’s faithfulness.

Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? These are constellations Job himself named when he praised God’s power (9:9): the Pleiades, the cluster of stars that seems held together by a chain; Orion, the hunter with his belt; the Bear with her cubs. Can Job lead them out night by night across the sky? God does.

The ordinances of the heavens. The stars keep God’s laws without fail. God once pointed to exactly that to assure his people of his faithfulness: “If this fixed order departs from before me… then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation” (Jeremiah 31:36). His promises are as fixed as the stars.

Uncertain wording. Not all the star names are certain. The Pleiades and Orion are the usual and likely identifications (the Hebrew name behind Orion means “fool”). “Mazzaroth” is unknown: probably the name of a constellation, as the ESV’s note says, and some think of the signs of the zodiac. “The Bear with its children” is often taken as the Great Bear, though some suggest another group of stars. Whatever their names, the point is certain: Job cannot move them, and God does.
verseByVerse.note: “Mazzaroth” is probably the name of a constellation (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that a flood of waters may cover you? Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go and say to you, 'Here we are'? Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind? Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can tilt the waterskins of the heavens, when the dust runs into a mass and the clods stick fast together?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clouds, lightning and the very wisdom in creatures answer to God, and the one who counts the clouds is where wisdom is found.

Can you send forth lightnings? Can Job shout at the clouds and make it rain, or dispatch the lightning like a messenger and have it report back, “Here we are”? The lightnings are pictured as God’s servants reporting for duty, as the heavenly beings came “to present themselves before the LORD” (1:6). Everything in the sky answers to him.

Who has put wisdom in the inward parts? Whatever wisdom any creature has, God gave it. And the rain clouds are waterskins God tips over, so that the dusty ground turns to mud and the clods stick together. Job has been asking where wisdom is (28:12). It is with the one who counts the clouds. And the God who gives wisdom to his creatures puts it in a heart: “you teach me wisdom in the secret heart” (Psalm 51:6).

Uncertain wording. The two rare words in v. 36, rendered “inward parts” and “mind”, may instead name birds: the ESV’s notes offer “the ibis” and “the rooster”, birds thought in the ancient world to sense a change in the weather. If so, the verse belongs with the weather around it: God gave even the birds their weather-wisdom. Either way, all wisdom is his gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 39–41 — Who Provides for the Raven?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first speech ends with God feeding hungry animals: his rule over the world is a Father’s care. Job cannot hunt prey for the lion or fill its cubs as they crouch in their dens (vv. 39–40). It is God who provides for the raven, whose hungry chicks cry to him and wander for lack of food (v. 41). The chapter that began with the foundations of the earth ends with the smallest cries in it, and God hears them all. Jesus drew the conclusion from the same picture: if God feeds the ravens, how much more will he care for his children.
verseByVerse.theology: The first speech ends with God feeding baby birds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you hunt the prey for the lion, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions, when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in their thicket? Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God for help, and wander about for lack of food?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God feeds the lion and hears the cries of raven chicks, so the world Job thought had no one in charge has a Father.

Can you hunt the prey for the lion? Now God turns to the animals. The lion is the king of beasts, and God, not Job, feeds him every day.

Who provides for the raven its prey. The first speech ends with baby ravens. Their parents are out looking for food; the chicks are squawking in the nest, and God says: that noise is a cry to me, and I answer it. “He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Psalm 147:9).

Consider the ravens. Jesus took this very picture and drew the conclusion Job needed: “Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!” (Luke 12:24). The God who hears raven chicks crying has heard every word Job has cried.

What this speech has done. It has not explained Job’s suffering; Job never hears about the scene in heaven, and never will. It has not accused him of any sin; the friends’ theory is not even mentioned. It has asked questions, dozens of them, and every one has turned Job’s eyes from himself to the Maker: his wisdom in the foundations, his power over the sea and the stars, his care for deserts and lions and raven chicks. There is humour in it, and tenderness: the sea in swaddling clothes, the baby birds. It is not the voice of a tyrant but of a Father showing his son the world he made. The answer to Job’s suffering is not a reason but a Person, and Job will say so: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (42:5).

For the sufferer. That is still the offer: not an explanation, but God himself, who made everything, rules everything and feeds the ravens. It is not a smaller gift than an explanation. It is the gift Christ gave at Bethany: he did not tell the grieving sisters why, but wept with them and told them who he was, “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25, 35).

38.theology: God answers Job not with an explanation but with himself. He brings no charge of sin, so the friends' theory falls without a word, and he shows Job the Maker and ruler of all things, who set limits to the sea as he set limits to Satan (1:12; 2:6). The one who laid the earth's foundation is the Son, the cornerstone of God's new building, the sunrise who visits those in the shadow of death, who holds the keys of death.
38.examples: Many sufferers have found that this chapter helps when explanations do not. Its pictures are tender as well as vast: the sea wrapped like a newborn and told thus far, rain on a desert no one will ever see, raven chicks whose squawking God counts as prayer. A God who cares for all that has not forgotten you.

keyVerse.quote: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.
keyVerse.note: God’s first great question sets the terms of everything that follows. Job has been judging the way the world is run, but he came late into a world he did not make and does not have the plans. The question humbles him without crushing him, and it is spoken by the Son through whom the earth was founded (Hebrews 1:10).

38.reflection:
God answers Job’s demand for a hearing not with an explanation but with questions about creation. Why might seeing God himself be a better answer to suffering than being told the reason for it?

God set limits to the sea, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther” (v. 11), as he set limits on Satan in chapters 1 and 2. How does it help in a hard time to know that God sets limits on what can reach us?

God sends rain “on the desert in which there is no man” (v. 26) and hears the young ravens when they cry (v. 41). What does this tell you about God’s care for the parts of your life no one else sees?

The God who would not be summoned by Job later let himself be put on trial for us. How does the cross change the way we bring our questions and complaints to God?

39.title: Who Has Let the Wild Donkey Go Free?
39.text: <sup>1</sup>"Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does?<sup>2</sup>Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth,<sup>3</sup>when they crouch, bring forth their offspring, and are delivered of their young?<sup>4</sup>Their young ones become strong; they grow up in the open; they go out and do not return to them.<sup>5</sup>"Who has let the wild donkey go free? Who has loosed the bonds of the swift donkey,<sup>6</sup>to whom I have given the arid plain for his home and the salt land for his dwelling place?<sup>7</sup>He scorns the tumult of the city; he hears not the shouts of the driver.<sup>8</sup>He ranges the mountains as his pasture, and he searches after every green thing.<sup>9</sup>"Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?<sup>10</sup>Can you bind him in the furrow with ropes, or will he harrow the valleys after you?<sup>11</sup>Will you depend on him because his strength is great, and will you leave to him your labor?<sup>12</sup>Do you have faith in him that he will return your grain and gather it to your threshing floor?<sup>13</sup>"The wings of the ostrich wave proudly, but are they the pinions and plumage of love?<sup>14</sup>For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground,<sup>15</sup>forgetting that a foot may crush them and that the wild beast may trample them.<sup>16</sup>She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers; though her labor be in vain, yet she has no fear,<sup>17</sup>because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding.<sup>18</sup>When she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider.<sup>19</sup>"Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane?<sup>20</sup>Do you make him leap like the locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying.<sup>21</sup>He paws in the valley and exults in his strength; he goes out to meet the weapons.<sup>22</sup>He laughs at fear and is not dismayed; he does not turn back from the sword.<sup>23</sup>Upon him rattle the quiver, the flashing spear, and the javelin.<sup>24</sup>With fierceness and rage he swallows the ground; he cannot stand still at the sound of the trumpet.<sup>25</sup>When the trumpet sounds, he says 'Aha!' He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.<sup>26</sup>"Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south?<sup>27</sup>Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high?<sup>28</sup>On the rock he dwells and makes his home, on the rocky crag and stronghold.<sup>29</sup>From there he spies out the prey; his eyes behold it from far away.<sup>30</sup>His young ones suck up blood, and where the slain are, there is he."
39.overview:
Where we are. God’s first speech from the whirlwind continues (38:1–40:2). He has shown Job the foundations of the earth, the sea, the sky and the weather, and ended chapter 38 with the lion and the raven. Now he turns to the wild animals.

The message. God shows Job a world full of creatures that owe nothing to man: births no one watches, a freedom no one gave, a strength no one can yoke, a foolish bird that outruns horses, a horse that laughs at fear, birds of prey that find their way and their food. God knows each one, made each one as it is, and delights in it. The world is not arranged around Job, and God’s care is far wider than Job’s case; if God tends the mountain goat and the wild donkey, he can be trusted with Job.

Why it was said. Job has spoken as if God’s attention were fixed on tormenting him, and as if the world had no wise ruler (see the introduction). God answers by turning Job’s eyes outward, to a creation that is wild, beautiful and sometimes terrible, and all of it in God’s hand.

How the chapter makes its case. The mountain goats and deer give birth where no one sees, and their young grow up and leave (vv. 1–4). God set the wild donkey free on the salt plains, far from the city (vv. 5–8). The wild ox will never serve at Job’s manger or bring in his harvest (vv. 9–12). The ostrich, careless of her eggs and given little sense, still laughs at the horse and his rider (vv. 13–18). The war horse, clothed with might, charges at the sound of the trumpet (vv. 19–25). The hawk flies south and the eagle nests on the crag, its young feeding where the slain lie (vv. 26–30). Each question asks Job: did you do this?

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him. The one who knows every birth on the mountains is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3), and Jesus spoke of the same care when he said that not one sparrow falls to the ground “apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). The war horse is no saviour (Psalm 33:17); Israel’s King came “humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), and conquered by dying.

For us. God’s world does not revolve around us, and that is good news: the God who tends what no one sees is tending us. Enjoy his creatures, trust his wisdom where his ways seem strange, and rest in a Father whose care is wider than our troubles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Who Has Let the Wild Donkey Go Free?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wild creatures live free of man, and God tends them all. God asks whether Job knows when the mountain goats and deer give birth, counts their months, or watches their young grow strong and leave (vv. 1–4). He set the wild donkey free, gave it the salt plains for a home, and lets it scorn the noise of the city and range the hills for every green thing (vv. 5–8). The wild ox, stronger than any farm animal, will never spend a night at Job’s manger, pull his harrow or bring his grain to the threshing floor (vv. 9–12). Each creature lives by God’s gift and beyond Job’s control.
verseByVerse.theology: Creatures no one feeds, tames or even sees: God knows each one. The world is larger than man, and all of it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does? Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth, when they crouch, bring forth their offspring, and are delivered of their young? Their young ones become strong; they grow up in the open; they go out and do not return to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows every birth that no human eye sees, and every young one that leaves and does not return.

Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? God turns from the sky to the animals, and the first thing he points to is a birth. High on the mountains where no shepherd goes, the wild goats give birth, and the deer in the thickets. No human being counts their months or sits with them in labour. God does. “The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth” (Psalm 29:9). Jesus said the same of the smallest bird: “not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29).

The wild creatures. Nearly every animal God chooses in this chapter is wild: goats, deer, donkey, ox, ostrich, hawk, eagle. Most never meet man, and even the war horse, the one tame creature here, has a courage no rider gave it. God tends them all, for their own sake. Job has spoken as if the whole world should be arranged around his case; God shows him a world full of creatures God cares for that have nothing to do with Job at all.

They go out and do not return to them. Here is a line a bereaved father would feel. The young grow up and leave, and do not come back. God knew every one of those births and every one of those leavings. He knew the births of Job’s ten children, and their going.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who has let the wild donkey go free? Who has loosed the bonds of the swift donkey, to whom I have given the arid plain for his home and the salt land for his dwelling place? He scorns the tumult of the city; he hears not the shouts of the driver. He ranges the mountains as his pasture, and he searches after every green thing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself set the wild donkey free, and he takes pleasure in the freedom he gave it.

Who has let the wild donkey go free? The wild donkey has run all through this book. Job compared his cry to its bray (6:5); Zophar used it as an insult (11:12); Job likened the homeless poor to wild donkeys in the desert (24:5). Now God speaks of it with obvious pleasure. He set it free and gave it the salt flats for a home; it scorns the noise of the city and the shouts of the driver, and roams the hills looking for every green shoot. What looks to us like barren waste, God calls a home he has given.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger? Can you bind him in the furrow with ropes, or will he harrow the valleys after you? Will you depend on him because his strength is great, and will you leave to him your labor? Do you have faith in him that he will return your grain and gather it to your threshing floor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wild ox has a strength no one can harness, a reminder that much of God’s world will never serve Job.

Is the wild ox willing to serve you? The wild ox, the great aurochs (a huge wild ox, now extinct), is stronger than any farm animal. Try to yoke it to a plough and see what happens. It will not sleep in Job’s stable, harrow his valleys or bring his grain to the threshing floor. Job once owned five hundred yoke of oxen (1:3), all tame. He cannot command this one. Older English versions called it the “unicorn”, but it is a real wild ox, with more than one horn (Deuteronomy 33:17).

The wild oxen of Psalm 22. Christian readers may also remember the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: “Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!” (Psalm 22:21). The link is only a shared picture, not this chapter’s meaning, but it is a true one: brute strength no man can yoke closed in on the Son of God in his suffering, and God rescued him by raising him from the dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Ostrich and the War Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s design includes both the foolish and the fearless, and neither is Job’s work. The ostrich waves her wings proudly but leaves her eggs on the ground as if they were not hers, because God gave her little wisdom; yet she outruns the horse and laughs at its rider (vv. 13–18). The war horse has a might Job did not give it: it leaps like a locust, snorts and paws, laughs at fear and charges the sword (vv. 19–22). It cannot stand still at the trumpet, and smells the battle from afar (vv. 23–25). God paints both with evident delight.
verseByVerse.theology: A silly bird and a fearless horse, both God's work and both beyond Job's control. God speaks of them with something like a smile.

verseByVerse.quote: "The wings of the ostrich wave proudly, but are they the pinions and plumage of love? For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground, forgetting that a foot may crush them and that the wild beast may trample them. She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers; though her labor be in vain, yet she has no fear, because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding. When she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the foolish ostrich is God’s deliberate work, and his design includes what looks careless or comic to us.

The wings of the ostrich wave proudly. The tone becomes almost comic. The ostrich flaps her great wings as if proud of them, but she cannot fly. She has fine feathers, but not love (see the uncertain wording below). The poem describes her as she looked to those who watched: eggs left on the warm ground, “as if they were not hers” (v. 16). Lamentations made her a byword: “Even jackals offer the breast; they nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness” (Lamentations 4:3).

She laughs at the horse and his rider. “God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding” (v. 17). God made a bird without much sense, on purpose, and she survives by the gift he did give her: speed. She can outrun a horse. Job called himself “a companion of ostriches” in his misery (30:29). God describes the ostrich with a smile. Even the foolish creatures are part of his wise design, and he is not embarrassed by them.

Uncertain wording. “Plumage of love” (v. 13) is a difficult phrase; the ESV’s note says the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. It is probably a play on the Hebrew name of the stork, a bird thought of as caring for its young, whose name sounds like the word for steadfast love, chesed. The ostrich has the stork’s fine feathers, but not its love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane? Do you make him leap like the locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying. He paws in the valley and exults in his strength; he goes out to meet the weapons. He laughs at fear and is not dismayed; he does not turn back from the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The war horse’s might and courage are God’s gift, not man’s, and Scripture admires that strength without trusting in it.

Do you give the horse his might? From the ostrich that laughs at the horse to the horse that laughs at fear. The war horse is one of the great portraits in the Bible: the arched neck and flowing mane, the leap like a locust, the snort, the stamping hoof, the charge straight at the sword. Who gave it that courage? Not Job.

A false hope for salvation. Scripture admires the war horse and will not trust it: “The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue” (Psalm 33:17). When Israel’s King came, he came “humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). And when he comes again, John saw him on another horse: “behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war” (Revelation 19:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Upon him rattle the quiver, the flashing spear, and the javelin. With fierceness and rage he swallows the ground; he cannot stand still at the sound of the trumpet. When the trumpet sounds, he says 'Aha!' He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The war horse’s fierce joy in battle shows a Creator who delights in his creatures, even the fierce ones.

He smells the battle from afar. The rider’s weapons clatter on his back; he swallows the ground at a gallop; he cannot stand still when the trumpet blows, and he snorts “Aha!” as if he loved the fight. The picture is full of life and noise. Job had thought God’s attention was fixed on tormenting him. God’s attention is on everything, and much of it is joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–30 — The Hawk and the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s wisdom guides even the birds of prey, and his world is wild and sometimes harsh, yet wholly in his hand. The hawk spreads its wings toward the south by an understanding Job did not give it (v. 26). The eagle mounts up at God’s command, not Job’s, and makes its home on the high crag (vv. 27–28). From there it spies out prey far away, and its young feed on blood wherever the slain lie (vv. 29–30). The survey of the animals ends not with a pretty picture but a hard one: God does not hide the harsh side of his creation, and that too is under his rule.
verseByVerse.theology: The birds find their way and their food by the wisdom God gave them. Job did not teach them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south? Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high? On the rock he dwells and makes his home, on the rocky crag and stronghold. From there he spies out the prey; his eyes behold it from far away. His young ones suck up blood, and where the slain are, there is he."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The birds of prey live by the wisdom God gave them, and even the harsh side of creation lies under his hand.

The hawk soars. Every autumn the hawks fly south. Who taught them the way? Not Job. “Even the stork in the heavens knows her times” (Jeremiah 8:7), because God built the knowledge into her. The eagle rises at God’s command and builds where no one can reach. “They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).

Where the slain are, there is he. The survey ends not with a pretty picture but a hard one: the eagle’s chicks feeding on blood, the great bird circling wherever there are bodies. God does not hide the harsh side of his world. Jesus used the same picture for the certainty of judgment: “Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather” (Matthew 24:28). The creation God shows Job is not tame or sentimental. It is wild, and beautiful, and sometimes terrible, and all of it is under his hand. That is the God Job must reckon with, and the God Job can trust.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word rendered “eagle” (v. 27) covers large birds of prey generally and can include the vulture, which suits the feeding on the slain in v. 30; the word for “hawk” may likewise cover several kinds of falcon. The point does not depend on the species.

39.theology: Every creature God names is wild and outside man's control, and God knows and tends each one. The world is not arranged around Job, and God's care is wider than Job's case. The one who knows each birth on the mountains is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3), and in Jesus that care came near enough to be seen. God delights in his creatures, and does not hide the harsh side of his world. The King who made the war horse came on a donkey, and will come again on a white horse.
39.examples: This chapter invites a slower look at the world: a walk outside, or a nature film, can become an act of worship when we remember that God saw every birth on the mountains and enjoys the wild donkey's freedom. For a parent whose children have grown and gone, or gone in death, the line about the young who do not return is a reminder that God knew every one of those leavings too.

keyVerse.quote: Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does?
keyVerse.note: The chapter opens with births on the mountains that no human eye ever sees, and that sets its theme. Every creature God names lives beyond Job’s knowledge and control, yet none lives beyond God’s care. If God attends to the labour of a wild goat, he has not forgotten Job.

39.reflection:
God shows Job animals that have nothing to do with him: wild goats, the wild donkey, the wild ox. Why might it help a suffering person to be reminded that the world is not arranged around them?

God describes the ostrich, who “laughs at the horse and his rider” (v. 18), with something like a smile. What does it tell you about God that he delights in creatures that seem foolish or strange to us?

“The war horse is a false hope for salvation” (Psalm 33:17), and Jesus came “humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Where are you tempted to trust strength rather than the Lord?

The chapter ends with a harsh picture of the eagle’s young feeding where the slain lie (v. 30). How can we trust God when his world, and our lives, include things that are hard and frightening?

40.title: Will You Condemn Me That You May Be in the Right?
40.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Job:<sup>2</sup>"Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? He who argues with God, let him answer it."<sup>3</sup>Then Job answered the LORD and said:<sup>4</sup>"Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth.<sup>5</sup>I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, but I will proceed no further."<sup>6</sup>Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:<sup>7</sup>"Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.<sup>8</sup>Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?<sup>9</sup>Have you an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his?<sup>10</sup>"Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor.<sup>11</sup>Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him.<sup>12</sup>Look on everyone who is proud and bring him low and tread down the wicked where they stand.<sup>13</sup>Hide them all in the dust together; bind their faces in the world below.<sup>14</sup>Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you.<sup>15</sup>"Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you; he eats grass like an ox.<sup>16</sup>Behold, his strength in his loins, and his power in the muscles of his belly.<sup>17</sup>He makes his tail stiff like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit together.<sup>18</sup>His bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.<sup>19</sup>"He is the first of the works of God; let him who made him bring near his sword!<sup>20</sup>For the mountains yield food for him where all the wild beasts play.<sup>21</sup>Under the lotus plants he lies, in the shelter of the reeds and in the marsh.<sup>22</sup>For his shade the lotus trees cover him; the willows of the brook surround him.<sup>23</sup>Behold, if the river is turbulent he is not frightened; he is confident though Jordan rushes against his mouth.<sup>24</sup>Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare?
40.overview:
Where we are. God’s first speech from the whirlwind (38:1–39:30) ends with a direct challenge to Job (vv. 1–2). Job answers briefly and falls silent (vv. 3–5). Then God begins his second speech, which runs on through chapter 41.

The message. God names the heart of the matter: in defending his own innocence, Job has been willing to put God in the wrong. “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (v. 8). God never says Job’s suffering was punishment, but he will not let any man justify himself by condemning his Maker. Only an arm like God’s can bring down the proud and save, and Job’s own right hand cannot save him. Then God shows him Behemoth, a creature far beyond Job’s strength, made by the hand that made Job: what is too strong for us is not too strong for God.

Why it was said. Job had demanded that God answer him and had charged God with taking away his right (27:2; see the introduction). Now God has answered, and Job must face what his words implied.

How the chapter makes its case. God challenges the faultfinder to answer (vv. 1–2). Job confesses that he is of small account, lays his hand on his mouth and will say no more (vv. 3–5). God speaks again from the whirlwind: will Job condemn God to be in the right, and has he an arm like God’s (vv. 6–9)? Then let him robe himself in majesty, humble the proud and tread down the wicked; if he can, his own right hand can save him (vv. 10–14). Finally God points to Behemoth, the mightiest creature on land, made as Job was made, at ease in the marsh and the torrent, which no man can capture (vv. 15–24).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and by the need it exposes. No man’s arm can save him, so God’s own arm brought salvation (Isaiah 59:16), and the arm of the LORD is revealed in the suffering Servant (Isaiah 53:1; John 12:38). Job’s dilemma, how God can be in the right while the sufferer is in the right too, is answered at the cross, where God shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And the powers no man can approach, Christ has disarmed (Colossians 2:15).

For us. When we suffer we are tempted to keep our own sense of being in the right by accusing God. The gospel frees us from that choice: God is righteous, and in Christ he declares us righteous. So we can lay a hand on our mouths, stop arguing, and trust the God whose arm saves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Lay My Hand on My Mouth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faced with God, Job stops arguing. The LORD ends his first speech with a challenge: will the faultfinder who has contended with the Almighty now answer (vv. 1–2)? Job, who once demanded a hearing, has nothing to say. He confesses that he is of small account, lays his hand on his mouth, and says that he has spoken once, twice, and will go no further (vv. 3–5). It is not yet repentance, which comes in chapter 42, but it is the right first response to God: silence before one far greater than he had thought.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who demanded a hearing has nothing to say. It is the beginning of wisdom, not yet the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Job: "Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? He who argues with God, let him answer it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns the questioning back on Job: the man who has argued with the Almighty must now answer.

Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? God pauses and turns to Job directly. Job had said, “Then call, and I will answer” (13:22), and ended his last speech, “Let the Almighty answer me!” (31:35). God has called, and asked question after question. Now it is Job’s turn: “let him answer it”.

He who argues. “He who argues” is one word in Hebrew, mokiach, the same word as the “arbiter” Job longed for: “There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both” (9:33). With no arbiter to be found, Job has been doing the job himself, sitting in judgment on God. God names it gently and unmistakably. The true Arbiter would come, not to judge God, but to stand between God and man: “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered the LORD and said: "Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth. I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, but I will proceed no further."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has nothing left to say, and he lays his hand on his mouth: the right first response to God.

I am of small account. The man who filled chapters with argument has nothing to say. The word means light, of little weight. The princes of his city once laid their hands on their mouths before him (29:9), and he told the friends to do it (21:5). Now he does it before God.

I have spoken once. “Once… twice” means more than enough. Elihu used the pattern of God (“For God speaks in one way, and in two”, 33:14), and so did the psalmist: “Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God” (Psalm 62:11). Job means: I have said all I had to say, and more. He does not yet withdraw a word; he stops adding to them.

I lay my hand on my mouth. Repentance will come in chapter 42. For now there is silence, the right first response to God. “The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him” (Habakkuk 2:20). David prayed it in his own trouble: “I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it” (Psalm 39:9). Paul says the law speaks “so that every mouth may be stopped” before God (Romans 3:19). A believer who has argued with God in the dark may come to the same place: not yet an answer, but a hand over the mouth.

What it does not mean. This is not the sullen quiet of someone beaten into submission, but the hush of a man beginning to see God as he is. God does not silence the honest cries of sufferers; he will say that Job spoke of him what is right (42:7). What he ends is their accusations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Will You Condemn Me That You May Be in the Right?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names Job’s real fault: to make himself right, he has put God in the wrong. God speaks again from the whirlwind with the same summons as before (vv. 6–7). Will Job condemn God that he may be in the right? Has he an arm like God’s, or a voice that thunders like his (vv. 8–9)? Then let him put on God’s robes of majesty, pour out anger on the proud, bring them low and bury the wicked in the dust (vv. 10–13). If he can do that, God will acknowledge that his own right hand can save him (v. 14). He cannot; only God can judge the world, and only God can save.
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of God's answer: Job has defended himself by accusing God, and no man's right hand can save him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: "Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me. Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s real fault was not a sin that caused his suffering, but this: to make himself right, he was willing to make God wrong.

Dress for action like a man. Silence is not enough; God is not finished. He speaks a second time, with the same summons as before (38:3).

Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? Here is the real charge. Not that Job sinned before his suffering; God never says that. It is that in defending his innocence, Job has put God in the wrong. To make himself right, he has been willing to make God unjust: an enemy, cruel, a God who mocks the innocent. That is exactly what Elihu said: “he justified himself rather than God” (32:2). Job was right that he was innocent. He was wrong to buy his innocence at God’s expense.

Will you even put me in the wrong? The first question turns Job’s own words round. Job said, “God has put me in the wrong” (19:6), and “As God lives, who has taken away my right” (27:2), where “my right” is mishpat, justice. God asks, literally, will you cancel my mishpat, my justice?

Every sufferer’s temptation. Every sufferer is tempted here: to keep our own sense of being in the right, we accuse God. Paul will not have it: “Let God be true though every one were a liar” (Romans 3:4). And the gospel shows that we do not have to choose between God’s righteousness and our own acquittal. God put forward Christ “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). At the cross God is in the right and the believer is declared righteous, both at once: no one has to condemn God to be saved.
verseByVerse.note: “Gird up your loins” means tuck up your robe for action, as a man does before a contest.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his? "Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No man has an arm like God’s, which is why God had to save by his own arm.

Have you an arm like God? Job has an arm; he swore it should be broken if he ever raised it against the orphan (31:22). But an arm like God’s, that holds up the world and brings down the proud?

Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity. Majesty and splendour are the robes God wears: “O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty” (Psalm 104:1). With holy irony, God invites Job to put on God’s robes and try being God for a day.

The arm of the LORD is a person. No man has such an arm, which is exactly why God himself had to act. Isaiah saw it: God “saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation” (Isaiah 59:16). And the prophet asked of the suffering Servant, “to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1), a question John applies to Jesus (John 12:38). Christ is God’s arm stretched out to save.

verseByVerse.quote: Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him. Look on everyone who is proud and bring him low and tread down the wicked where they stand. Hide them all in the dust together; bind their faces in the world below. Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God can humble every proud man and judge the wicked, and only God can save; Job’s own right hand cannot.

Look on everyone who is proud and abase him. Job has complained for chapters that the wicked prosper and God does nothing (chapters 21 and 24). Very well: humble every proud man, tread down the wicked where they stand, “hide them all in the dust together” (v. 13), and see that justice is done in the world yourself. Job cannot even heal his own sores.

Only God can do this. And he will. “The LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty” (Isaiah 2:12); “he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts” (Luke 1:51). The wicked will be judged, but on God’s day and by God’s arm.

Your own right hand can save you. If Job could do all that, God says, his own right hand could save him, and he would not need God. He cannot, and neither can anyone. “His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him” (Psalm 98:1). “By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing” (Ephesians 2:8). The right hand that saves is God’s, and the one who sits at it is Christ (Hebrews 1:3).

Uncertain wording. “Bind their faces in the world below” (v. 13) is literally “in the hidden place”. Most take the hidden place as the grave, and the binding as the wrapping of the dead for burial or the darkness of a prisoner shut away. Either way it pictures the final humbling of the proud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — Behemoth, Which I Made as I Made You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behemoth, the mightiest creature on land, is made by the same hand as Job and is wholly in God’s power. God bids Job look at the beast he made as he made Job, a grass-eater of enormous strength in loins, belly, tail, thighs and bones (vv. 15–18). It is the first of God’s works, and only its Maker can approach it with a sword (v. 19). The hills feed it; it lies at ease in the shade of the lotus and the reeds, untroubled though the river rushes against its mouth (vv. 20–23). No one can capture it (v. 24). What Job cannot master, God made and rules.
verseByVerse.theology: Behemoth is a creature Job could never master, made by the same hand that made him and wholly in God's power.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, Behemoth, which I made as I made you; he eats grass like an ox. Behold, his strength in his loins, and his power in the muscles of his belly. He makes his tail stiff like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit together. His bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows Job Behemoth, a creature of overwhelming strength, and the first thing he says of it is that he made it, as he made Job.

Behold, Behemoth. Now God shows Job two great creatures, and the first is Behemoth. The name is a plural of the ordinary word for “beast”: the beast of beasts. God does not name the species; he describes it until Job can feel its weight: loins, belly, thighs, bones like tubes of bronze, limbs like bars of iron.

Which I made as I made you. Look at the first words. Behemoth and Job are fellow creatures, made by the same hand, and God is not threatened by what threatens us.

Where Christians differ. What was Behemoth? Many readers see the hippopotamus, a grass-eater of enormous strength living in the marshes; others see a picture of all the untamed power on the land, as Leviathan pictures the power of the sea. Some young-earth readers think it a dinosaur, pointing to “He makes his tail stiff like a cedar” (a hippopotamus has a short, stubby tail) and to “the first of the works of God” (v. 19). On this commentary’s view of a young creation, in which the land animals and man were made on the same sixth day (Genesis 1:24–27), the idea is not impossible.

This commentary’s view. God tells Job to “behold” it, a creature Job could see, made “as I made you”. This commentary takes the likeliest reading to be a real animal Job knew, perhaps the hippopotamus, drawn larger than life in poetry, as Leviathan is.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV note calls Behemoth a large animal of uncertain identity; the elephant has also been suggested.

verseByVerse.quote: "He is the first of the works of God; let him who made him bring near his sword! For the mountains yield food for him where all the wild beasts play. Under the lotus plants he lies, in the shelter of the reeds and in the marsh. For his shade the lotus trees cover him; the willows of the brook surround him. Behold, if the river is turbulent he is not frightened; he is confident though Jordan rushes against his mouth. Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behemoth lies at ease where no man dares approach, yet it is God’s creature, fed by him and within reach of his sword alone: what is too strong for us is not too strong for God.

He is the first of the works of God. He is the chief of God’s land creatures, and only the one who made him can come near him with a sword. The mountains feed him while the wild animals play around him. He lies at complete ease in the shade of the lotus, the river roaring against his mouth, and he does not care. “Jordan” probably stands here for any rushing torrent.

Why a river beast? It is fair to ask why God answers a bereaved and diseased man with a description of a river beast. Here is why. Job has been living as though the power that crushed him were outside God’s control, or worse, were God turned enemy. So God takes the most unmanageable thing Job can picture and says: I made that, as I made you; it grazes where I feed it; only my sword comes near it. Whatever is too strong for you is not too strong for me. If you are in a trouble you cannot master, any more than a man can take Behemoth by the eyes or lead him by the nose (v. 24), this is the God you are dealing with, and he is not describing his rival. He is describing his livestock.

What Job could not approach. The New Testament shows the Maker doing exactly that to every power that sets itself up against him: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). What Job could not approach, Christ has conquered.

Uncertain wording. Several phrases here are hard. “The first of the works of God” (v. 19) may mean first in rank, the chief, rather than first in time. “Let him who made him bring near his sword” seems to mean that only his Maker can approach him armed, though some take the “sword” as the great teeth God gave him. “Can one take him by his eyes” (v. 24) is obscure Hebrew, perhaps meaning “while he is watching”, that is, in the open; the answer expected is no. The overall picture is clear: no man can master Behemoth.

40.theology:
God's charge is that Job put God in the wrong to justify himself (v. 8; 32:2). God is true though every man be a liar (Rom 3:4), and in Christ he is both just and the justifier (Rom 3:26).

No man's arm can save him (vv. 9, 14); God's own arm brought salvation (Isa 59:16). Behemoth, beyond Job's power, is wholly in God's (v. 19), and Christ has triumphed over every power (Col 2:15).
40.examples: The man who wanted an arbiter (9:33) has been sitting as God's judge; called to answer, he lays his hand on his mouth. Anyone who has felt wronged by life meets God's question here, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?, and the gospel's answer to it: in Christ God is just and the believer is acquitted.

keyVerse.quote: Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?
keyVerse.note: This is God’s one real charge against Job. He never says Job’s suffering was punishment, but he will not let Job prove his own innocence by condemning God. The gospel answers the dilemma at the cross, where God is shown to be “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

40.reflection:
Job says, “I lay my hand on my mouth” (v. 4). When is silence before God the right response, and how is it different from simply giving up?

God asks, “Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?” (v. 8). In what ways are we tempted to defend ourselves by blaming God, especially when we suffer?

God tells Job that if he could judge the proud himself, “your own right hand can save you” (v. 14). Why can no one save themselves, and how does Christ, God’s arm stretched out, change that?

God shows Job Behemoth, “which I made as I made you” (v. 15). What trouble in your life feels too strong to master, and what does it mean to trust that it is not too strong for God?

41.title: King Over All the Sons of Pride
41.text: <sup>1</sup>"Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook or press down his tongue with a cord?<sup>2</sup>Can you put a rope in his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook?<sup>3</sup>Will he make many pleas to you? Will he speak to you soft words?<sup>4</sup>Will he make a covenant with you to take him for your servant forever?<sup>5</sup>Will you play with him as with a bird, or will you put him on a leash for your girls?<sup>6</sup>Will traders bargain over him?
