Around his teeth is terror.<sup>15</sup>His back is made of rows of shields, shut up closely as with a seal.<sup>16</sup>One is so near to another that no air can come between them.<sup>17</sup>They are joined one to another; they clasp each other and cannot be separated.<sup>18</sup>His sneezings flash forth light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn.<sup>19</sup>Out of his mouth go flaming torches; sparks of fire leap forth.<sup>20</sup>Out of his nostrils comes forth smoke, as from a boiling pot and burning rushes.<sup>21</sup>His breath kindles coals, and a flame comes forth from his mouth.<sup>22</sup>In his neck abides strength, and terror dances before him.<sup>23</sup>The folds of his flesh stick together, firmly cast on him and immovable.<sup>24</sup>His heart is hard as a stone, hard as the lower millstone.<sup>25</sup>When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid; at the crashing they are beside themselves.<sup>26</sup>Though the sword reaches him, it does not avail, nor the spear, the dart, or the javelin.<sup>27</sup>He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.<sup>28</sup>The arrow cannot make him flee; for him, sling stones are turned to stubble.<sup>29</sup>Clubs are counted as stubble; he laughs at the rattle of javelins.<sup>30</sup>His underparts are like sharp potsherds; he spreads himself like a threshing sledge on the mire.<sup>31</sup>He makes the deep boil like a pot; he makes the sea like a pot of ointment.<sup>32</sup>Behind him he leaves a shining wake; one would think the deep to be white-haired.<sup>33</sup>On earth there is not his like, a creature without fear.<sup>34</sup>He sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride."
41.overview:
Where we are. God’s second speech from the whirlwind reaches its climax. After Behemoth (40:15–24) comes Leviathan, the last and most fearsome creature in the book; then Job speaks (42:1–6).

The message. If no human being can catch, tame, bargain with or even face a creature God made, then no one can stand before God as his accuser, and no one has ever put God in his debt (vv. 10–11). The most terrifying power in the world, king over all the proud, is still a creature, made and governed by its Maker. Job does not need to master the chaos; he needs to trust the one who does.

Why it was said. Job had summoned God to court and spoken as though a blameless life put God under obligation to him (see the introduction). In his first lament he even called on those “who are ready to rouse up Leviathan” (3:8). God answers by showing him what he was calling up, and who rules it.

How the chapter makes its case. First the impossibilities: no hook, rope, covenant, leash, market or harpoon can deal with Leviathan, and one battle cures anyone of trying (vv. 1–9). Then the hinge: if no one dares rouse him, “Who then is he who can stand before me?”, and who has ever given God anything first (vv. 10–11)? Then God’s portrait of the creature: sealed armour, fire and smoke, a neck of strength and a heart of stone (vv. 12–25); every human weapon useless, the sea churned white behind him (vv. 26–32); and the final verdict, without equal, without fear, king over all the sons of pride (vv. 33–34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. Elsewhere Scripture makes the sea-dragon its picture of the evil power God will slay (Isaiah 27:1), and the New Testament names “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9). The Son of God took our flesh “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14), and the sea that boils under Leviathan lay still at his word (Mark 4:39). Paul takes up verse 11 to praise a salvation that is all gift (Romans 11:35–36).

For us. Whatever we cannot master, a craving, an illness, a fear, the power of evil itself, stands on the creature’s side of the line, under the Maker’s hand. We cannot put God in our debt, and we need not try: in Christ he gives freely what no one could earn. The proud are undone, and the humble receive grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Will You Put Him on a Leash for Your Girls?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one can master Leviathan, so no one can stand before the God who made him, or claim that God owes him anything. God piles up teasing questions: can Job catch him with a hook, rope his nose, hear his pleas, sign him on as a servant, keep him as a pet for the girls, sell him at market or fill his hide with harpoons (vv. 1–7)? Lay a hand on him once and you will not try again; human hope against him is false (vv. 8–9). Then the point of the whole speech arrives. If no one dares stir up this creature, who can stand before his Maker? And no one has ever given God anything first, for everything under heaven is his (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: If no man can face the creature, no man can face the Creator, and no one has ever put God in his debt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook or press down his tongue with a cord? Can you put a rope in his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook? Will he make many pleas to you? Will he speak to you soft words? Will he make a covenant with you to take him for your servant forever? Will you play with him as with a bird, or will you put him on a leash for your girls?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No human skill or strength can capture, tame or own Leviathan, yet God made him for sport.

Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook? The questions begin where the last chapter ended: “Can one take him by his eyes, or pierce his nose with a snare?” (40:24). Much in the description fits the crocodile, and much of it, as we will see, goes far beyond any animal.

Will he make many pleas to you? Four impossibilities, each a little joke at human mastery: he will not beg you, negotiate terms, sign on as a lifelong servant, or be walked on a string for the children. The words also turn back on Job, who has been the one pleading: “Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser” (9:15). The beast will not plead with Job; Job has been pleading all along, and with the only one who hears.

Made for sport. The psalm says of the same creature: “There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it” (Psalm 104:26). What no man can leash is, to God, a creature at play.

The background. Texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, tell of a sea dragon, Lotan, fought by their gods. Scripture uses the name in poetry and turns the story upside down: Leviathan is a creature God made, not a rival god.

Uncertain wording. The identity of Leviathan is uncertain (ESV note). The crocodile fits the armoured hide and the teeth; some suggest a whale. But the fire of verses 18–21 fits no animal, and elsewhere the name belongs to the sea-dragon of poetry (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1). Most likely God starts from a real beast, probably the crocodile, and lets the portrait grow into the dragon that stands for every power beyond human control.
verseByVerse.note: Job 41:1–8 is 40:25–32 in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Will traders bargain over him? Will they divide him up among the merchants? Can you fill his skin with harpoons or his head with fishing spears? Lay your hands on him; remember the battle—you will not do it again! Behold, the hope of a man is false; he is laid low even at the sight of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leviathan cannot be traded, harpooned or fought, and hope that rests on human strength is false.

You will not do it again! No market will handle him and no harpoon will hold him. Then God says something almost amused: try it once, and you will remember the battle and never try again.

The hope of a man is false. This is Job’s own theme: he said his days come to their end “without hope” (7:6) and that God destroys “the hope of man” (14:19). One look at what is really out there flattens it. That is not cruelty but the clearing of the ground: false hope has to die before true hope can be planted.

The battle we remember. Most of us have a Leviathan we have laid hands on once and remember the battle: a craving, an illness, an enemy, a grief, the death we cannot out-wrestle. The point is not to try harder. It is to notice who is speaking about the creature as casually as a farmer speaks about his cattle.

verseByVerse.quote: No one is so fierce that he dares to stir him up. Who then is he who can stand before me? Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If no one dares rouse a creature God made, no one can stand before God, and no one has ever put him in debt.

No one is so fierce that he dares to stir him up. Yet in a manner of speaking Job had dared. In his first bitter speech he called for the cursers of days, “who are ready to rouse up Leviathan” (3:8), to blot out the night he was conceived: he summoned the monster as an ally against his own life. God now tells him what he was playing with.

Who then is he who can stand before me? Here is the turn the whole speech has been building towards. This is no lesson in zoology. The argument is: you cannot look this creature in the eye, and I made him; if the works of my hands overwhelm you, what will you do with me, whom you have summoned to court? Every question about the creatures has carried this one on its back.

Who has first given to me? The question quietly demolishes Job’s case. Job had reasoned that a blameless life put God under some obligation to him. But no one hands God anything first: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (Psalm 50:12).

Paul’s song. Paul sings this very line at the end of eleven chapters on salvation: “Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:35–36). So God never owes any believer anything, and yet no believer need go without: what cannot be earned can still be given freely, and in Christ it has been.
verseByVerse.note: Job 41:9–34 is 41:1–26 in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — His Sneezings Flash Forth Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God describes Leviathan with evident delight, and the portrait grows until it reaches past any animal. No one can strip his hide, bridle him or open the doors of his face (vv. 12–14). His back is a wall of sealed shields with no gap to strike (vv. 15–17). Light flashes from his sneezes, fire and smoke pour from his mouth and nostrils, and his breath kindles coals (vv. 18–21). Strength lives in his neck, terror dances before him, his flesh is cast solid and his heart is as hard as a millstone, so that even the mighty panic when he rises (vv. 22–25). This is the most fearsome power in the world, and God speaks of it as its Maker.
verseByVerse.theology: The description reaches past any living animal, towards the evil power that Scripture elsewhere pictures as a sea-dragon.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will not keep silence concerning his limbs, or his mighty strength, or his goodly frame. Who can strip off his outer garment? Who would come near him with a bridle? Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror. His back is made of rows of shields, shut up closely as with a seal. One is so near to another that no air can come between them. They are joined one to another; they clasp each other and cannot be separated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God delights in Leviathan’s armour, so complete that there is no way in.

The doors of his face. Who will pull off his hide as you would a coat, bridle him like a horse, or reach in and prise open his jaws? “The doors of his face” is a marvellous phrase for a mouth that opens like a gate, with a ring of terror set round it.

His back is made of rows of shields. This is a soldier’s wall of shields: overlapping, sealed, airtight, interlocked and impossible to prise apart. To us who stand beneath it, evil often looks like this: sealed, seamless, with no way in.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 may also be read “His pride is his rows of shields” (ESV note); the Hebrew words for “pride” and “back” differ only slightly. That reading fits verse 34, where he is king over the proud; either way the armour is the point. In verse 12, “his goodly frame” renders an unusual expression, probably the fine proportion of his build.

verseByVerse.quote: His sneezings flash forth light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn. Out of his mouth go flaming torches; sparks of fire leap forth. Out of his nostrils comes forth smoke, as from a boiling pot and burning rushes. His breath kindles coals, and a flame comes forth from his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With fire and smoke, the portrait passes beyond any animal towards the evil power Scripture pictures as a dragon.

His sneezings flash forth light. A crocodile surfacing and blowing spray in the sunlight could account for some of this, and “the eyelids of the dawn” is a lovely line: eyes that open like daybreak over the water. But torches, sparks, smoke and burning coals are not natural history. The description has grown into something else, and the reader is meant to notice.

The evil power broken. Elsewhere this sea-dragon pictures the evil power God has broken and will destroy. “You crushed the heads of Leviathan” (Psalm 74:14). “Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon?” (Isaiah 51:9; compare Job 9:13). Isaiah promises the day: “In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent … and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea” (Isaiah 27:1). John names him: “the great dragon … that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9; 20:2).

What Job 41 does not say. The chapter does not say Leviathan is the devil. It says the most terrifying power in the world is a creature God made, describes, feeds and governs. The reader, who has seen the Accuser in chapter 1, is told where such power stands: on the creature’s side of the line between Maker and made, and under the Maker’s sword. And the Maker came in flesh “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: In his neck abides strength, and terror dances before him. The folds of his flesh stick together, firmly cast on him and immovable. His heart is hard as a stone, hard as the lower millstone. When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid; at the crashing they are beside themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leviathan is strength and terror through and through, with a heart that nothing can move.

Terror dances before him. Terror goes ahead of him like a dancer: you feel him coming before you see him. His flesh is cast solid, like metal poured in a mould, and his heart is the lower millstone, the one that never moves and takes all the grinding. He only has to rise out of the water and the strongest men lose their nerve.

His heart is hard as a stone. Hold that heart beside Job’s, broken open, made bitter, wrung with grief. He might well have envied a heart of stone that feels nothing. But the millstone heart belongs to the beast, and a heart that can be broken is the heart God can teach. God promises to take out hearts of stone, not to give them (Ezekiel 36:26).

Uncertain wording. “The mighty” in verse 25 may be read “the gods” (ESV note), for the Hebrew word can mean either: even the powers the nations feared would flinch. The last line is obscure; “at the crashing they are beside themselves” is a likely rendering, and the sense is plain: when he rises, the strong lose their heads.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–34 — On Earth There Is Not His Like
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every human weapon fails against Leviathan, and he reigns over everything proud; yet he remains a creature. Sword, spear, dart, javelin, arrow, sling and club are straw and rotten wood to him (vv. 26–29). He scores the mud beneath him, churns the deep like a boiling pot and leaves a white wake behind (vv. 30–32). God’s last words about him are a verdict: on earth there is none like him, a creature without fear, king over all the sons of pride (vv. 33–34). The last thing God shows Job is the fiercest thing in the world, and it has a Maker and a sword over it. Then Job answers.
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing God shows Job is the fiercest thing in the world, and it is a creature with a Maker and a sword over it. Then Job answers.

verseByVerse.quote: Though the sword reaches him, it does not avail, nor the spear, the dart, or the javelin. He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood. The arrow cannot make him flee; for him, sling stones are turned to stubble. Clubs are counted as stubble; he laughs at the rattle of javelins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every weapon human beings have made is useless against him; only the Maker’s sword prevails.

Though the sword reaches him, it does not avail. The whole armoury of the ancient world is laid out and dismissed, weapon by weapon: sword, spear, dart, javelin, arrow, sling, club. Iron might as well be straw, bronze rotten wood, and he laughs at the rattle of javelins.

The one weapon left. There is one weapon the chapter has not dismissed. Of Behemoth God said, “let him who made him bring near his sword” (40:19), and of Leviathan the prophet says the day is coming when “the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword” will kill the dragon in the sea (Isaiah 27:1). The Maker’s sword is the only one that does not fail. To anyone fighting something too big for them: our own weapons are not the answer, and God’s sword is.

verseByVerse.quote: His underparts are like sharp potsherds; he spreads himself like a threshing sledge on the mire. He makes the deep boil like a pot; he makes the sea like a pot of ointment. Behind him he leaves a shining wake; one would think the deep to be white-haired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wherever Leviathan goes, the mud is torn and the deep churned white.

He makes the deep boil like a pot. He drags his belly over the mud like a threshing sledge, all broken pottery and edges. He churns the sea until it boils and froths like ointment stirred in a pan, and the white water trails behind him so that the deep looks white-haired, like an old man’s head.

The deep lies down at his voice. In the Gospels there is a boat on such a sea, men certain they are going to die, and a man asleep in the stern. “And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.” Then: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:39, 41). God asked Job, “Who then is he who can stand before me?” (v. 10), and the answer was: no one. The disciples ask who this man can be; their Scriptures said it is the LORD who stills the sea (Psalm 107:29), and they are looking at him. The deep that boils under Leviathan lies down at the voice of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: On earth there is not his like, a creature without fear. He sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leviathan is unequalled because he fears nothing, king of all the proud, and still a creature with a Maker.

On earth there is not his like. God has said this once before, of a very different creature: “there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil” (1:8; 2:3). Two have no equal on earth, and the difference between them is one word. The man is unequalled because he fears God; the beast is unequalled because he fears nothing. Fearlessness is not the summit of creation; it is the mark of the monster.

He is king over all the sons of pride. The “proud beasts” of 28:8 are his subjects, and the phrase makes him king of everything that will not bow. If pride has a throne, this is who sits on it. The Accuser of chapters 1 and 2, who thought love of God was self-interest in disguise, belongs to that kingdom. So, in a smaller way, does the self-justifying that God has just named in Job (40:8).

How God ends. Two chapters of questions, and the last word is not Job’s sin but a creature: fearless, crowned over the proud, and made. Nothing in the speech says that God’s power is a reason to stop asking questions; it says the King of all the proud has a Maker who keeps him, feeds him, and will one day run him through.

The Lamb who conquered. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The Lion of Judah has conquered, and he did it as “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:5–6). He won by humbling himself to death. That is how the sons of pride are undone, and why a broken man kneeling in ashes is closer to the throne than the king of the fearless will ever be. Job has heard enough. The next words in the book are his.

Uncertain wording. “Sons of pride” uses a rare Hebrew word found only here and at 28:8 (“the proud beasts”). It probably means lordly wild animals, and widens naturally to everything proud.

41.theology:
No one can stand before the creature, so no one can stand before the Creator (v. 10); and no one has ever given God anything first (v. 11; Rom 11:35-36). Job’s case assumed that God owed him something, and God owes no one.

The description passes beyond any living animal, and Scripture elsewhere makes the sea-dragon its picture of the evil power God has broken and will destroy (Ps 74:14; Rev 12:9). Job 41 does not identify Leviathan with Satan, but it places every such power on the creature's side of the line, under the Maker's sword, which Christ wielded through death (Heb 2:14-15). The sea that boils under Leviathan lies still at his word (Mark 4:39-41).

The creature is unequalled on earth because he fears nothing (v. 33); the man was unequalled because he feared God (1:8). Fearlessness is the mark of the monster, and pride its kingdom (Jas 4:6).
41.examples: Most of us have laid hands on some Leviathan once and remember the battle: a craving, an illness, a grief. This chapter does not tell us to try harder. It shows us the Maker who speaks of such powers as a farmer speaks of his cattle, whose sword alone does not fail, and whose Son stilled the sea with a word (Mark 4:41).

keyVerse.quote: Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine.
keyVerse.note: This is where the whole Leviathan speech has been heading. Job had argued as though his blameless life put God in his debt; God answers that no one has ever given him anything first, because everything already belongs to him. Paul takes up the question to close his great account of salvation (Romans 11:35–36): what can never be earned is given freely in Christ.

41.reflection:
God describes Leviathan as a creature no one can capture or tame, yet the psalm says God formed him “to play” (Psalm 104:26). What in your life feels too strong for you, and how does it help to remember that it stands on the creature’s side of the line, under the Maker’s hand?

“Who has first given to me, that I should repay him?” (v. 11). In what quiet ways do we expect God to owe us something for our obedience? How does Paul’s use of this verse in Romans 11:35–36 turn it into praise?

Job and Leviathan are both said to have no equal on earth, one because he feared God, the other because he feared nothing (1:8; 41:33). Why is fearlessness before God the mark of the monster rather than of greatness? Where does pride show itself in you?

The sea that boils under Leviathan lay still at Jesus’ word (Mark 4:39–41), and he came to destroy the devil through his death (Hebrews 2:14–15). How does Christ’s victory help you face what frightens you?

42.title: But Now My Eye Sees You
42.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered the LORD and said:<sup>2</sup>"I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.<sup>3</sup>'Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.<sup>4</sup>'Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'<sup>5</sup>I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you;<sup>6</sup>therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes."<sup>7</sup>After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.<sup>8</sup>Now therefore take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and offer up a burnt offering for yourselves. And my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer not to deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has."<sup>9</sup>So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD restored the fortunes of Job, when he had prayed for his friends. And the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.<sup>11</sup>Then came to him all his brothers and sisters and all who had known him before, and ate bread with him in his house. And they showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. And each of them gave him a piece of money and a ring of gold.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning. And he had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys.<sup>13</sup>He had also seven sons and three daughters.<sup>14</sup>And he called the name of the first daughter Jemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch.<sup>15</sup>And in all the land there were no women so beautiful as Job's daughters. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.<sup>16</sup>And after this Job lived 140 years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, four generations.<sup>17</sup>And Job died, an old man, and full of days.
42.overview:
Where we are. God has finished speaking from the whirlwind (38:1–41:34). Job, who once demanded a hearing, gives his last answer, and the prose story that opened the book returns to close it.

The message. Job is given no explanation, only God himself, and that is enough: “now my eye sees you” (v. 5). Satan’s question, whether anyone will fear God for nothing (1:9), is answered by a man who has lost everything and still bows before him. God then vindicates his honest servant, condemns the tidy theology that misrepresented him, forgives the friends through sacrifice and Job’s prayer, and restores Job with open hands, while the book stays honest that ten graves remain and death still comes.

Why it was said. The book has asked whether God is worth loving for himself, and whether great suffering is always a verdict on the sufferer (see the introduction). Here it gives its answer to both: God himself is the treasure, and the friends’ verdict on Job was false.

How the chapter makes its case. Job confesses that no purpose of God’s can be thwarted, takes back his words, and repents in dust and ashes, because he has seen God (vv. 1–6). The LORD’s anger falls on Eliphaz and his friends, who have not spoken rightly of him as Job has; they must bring a great burnt offering, and Job must pray for them (vv. 7–9). When he prays, the LORD restores his fortunes double: family and friends return, his flocks are exactly doubled, he has seven sons and three named daughters who share the inheritance, and he dies old and full of days (vv. 10–17).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The innocent sufferer, vindicated by God, becomes the one through whose sacrifice and prayer his accusers are forgiven: a shadow of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) and “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Job’s restoration is real but partial. He still dies, and his hope, “in my flesh I shall see God” (19:26), waits for the resurrection that Christ has begun.

For us. God may not tell us why, but he gives himself, and that is the deeper answer. Speak to God honestly rather than about him smoothly, pray for those who have wronged us, and hold every restoration in this life as a foretaste of the one kept for us in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Now My Eye Sees You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job answers God without protest, because he has seen him. He confesses that God can do all things and that no purpose of his can be thwarted (v. 2). He takes up God’s own words from the storm and admits that he spoke of things too wonderful for him, which he did not understand (vv. 3–4). Then comes the summit of the book: he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees him, and so he takes back his words and repents in dust and ashes (vv. 5–6). He receives no explanation, and needs none. A man who has lost everything still wants God, and Satan’s question is answered.
verseByVerse.theology: Job gets no explanation and needs none: he has seen God, and that ends the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered the LORD and said: "I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job confesses not only that God can do all things, but that God has a purpose nothing can break.

I know that you can do all things. For the first time since chapter 3, Job’s answer is not a protest. That God can do all things he always believed, even in his bitterness (9:4–12). What is new is the second half: God’s “purpose”. Job had come to suspect that God’s purpose was against him, or that God had no purpose at all and simply crushed whatever came under his hand. Now he says the word without flinching. There is a plan; it is God’s; nothing can break it.

No purpose of yours can be thwarted. Job still does not know why his children died. He has not been told about chapter 1. He walks out of the whirlwind with no more information than he walked in with, and with his questions answered in a way he never asked for: not an explanation, but a Person. Hold that in mind before the restoration begins, because most sufferers are given the same thing in the same order: God first, restoration afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know. 'Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job repeats God’s charge and agrees with it: he spoke about what he did not understand.

Who is this that hides counsel without knowledge? Job quotes God’s first words from the storm, “Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2), and accepts the charge, not because he is cornered but because he agrees. He had spoken about “things too wonderful for me” as though he had the file in front of him. He did not.

Hear, and I will speak. He quotes God a second time (38:3; 40:7), almost humorously: he repeats the summons to answer and then, after demanding a hearing for chapters, does not argue his case at all.

Uncertain wording. Hebrew has no quotation marks. The ESV takes the first line of verse 3 and all of verse 4 as Job quoting God (38:2–3; 40:7), which fits their close echo; a few read them as Job’s own words. Either way, Job yields the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job has met God for himself, and in that light he takes back his words and bows.

Now my eye sees you. Here is the summit of the book. Job’s faith before the test was real: God himself called him blameless and upright, with none like him on the earth (1:8). But it was faith by report: true, and not enough for this. Now he has met him. The whirlwind speeches gave Job no fact to write down as an answer. They gave him God, and that turned out to be the thing he actually wanted.

Sight of God. Sight of God always humbles honest people. “Woe is me! For I am lost … for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” (Isaiah 6:5). “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). Job’s own hope had been exactly this: “whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (19:27). He is given it early, in this life, before he has died and been raised. And the God he glimpsed in the storm has since shown his face in his Son: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

What does he repent of? Not the sins the friends invented: God is about to call their speeches wrong (v. 7), and he never charges Job with the crimes of chapter 22. Job is taking back what he said about God and letting go of the case he had built. Dust and ashes is where he has been sitting since 2:8, and what he called himself in bitterness: “I have become like dust and ashes” (30:19). The place has not changed. The man in it has.

The first question answered. With this verse the question that started everything is answered: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9). Job has lost his flocks, his children, his health, his standing and any explanation. What is left is God, and Job wants him. That is the answer, and the Accuser has nothing to say to it.

Uncertain wording. The verb rendered “I despise myself” has no object stated in the Hebrew, so it may mean that Job rejects what he has said rather than himself. And “repent” may also be rendered “am comforted” (ESV note), for the verb can mean either. Both describe one turning: Job lets go of his case and finds rest in God, there in the dust.
verseByVerse.note: “Repent” may also be rendered “am comforted” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — You Have Not Spoken of Me What Is Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives his verdict: the friends’ tidy theology was false speech about him, and Job’s anguished honesty was right. The LORD’s anger burns against Eliphaz and his two companions, because they have not spoken of him what is right, as his servant Job has (v. 7). Their pardon requires a great burnt offering of seven bulls and seven rams, and the prayer of the very man they accused (v. 8). They obey, and the LORD accepts Job’s prayer (v. 9). The sufferer becomes the priest of his accusers, a picture of the greater innocent sufferer who intercedes for those who wronged him.
verseByVerse.theology: God's verdict: the friends' tidy orthodoxy was false speech about him, and Job's anguished honesty was true. The accused man becomes their priest.

verseByVerse.quote: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends, for all their orthodox-sounding speeches, spoke wrongly of God; Job, for all his anguish, spoke rightly.

My anger burns against you. God turns from the sufferer to the counsellors, and his first word to them is anger. Eliphaz, the first to speak and the gentlest (chapter 4), is addressed by name; the other two are “your two friends”. The three of them said many things that would pass in any pulpit: God is great, he does not pervert justice, the wicked come to grief, no man is pure before his Maker. And the verdict on all of it is: you have not spoken of me what is right.

Recorded, not therefore true. The friends’ speeches sit in Scripture and can be quoted like any other verse. They are faithfully recorded; they are not therefore true. Where they described God rightly, they used the description as a weapon to convict an innocent man, which is a lie about God’s character even when every sentence is correct in itself. Where they went further and told Job what he must have done, they were simply inventing. Never take a sentence from the friends as God’s word without remembering this verdict (see the introduction).

As my servant Job has. Job, who called God his enemy and said God mocks the innocent and laughs at calamity: how can that be right speech? Because Job spoke to God and not merely about him; because he refused to tell a lie in God’s favour or a lie against himself; because he kept coming, and his worst words were addressed to the one he could not stop believing in. God prefers a man who shouts at him to a man who explains him away. The friends never once spoke to God in nine chapters of speeches.

Where Christians differ: Elihu. The verse says nothing about Elihu. He is not rebuked and not commended; after chapter 37 the book simply drops him. Some see him as a fourth friend repeating the same formula; others as a forerunner of God’s own answer.

This commentary’s view. The likelier reading lies between: Elihu speaks partly truly, and God’s answer out of the storm goes beyond him without needing to correct him.
verseByVerse.note: What is right also carries the sense of what is true and firmly grounded.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and offer up a burnt offering for yourselves. And my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer not to deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has." So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friends are forgiven through a sacrifice and the prayer of the man they accused.

Take seven bulls and seven rams. The friends are in real danger, and the remedy has two parts: a blood sacrifice and a mediator, a man to stand between them and God. Seven bulls and seven rams is the largest offering in the book, and it is not enough by itself: they must also stand before the man they have been lecturing and ask him to pray. Their theology has been called “folly”, and their forgiveness comes through the one they accused.

No temple and no priest. There is no temple or Levitical priest in this story: as in the days of the patriarchs, the head of a household offered sacrifice himself, and Job does for these three men what he once did for his own children (1:5).

What Eliphaz had said. Eliphaz had said it himself without knowing it. Promising Job restoration if he would only repent, he ended: “He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands” (22:30). Eliphaz is now the one who is not innocent, delivered through the cleanness of hands he had called filthy. Job had longed for someone to stand between himself and God: an arbiter (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), a Redeemer who lives (19:25). He never gets a man in the middle for himself; he becomes the man in the middle for the men who wronged him.

Father, forgive them. So the scene looks ahead to a greater one. The innocent sufferer, vindicated by God, prays for those who accused him: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Christ Jesus “is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34); “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Job’s one prayer is heard for three men. The prayer of Christ, the Redeemer Job was waiting for, is heard for everyone who comes to him.

They went and did what the LORD had told them. To their credit, they went, named in full one last time. No apology is recorded, and none is asked for. Job prays for them, which answers everything they had said about his character. Four times in two verses God calls him “my servant Job”, the name he used of him to the Accuser before any of this began (1:8; 2:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The LORD Restored the Fortunes of Job
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD restores Job when he prays for his friends, generously and publicly, yet not completely. His fortunes are restored twice over (v. 10), and the family and friends who abandoned him come back to eat with him, comfort him and bring gifts (v. 11). Every figure of his livestock is exactly doubled, but his children are not: seven sons and three daughters again, the daughters named, famed for their beauty and given an inheritance with their brothers (vv. 12–15). He lives 140 years and sees four generations, and then he dies, old and full of days (vv. 16–17). Ten graves remain, and the hope of 19:25–27 still waits.
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is real, generous, public, and not the whole answer: ten graves remain, and the Redeemer of 19:25 has not yet stood on the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD restored the fortunes of Job, when he had prayed for his friends. And the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD restores Job’s fortunes twice over as Job prays for the friends who wronged him.

When he had prayed for his friends. The timing is the message. Not when Job stopped complaining, nor when he confessed, but when he lifted empty hands in prayer for the men who had tormented him. This is not a last condition Job met to earn his goods back. It shows how God works: the blessing comes as Job prays for others, and a man who can pray for his accusers is a man in whom God’s work has already been done.

For anyone waiting. If you have been wronged and are waiting for restoration, look hard at this verse: the waiting is not usually ended by winning the argument. Pray for them, as Christ prayed for us while we were his enemies. It is the last thing our sinful nature wants to do, it is what the Spirit given to believers makes possible, and it is the first thing that makes a person free.

What it does not mean. Praying for those who wronged you is not the same as going back to them, trusting them again, or calling the wrong small. Anyone who is being abused should seek safety at once, and can pray from there.

Does God always restore the faithful sufferer in this life? No. Many of the faithful “did not receive what was promised” in this life (Hebrews 11:39), and Paul says that “all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). Job’s restoration is God’s public verdict on his servant and a foretaste of the final restoration. It is not a promise of wealth to those who suffer well; the book has spent forty chapters refuting that idea.

If your losses have not been given back. This chapter is not a rebuke to you. Christ, the innocent sufferer, had nothing restored to him in this life: he was vindicated by being raised, and his people’s restoration waits in him, an inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). Job’s doubled flocks are an early picture of that day, and your restoration is not cancelled because it has not yet come.

Uncertain wording. “Restored the fortunes” translates a Hebrew phrase that older English versions rendered “turned the captivity of Job”. Job was never a captive; the phrase is now generally taken to mean restoring what was lost, as in the prophets’ promises (Jeremiah 29:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Then came to him all his brothers and sisters and all who had known him before, and ate bread with him in his house. And they showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. And each of them gave him a piece of money and a ring of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The relatives who deserted Job return, and the narrator says plainly that the evil came from the LORD.

All his brothers and sisters. These relatives were nowhere to be found in his trouble: “He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me” (19:13). Now they are at his table eating his bread, sympathising, bringing money and gold rings. Job takes it.

All the evil that the LORD had brought upon him. The narrator writes a sentence that should stop the reader. Not the evil the Accuser brought, though he struck the blows (1:12; 2:6–7). The book closes by laying the disaster at God’s door. “Evil” here means disaster, not wickedness: God brought trouble on Job, not sin. That is Job’s own theology from the first day: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (1:21); “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (2:10). Scripture will not let us excuse God by saying the disaster was outside his control. Nor will it let us doubt his goodness, having shown us his face in the whirlwind and, later, in his Son.

Uncertain wording. “A piece of money” translates the Hebrew qesitah, a unit of money of unknown value (ESV note). The word appears elsewhere only for Jacob’s purchase of land at Shechem (Genesis 33:19; Joshua 24:32), a sign of the patriarchal age (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: A qesitah was a unit of money of uncertain value (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning. And he had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys. He had also seven sons and three daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s possessions are exactly doubled, but not his children, because children cannot be replaced.

Twice as much as he had before. Job had 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys (1:3); every figure is now exactly doubled. In the law, double is what a thief pays back to the man he robbed (Exodus 22:4). God is not paying damages, and no one robbed Job. But the doubling is a public statement in the only language the ancient world read fluently: this man was not under judgment.

Seven sons and three daughters. There the doubling stops: ten children, as before (1:2). The point is simple and hard: livestock can be replaced and children cannot. Ten new children do not cancel ten graves, and the text does not pretend otherwise.

Were the children doubled after all? Some readers have said so, because the first ten are not lost but waiting for the resurrection, so that Job has twenty. The book gives grounds for that hope (19:25–27), but this verse does not say so.

If you have buried a child. Anyone who has buried a child and never been given another may take this from it: the book will not call new children a replacement, and it does not measure God’s love by what has been given back.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the name of the first daughter Jemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch. And in all the land there were no women so beautiful as Job's daughters. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job’s new daughters are named, praised for their beauty and given an inheritance: the household of a man whom grace has made generous.

Jemimah, Keziah, Keren-happuch. Not one of Job’s first ten children is named. Now three daughters are named, and their beauty remarked on; after forty chapters of dust the naming is itself sunlight. These are the names of a man come out of the dark, delighting in his girls.

An inheritance among their brothers. Then the quiet, radical line. Daughters did not ordinarily inherit at all; under Moses’ law they inherited only where there was no son, as the case of the daughters of Zelophehad established: “You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father’s brothers” (Numbers 27:7–8). Job, of his own accord, gives his daughters a share while their brothers are living.

Grace received comes out as generosity. A man who has met God does not go home and rule harshly; grace shows up first in the way a man treats the people with the least claim on him. The gospel goes further still: in Christ “there is no male and female”, and all who belong to him are “heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:28–29).
verseByVerse.note: Jemimah may mean “dove,” Keziah “cinnamon,” and Keren-happuch “horn of eye-paint.”

verseByVerse.quote: And after this Job lived 140 years, and saw his sons, and his sons' sons, four generations. And Job died, an old man, and full of days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job lives long and dies full of days, yet he still dies, and his greatest hope lies beyond the grave.

Job lived 140 years. The man who begged to die (3:21; 7:15) lives 140 years, a lavish number beside the psalm’s “seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty” (Psalm 90:10). The house that lost ten children in one day fills up for four generations. The last sentence gives him the patriarch’s death: Abraham too died “an old man and full of years” (Genesis 25:8). Not emptied. Full.

And Job died. And still he dies: the book’s last piece of honesty. Job never learned why. The children of chapter 1 are not given back. The Accuser is never mentioned again, and Job never knows he was there. The great hope he confessed is still ahead of him: “after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God” (19:26). He glimpsed God from the whirlwind while his sores were fresh; he waits, like every believer who has ever closed his eyes, for the day when “he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4).

The steadfastness of Job. That is why the New Testament can hold this whole book up as an encouragement without softening a line of it: “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (James 5:11). The purpose was there all along, in the silence and behind the wind. The one who held Job has since stood on this earth himself with a body that could be struck, and let it be struck, and risen. Job’s Redeemer lives. That is the answer this book was waiting for, and it has come.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, adds a line after verse 17 saying that Job will rise again with those the Lord raises up. It is not in the Hebrew and is a later addition, but it shows how early readers heard this ending.

42.theology:
Job receives no explanation and is satisfied: now my eye sees you (v. 5). Sight of God, not information about him, ends the argument, and a man who has lost everything and still wants God is the answer to the Accuser (1:9).

The friends have not spoken of me what is right (vv. 7-8); Job, who said wild things to God's face, spoke rightly, because he spoke to God and would not lie about him or about himself. Their forgiveness comes through sacrifice and the prayer of the man they accused (v. 8), a picture of Christ's intercession (Rom 8:34; Heb 7:25).

The narrator lays the evil at the LORD's door (v. 11) without doubting his goodness. The restoration is real and incomplete. Livestock is doubled; children are not. Job dies (v. 17), and the hope of 19:26 waits for the resurrection (Rev 21:4; Jas 5:11).
42.examples: Most sufferers receive what Job received, and in the same order: not an explanation, but God himself, and only afterwards whatever restoration he gives. The man who longed for a mediator becomes one for the friends who wronged him, and his blessing comes when he prays for them. The restoration is generous and still incomplete: every figure is doubled except the children, and the daughters, named at last, receive an inheritance. Job dies full of days, still waiting for the day of 19:26.

keyVerse.quote: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you;
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the whole book. Job is never told why he suffered, but he has met God, and that answers his longing and Satan’s accusation together (1:9). Faith by report has become sight, a foretaste of the day when believers will see God in the face of Christ.

42.reflection:
Job received no explanation for his suffering, but he saw God (v. 5). What is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him? How have hard times affected that in your own life?

God said the friends had not spoken rightly of him, though much of what they said sounded orthodox, while Job, who argued with God, had (v. 7). What does this teach us about how to speak to God in suffering, and how to speak to those who suffer?

Job’s fortunes were restored when he prayed for the friends who had wronged him (v. 10). Is there someone you need to pray for in this way? How does Christ’s prayer for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) make that possible?

Job’s possessions were doubled but his children were not, and in the end he died (vv. 13, 17). How does the hope of resurrection in Christ help us live with losses that will not be made up in this life?
